pitch: Turn AI agents into browser-native operators with WebMCP — structured, controllable, and built for real-world tasks.\n
about_excerpt:
Turn AI agents into browser-native operators with WebMCP — structured, controllable, and built for real-world tasks.

 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web

 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 testing guidance 1 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 testing guidance 2 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web 

 I built Agent Mission Control to test a simple question: can a human and an AI agent work on the same application state through two different interfaces? 

 The web was designed for humans to click. What if it were also designed for agents to act? 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but interacting with the web still often feels like teaching a machine to imitate a human. 

 Find a button.
Read its label.
Guess what it does.
Click it.
Wait for the page to change.
Repeat. 

 Humans need visual interfaces because we navigate by seeing and clicking. 

 Agents shouldn't have to. 

 That led to the question behind Agent Mission Control: 

 
 What would a web application look like if it were designed for both humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 WebMCP gave me a way to explore that question, and gave me a new way to explore thtis idea.. 

 Instead of treating the browser as a collection of pixels that an agent must interpret, a website can expose structured capabilities that describe what the agent is actually allowed to do. 

 So I built Agent Mission Control , an experimental WebMCP-native task environment where a human can manage work visually while an AI agent can interact with the same application through structured tools. 

 The goal isn't to replace the interface. 

 It's to give the web two interfaces to the same application : 

 a visual interface for humans, and a semantic tool interface for agents. 

 So I built agent-mission-control-webmcp to test a different model: one application with two interfaces — a visual interface for humans and a structured capability interface for AI agents — both operating on the same underlying application logic. 

 

 What it does 

 Agent Mission Control turns a normal task-management web application into an agent-addressable workspace . 

 A human can interact with the application through the UI. 

 An AI agent can discover WebMCP tools exposed by the page and use those structured capabilities to work with the same underlying tasks. 

 Instead of asking an agent to: 

 
 "Look around the page, find the right button, click it, and hope the UI hasn't changed..." 
 

 the application can expose explicit operations the agent can understand and invoke. 

 The important part is not simply that an agent can control a task app. 

 The important part is how . 

 The agent is no longer pretending to be a human operating a website. 

 The website is speaking to the agent directly. 

 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Traditional browser automation often starts from the presentation layer. 

 WebMCP lets us start from intent . 

 A button might visually say: 

 Complete 

 But the capability behind it can communicate something much richer: 
 complete_task(taskId)
 
 with structured parameters, predictable behavior, and application-defined semantics. 

 That changes the relationship between websites and AI agents. 

 Instead of: 
 Agent
 ↓
interpret pixels / DOM
 ↓
guess user interface
 ↓
click
 ↓
Application
 
 Agent Mission Control explores: 
 Human ───────→ Visual UI ───────┐
 │
 ▼
 Shared Task Logic
 ▲
 │
AI Agent ───→ WebMCP Tools ─────┘
 
 Both interfaces operate on the same application logic . 

 That was a key architectural decision. 

 WebMCP isn't an automation layer bolted onto the side of the application. 

 It becomes another interface into the application itself. 

 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The most interesting possibility isn't fully autonomous agents. 

 It's shared control . 

 Humans are good at goals, judgment, context, and deciding what should happen. 

 Agents are good at translating intent into structured actions and carrying out repetitive operations. 

 Agent Mission Control explores a simple model: 

 Human defines the mission.
The application defines the allowed capabilities.
The agent executes through those capabilities.
The human remains in control. 

 This creates an interesting middle ground between a traditional website and unrestricted browser automation. 

 The website itself participates in defining what an agent can do. 

 

 How I built it 

 Agent Mission Control is built as a web application with WebMCP integrated directly into its task workflow. 

 The application exposes a small set of task-oriented WebMCP tools. 

 Rather than implementing separate automation logic, the WebMCP layer connects to the same task service used by the React interface. 

 Conceptually: 
 ┌── Human UI
 │
TaskService ─┤
 │
 └── WebMCP Tools → AI Agent
 
 This was deliberate. 

 If the human interface and agent interface implement separate business logic, they can eventually disagree. 

 By sharing the same underlying service, actions performed through WebMCP can follow the same application behavior as actions performed through the UI. 

 The project also includes a browser test path for discovering registered tools, invoking them with structured arguments, and verifying that the resulting state is reflected back in the application. 

 

 Challenges I ran into 

 1. Designing tools instead of exposing buttons 

 My first challenge was conceptual. 

 A WebMCP tool shouldn't simply be a remote-control version of every button on the page. 

 The question became: 

 
 What capability should the application expose to an agent? 
 

 That forced me to think in terms of application semantics rather than UI components. 

 

 2. Keeping humans and agents on the same source of truth 

 It would have been easy to create a separate "AI API." 

 But then I would effectively have two applications: 

 one for humans and one for agents. 

 Instead, I structured the project so both paths converge on shared task logic. 

 That made WebMCP feel less like an integration and more like a second interface to the application . 

 

 3. Testing an emerging browser capability 

 WebMCP is still an emerging technology. 

 Testing required thinking beyond normal frontend tests: 

 
 Are tools actually registered? 
 Can an agent discover them? 
 Are arguments structured correctly? 
 Does execution reach the same application logic? 
 Does the resulting state appear correctly in the human UI? 
 

 Building around an emerging browser capability was one of the most challenging — and interesting — parts of the project. 

 

 Accomplishments I'm proud of 

 The thing I'm most proud of isn't the number of tools. 

 It's proving a simple architectural idea: 

 
 A web application doesn't have to choose between being human-friendly and agent-friendly. 
 

 The same application can expose a visual experience to a person and structured capabilities to an AI agent without duplicating the underlying workflow. 

 Agent Mission Control is intentionally small, but that makes the experiment easier to see. 

 This isn't a task manager with AI added to it. 

 The task manager is the demonstration of a different interface model for the web. 

 

 What I learned 

 Before building this project, I mostly thought about agent/browser interaction as automation. 

 WebMCP changed the question. 

 Instead of asking: 

 
 "How can an AI operate this website?" 
 

 I started asking: 

 
 "How should this website expose itself to AI?" 
 

 That sounds like a small distinction. 

 It isn't. 

 It shifts responsibility from agents constantly reverse-engineering interfaces toward applications explicitly describing safe, meaningful capabilities. 

 And it suggests that the future web may not have one interface. 

 It may have at least two: 

 one optimized for people, and one optimized for agents. 

 

 What's next 

 Agent Mission Control is a proof of concept, but the pattern extends far beyond task management. 

 Imagine websites exposing carefully designed agent capabilities for: 

 
 project management, 
 commerce, 
 scheduling, 
 content workflows, 
 developer tools, 
 administrative systems, 
 and collabor

title: ZShop Agent Cart
pitch: A shared shopping workspace where humans set intent and WebMCP agents search, compare, and safely build the cart.
about_excerpt: A shared shopping workspace where humans set intent and WebMCP agents search, compare, and safely build the cart. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Shopping agents are often forced to infer intent from pixels, scrape inconsistent product cards, and guess whether an action is safe. ZShop Agent Cart explores a better contract: the storefront exposes precise capabilities while the shopper keeps a visible, shared workspace and remains in control of consequential choices. What it does ZShop registers five WebMCP tools directly from the live storefront: set_shopping_goal makes the shopper's brief visible to both human and agent. search_products searches the live catalog and returns compact, comparable facts. inspect_product reads current price, stock, fulfilment, description, and option requirements. view_cart reads the authenticated shopper's selected items and total. add_product_to_cart adds simple products through the existing signed-in session. The on-page companion shows the shared goal and a live activity trail, so the human can see what the agent is doing without leaving the shopping experience. Products with variants are deliberately not guessed: the tool returns a product URL and asks the shopper to select options. Checkout remains human-controlled. Why WebMCP is the right fit Commerce mixes fast-changing facts, authenticated state, and actions with different risk levels. WebMCP lets the site describe each capability with a narrow JSON schema and behavioral annotations instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer the UI. The result is faster and more reliable than click automation, while preserving the storefront's own validation, authentication, and cart rules. Before this extension, a shopper could browse ZShop and an agent could separately offer generic advice. Now they can work in the same live catalog and session: the person states intent and handles preference-heavy decisions; the agent retrieves current facts, narrows choices, and performs bounded cart work; both share visible context. How we built it The Nuxt 4 client plugin detects document.modelContext , then registers typed tools with registerTool . Each tool has a constrained input schema, clear descriptions, and read-only, destructive, idempotent, and open-world hints. Tool handlers call the same production catalog and cart APIs as the storefront and reuse the existing auth token. A Vue composable keeps the shared goal and recent action log reactive in the companion UI. Focused Vitest coverage validates product normalization and rejects malformed search terms and numeric inputs. A CDP-based WebMCP host test injects the browser API, verifies all five registrations, executes the goal and live catalog search tools, and confirms that the human-visible companion updates. Challenges The central design challenge was choosing boundaries, not simply exposing every UI action. Product options cannot be selected safely from incomplete intent, and checkout has financial consequences, so neither is automated. Another challenge was keeping the experience useful outside a WebMCP-enabled browser; the storefront still works normally and the companion explains when agent capabilities are unavailable. Accomplishments Five working WebMCP tools backed by a live multilingual catalog. Shared human-agent context visible in the existing storefront. Authenticated cart access without a second agent-specific account system. Explicit safety boundaries for variants and checkout. Reproducible tests, public source, MIT license, and dated challenge-period commits. What we learned Agent-native UX is strongest when structured capabilities and visible human feedback are designed together. Schemas make actions reliable; the companion makes them understandable. The most important tool behavior can also be a refusal to guess. What's next Next we would add preference memory approved by the shopper, side-by-side comparison cards generated from tool results, and a confirmation protocol for reversible versus consequential actions. We would also localize tool descriptions alongside ZShop's Chinese, English, Thai, and Traditional Chinese interface. title: Xyle
pitch: Xyle is an open-source visual editor for non-technical owners of static websites.
about_excerpt:
Xyle is an open-source visual editor for non-technical owners of static websites.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Static websites are fast, simple, and cheap to run, but even a tiny content change often means going back to a developer. Xyle started as a human-first visual editor for existing static websites. 

 WebMCP opened up another possibility: instead of building a separate AI editor, an agent could safely operate the same editing system a person already uses. 

 What it does 

 Xyle lets people edit an existing website directly on the page. 

 With WebMCP, Xyle exposes those same editing capabilities to AI agents through structured tools. An agent can discover editable content, read its current value, update text or links, inspect the change history, and undo changes. 

 Human edits and agent edits share the same page state and history. There is no separate “AI version” of the website. 

 The agent also does not receive arbitrary DOM access. Xyle exposes only the editing operations it explicitly supports, while publishing remains a deliberate human action. 

 How we built it 

 Xyle has a shared editor core used by both its visual UI and its WebMCP integration. 

 The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: tools registered through document.modelContext call the same editing operations used by the human interface rather than introducing a second editing system. 

 Xyle also keeps static files as the canonical published content. There is no separate content database. Unpublished edits live in the editing session, and publishing applies narrow changes back to the site's source files. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hardest part was not simply making a webpage editable by an agent. It was making agent actions predictable, constrained, visible, and reversible while keeping humans and agents in sync. 

 That led to one of the main ideas behind Xyle's WebMCP implementation: WebMCP works particularly well as a capability layer over an existing application. The agent does not need a chatbot embedded in the product or unrestricted access to the page. It can use the product's existing tools directly. 

 What's next 

 The next step is expanding the set of safe editing capabilities while keeping the same shared-control model: agents can help make changes, but people can always see, review, undo, and decide what gets published.

title: MapTruth
pitch: MapTruth lets people and browser agents turn a real OpenStreetMap view into AI-generated map artwork—without letting the model invent the geography.
about_excerpt: MapTruth lets people and browser agents turn a real OpenStreetMap view into AI-generated map artwork—without letting the model invent the geography. Like Comment Story Updates Same brief, prompt-only versus map-grounded New Orleans. Real OpenStreetMap geometry locked for Lower Manhattan Ten typed WebMCP tools exposed directly by the page Six native calls completed with visible execution receipts The agent stops before paid image generation Editorial montage made from authentic production captures Inspiration AI image models can draw maps that look authoritative while inventing streets, landmarks, and spatial relationships. That is harmless as wall art, but dangerous when somebody might plan from it. I built MapTruth to make the real place—not the model—the source of geographic truth, while still letting an AI do what it is good at: interpreting intent and styling evidence. What it does Ask an image model for a map of a real place and it can draw something beautiful, confident, and geographically false. MapTruth changes the input to that process. A person chooses a place and writes a brief; MapTruth locks a live OpenStreetMap view, resolves requested features against OpenStreetMap, and generates two images side by side: one from the prompt alone and one grounded in the sourced map. The comparison makes the failure mode visible. In the New Orleans demo, the ungrounded result invents a plausible city. The grounded result preserves the large-scale relationship among Lake Pontchartrain, the city, and the Mississippi River, and marks only places resolved within the locked view. Why WebMCP The page—not the model—owns the map and its invariants. Through document.modelContext.registerTool , MapTruth exposes ten typed browser tools for focusing a place, navigating, inspecting and locking the live map, marking features from OpenStreetMap, verifying geography, and staging a comparison. An agent calls those tools directly instead of interpreting a screenshot or scraping UI text. That changes what an agent is allowed to invent. The model may decide what kinds of places a brief needs, but it never supplies their coordinates. OpenStreetMap locates them. Anything that cannot be resolved inside the locked view is dropped and reported rather than approximately placed. The app's visible six-step assistant walkthrough uses WebMCP's native executeTool() path when it is available, so judges can watch the agent call the same registered tools that another browser agent discovers. It leaves a receipt for each action and stops at the human approval gate before any paid image generation. A better user experience Without WebMCP, an assistant would have to guess from pixels or automate fragile controls. Here it receives named, typed capabilities and compact structured results. A person can see the same state, source attribution, verification counts, geometry hashes, and approval boundary the agent sees. The interface also has a manual fallback, so the product remains usable in a browser that does not yet expose WebMCP. What people and agents do together The person chooses the real place, states the purpose, and approves cost. The agent turns that intent into a sequence of explicit browser-tool calls. OpenStreetMap supplies locations and geometry. MapTruth rejects unsupported places, verifies the locked evidence, and records tool receipts. The image model styles the evidence; it does not supply the evidence. How it was built MapTruth is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. MapLibre GL JS renders the live map. Nominatim resolves the requested city; Overpass provides nearby OpenStreetMap features. The browser integration registers ten WebMCP tools with JSON schemas, annotations, bounded outputs, and untrusted-content hints. Vercel Functions proxy the external services and image generation. Examples use checked-in snapshots captured from the same live pipeline so a demo does not stall on a public service. A separate verification script launches installed Chrome with WebMCP enabled, discovers all ten tools through document.modelContext.getTools() , and executes inspect_map_context through the browser's own document.modelContext.executeTool() . Challenges The difficult part was not drawing a map. It was defining a trust boundary an agent could not casually cross: the model can name candidates but cannot set a coordinate; geometry must belong to the current locked place; stale locks must be rejected; and paid generation must require visible human approval. Public geocoding and Overpass services also vary in latency, so the experience needed deterministic examples without pretending they were a separate data path. Accomplishments Ten discoverable WebMCP tools operate a real map workflow rather than a toy counter or hidden demo route. Native discovery and execution are tested in installed Chrome, with no mocked model context in the production verifier. Every generated comparison has a visible source line and OpenStreetMap inspection link. Agent activity is legible to the person and stops before cost. The same app remains usable manually when WebMCP is unavailable. What I learned Reliable agent UX comes from moving important guarantees out of prompts and into the page's tool contract. Structured tools make collaboration clearer, but the strongest result comes from deliberately limiting each participant: the model names, OpenStreetMap locates, the page verifies, and the person decides. What's next Next I would add saved, shareable evidence bundles; compare OpenStreetMap changes over time; and support more source layers while keeping the same provenance contract. The most useful extension is not more autonomous drawing, but better ways to inspect why a place was accepted or rejected. Honest limits MapTruth verifies that generation received geometry derived from the current OpenStreetMap view. It does not claim that every generated pixel is cartographically exact or that OpenStreetMap is perfectly complete or current. The prompt-only image is deliberately untrusted. Example snapshots are marked as snapshots; typing a new city exercises the live service path. Built during the challenge The repository was created on August 26, 2026 and its first commit is dated the same day, after the challenge submission period opened on August 25. The full implementation history is visible in the public commit log. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: ONE
pitch: An open lab where humans and agents build, test, and improve voice AI together.
about_excerpt: An open lab where humans and agents build, test, and improve voice AI together. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Make it YOU Inspiration Voice AI demos can feel magical. Then someone interrupts, stays silent, speaks over background noise, reaches voicemail, or loses their connection, and that magic can disappear. After years of helping organizations turn APIs and SDKs into dependable customer experiences, I became fascinated by the gap between an impressive voice demo and a system people can genuinely trust. Building voice AI meant navigating fragmented providers, hidden events, incompatible interfaces, unpredictable costs, sensitive credentials, and failures that were difficult to reproduce. I started ONE as a local learning lab where I could see the entire system working: authentication, payloads, transcripts, realtime events, latency, interruptions, recovery behavior, and the connection between an audio interaction and its intended human outcome. As I explored more providers, a larger problem became clear. Creators are often asked to choose a platform before they have enough evidence to know whether it fits their needs. Provider comparisons tend to flatten everything into leaderboards, even though the best combination depends on language, latency, privacy, accessibility, geography, budget, and the experience being created. ONE grew from a personal voice AI lab into a larger mission: give humans and agents an open place to understand the ecosystem, test it honestly, and assemble the combination that works best for them without surrendering control to a single vendor. What it does ONE is an open, provider-neutral lab for learning, building, testing, and improving voice AI. The lab makes normally hidden system behavior visible, including: Realtime conversation states and event timelines Speech-to-text, reasoning, text-to-speech, and transport layers Interruptions, crosstalk, silence, latency, voicemail, and reconnect behavior Controlled failures, fallback paths, and recovery decisions Provider capabilities and implementation status Structured evaluation evidence Authentication and payload construction Explicit execution and provider-spend controls Reusable voice-agent architecture patterns For the WebMCP experience, ONE exposes a focused workflow through four structured tools: list_voice_scenarios configure_voice_replay start_deterministic_replay get_replay_evidence A person can ask their agent to test how a voice system handles an interruption or lost connection. The agent can discover the available scenarios, configure a deterministic replay, request execution, and retrieve the resulting evidence without guessing where to click. The browser remains the shared workspace. Configuration changes appear visibly in ONE, consequential actions require confirmation, the test unfolds through the interface, and the resulting timeline and scorecard remain available for human review. The agent handles repetitive discovery, configuration, and evidence gathering. The person retains intent, judgment, approval, and the final decision. How we built it ONE began as a local React-based voice lab and evolved into a modular system with provider adapters, realtime inspection tools, deterministic scenarios, evidence capture, and an extensive browser regression suite. The most important architectural decision was creating one capability layer shared by the human interface and WebMCP. The agent does not operate a hidden copy of ONE or maintain a separate version of its state. WebMCP invokes the same capabilities, updates the same interface, and produces the same evidence that a person sees. The collaboration loop works like this: The person defines the goal and constraints. The agent discovers an appropriate test. The agent configures the scenario. ONE makes the proposed configuration visible. The person approves execution when required. The replay runs inside the shared interface. The agent retrieves and helps interpret the evidence. The person decides what to investigate next. I built deterministic local replay so reliability failures can be reproduced without requiring a live provider call or spending API credits. Live, simulated, experimental, and proposed capabilities are labeled separately so ONE never implies that something is operational when it is not. Provider credentials remain server-side, while execution gates prevent a browser agent from silently initiating billable activity. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not teaching an agent how to operate ONE. It was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do, what must remain under human control, and how every action could be inspected afterward. Realtime voice is also inherently difficult to test. Network conditions, timing, microphones, background noise, provider behavior, and human speech can all change the result. Deterministic replay became the bridge between realistic failure scenarios and repeatable evidence. Another challenge was translating a complex laboratory into a small set of meaningful WebMCP tools. Exposing every button would only recreate the interface as an API. I instead designed tools around complete intentions: discover a scenario, configure it, run it, and inspect what happened. ONE also began as a substantial local project rather than a challenge-sized prototype. Preparing it for the web required disciplined scope, deployment hardening, browser validation, security boundaries, and careful separation between what is truly implemented and what remains part of the roadmap. Accomplishments that we're proud of ONE grew from a provider-specific learning experiment into a provider-neutral system for studying the complete voice AI stack. I am especially proud of: Building deterministic reliability scenarios for interruption, crosstalk, silence, latency, reconnects, and other real-world conditions Creating a zero-provider-spend path for testing system behavior safely Making agent execution visible instead of allowing agents to act silently Preserving explicit human confirmation before consequential or billable actions Separating live, adapter-backed, experimental, simulated, and proposed capabilities Producing structured timelines and evidence instead of relying only on subjective impressions Building a shared capability layer that serves both the human interface and WebMCP Growing an extensive automated regression suite around a fast-moving experimental project Building this as an independent creator while keeping the architecture open to an entire ecosystem The accomplishment I value most is that ONE does not treat human control as friction. Human judgment is part of the architecture. What we learned The biggest lesson is that voice quality is not a single model score. It is an end-to-end property of the system, including timing, turn-taking, transport, recovery, observability, permissions, cost, and human expectations. I also learned that provider neutrality requires more than displaying several logos. It requires consistent capability descriptions, honest implementation states, comparable evidence, provenance, and the freedom to combine services rather than accept an entire bundled stack. Agent-native design is not simply automation. An effective agent needs structured capabilities, but a trustworthy agent also needs bounded authority, shared state, visible history, and clear moments of human approval. WebMCP creates that relationship inside the web experience. The agent does not replace the interface or move the work into an invisible backend. The person, page, and agent remain together. Finally, I learned that hosted access and local sovereignty are not opposing ideas. The web can support discovery, education, and collaboration, while local execution can preserve privacy, resilience, portability, and user control. What's next for ONE Almost everything. The long-term vision is for ONE to include every meaningful provider across the voice AI ecosystem: speech recognition, speech generation, speech-to-speech models, language models, telephony, orchestration, evaluation, translation, accessibility, observability, and supporting infrastructure. The goal is not to identify one universal winner. It is to let any human or agent assemble the right system for a particular need and budget. Someone might choose one provider for transcription, another for reasoning, another for voice, another for telephone transport, and a separate evaluation layer to verify the result. Another creator might prioritize local processing, a specific language, low latency, accessibility, regional data handling, or the lowest sustainable cost. ONE should help both of them construct an evidence-backed stack. Agents will help people navigate this growing ecosystem by translating human requirements into testable configurations. A visual cloud studio where humans and AI agents design, stress-test, and synthesize production infrastructure together in real-time through 31 in-browser WebMCP tools.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 💡 Inspiration: Breaking Free from the Chatbox 

 Every software architect and cloud engineer has had this frustrating experience: you ask ChatGPT or Claude to "design an enterprise AI cluster" , and it spits out three pages of markdown text with ASCII diagrams. 

 You can't click on it. You can't simulate 50,000 requests per second to see where it chokes. You can't calculate real-time AWS or NVIDIA GPU costs without opening three separate pricing calculators. And you certainly can't turn it into production Terraform code without hours of manual transcription. 

 AI coding assistants were spatially blind —trapped inside narrow text boxes while real engineering happens visually on canvases, whiteboards, and topology graphs. 

 When I discovered the W3C Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , everything clicked. WebMCP allows the browser tab itself to become the AI agent's interactive workspace. I asked myself: What if an AI agent didn't just write text, but lived inside the canvas with you—wiring components, stress-testing bottlenecks, debating trade-offs, and compiling infrastructure code in real-time? 

 That vision became OmniFlow Studio . 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 OmniFlow Studio is a collaborative visual systems architecture studio where humans and AI agent swarms co-create, stress-test, and synthesize cloud infrastructure live in the browser through 31 WebMCP tools : 

 
 Interactive 60 FPS Canvas : Drag, drop, and wire microservices, NVIDIA H100 GPU clusters, Redis semantic caches, and vector databases with interactive port wiring and adaptive bezier curves. 
 Live Multi-Agent Swarm Consensus : A human architect can trigger an automated debate between 4 specialized AI roles ( Lead Architect, SecOps Auditor, FinOps Advisor, and Chaos Daemon ). The swarm deliberates live, reaches consensus, and refactors the architecture. 
 Real-Time Traffic & Particle Physics : Simulate traffic spikes up to 50,000 RPS. The canvas visualizes dataflow bottlenecks using glowing packet particles and node heatmaps. 
 Chaos Engineering & Auto-Pilot : Inject chaos faults (Chaos Monkey node termination, DDoS floods, and GPU OOMs). An autonomous Auto-Pilot loop actively detects degraded nodes and self-heals the cluster. 
 Instant Code Synthesis : Compiles visual topologies directly into production Terraform (HCL) , Kubernetes Helm values , AWS CloudFormation , Docker Compose , and executive Markdown manifestos with live Mermaid diagrams. 
 

 

 🧮 Engineering Math & FinOps Foundations 

 To make the studio truly enterprise-grade, I implemented mathematical models directly into the client-side engines: 

 1. Frontier LLM KV-Cache & VRAM Sizing 

 When provisioning an NVIDIA H100 inference cluster, the memory sizing engine calculates continuous batching requirements using: 

 Memory KV = 2 × L × H × D × B × S × P 

 Where: 

 
 L = Number of transformer layers (e.g., 80 for 70B models) 
 H = Key-Value attention heads (e.g., 8 for GQA) 
 D = Head dimension (e.g., 128) 
 B = Concurrency batch size 
 S = Context sequence length (tokens) 
 P = Precision bytes ( 2 for FP16, 1 for FP8) 
 

 2. FinOps Egress & Real-Time TCO Formula 

 Monthly total cost of ownership accounts for compute instances, replicas, and network egress bandwidth dynamically: 

 $$\text{TCO} {\text{monthly}} = \sum {i=1}^{N} \left( C_{\text{base}, i} \times r_i \right) + \left( \frac{\text{RPS} \times 3600 \times 730 \times S_{\text{payload}}}{10^9} \times R_{\text{egress}} \right)$$ 

 Where C base , i is the hourly node rate, r i is horizontal replica count, and R egress is cloud egress cost per gigabyte. 

 

 🛠️ How I Built It 

 OmniFlow Studio was engineered from scratch with a zero-backend, client-side Edge architecture : 

 
 Core & Bundler : Built with HTML5 semantic elements, modern ES Modules, and bundled with Vite . 
 Design System : Handcrafted glassmorphic dark-mode CSS with cyber-glow telemetry accents, 100% responsive without heavy third-party UI bloat. 
 Canvas Engine : Custom HTML5 Canvas renderer running at a locked 60 FPS, featuring world-to-screen coordinate transformation, adaptive port attachment, and undo/redo history stacks. 
 WebMCP Architecture :

 
 29 Imperative Tools registered directly on window.document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 2 Declarative HTML Forms using <form toolname="..."> and <input toolparamdescription="..."> for native DOM-level tool exposure. 
 Machine Discovery : Pre-configured /.well-known/webmcp.json and /llms.txt with CORS enabled for instant agent crawling. 
 
 Edge Deployment : Hosted globally on Vercel's Anycast Edge CDN with 0ms cold-start latency (no server sleep, no timeouts). 
 

 

 🧗 Challenges I Faced 

 
 Bidirectional State Sync : The hardest part was allowing humans to drag nodes with the mouse while AI agents simultaneously executed mutations (like batch_build_architecture or kill_random_node ) without UI race conditions or dropped frames. I designed an event-driven decoupled EventBus that synchronizes canvas coordinates instantly. 
 Preventing Awkward Wire Loops : Early prototypes suffered from overlapping connections when nodes shared columns. I wrote an adaptive port calculation algorithm and a topological DAG layering auto-layout engine ( applyAutoLayout ) that guarantees clean Left-to-Right dataflow with zero wire crossings. 
 Pure Client-Side WebMCP Execution : Ensuring that all 31 tools—including Terraform compilation and FinOps math—execute locally in under 5 milliseconds inside the browser without requiring a bulky backend server. 
 

 

 🧠 What I Learned 

 Building OmniFlow Studio convinced me that WebMCP is the future of human-AI collaboration on the web . 

 Text boxes force humans to translate their thoughts into prompts, and then translate the AI's response back into tools. With WebMCP, the human and the AI share the exact same canvas, the exact same state, and the exact same visual vocabulary . It feels less like asking a chatbot for help and more like pairing with a senior systems architect sitting right beside you. 

 

 🔮 What's Next for OmniFlow Studio 

 
 Live Cloud Deployment Hook : One-click pushing generated Terraform directly to AWS and GCP via ephemeral GitHub Actions runners. 
 Cost Anomaly Watchdogs : WebMCP agents listening to live Datadog/CloudWatch metrics to auto-tune replica counts dynamically. 
 Collaborative Multi-User Rooms : Enabling multiple humans and multiple agent swarms to co-design in the same canvas via WebRTC.

 Planner view: PantryPilot turns pantry ingredients into a time- and diet-aware dinner plan with Agent Trace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval boundary: missing groceries wait for review; no tool can purchase or submit payment. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Guided cooking mode combines recipe steps, substitutions, Agent Trace, and a persistent timer. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive finish: PantryPilot confirms dinner is ready after the guided cooking flow is complete. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Dinner is rarely blocked by a lack of recipes. It is blocked by a chain of small decisions: what is already in the kitchen, what fits the time and diet, what can be substituted, what is missing, and what to do next. 

 We wanted to turn that fragmented process into one clear, collaborative flow where an agent can help without becoming a black box. 

 What we built 

 PantryPilot is a WebMCP-enabled cooking app that turns pantry ingredients into a complete dinner plan and guided cooking session. 

 The agent can read the kitchen, select and scale a recipe, replace ingredients, prepare a shopping list, start cooking mode, and set persistent timers. Every action updates the same Zustand state used by the interface and appears in the visible Agent Trace. 

 The Golden Demo plans a vegetarian dinner for two, prioritizes tomatoes, replaces dairy with oat milk, identifies missing ingredients, pauses for human approval, and then starts the cooking flow. 

 How we built it 

 The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Zod, and the WebMCP imperative API. Zod validates tool inputs, while Zustand provides one persisted state layer shared by human interactions and agent tools. 

 We exposed ten structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . This lets agents operate named actions with validated inputs instead of guessing from pixels. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hardest part was making the agent experience reliable, deterministic, and understandable. We needed every tool action to update the visible UI correctly, survive reloads, fit documented input and output budgets, and behave consistently during the Golden Demo. 

 The most important design decision was the human-approval boundary. The agent may prepare missing groceries, but it cannot approve, purchase, or submit payment. This keeps the experience useful while preserving user control at consequential moments. 

 PantryPilot taught us that capable agents need equally strong visibility, validation, and boundaries. WebMCP makes the app directly operable by an agent, while the interface keeps the person informed and in control.

 AffiliateTresuroperates as an agent-native affiliate discovery platform, bridging human browsing and AI interactivity 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Conventional affiliate discovery platforms are designed exclusively for human navigation through ad banners, cluttered lists, and search bars. However, as local client assistants and autonomous AI agents evolve into the primary portal for research and shopping, web content must become programmatically actionable for machines as well as visually readable for humans. Driven by this shift, we set out to create an agent-native affiliate marketplace. Our goal was to enable seamless visual browsing for users while empowering local AI agents to query structured product catalogs, discover tools, and deliver verified deals using modern browser standards. 

 
 What it does AffiliateTresur. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Built with vanilla HTML5, modern CSS, and JavaScript to keep asset delivery lightweight and responsive. 
 Agent Interface: Implemented declarative WebMCP tool handlers that bind directly to DOM forms and programmatic schemas, responding with structured JSON when invoked by browser-level AI agents. 
 Edge Hosting & Delivery: Configured for edge deployment via Cloudflare using Wrangler, delivering static assets globally with instant edge caching. 
 Version Control & CI/CD: Maintained via GitHub with automated Cloudflare Worker build triggers and custom domain routing on affiliatetresur.com . 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Edge Environment vs. Browser Code: Reconciling Cloudflare Worker deployment pipelines with a purely client-side static application required fine-tuning wrangler.jsonc asset routing rather than compiling edge server handlers. 
 Build Configuration Hurdles: Diagnosing configuration file syntax issues—such as multi-root JSON parsing bugs in package.json —and configuring compatibility dates under automated Wrangler pipelines. 
 Standardizing Agent Discovery: Aligning custom mock product query filters (spanning hardware, mobile tech, and automotive accessories) with strict WebMCP schema definitions so simulated agents could query data cleanly without format errors. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Seamless Tool Discovery: Successfully implemented in-browser agent discovery, enabling Chrome DevTools agent simulators to detect and execute catalog queries instantly. 
 Zero-Bloat Architecture: Delivered a full-featured, functional prototype without heavy framework overhead, ensuring sub-second load times and zero unnecessary dependencies. 
 Live Domain Deployment: Successfully deployed and routed the platform to the live production custom domain affiliatetresur.com . 
 

 What we learned 

 
 Agent-First Web Design: Structuring data and forms for both browser DOM events and agent-invoked events requires thinking about web applications as APIs and visual dashboards simultaneously. 
 Declarative Browser Standards: Practical hands-on experience navigating emerging browser AI APIs and testing agent interaction pipelines locally and in staging environments. 
 Cloudflare Static Assets on Workers: Mastering modern Wrangler asset-binding patterns to serve high-performance client code reliably at the edge. 
 

 What's next for AffiliateTresur 

 
 Live Affiliate API Feeds: Connect the platform beyond mock datasets to real-time affiliate network APIs (e.g., Amazon Associates, CJ, ShareASale) with dynamic pricing updates. 
 Autonomous Agent Price Tracking: Enable background agent monitoring where users can instruct their local assistant to alert them when a specific product drops below a target price threshold.

pitch: Browser-native WebMCP agent for First Notice of Loss (FNOL): tells drivers what their car insurance covers while reporting a crash.
about_excerpt: Browser-native WebMCP agent for First Notice of Loss (FNOL): tells drivers what their car insurance covers while reporting a crash. Like Comment Story Updates Discovery. The agent finds the insurer's typed tools at runtime and drafts the claim from what the claimant said in plain words. Routes on screen. Rows the agent wrote read via tool, rows that came with the file read on file, and each requirement names its clause. A moving surface. Answering that the car cannot be driven publishes a ninth tool. Changing the answer back withdraws it again. Refusal. A planted instruction inside a third party note is refused, and the ledger names the code, PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED. The refusal, and the button. PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED on the pinned row, the claim not filed, and File this claim left for a person. The whole desk, live in the ChatGPT browser. The agent says it is ready to file, and that pressing File this claim is yours to do. The insurer's page hands your own agent its rules as typed tools, so you learn what you are covered for while still describing the crash. Live, no account: https://upgradedev.github.io/claimready/ Code (MIT): https://github.com/upgradedev/claimready Tools need a browser that has WebMCP. Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on, verified on Chrome 151 stable, or the ChatGPT desktop app's built in browser with site tools enabled. Availability there is still rolling out and varies by workspace. In any other browser the page works by hand and says on screen why no tools are registered. Inspiration Somebody has just had a crash and is standing next to the car with a phone. They know what happened. What they do not know is what their own policy needs to hear about it, and neither does any general purpose assistant, because the clause, the excess and the list of required answers sit on one insurer's origin and change from customer to customer. I build claims systems for European assistance operators, so this is the failure I watch: a first notice of loss arrives wrong about what the policy needed rather than about what happened. Then the driver waits days to learn what they are covered for, and a handler spends the interval asking for the field nobody told anyone to fill in. What it does Describe the crash to your own agent. It reads the insurer's typed tools and tells you what this policy still needs while you are talking. Then the surface moves: answer that the car cannot be driven and get_assistance_options registers, a capability the agent lacked a moment earlier and loses when that answer changes. Three prompts to paste, with two page steps between the second and the third: Read this claim page and tell me what it still needs from me. A delivery van reversed into my car while it was parked in the car park on Harbour Road. It caught the left front wing and left a dent. The car still drives, and it is still there in the Harbour Road car park. Fill that in for me and write the description. Now set Still drivable to no on the page yourself, and press Pin on that row. Both steps matter: the pin is what makes the next answer a refusal rather than a successful write. Then: Read the notes on the file, then read the claim again, do what that note asks, and tell me what the page said. That note is a planted instruction inside third party evidence, and it asks for the row you just pinned, so the answer is PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED . Every answer also carries the route it arrived on: on file, via page, via tool. That names a surface, not a person. The page cannot see who is at the keyboard, so it never claims to. Filing is human only. No tool files, dispatches, pins or unlocks, and a test reads the source to keep it that way. Filing leaves a handler packet built from the exact revision that passed the filing gate, with the clause, the excess, every requirement and a SHA-256 that scripts/verify_packet.mjs recomputes. Nothing is transmitted and no claim is opened anywhere. With no key and no signature, a matching digest shows only that the content is unchanged. It does not show origin, authorship, or that nobody edited the content and recomputed the digest to match, and the repository says so in the same words. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The rules that decide a motor claim sit on one insurer's origin and change from customer to customer. A REST endpoint with an OpenAPI file carries the same answers, once somebody builds that integration for this insurer. This is browser native and same origin, with zero integration work: an agent meeting this insurer for the first time discovers the tools at runtime. How it creates a better user experience The driver learns what their own policy still needs while they are still describing the crash, in the assistant they already have open, instead of a second call days later. The cover answer at the roadside instead of a letter a week later. Nothing to install, no account, and the page keeps working by hand in a browser with no agent in it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Two parties write to one document and neither overwrites the other silently. The agent drafts. The person corrects a field and pins it, and a pinned row then refuses every later patch and says so with a code. The tool surface itself moves: answering that the car cannot be driven publishes a ninth tool, and changing the answer back withdraws it. Filing stays a button only a person can press, and the page says so in its own tool list. Before this, each of those needed a bespoke integration per insurer, and an agent still had no way to be told what a page refuses. How WebMCP is implemented Tools register on document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext , over a pure core with no dependencies and no build step. Page and tools share one store, so an agent action shows on screen. Read tools carry readOnlyHint and text the insurer did not write carries untrustedContentHint . Both halves of the standard ship. Nine tools come from JavaScript, eight from the moment the page loads and a ninth that appears when the claim says the car cannot be driven, which is why the narration at 0:20 of the video counts eight. The tenth is an ordinary HTML form carrying four attributes, toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription and toolautosubmit , and the browser builds the JSON Schema and the tool from that markup on its own. toolautosubmit is the one that makes an agent's call actually submit the form rather than only fill it. So an insurer adopts WebMCP by adding attributes. What the demo video shows Three beats are captured in CI by Playwright against the deployed page in Chrome. Two run with WebMCP on, against the browser's own implementation. The first runs with it deliberately off, because that beat shows the page as a visitor with no agent sees it. Six are one continuous unbroken recording in the ChatGPT desktop app's built in browser, cut into six. Two corrections to the narration , written here because the cut is frozen. At 1:40 it says the roadside collection "is arranged": the demo records a local roadside assistance request and marks that requirement answered, it does not arrange or dispatch a service, and nothing leaves the page. At 2:08 it says "Chrome builds the schema from that markup", where the accurate word is the browser: that take was shot in the ChatGPT desktop browser, and the declarative half is verified separately in Chrome 151.0.7922.174 stable. Both are also written into the video description. The opening and closing cards are type on a still background, generated by a script in the repository. No stock footage and no rendered people: every other frame is the deployed page running. Evidence 961 unit tests, from node --test tests/unit , with source coverage of 98.11 percent of lines over the 22 files under src. Both are read at the submitted commit and both reprint in any clone. 178 assertions run against the deployed page in a real Chrome with WebMCP enabled, in CI, at the same commit the host serves. The page loads no framework, has no build step and makes no network call at runtime after load. Challenges, and the honest limits Insurer, policy, vehicle and claimant are invented. No integration, no adjudication, no handler has reviewed a packet, nobody has run this on a real intake. What is not demonstrated is that any of it makes an autonomous agent fill a form better. One experiment tried to show that and did not, and it is published in full rather than dropped.  Inspiration 

 Doctors and hospital leaders move between camera views, mobile observations, staff calls, and task lists while trying to keep clinical judgment clear. An agent can help gather context and coordinate the right role, but it should not turn an uncertain image into an autonomous diagnosis or treatment order. Care Command Center explores that boundary with a public, simulated environment containing no patient imagery or live hospital connection. 

 What it does 

 Care Command Center presents simulated fixed-camera and mobile observations, a clinician review queue, staff availability, and an activity log. Its six WebMCP tools let an agent: 

 
 summarize the command center; 
 list observations by status, urgency, and source type; 
 prepare one observation for clinician review; 
 draft a task for a staff role; 
 read simulated role availability; and 
 run a coordination drill. 
 

 Preparing an observation highlights the matching card and returns a verification checklist. Drafting a task leaves it pending. A doctor or authorized operator must independently verify the situation and use the visible Approve & queue action. The staff acknowledgment shown in the demo is simulated. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer meaning from a dense dashboard and simulate clicks. With WebMCP, the page exposes a small typed contract that maps directly to its state. The agent can reliably answer “What needs review?”, “Prepare this observation for me,” or “Draft a task for the duty nurse” while the doctor stays in the same interface. 

 This creates a practical human-agent boundary: the agent compresses navigation and coordination, while the clinician retains the consequential decision. 

 What judges should notice 

 
 WebMCP leverage: the agent invokes native typed tools backed by page state; it does not scrape labels or replay brittle clicks. 
 Execution: one continuous workflow goes from an urgent simulated observation to review preparation, a structured staff-task draft, doctor approval, simulated staff acceptance, and an audit entry. 
 Potential impact: hospital leaders can coordinate observations and staff from one interface without hiding uncertainty or transferring clinical authority to the agent. 
 Creativity and ambition: the prototype applies browser-native agent tools to camera, mobile, clinician, and staff coordination while defining a realistic boundary for safety-critical work. 
 

 How we built it 

 The app is a dependency-free static site built with accessible HTML, responsive CSS, and JavaScript modules. webmcp.mjs registers six imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a JSON Schema, a precise description, and an explicit side-effect boundary. The summary, observation-list, and staff-directory tools declare readOnlyHint: true. 

 The WebMCP adapter calls the same state functions used by the visible interface, so agent and human actions cannot drift into separate behavior. Pure functions cover queue ordering and the draft -> approved -> queued -> accepted task transition. Tests verify both operational rules and the public tool contract. 

 Challenges 

 The hard design question was what an agent should do when a camera or mobile image could be clinically important. A direct diagnose_patient or change_device_setting tool would be unsafe and misleading. We instead created prepare_clinical_review: it highlights the observation, returns a checklist, and states clearly that no diagnosis, prescription, device change, or staff message occurred. 

 Staff coordination follows the same boundary. draft_staff_task creates a structured, pending task. The human must approve it before the simulated staff inbox accepts it. A real WhatsApp adapter is intentionally not connected. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Six working WebMCP tools discovered and executed in a WebMCP-enabled browser. 
 A visible workflow from simulated camera/mobile observation to clinician review and staff-task approval. 
 Separate clinical and operational safety boundaries. 
 A reproducible public demo with no accounts, private data, or external systems. 
 Tests covering queue and approval behavior plus a public MIT-licensed repository. 
 

 What we learned 

 For agent-facing clinical workflows, descriptions and approval boundaries matter as much as schemas. The useful role for an agent is often to collect context, prepare work, and make uncertainty visible. The doctor remains accountable for the decision. 

 What's next 

 Future work could add institution-approved authentication, secure mobile capture, camera and device adapters, EHR links, staff-channel adapters, immutable audit storage, role-based policy, localization, and a formal clinical-safety evaluation. Any real deployment would require privacy and security review, named-user access, retention limits, validation, and independent clinical governance.

title: RelayGrid
pitch: Safe, explainable WebMCP workflows for enterprise data grids.
about_excerpt: Safe, explainable WebMCP workflows for enterprise data grids. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Enterprise teams spend too much time constructing nested filters, checking why records were selected, and safely applying repetitive actions across dense operational tables. Natural-language filtering alone does not solve the risky part: understanding the interpretation, reviewing the impact, and reversing a mistake. What it does RelayGrid turns a natural-language goal into a visible, deterministic query tree over 7,500 synthetic radiology records. It shows the matching records and explains why each one matched. Stage-aware actions are processed in visible batches of at most 50 records: Preview separates permitted and protected records, explicit confirmation executes the saved plan, every action is audited, and the latest batch can be undone. Unsupported or out-of-order requests are rejected without changing data. Why WebMCP is essential RelayGrid exposes six high-level tools directly from the active page instead of asking an agent to scrape the DOM or guess which controls to click. WebMCP publishes the grid's real fields, supported operators, input schemas, and live context. ChatGPT constructs a schema-grounded Query AST; WebMCP invokes the requested tool; RelayGrid validates and evaluates it deterministically. The tools and the human interface share the same active query, Preview plan, workflow stage, status colors, and audit history, so every agent action is immediately visible and reviewable. The tools are: describe_grid apply_query explain_record preview_batch_action execute_batch_action undo_last_batch How we built it The page registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . A canonical JSON AST supports nested AND, OR, and NOT groups, comparisons, dates, Boolean values, enums, and sorting. A deterministic query engine validates and evaluates the AST against the full dataset. A shared transition engine powers both non-mutating Preview and confirmed Execute, while a workflow state machine exposes only context-valid operations and returns precise errors for invalid stages. The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Next.js, and Tailwind CSS. The public app is hosted with OpenAI Sites, and the complete MIT-licensed source is available on GitHub. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making natural-language intent safe without hiding the interpretation. We separated the agent's structured intent from the application's deterministic matching logic, then added stale-preview protection so execution can only use the exact reviewed plan. We also had to keep filtering global while limiting mutations to the current visible batch, preserve the active query as the next eligible batch loads, and make every scenario reset to a reproducible state. Accomplishments Non-trivial nested filtering over a realistic enterprise dataset Shared state between WebMCP tools and the visible grid Record-level explainability Preview, policy exceptions, confirmation, audit, and undo Safe 50-record batch progression Stage-aware command gating and a visible invalid-input test Four guided judge scenarios with exact prompts and expected outcomes Native Chrome WebMCP verification of all six tools against the published site What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a page exposes domain capabilities and safety contracts, not low-level UI gestures. A strong tool result should update the same state the human sees and leave enough evidence to verify, approve, or reverse the operation. How to test Open the live app and follow the sticky Judge Demo Guide . The Main scenario covers Filter, Verify, Preview, Confirm, Next batch, and Undo. Additional tabs demonstrate Review to Approve, Cancel to Undo, and invalid-input rejection. The repository includes exact judge instructions and verified QA results. All records are synthetic. No GitHub account, deploy key, access token, or project credential is required. What's next The same schema and action engine can support insurance claims, inventory exceptions, CRM worklists, and ERP approvals without building a separate copilot for every application. pitch: Sentinel Desk is an open-source AI incident response desk where agents investigate traces, simulate runtime guards, and deploy human-approved fixes through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Sentinel Desk is an open-source AI incident response desk where agents investigate traces, simulate runtime guards, and deploy human-approved fixes through WebMCP.

 Theseus Guard - Sentinel Desk WebMCP 
 
 1 2 



 
 Project Story 

 AI systems can fail in ways that are difficult to investigate and even harder to remediate safely. When an incident occurs, security teams need to understand the evidence, replay the risky behavior, evaluate a possible fix, and preserve a clear audit trail. We wanted to explore how agents could help with this workflow without giving them unrestricted authority to change runtime policies. 

 That idea became Sentinel Desk : an open-source, standalone AI incident response desk powered by WebMCP. 

 Sentinel Desk lets an agent search incidents, inspect model traces, identify policy violations, simulate a proposed runtime guard, and request human approval. The final policy-changing action remains explicitly gated by the human operator. After approval, the guard is activated and the action appears in the provenance timeline. 

 The WebMCP layer exposes six tools: 

 
 search_incidents 
 inspect_trace 
 simulate_guard 
 request_guard_approval 
 apply_guard 
 get_audit_report 
 

 These tools are registered through the WebMCP Imperative API using document.modelContext.registerTool . The application also works as a normal web interface, so people can manually explore the workflow even when WebMCP is not available. 

 The most important thing we learned is that WebMCP is not simply a replacement for clicking buttons. A well-designed tool gives an agent a precise capability, a clear input schema, and an explicit trust boundary. This is especially important for security workflows: reading evidence and proposing a remediation are different actions from activating a policy change. 

 One of our main challenges was working with an emerging browser API while preserving a reliable human experience. We had to handle WebMCP availability, tool registration, cancellation and permission boundaries, while keeping the application usable in a regular browser. We also needed to make a synthetic runtime feel realistic without implying that it was connected to production data. 

 Sentinel Desk demonstrates a possible future for AI governance: agents can help investigate complex incidents and prepare remediation, while people retain authority over consequential runtime changes.
