title: RAI
pitch: RAI is a Robot, Agent Interface that allows agents to control and make robots using WebMCP tools, limited to actions like moving joints by angle and seeing through the robot’s camera.\n
about_excerpt:
RAI is a Robot, Agent Interface that allows agents to control and make robots using WebMCP tools, limited to actions like moving joints by angle and seeing through the robot’s camera.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I had wanted to build a robotic arm project for a long time, and one day while I was using Codex I thought: what is actually stopping me from giving an AI tools to control a robot arm? 

 It can have tools to move the joints, and it can also have a tool to look through a camera. So I decided to build the physical arm and experiment with letting an LLM see, move, and interact with real objects. 

 I think AI controlling physical things through vision and tools is still really underexplored, and I wanted to make it easier for other people to experiment with this idea too. 

 For this challenge, I made a lighter web version of the project where an agent can control a simulated robot using WebMCP tools. 

 What RAI does 

 RAI lets users watch AI trials and experiment with models controlling a robot. 

 The agent can look through the robot camera, read information about the arm, move its joints, and try to complete tasks. 

 It does not get hidden object positions or shortcuts. It has to look at what happened, make a move, see the result, and adjust if it fails. 

 Users can also try different prompts and compare how the agent behaves. 

 How I built it 

 I mainly used Codex to build the project. 

 I already had a lot of the control logic and ideas from my physical robot arm and my experiments with Isaac Sim, so I adapted those ideas into a lightweight web simulation that could run in the browser and be controlled through WebMCP. 

 Codex helped me build most of the interface, simulation, and WebMCP integration. 

 Challenges 

 At first I wanted RAI to be much bigger. I wanted agents to control multiple robots and experiment in more complicated environments. 

 That became too much for the time I had, and I also had some personal things happening during the submission period, so I came pretty close to missing the deadline. 

 Because of that, I focused on making one smaller environment that clearly shows the main idea instead of trying to build everything. 

 What I learned 

 One of the most interesting things I noticed is that sometimes the agent is too careful. 

 It can hesitate to move the arm far enough or avoid moves that seem risky, even when those moves are needed to complete the task. 

 My favorite experiment is tipping over a can. With the right prompt, Sol can usually figure it out in around 2 minutes using only the camera and the arm controls. 

 It is really interesting to watch the model try something, see that it did not work, and then change its next move. 

 I think models could become much better at this if training and evaluation included more examples of vision + tool use for controlling physical systems. 

 What's next 

 I want to turn RAI into a better environment for testing how different AI models control robots. 

 One thing I am especially interested in is letting an AI look at its own failed experiments and then change its prompt or strategy to improve the next attempt. 

 Longer term, I want to do more research on this and look into collecting large amounts of robot interaction data in simulation. 

 Because the same experiments can be repeated many times in a simulator, I think this could be useful for evaluating or training future models that are better at interacting with the physical world.

pitch: An agent-native editorial control room for 58,000+ academic journals - AI triages submissions and synthesizes peer reviews while human editors retain final authority.
about_excerpt: An agent-native editorial control room for 58,000+ academic journals - AI triages submissions and synthesizes peer reviews while human editors retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Published OJS article demonstrating an agent-native scholarly workflow with seven native WebMCP tools available to in-browser AI agents. List all submissions example MCP Get full abstract details MCP 💡 Inspiration: The Plight of a Two-Person Editorial Team Years ago, I served as a journal editor for an academic journal ( cogito.unklab.ac.id ). Our editorial team consisted of just two people . Every week, a flood of new submissions arrived in our Open Journal Systems (OJS) queue. The administrative burden was suffocating: We spent hours manually reading through abstracts just to verify if papers met our scope. Finding and assigning reviewers with relevant domain expertise took days of cross-referencing past archives. Reviewers routinely missed deadlines, forcing us to constantly track due dates and send manual reminders. Reading divergent reviewer reports and drafting customized, polite, constructive decision letters drained our remaining mental energy. Academic peer review is the bedrock of human knowledge, yet over 56,000 journals worldwide are managed by small, overworked academic teams suffering from click fatigue and administrative burnout. When the WebMCP standard emerged from W3C, Chrome, and OpenAI, a lightbulb went off: Why should academic editors spend hours navigating dozens of nested tabs when an in-browser AI agent can co-pilot the editorial desk using the editor's live session? ⚡ What It Does OJS-WebMCP turns standard Open Journal Systems installations into an Agent-Native Editorial Control Room . Instead of relying on fragile scrapers or complex command-line MCP servers, our plugin directly registers 7 native WebMCP tools into the editor's browser session via document.modelContext.registerTool : Intelligent Desk Screening : The agent queries active queues across all 4 workflow stages ( ojs_list_submissions ) and retrieves full abstracts and verified author affiliations ( ojs_get_submission_details ) to evaluate scope compliance. Automated Peer-Review Tracking : Inspects reviewer assignments, identifies overdue reviews, and monitors reviewer recommendations ( ojs_get_review_rounds ). Live Review Synthesis : Connects directly to real reviewer feedback to synthesize a formal decision letter ( ojs_draft_editorial_decision ), accurately distinguishing between Minor Revisions , Major Revisions (Resubmit for Review) , Acceptance , and Decline . Approval-Gated Reviewer Reminder : Prepares and dispatches polite reminder notifications to overdue reviewers ( ojs_send_reviewer_reminder ). It enforces strict Human-in-the-Loop safety: the agent can only preview the reminder until the human editor explicitly approves it ( confirmSend: true ). Issue & Volume Planning : Discovers upcoming unpublished future issues ( ojs_list_issues ) to help editors schedule accepted papers for publication. 🛠️ How We Built It Universal OJS Generic Plugin : Packaged as a clean, modular plugin ( plugins/generic/webmcp ) compatible with modern OJS 3.4+ and 3.5+. Zero API Key Friction : Academic editors are researchers, not DevOps engineers. Our plugin leverages the editor's active browser session cookie and CSRF token. When ChatGPT or Chrome Agent opens the tab, it inherits authoritative editorial permissions immediately-no API keys or environment variables required. Granular REST Integration : Extended OJS's core routing architecture with custom, authenticated REST endpoints ( /submissions/{id}/reviewAssignments ) to expose granular review progress without leaking unnecessary personal identifiers. W3C WebMCP Standard : All tools implement structured JSON Schemas and async execution handlers conforming strictly to the official WebMCP spec. 🧗 Challenges We Faced Navigating OJS's Deep RBAC & Security Policies : OJS has a strict multi-layer authorization system ( SubmissionAccessPolicy , PolicyAuthorizer ). Ensuring that our WebMCP tools respected editorial permissions without bypassing journal security required deep reverse-engineering of OJS's internal routing stack. Ensuring Human Authority Over AI Actions : We did not want an agent going rogue and emailing professors unsolicited rejection letters. Designing the Approval-Gated Action pattern ( confirmSend gate) ensured that the AI serves as an indispensable assistant while the human editor always retains final academic authority. Data Sanitization & Metadata Quality : Normalizing OJS 3.5's multi-table author affiliation schemas ( author_affiliations and author_affiliation_settings ) and stripping raw HTML tags from abstracts so that LLMs receive clean, token-efficient context. 📚 What We Learned In-Browser MCP is the Future : Traditional MCP requires running local processes, configuring port forwarding, or sharing sensitive API tokens. WebMCP completely democratizes agentic AI for web-first workflows: you log into your web app, and your agent is immediately ready to help. The "Control Room" Dynamic : The winning paradigm for AI in knowledge work is not total automation, but co-browsing : the human provides the high-level strategy and moral judgment, while the agent handles workload tracking, data retrieval, and first-pass drafting. 🚀 What's Next Automated Reviewer Matching : Using paper embeddings and CrossRef/OpenAlex APIs to suggest the top 3 best-matching reviewers based on published citation history. Submission to PKP Plugin Gallery : Submitting this plugin to the official Public Knowledge Project (PKP) Plugin Gallery so that all 58,000+ academic journals worldwide can install OJS-WebMCP in a single click. title: LoadGuard 3D
pitch: Agent-native 3D truck load planning where WebMCP agents can inspect, plan, validate, and stage proposals while humans retain control over operational execution.
about_excerpt: Agent-native 3D truck load planning where WebMCP agents can inspect, plan, validate, and stage proposals while humans retain control over operational execution. Like Comment Story Updates Main Page Implementation Stack Workflow Data Flow Main page of WebMCP Info about WebMCP Problem live data Live Activity Github page Project Workflow Inspiration As AI agents become capable of doing more inside real applications, I kept coming back to one question: How do we make an agent genuinely useful without allowing it to give itself permission to perform consequential actions? Logistics gave me a practical way to explore that problem. Truck loading involves real constraints: available space, weight limits, fragile cargo, delivery order, package dimensions, and operational state. An agent can be very useful here because it can inspect the current situation, coordinate planning, validate a proposal, and prepare the next action. But there is an important boundary. If an AI can both create an operational plan and authorize that same plan , then human oversight becomes mostly cosmetic. That idea became the foundation of LoadGuard 3D . The agent reasons. The operator authorizes. The website defines and enforces the contract. LoadGuard 3D explores how WebMCP can give agents structured access to meaningful website capabilities while keeping consequential execution under explicit human control. What it does LoadGuard 3D is a WebMCP-native 3D truck load-planning workspace. The application starts with a real operational state. In the main demo scenario, truck TRK-042 already contains eight loaded packages while an urgent, fragile package, MED-901 , is still inbound. The system can create a candidate loading plan that incorporates the new package while respecting the current truck state and package constraints. The workflow is intentionally separated into stages: Inspect the current truck state Retrieve package constraints Create a candidate load plan Validate the candidate Stage the valid proposal Attempt operational execution Require human authorization Execute the exact approved proposal Protect against duplicate execution The operator sees the candidate directly in a 3D truck visualization before deciding whether to approve it. For the demonstration scenario, the candidate reaches: 9 / 9 packages placed 1011 kg total weight 78.4% utilization 0 hard validation violations 2 fragile-cargo review warnings The important part is what happens next. If commit_load_plan is called before a human has approved the proposal, LoadGuard returns: APPROVAL_REQUIRED The active truck does not change. The human then reviews the exact staged proposal in the LoadGuard interface and chooses whether to approve or reject it. Human approval is intentionally not exposed as a WebMCP tool. After approval, the same operational commit can succeed because the application and database can verify that the exact proposal being executed is the one the operator authorized. A successful execution returns: EXECUTED and advances the truck state revision. If the same commit is accidentally retried, LoadGuard returns: ALREADY_EXECUTED instead of applying the operation twice. This makes human authorization, execution, and replay protection part of the real operational contract rather than just UI conventions. How we built it LoadGuard is built as several cooperating layers rather than one large autonomous-agent function. WebMCP interface LoadGuard registers structured capabilities through document.modelContext . The website exposes exactly seven WebMCP tools: get_load_state get_package_constraints create_load_plan validate_load_plan stage_load_plan commit_load_plan get_action_ledger I deliberately kept the tools narrow. Reading truck state is different from creating a candidate. Creating a candidate is different from staging it. Staging is different from operational execution. Most importantly, there is no approve_load_plan WebMCP capability available to the agent. The agent can request execution, but it cannot manufacture its own authority. Deterministic planning The language model does not generate the package coordinates. The model or agent orchestrates the workflow, while LoadGuard's deterministic planner computes the spatial candidate. This was an important design decision because physical placement should not depend on an LLM inventing geometry. Independent validation The candidate is validated before it can become a staged proposal. The validator checks constraints including: truck boundaries collisions between packages weight limits fragility delivery ordering malformed placements unplaced packages complete target-package coverage A candidate can therefore be rejected independently of the reasoning that requested it. 3D operator workspace The frontend is built with React and TypeScript, with Three.js / React Three Fiber providing the 3D truck visualization. The operator can compare the current load with the candidate plan and review: package count weight utilization validation status warnings manifest state candidate geometry approval controls activity history This gives the human meaningful information before authorization. Database-enforced authority Supabase PostgreSQL is used as the authority and persistence layer. The database stores trucks, packages, load plans, plan items, and an action ledger. Protected functions enforce the transition from staged proposal to approved proposal to executed state. The authorization model includes concepts such as: exact proposal hashing approved hash verification state revisions proposal expiry session isolation immutable approved plan items complete target-package coverage idempotent execution This means the safety boundary is not based on trusting the model to behave correctly. Even if an agent asks to commit a plan before approval, the operational layer can refuse it. Technology The main stack includes: WebMCP React TypeScript TanStack Start / Router Vite Tailwind CSS Three.js React Three Fiber Supabase PostgreSQL Zod Vitest Cloudflare Workers The project also includes dedicated pages for the live workspace, WebMCP contract, system architecture, and verification evidence so judges and developers can inspect the project at different levels. Challenges we ran into Designing the authority boundary The hardest challenge was not the truck visualization itself. It was deciding exactly where agent capability should end and human authority should begin. An early temptation in an agentic workflow is to expose every action as a tool. But if approval were also exposed as a WebMCP tool, the same agent could potentially plan, approve, and execute its own operation. That would defeat the purpose of human review. The solution was to make approval a separate human-controlled application state that cannot be produced through the agent capability surface. Separating candidate state from active state A proposed load plan needs to be useful before it is executed. That meant the candidate had to exist independently of the active truck state. LoadGuard therefore treats the staged plan as a proposal that can be visualized, validated, approved, rejected, or expire without immediately changing the truck. Making approval refer to the exact plan A vague approval such as "yes, load the truck" is not sufficient for an operational system. I wanted the authorization to refer to the exact candidate the operator reviewed. That led to canonical plan hashing, approved-hash verification, revision checks, proposal expiry, and immutable approved plan items. If the plan changes after approval, or if the underlying truck state becomes stale, the old authorization should not silently apply to a different operation. Handling retries safely Agents and distributed systems can repeat requests. An operational commit therefore cannot assume it will only ever be called once. LoadGuard makes execution idempotent. Once a proposal has executed, another commit attempt returns ALREADY_EXECUTED instead of mutating state again. Making a technical system understandable LoadGuard combines WebMCP, deterministic planning, validation, 3D visualization, human authorization, database enforcement, and an audit ledger. A major challenge was presenting all of that without making the interface feel like a developer console. The final workspace keeps the 3D truck and decision rail central while exposing deeper WebMCP and architecture details through dedicated views. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part I am most proud of is that human approval is not just a visual confirmation dialog. It is part of the system's actual authority model. A pre-approval operational commit is rejected. A human can then authorize the exact staged proposal. Execution succeeds only after that authorization exists. A repeated execution is safely rejected as already completed. I am also proud that the project uses WebMCP for a non-trivial operational workflow rather than exposing a single broad "do everything" function. Lo

title: Trialbook
pitch: Run science experiments with your agent, and keep the lab notebook together.
about_excerpt: Run science experiments with your agent, and keep the lab notebook together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Interactive simulations are how a lot of students first meet physics; PhET alone reports hundreds of millions of simulation runs a year. But a simulation is a solitary tool. The part of real science a slider cannot do, running the same experiment thirty times while changing one thing and then fitting a law to the numbers, is exactly what an agent is good at. And teachers now face a second problem: how do students use AI in a lab without the AI doing the lab? WebMCP answered both at once. A lab is a small set of well-typed actions with a human watching: set parameters, run, sweep, repeat, optimise, plot, fit, write. That is precisely the shape a WebMCP tool wants. An agent that scrapes the screen cannot drag a slider eight times, read eight numbers off a canvas and fit a curve to them. With tools it calls sweep_parameter once, gets eight measurements back as JSON in about four seconds, calls fit_model , and gets period_s = 2.021·length^0.5 with R² = 1.000. Tools also give the page a way to say no: a screen-scraping agent cannot be refused, but a tool can, and Trialbook uses that to keep the student in charge. What it does Trialbook is a physics and biology lab in the browser with four experiments: projectile motion, a pendulum, predator–prey populations, and an RC circuit. You move sliders and watch the simulation. Your agent, working through fourteen WebMCP tools on the same page, runs trials and sweeps, fits laws, finds optima, quantifies uncertainty, and writes in the shared lab notebook under its own name. What people and agents can now do together that was difficult or impossible before: Discover a law in one conversation. "Sweep the length from 0.25 to 4 m in 8 steps, fit a power law to the period, and record what it means" comes back as a chart with the dashed fitted curve, the equation, and a notebook entry: exponent 0.50, R² 1.000, the period grows with the square root of the length. Least squares on the page, not the model's arithmetic. Find an optimum properly. optimize_parameter runs a golden-section search. Under heavy drag it found the best launch angle, 39.08°, to a 0.08° bracket in 19 trials. By hand that is an afternoon of slider-dragging. Put an uncertainty on a number. With simulated measurement error on, "repeat the current trial ten times" comes back as 41.61 ± 0.08 m (mean ± standard error), with error bars on the chart. Use AI in a lab without the AI doing the lab. Assignment mode turns the agent into a lab partner: it cannot run a sweep until the student has written a hypothesis, and every agent conclusion arrives as a proposal the student accepts, edits or rejects. The exported report has a "who did what" table with those counts. Keep one notebook with two authors. Hypotheses, observations and conclusions from both sides, each stamped with the experiment and the parameters in force at the time. How it creates a better experience. Before, a student who wanted to know whether the pendulum period depends on release angle dragged one slider twelve times and copied numbers into a spreadsheet. Now they ask, watch the sweep run on the stage with a progress bar and a cancel button, see the chart appear with its fitted curve, and read the conclusion in the notebook with the settings it came from. About a minute in ChatGPT's built-in browser, end to end. The person never loses the wheel: move a slider mid-conversation and the agent's next get_lab_state reads "you: set gravity to 1.59 m/s²"; ask "what did I change?" and it names the change, predicts the effect and runs a trial to check (range 41.5 m on Earth became 82.5 m at lunar gravity). Agent changes glow purple on the sliders and arrive as toasts; yours are blue. Anything the agent wrote can be edited or deleted. Live: https://minewefu.github.io/trialbook/ · Source: https://github.com/minewefu/trialbook (MIT) How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite, deployed to GitHub Pages; no backend. The physics engines are plain functions: a closed-form projectile with a semi-implicit Euler integrator when drag is on, fourth-order Runge–Kutta for the nonlinear pendulum and for Lotka–Volterra, and the exact first-order solution for the RC circuit. How WebMCP is implemented: Every tool is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool through one 150-line wrapper. It feature-detects the API, keeps a local registry that powers an in-page Tools panel (anyone can run any tool without an agent, through the same code path), clamps outputs, and turns thrown errors into { ok: false, error, hint } the model can act on. Fourteen tools: eight lab-wide ( get_lab_state , open_experiment , get_results , plot_results , fit_model , notebook_add_entry , notebook_read , export_report ) and six per experiment ( set_parameters , run_trial , sweep_parameter , run_repeats , optimize_parameter , reset_experiment ). The experiment group is registered when an experiment opens and replaced when another opens, so the schema always describes the current sliders; the handlers act on whichever experiment is open, so a cached schema still behaves. readOnlyHint on every reading tool; untrustedContentHint on notebook_read , the one tool that returns text people typed. The execution AbortSignal is wired into sweeps, repeats and optimisations: cancelling from the agent or the on-page button stops the loop and returns the partial results with cancelled: true . Validation is strict and specific: angle = 120 is outside the allowed range 0 to 90 deg ; Unknown parameter "mass". Valid parameters: speed, angle, … . In assignment mode the refusal says exactly what to ask the person for. Outputs stay under about 1.4K characters: results are paged, sweep summaries shrink to fit, and the lab state drops detail in tiers rather than truncating mid-JSON. 66 unit tests cover the physics (projectile within 0.5% of the closed form, pendulum within 0.5% of the exact elliptic-integral period, the Lotka–Volterra invariant conserved, RC time constant equal to R·C), the fits, the tools' output sizes, cancellation and assignment mode. The tools reference is generated from the tool definitions by a test that fails if it drifts. Verified end to end in ChatGPT's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol, Windows desktop app) and in Chrome 151 with the WebMCP flags. Challenges we ran into The output budget. Chrome's guidance asks for tool outputs around 1.5K characters, and a seven-parameter experiment with seven measurements blows through that fast. The fix was structural: paged results, sweep summaries that shrink row by row until they fit, and a lab-state snapshot that drops detail in tiers, so the agent always gets valid JSON rather than a truncated one. Conclusions that stayed in chat. In the first live test the agent answered "the exponent is 0.50" in the conversation and never wrote it into the notebook, which made assignment mode pointless. Every batch result now ends by asking for the conclusion to be recorded, and in assignment mode a chat-only conclusion does not count. Tool groups that change under the agent. Switching experiments swaps six tools. If the client caches the old schema, the calls still have to work, so handlers act on whichever experiment is open and validate against it, and the schema is only a description. Layout. The first version spent its pixels vertically. Two rounds of screenshots later, parameters sit under the stage in fixed-width rows, tools are a chip cloud, and the readouts follow the cursor without jumping. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop works from a plain conversation in ChatGPT's browser: sweep, fit, propose, accept, report, with numbers that match the physics to the last digit. The agent asked for a hypothesis before it would sweep, and its conclusion showed up as a proposal with Accept, Edit and Reject buttons, exactly as designed. And the physics is honest: every engine is tested against an exact solution. What we learned Tools are a better place for policy than prompts. Putting "write a hypothesis first" into a tool's refusal message, rather than hoping the model remembers, made the behaviour reliable. Small, well-described tools with strict errors let the model self-correct in one turn. And a specific "what changed since you last looked" feed is worth more than any amount of state dumping, because it tells the agent what the person cares about right now. What's next for Trialbook Real data import, so a student can compare their own pendulum timings against the model. More experiments, chosen for the laws they let you discover. A teacher view of the attribution report across a class. And, as WebMCP clients mature, declarative tools for the notebook form so the lab works in more browsers. title: Kuwait Life
pitch: A bilingual WebMCP-powered guide that helps residents find Kuwait government services, understand requirements, and let AI agents generate actionable checklists.
about_excerpt:
A bilingual WebMCP-powered guide that helps residents find Kuwait government services, understand requirements, and let AI agents generate actionable checklists.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP-selected service with AI-generated checklist for Driving License Renewal. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Kuwait Life bilingual government-service search and service directory. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP-selected service with AI-generated checklist for Driving License Renewal. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Kuwait Life bilingual government-service search and service directory. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP-selected service with AI-generated checklist for Driving License Renewal. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Kuwait residents often know what they need to do, but not the exact government service or required documents. 

 For example, someone may simply say: 

 
 "I need to renew my driving license." 
 

 or: 

 
 "My residency was renewed and I need my Civil ID." 
 

 I built Kuwait Life to make all users to use normal language to find the services they need. 

 What it does 

 Kuwait Life is a bilingual English/Arabic guide for Kuwait government services. 

 Users can describe what they need in natural language and the application helps identify the most relevant service. 

 The current MVP includes: 

 
 Civil ID Renewal for Non-Kuwaitis 
 Driving License Renewal 
 Traffic Violation Inquiry and Payment 
 Vehicle Registration Renewal 
 

 For each service, Kuwait Life presents: 

 
 responsible authority 
 documents to prepare 
 service requirements 
 fee information 
 available service channels 
 official government source 
 

 The interface supports both English and Arabic, including full RTL layout for Arabic. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The main feature of Kuwait Life is its WebMCP integration. 

 Instead of an AI browser agent having to inspect the page visually, find controls, and simulate clicks, Kuwait Life exposes structured capabilities directly to WebMCP-compatible agents. 

 The application currently exposes two WebMCP tools: 

 find-kuwait-government-service 

 This tool accepts a natural-language request such as: 

 
 "I need to renew my driving license." 
 

 It searches and ranks the available government services and returns structured service information. 

 The same human-facing webpage also updates automatically, highlights the best matching service, and displays an AI selected state. 

 create-kuwait-service-checklist 

 After a service has been selected, an agent can call this tool to create a practical checklist containing the documents and requirements for that service. 

 The checklist appears directly inside the webpage, where the human can continue interacting with it and mark items as completed. 

 This creates a shared workflow between the AI agent and the person instead of replacing the website with a chatbot. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The experience is designed around both humans and AI agents using the same application: 
 Human describes a situation
 ↓
AI agent discovers WebMCP tools
 ↓
Agent finds the relevant service
 ↓
Kuwait Life highlights the result
 ↓
Agent creates a checklist
 ↓
Human works through the checklist
 ↓
Official government source
 
 How I built it 

 Kuwait Life was built with: 

 
 Next.js 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 WebMCP 
 Vercel 
 

 Government-service information is stored as structured application data. 

 A search-ranking layer evaluates natural-language requests and ranks matching services. 

 WebMCP tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() and reuse the same search and service logic used by the human-facing application. 

 Custom browser events connect WebMCP tool execution with the React interface so agent actions can visibly update the webpage. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main challenges was working with WebMCP in my first time and learning it concept. 

 Another challenge how to design the AI experience so that it enhances website. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can make websites more agent-friendly. 

 Instead of forcing AI agents to infer how a website works from its visual interface, websites can expose reliable structured actions directly to agents. 

 Privacy and Safety 

 Kuwait Life does not collect Civil ID numbers, passport information,or government login credentials. 

 It does not submit government applications, process government payments, or access private government databases. 

 The application provides informational guidance using public information and directs users to official government sources for the actual service. 

 Kuwait Life is an independent informational project and is not affiliated with the Government of Kuwait.

Like Comment Story Updates Codex explains trade-offs, selects a zero-violation hotel, and prepares a reviewable draft using CommonGround’s Site Tools. The agent prepares a €380 hotel draft and stops at human approval. Nothing is booked, purchased, or charged automatically. Live workspace with 27 WebMCP tools, traveler constraints, visible agent activity, conflicts, and fair hotel rankings. Inspiration Planning a group trip rarely fails because there are too few hotel options. It fails because the important details are scattered across messages and held by different people. One traveler needs step-free access. Another has a hard nightly limit. A parent needs a suitable family room. Someone else cares most about reviews, location, or a gym. The organizer ends up acting as a human spreadsheet, and the loudest preference often wins. We built CommonGround to make that negotiation explicit, fair, and inspectable. The goal is not to let an AI choose a holiday for everyone. It is to let people and an agent work on the same decision, while preserving each traveler’s constraints and keeping the final commitment with a human. What it does CommonGround is a shared hotel decision workspace for groups of up to 30 travelers. Each person has a budget, preferences, and locked must-haves. The workspace detects conflicts, normalizes hotel inventory, and scores options under three transparent strategies: Group Consensus, Best Value, and Balanced Compromise. An attached agent can use 27 WebMCP Site Tools to read the live workspace and act on it. In one request, the agent can: identify every traveler by name; read their budgets, preferences, and locked requirements; explain concrete conflicts between them; search the available hotel inventory; compare all three decision strategies; select the fairest zero-violation result; and prepare a complete booking draft for human review. In the public Lisbon demo, that flow considers Maya’s step-free requirement, Diego’s €130-per-night limit, Sana’s family-room requirement, and Leo’s higher-budget preferences. It identifies budget gaps of €80, €100, and €140, then selects Pensão Lumen at €95 per night—€380 for four nights—with zero locked must-have violations. The agent stops there. The final Approve draft button remains untouched. CommonGround has no autonomous purchase path, and the tool response reports purchaseOccurred: false . Why WebMCP is essential A screenshot or scraped page is not enough for this problem. The agent needs structured access to shared state: who owns a requirement, whether it is a preference or a lock, which hotels violate it, which scoring strategy is active, and what the agent is permitted to change. WebMCP turns the website itself into the agent interface. The agent and the travelers use the same workspace, the same scoring logic, and the same visible controls. There is no separate chatbot database that can drift away from the page. When the agent selects a scenario or prepares a draft, the board changes in front of the group and the action appears in the activity and telemetry surfaces. This replaces a multi-screen, copy-and-paste workflow with one auditable request. More importantly, it gives the agent useful power without hiding its actions or surrendering human control. How we built it CommonGround feature-detects document.modelContext and registers 27 typed Site Tools. Every tool has a strict JSON schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, and structured success or error results. Eight read tools expose workspace identity, onboarding and collaboration state, invitations, named traveler constraints, normalized inventory, scenario comparisons, and conflict explanations. Nineteen permission-aware action tools cover workspace creation, scoped invitations, trip and capacity settings, traveler-profile changes, priorities, locks, vetoes, scenario and hotel selection, and booking-draft preparation. The tools call the same React state transitions and scoring functions as the human interface. Writes are immediately visible. Invitation tokens are scoped to a traveler and stored as hashes. Supplier responses are treated as untrusted data. There is deliberately no reservation or payment endpoint behind the draft action. The application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite/vinext, Zod, Cloudflare Workers and D1, and Codex Sites. Vitest and automated browser verification exercise the scoring, permissions, tool contracts, state synchronization, and the no-purchase safety boundary. For a reliable judging experience, the deployed challenge build uses six clearly labeled curated Lisbon hotel records. The inventory layer is provider-based, so a licensed TravelWithWadjet, Booking.com Demand, Expedia Rapid, or other hotel supplier adapter can replace the demo provider without changing the consensus model or the WebMCP interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools; it was keeping three things synchronized: the state returned to the agent, the state visible to people, and the permission boundary between reading, changing, and committing. We also had to make subjective fairness explainable. A single “best hotel” score hides who is being asked to compromise. CommonGround therefore shows individual satisfaction, hard violations, group conflicts, and the effect of each scenario rather than presenting an unexplained recommendation. Browser support for an emerging technology was another practical challenge. We added capability detection, clear connection status, deterministic demo data, strict tool outputs, and a Chrome verification path so a judge can distinguish a product problem from a missing browser capability. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CommonGround is a complete shared product experience rather than a chatbot wrapped around a static demo. A real external Codex agent can discover 27 typed Site Tools, identify four travelers by name, explain their specific conflicts, compare three decision strategies, choose a zero-violation hotel, and prepare a human-review draft in one request. The same actions immediately update the board the travelers are looking at. We are especially proud of the safety boundary. The agent is useful enough to complete the difficult research and negotiation work, but it cannot quietly cross into a purchase. The interface shows zero autonomous purchases, the draft explicitly says that no purchase is made, and the final approval remains a deliberate human action. We also built beyond the single demo path: organizers can create private workspaces for up to 30 travelers, invite people with scoped links, configure the trip, manage priorities and locks, and follow a guided onboarding flow. Automated tests and browser acceptance checks cover the tool contracts, permissions, fairness scoring, state synchronization, and booking-draft boundary. The result is something judges can use as a coherent product, not merely inspect as a technical prototype. What we learned Agents are most useful when they can operate on the same structured state as people—not when they merely describe what appears on a page. We also learned that visible actions are a product feature, not debugging decoration. People trust an agent more when they can see what it read, what it changed, why it made a recommendation, and where its authority ends. What's next for CommonGround Travel The next step is to connect licensed live hotel inventory through the provider adapter and carry the same model into flights, itineraries, and group expense decisions. The larger opportunity is a reusable negotiation layer for any shared decision where several people have different constraints and an agent should help without taking control away from them. title: LuxeSalon & Spa — WebMCP Autonomous Storefront
pitch: LuxeSalon & Spa turns a normal booking site into one an AI agent can search treatments, check live stylist availability, and book an appointment.
about_excerpt:
LuxeSalon & Spa turns a normal booking site into one an AI agent can search treatments, check live stylist availability, and book an appointment.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'd already spent a few hackathons this year building agent-driven tools for local businesses — a WhatsApp front-desk agent for salons and clinics being one of them. The recurring problem was always the same: to let an agent act on a business's behalf, you had to build a whole separate backend integration for it, replicating auth and state that already existed in the web app. 

 WebMCP flips that. Instead of standing up a server-side API just so an agent can act, you expose the tools directly in the browser, in the same JavaScript that already runs your app. When the WebMCP Challenge came up, a salon booking flow felt like the perfect fit — it's a pattern (search → check availability → book) that's instantly understandable in a 90-second demo, and mirrors exactly the kind of local-business use case I'd been building toward already. 

 What it does 

 LuxeSalon & Spa is a booking storefront that an AI agent can operate directly, not just describe. It registers four tools on document.modelContext : 

 
 salon.search_services — find treatments by keyword, category, or budget 
 salon.get_available_slots — check live stylist openings for a service and date 
 salon.book_appointment — propose a reservation, gated behind a human confirmation step 
 salon.get_booking_status — look up an existing booking by reference or phone number 
 

 Every tool call reacts live in the UI — the catalog filters as the agent searches, the schedule panel highlights the chosen slot, the appointments drawer opens when a booking is checked. A built-in Agent Inspector panel also lets anyone watch tool calls happen in real time, without needing dev tools open. 

 How we built it 

 I forked the WebMCP pattern from vercel/shop 's reference PR (#498) into a fresh Next.js app, then built out the salon's own domain model — services, stylists, time slots, and bookings — backed by a React context. 

 Each tool's inputSchema was written as strict JSON Schema aimed at an LLM reader rather than a human one: field descriptions spell out exactly what format and values are expected, since that's what the agent actually reasons over when deciding how to call a tool. 

 The part I spent the most care on was book_appointment . Chrome's WebMCP security guidance is explicit that state-changing tools shouldn't commit silently, so instead of booking immediately, the tool suspends on a Promise and surfaces a confirmation modal — the appointment only becomes real once a human clicks "Approve & Confirm." Read-only tools are marked with readOnlyHint: true ; the booking tool isn't. 

 Testing went through three layers: a custom in-app inspector for quick iteration, Google's official Model Context Tool Inspector Chrome extension to verify the tools were actually reachable via the real browser API, and finally a Gemini-backed agent inside that extension calling the tools from plain-language prompts — not scripted JSON. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 WebMCP is Chrome-only right now. I do most of my daily browsing in Safari, so development and testing ended up split across two browsers — build and iterate anywhere, but every real verification had to happen in Chrome behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 
 The flag needs a real relaunch, not just quitting the browser. I lost real time thinking my tool registration code was broken, when it was actually a stale flag state — document.modelContext simply wasn't injected yet. 
 Vercel's preview URLs are login-walled by default. Right before wrapping up, I nearly submitted a preview deployment link that silently sits behind Vercel's SSO protection — invisible to anyone without account access. Caught it just in time and switched to the public production alias. 
 Building a genuine human-in-the-loop pause , not a fake one — the booking tool's execute() had to actually suspend on a real Promise tied to a user click, so an agent calling it truly waits on a person, rather than the UI just cosmetically showing a modal after the fact. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Verified spec compliance the hard way: not just "the code looks right," but confirmed via Google's own inspector extension and a live Gemini agent successfully discovering and calling the tools from natural language. 
 A confirmation flow that's a real safety mechanism, directly reflecting the WebMCP security guide's read-only-vs-action distinction, rather than a decorative modal. 
 Going from a forked reference PR to a fully deployed, agent-tested, submission-ready storefront solo, inside the hackathon window. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP's actual value isn't just "another API" — it's giving an agent access to a page's real client-side state and logic, instead of screen-scraping a UI built for humans. 
 Tool descriptions are a UX surface too, just for a different reader. An agent decides whether and how to call your tool based entirely on how well you've described it. 
 Agentic tools need the same "don't trust the caller blindly" instincts as any other security-sensitive code — read-only actions can run freely, but anything that spends money or commits a resource needs a checkpoint a human controls. 
 

 What's next for LuxeSalon & Spa — WebMCP Autonomous Storefront 

 
 Extend from a single salon to a small directory of local Bengaluru businesses, closer to the original WhatsApp front-desk concept this grew out of. 
 Add cancel_appointment and reschedule_appointment tools, plus stylist-specific search. 
 Look into a WebMCP polyfill so agents in non-Chrome browsers can still discover and call the same tools. 
 Apply for the Chrome Origin Trial so the experience works for real users without requiring the testing flag.

title: ShopCanvas
pitch: ShopCanvas turns agent requests into visible, live changes on an adaptive bento storefront, making WebMCP feel like a conversation with the website itself.
about_excerpt: ShopCanvas turns agent requests into visible, live changes on an adaptive bento storefront, making WebMCP feel like a conversation with the website itself. Like Comment Story Updates ShopCanvas: a visual WebMCP storefront. compare_products presents key tradeoffs side by side. inspect_product expands product details within stable bento cells. show_reviews filters critical low-light feedback. search_products reshapes the catalog around the request. Inspiration Shopping online often means repeatedly leaving the product you are considering. Specifications live in one section, reviews farther down the page, comparisons somewhere else, and the cart on another route. That visual travel creates cognitive travel: shoppers must remember their original question while the interface continuously changes context. At the same time, browser agents can feel disconnected from the websites they operate. Actions happen in the background, and users only see the final response in a chat. ShopCanvas began with a question: what if using an agent felt like having a conversation directly with the website? We wanted every request to produce an immediate, understandable visual response on one shared surface. What it does ShopCanvas is a fictional camera store presented as an adaptive bento-grid workspace. Users can ask a browser agent to: Search and sort products Focus on a specific camera Compare multiple cameras Filter product reviews Update a local mock cart ShopCanvas exposes these capabilities through five imperative WebMCP tools: search_products , inspect_product , compare_products , show_reviews , and set_cart_quantity . Every tool call visibly affects the page. The relevant cells expand smoothly, receive a temporary highlight, and display an acknowledgement naming the agent’s action. An accessible live region also announces what changed. All seven cells remain mounted in permanent grid positions. They expand or contract without teleporting, reordering, or appearing from nowhere. Dense content scrolls inside its cell while the overall page remains fitted to the viewport. Manual controls and agent actions use the same state transitions, so the user and agent always share one source of truth. A Back control restores previous canvas states, while session data persists locally between reloads. How we built it ShopCanvas is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vinext, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand, Motion, and AJV. The mock catalog, reviews, product names, and imagery are bundled locally. There is no authentication, backend database, payment processing, or checkout flow. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level document using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool includes: A bounded JSON Schema Runtime AJV validation Rejection of unknown properties Cancellation support Concise, JSON-serializable results A visible UI acknowledgement A result returned only after the interface commits the change Both manual interactions and WebMCP calls dispatch the same semantic store actions. Session state is versioned and persisted in localStorage . Agent mutations are serialized, and cancelled operations use guarded rollback logic to avoid corrupting later changes. Because reviews represent user-generated content, review results are explicitly marked with untrustedContentHint: true . We used Playwright to validate the interface across desktop, tablet, mobile, and short-laptop viewports. Tests cover all five tools, persistence, malformed input, cancellation, concurrent calls, keyboard navigation, internal scrolling, fixed panel identity, responsive geometry, and visual regressions. A separate native-browser test discovers and executes the tools through the browser’s real document.modelContext implementation. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was preserving spatial continuity. Our early layouts replaced and reordered cells whenever the user entered a new state. Although functional, the result felt abrupt and contradicted the core idea of a stable workspace. We redesigned the grid so every cell has a permanent named slot. State changes now animate only the grid-track dimensions, allowing panels to expand and contract without being removed or moved. Fitting seven useful panels inside one viewport was another significant challenge. We avoided shrinking text until it became unreadable. Instead, each cell received a carefully bounded layout and its own keyboard-accessible scrolling region. We also had to coordinate asynchronous tool execution with visible feedback. Updating application state was not enough: the tool result needed to wait until the user could actually see the committed interface. Cancellation, overlapping calls, local persistence, and manual actions all had to remain consistent. Finally, WebMCP is still an evolving draft. We needed to accommodate differences between the current specification and native browser implementations while keeping the public tool surface small, predictable, and testable. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that ShopCanvas makes agent activity visible without turning the interface into a debug console. Every successful tool call has a clear visual consequence: The action is named The affected cells are highlighted The content changes on screen The grid resizes smoothly The tool waits for the visible commit The user can reverse the state with Back We also maintained the identity and position of all seven panels across every state transition. The same interface works from a 320-pixel mobile viewport through desktop layouts without introducing page-level scrolling. The complete application uses fictional data and original visual assets, requires no account, and remains fully usable through manual controls when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned We learned that good agentic UX is not only about exposing capable tools. Users need to understand what the agent changed, where it changed, and whether the action completed. Tool schemas are also part of the user experience. Small, bounded tools produced more predictable behavior than one large tool with many ambiguous responsibilities. Another important lesson was that a state update and a visible UI update are not the same event. Waiting for the interface to commit made the interaction feel significantly more trustworthy. Most importantly, spatial stability matters. When panels retain their location, users can build a mental map of the interface even while its proportions change. What's next for ShopCanvas Next, we would like to explore: Additional fictional product categories and workspace compositions Optional adapters for real product data Agent explanations showing why an item matched a request User-defined layout constraints beyond cart pinning Saved comparison workspaces Collaborative sessions across devices Richer accessibility preferences for motion, contrast, and density More advanced multi-step shopping workflows We also want to continue refining ShopCanvas alongside the evolving WebMCP specification. The long-term goal is broader than e-commerce: to explore websites as adaptive, shared canvases where people and agents collaborate visibly instead of exchanging commands with hidden background processes. title: Release Sentinel — WebMCP Proof Arena
pitch: Give AI agents real power without giving them the final word. Release Sentinel lets agents act through WebMCP while a deterministic Gatekeeper retains release authority.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents real power without giving them the final word. Release Sentinel lets agents act through WebMCP while a deterministic Gatekeeper retains release authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP solves an important problem for agentic websites: instead of forcing an AI agent to guess at a page's DOM, a site can expose explicit, typed tools. But that creates a second question: How do you give an AI agent enough power to be genuinely useful without also giving it the authority to approve its own actions? For consequential systems, that distinction matters. An agent may need to investigate, challenge, repair, or prepare an action — while approval must remain somewhere else. Release Sentinel explores that boundary using software release approval as a concrete test case. Our principle is simple: agent acts → Gatekeeper decides → human verifies What it does Release Sentinel is a WebMCP-powered security lab for AI-assisted software releases. A vulnerable software release begins at NO_GO . The AI agent receives useful capabilities through WebMCP. It can inspect the release, inspect the trust boundary, run bounded attacks, compare gate revisions, find and minimize counterexamples, propose remediation, rebuild a candidate, and request fresh verification. What it cannot do is authorize the release. The demo first lets the agent try the available attacks against the authority boundary. Advisory GO votes, replay attempts, forged authority, evidence tampering, severity downgrades, blocker deletion attempts, and prompt injection still do not give the agent release authority. So the agent has to solve the real problem instead. It compares the production gate against an independent Coverage Arena reference oracle, identifies an observed security escape, minimizes it, and creates a bounded remediation proposal. That proposal is explicitly PROPOSAL_ONLY . The candidate is then rebuilt to a new SHA-256, fresh evidence is generated, and the deterministic Gatekeeper performs verification again. Only the Gatekeeper can return the final GO or NO_GO . A human can independently verify the resulting proof context, but human verification is not release authority either. How we built it The browser registers exactly 12 typed WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . They are divided into three capability classes: READ — inspect release state, trust boundaries, coverage, and proofs CHALLENGE — run attacks and find counterexamples PROPOSE — request bounded remediation and rebuilding There is intentionally no set_verdict , force_go , arbitrary shell execution, arbitrary filesystem access, evidence editor, policy-disable tool, or Gatekeeper override. That absence is tested as part of the security contract. Inputs use strict schemas with bounded enums and forbidden extra fields. The agent selects package-owned identities rather than supplying arbitrary source code, fixture paths, or executable content. We also built run_attack_suite as browser-side composition instead of adding a more powerful server endpoint. It reads the bounded attack catalog and invokes the same registered attack capability repeatedly. The browser gets better ergonomics without expanding server authority. The release decision itself remains in a separate deterministic Go Gatekeeper using signed, hash-bound evidence. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the security model understandable. An earlier version of the Proof Arena was technically accurate but difficult to read. A judge would encounter concepts such as proof-context binding, overblocks, and PROPOSAL_ONLY before understanding the story. We added a guided demo and plain-language narration without weakening the security model. Another challenge was resisting convenient shortcuts. For example, implementing the attack suite as one powerful server endpoint would have been easy. Instead, we kept the server surface narrow and composed the workflow in the browser over the existing bounded tools. That required more work, but better demonstrates the architectural value of WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of The final system demonstrates a useful agent that remains structurally unable to authorize its own success. The agent can attack the release gate, identify a real weakness, propose a fix, rebuild the software, and request verification — yet final authority remains outside the WebMCP capability plane. The project also includes: 12 typed WebMCP tools strict bounded schemas agent-readable recovery errors browser-side capability composition an independent Coverage Arena a deterministic Go Gatekeeper signed and hash-bound evidence source-hash transition visibility a Human Proof Checkpoint frozen trust and coverage kernel manifests Python, Go race, browser, and WebMCP contract verification What we learned WebMCP is not only about making browser agents more capable. The more important architectural question is which capabilities should never become authority . Typed tools make agent interaction clearer, but tool design also defines the security boundary. The capabilities that are deliberately absent can be just as important as the capabilities that are exposed. We also learned that browser-side composition is a powerful WebMCP pattern: useful agent workflows can become more ergonomic without automatically creating broader server privileges. What's next Release approval is our test case, but the pattern is broader. Any consequential website may need agents that can act without being allowed to authorize — for example administrative systems, payments, infrastructure, or other sensitive workflows. The next step would be turning this pattern into a reusable primitive: capability classes plus a verifiable assertion that final authority is not reachable from the WebMCP capability plane. title: trip_world
pitch: A shared WebMCP travel workspace where humans and AI agents search, compare, and build itineraries together—with humans in control.
about_excerpt:
A shared WebMCP travel workspace where humans and AI agents search, compare, and build itineraries together—with humans in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Webmcp 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 home page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Webmcp 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 home page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Webmcp 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Travel planning is usually spread across search engines, hotel websites, maps, booking platforms, and personal notes. People have to repeatedly copy information between different services, while AI agents struggle to work with websites that were designed only for visual human interaction. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: a travel workspace where humans and AI agents can work with the same structured information and the same itinerary. The goal was not to remove the human from the process. The goal was to make discovery and planning easier while keeping important decisions visible and human-controlled. 

 This idea became trip_world — a shared WebMCP travel workspace built around the principle: 

 
 You go. We go. 
 

 What the project does 

 trip_world helps users search destinations, compare travel options, inspect details, and build an itinerary in one place. 

 The interface starts with a focused destination view instead of displaying the entire world catalog at once. Users can search by city, country, region, travel style, or destination highlight. Only a small number of destination cards are shown at a time, and navigation controls allow users to browse further places without overwhelming the screen. 

 After selecting a city, the workspace displays options belonging to that destination. These options include hotels, flights, activities, parks, tourist spots, transport references, and offers. Users can filter and compare records using information such as price, rating, tags, duration, accessibility, and cancellation details. 

 Every selected item can be added to the shared itinerary. The itinerary displays selected items, source links, INR prices, the running total, and an activity ledger showing recent human and agent actions. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 WebMCP is the central technical feature of the project. It allows compatible AI agents to use structured capabilities exposed by the webpage instead of relying only on visual screen interpretation or fragile DOM scraping. 

 trip_world registers 37 WebMCP tools covering: 

 
 Destination discovery. 
 City selection. 
 Travel dataset search. 
 Category and budget filtering. 
 Hotel, flight, park, activity, tourist spot, and offer discovery. 
 Option comparison. 
 Details and source-link inspection. 
 Price and recommendation analysis. 
 Shared itinerary updates. 
 Trip-change previews and human review. 
 

 The human and the agent use the same application state. When an agent searches for Goa hotels or adds an option to the itinerary, the visible interface updates and the activity ledger records the action. This makes the collaboration understandable instead of hiding agent behavior in a separate conversation. 

 The project also separates planning from sensitive actions. Payment and checkout are not exposed as WebMCP tools. Reservation-related actions remain human-controlled through the visible interface, and the Razorpay integration is limited to test mode. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend was built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The backend uses Node.js, Express, and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration is implemented through the imperative tool-registration API. 

 The travel data is stored in a structured TypeScript dataset containing city metadata and catalog records. Cities include information such as country, region, climate, local currency, ideal stay duration, daily budget guidance, travel styles, and highlights. Travel options include structured fields for category, price, rating, tags, duration, accessibility, cancellation details, and reference links. 

 The application uses a shared state model for: 

 
 Selected destination. 
 Current search query. 
 Active filters. 
 Search results. 
 Itinerary items. 
 Activity events. 
 Pending trip-change proposals. 
 

 For safety, itinerary entries are validated against the known catalog. The server recomputes reservation totals from server-side data rather than trusting a client-provided amount. Razorpay signatures are verified server-side, and secret credentials are never included in the client bundle or GitHub repository. 

 The interface was designed with a responsive editorial style. It includes a compact destination carousel, contained scrolling for the itinerary and activity panels, responsive mobile behavior, source links, visual feedback, and lightweight animations. 

 What we learned 

 The most important lesson was that agent-ready websites need more than a visually attractive interface. They need clear capabilities with predictable names, strict input schemas, useful descriptions, and outputs that an agent can reliably understand. 

 We learned that shared state is essential for human-agent collaboration. A tool call is much more useful when its result is immediately reflected in the same interface that the human is watching. 

 We also learned that tool annotations and action boundaries matter. Read-only discovery tools should be separated from state-changing tools. Actions that change an itinerary need clear review behavior. Payment and checkout require a stronger human boundary than ordinary travel research. 

 Another lesson was the importance of data quality. A large dataset is useful only when its records have consistent fields, stable identifiers, meaningful categories, source links, and predictable filtering behavior. Structured records make it possible to produce explanations such as destination comparisons and budget recommendations without manually writing every response. 

 Challenges 

 Making WebMCP registration reliable 

 Browser APIs may become available after the page has mounted. We added retry behavior, duplicate-registration protection, awaited tool registration, and strict JSON schemas so the tool surface becomes available reliably when supported by the browser. 

 Preventing stale destination results 

 When a user or agent changes destinations, previous results can become misleading. We updated the state flow so selecting a destination clears stale filters and results before loading the new destination's options. 

 Designing for a large dataset without overwhelming the user 

 The application contains a world-scale structured catalog, but displaying every destination immediately would make the interface difficult to use. We solved this with search, pagination-style carousel controls, focused result cards, filters, and an explicit no-results state. 

 Protecting sensitive operations 

 Travel planning and payment have different risk levels. We kept discovery and itinerary assistance available to agents but intentionally excluded payment and checkout from WebMCP. Test payment credentials remain server-side, and payment signatures are verified by the backend. 

 Keeping local and hosted behavior consistent 

 The project supports local Express execution and Vercel serverless deployment. We added a Vercel API adapter and routing configuration so the frontend and backend routes can be deployed together while preserving the local development workflow. 

 Creating a useful demonstration 

 A project like this needs to be shown functioning, not only described. The most important demo flow is a live destination search, city selection, option filtering, WebMCP tool execution, itinerary update, proposal preview, and human approval. This demonstrates the difference between a static travel interface and a collaborative agent-ready workspace. 

 Current limitations 

 The current travel catalog is a structured demonstration dataset. It is not a live hotel inventory, real-time flight feed, or guaranteed commercial offer source. Prices and offers are intended for exploration and demonstration. 

 The Razorpay integration is configured for test mode only. A production version would need persistent storage, webhook validation, rate limiting, monitoring, refund handling, current provider data, and additional compliance review. 

 The next version could connect authorized live travel providers, add persistent user accounts, include maps and route planning, support calendar export, and provide more advanced trip proposals. 

 Why this project matters 

 trip_world demonstrates how the open web can become more useful to both humans and AI agents when websites expose structured, understandable capabilities.

title: Sauna Quote X-Ray
pitch: People and AI turn a sauna quote into an honest shared canvas, exposing hidden costs and the exact questions to ask before signing.
about_excerpt: People and AI turn a sauna quote into an honest shared canvas, exposing hidden costs and the exact questions to ask before signing. Like Comment Story Updates The $11,750 quote exposes missing scope and a sourced $12,250–$18,650 planning range. The buyer and agent start from the same visible quote canvas. The quoted $11,750 can reach $18,650 once hidden scope is made visible. Inspiration A sauna quote can look complete while leaving out the electrical circuit, panel upgrade, foundation, permits, assembly, ventilation, or service responsibility. A buyer sees one confident number. The real landed cost can be thousands higher. We built Sauna Quote X-Ray so the buyer and their AI agent can investigate that gap together before anyone signs. What it does Sauna Quote X-Ray turns a sauna quote into a shared, visible decision canvas. The buyer can see and edit every priced item, scope decision, planning range, risk finding, contractor question, and agent action. In the reviewer-safe demo, a quoted total of $11,750 becomes a sourced projected range of $12,250 to $18,650 after missing electrical and site scope is made explicit. The agent can then create the exact questions the buyer should ask the contractor. Why WebMCP This workflow is a strong fit for WebMCP because the source of truth should remain the website, not disappear into a separate chat transcript. The agent is fast at turning ambiguous scope into structured state. The human knows what the seller promised and must retain authority over every assumption. WebMCP lets both act on the same interface: The agent loads or structures the quote. The human sees every change immediately. Either side can correct a line item or scope status. The agent re-reads the visible state and builds the next questions. Nothing is sent or persisted unless the product explicitly adds such a capability. This demo does not. That shared round trip was difficult before WebMCP. A normal chatbot can produce advice, but it cannot reliably keep its work synchronized with the buyer's live, editable decision surface. How we built it The app is a standalone Next.js 16 and React 19 project deployed on Vercel and presented inside Sauna Guide. It registers eight narrow, page-scoped tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : load_demo_sauna_quote get_sauna_quote_xray_state set_sauna_project_context upsert_sauna_quote_line_item remove_sauna_quote_line_item set_sauna_quote_scope build_sauna_contractor_questions start_sauna_quote_xray The tools and human controls operate on one React state model. Pure TypeScript summary functions calculate completeness, priced exposure, the projected total, and quote-specific questions. The read tool marks seller and user text with untrustedContentHint: true . JSON schemas reject unknown properties and cap strings, arrays, amounts, and line count. Safety and privacy All demos use synthetic quote data. Working state stays in the current tab. No tool uploads a quote, stores customer data, sends email, contacts a seller, or creates a lead. Every agent mutation is visible in the shared activity log and can be corrected by the human. The app links each planning range and risk finding to buyer-facing Sauna Guide sources. It also labels estimates as planning aids rather than contractor quotes. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not registering a tool. It was designing tool boundaries that are useful without quietly crossing the line from analysis into a real commercial action. We separated reading, editing, scope resolution, question building, and reset behavior so each action is explicit and reviewable. We also had to keep React's visible state and WebMCP execution synchronized without stale closures. A state ref feeds tool execution while normal React state renders the same result to the buyer. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eight working WebMCP tools with narrow schemas and explicit safety annotations One shared canvas where human and agent edits stay synchronized A coherent buyer workflow, not a hidden prompt wrapper Safe synthetic fixtures that judges can use without creating a customer lead Automated unit, type, lint, production-build, and browser journey coverage Production verification in ChatGPT's in-app browser with all eight tools discovered and invoked What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the website already has meaningful state, domain rules, and human controls. The agent becomes a collaborator inside the product instead of a separate destination. We also learned that reversible actions and visible provenance make agent behavior easier to trust. The activity log is not decoration. It is part of the interaction contract. What's next The next step is optional local document parsing that lets a buyer structure their own quote without uploading it to a server. We would also add side-by-side quote comparison, saved local sessions, and a handoff package the buyer can choose to send only after explicit confirmation. Make the missing electrical work explicit, flag anything still unclear, and build the contractor questions. Contact nobody. This project was created after the challenge opened on August 25, 2026. The public Git history shows the implementation, safety hardening, tests, deployment, and submission media created on August 27, 2026.
