title: Semantic Loop DevOps Demonstrator
pitch: A shared schema-design workspace where people shape the model visually and WebMCP agents inspect, edit, seed, and export the same live project.
about_excerpt:
A shared schema-design workspace where people shape the model visually and WebMCP agents inspect, edit, seed, and export the same live project.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Database design often splits into two disconnected experiences. A person works visually in a browser while an AI assistant receives pasted fragments, guesses at current state, or drives the page through brittle clicks. That gap makes collaboration slow and risky: the person cannot easily review what the agent believes, and the agent cannot reliably act on the model the person is seeing. 

 Solution 

 Semantic Loop turns the browser page into a shared, structured workspace. The person can continue using the visual schema editor while an agent discovers purpose-built WebMCP tools on that same page. The agent can inspect the current project, create or revise a schema, add sample data, and export the project through typed operations. Every change flows through the application's real React state, so the interface immediately shows the result for human review. 

 This is stronger than generic browser automation: the agent works with domain concepts such as tables, columns, keys, sample data, and project exports instead of screen coordinates or incidental DOM text. 

 Why This Matters 

 The target users are developers, data architects, product teams, and technical operators who need to turn requirements into a reviewable data model. WebMCP gives them a collaboration loop that was previously awkward: 

 
 A person describes intent and watches the model evolve. 
 An agent reads the exact current project state. 
 The agent proposes or applies a structured change. 
 The person reviews the result in the visual interface and can edit it directly. 
 Either participant can continue from the same state and export a portable result. 
 

 That shortens the path from conversation to an auditable artifact while keeping the person in control of the visible source of truth. 

 How We Used AI 

 
 WebMCP-enabled agents operate the application through explicit, typed tools rather than DOM scraping. 
 A provider-neutral server-side gateway supports optional natural-language schema, data, visualization, and artifact generation using Gemini, OpenAI, or Anthropic when the operator configures credentials. 
 The core WebMCP demonstration is designed to remain usable without sharing any provider credential: judges can exercise the page-state tools and review their visible effects directly. 
 

 How We Used Codex 

 Codex helped inspect the existing codebase, separate pre-challenge product work from the new challenge contribution, design the WebMCP tool boundary around the application's existing state model, implement and test the adapter, harden the no-secret judge path, and prepare the Netlify and Devpost materials. Human review remained the decision point for project selection, rules acceptance, product positioning, and final submission. 

 Key Features 

 
 A visual React schema-design workflow that remains usable by a person. 
 Discoverable WebMCP tools with JSON schemas and focused descriptions. 
 A single shared project state for human UI actions and agent tool calls. 
 Structured read, create, update, sample-data, and export operations. 
 Visible feedback after agent mutations so the person can review the outcome. 
 A no-secret judge path for the core WebMCP flow, with multi-provider AI features as an optional enhancement. 
 Browser code never receives provider keys. Local development can load them using macOS Keychain, production reads protected Netlify secrets, and the gateway sends credentials only to the selected provider over HTTPS. 
 Portable project export for continuing the work outside the current browser session. 
 

 WebMCP Tools 

 The source registers these tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 webmcp/tools.ts defines registerWebMcpTools ; webmcp/useWebMcpTools.ts mounts the document.modelContext.registerTool registration into React. export_project returns files: [{name, mediaType, content}] . 

 Architecture 

 The application is a Vite-built React 19 and TypeScript single-page app. React Context and a reducer hold the canonical project state. The WebMCP adapter registers browser-native tools, validates structured inputs, and dispatches through that existing state boundary. UI components subscribe to the same state and immediately render agent-initiated changes. Browser persistence keeps the working project local, and the export path produces a portable project representation. 

 Gemini, OpenAI, and Anthropic are optional service integrations behind one provider-neutral server-side boundary. They are not the state store and are not required for the basic WebMCP tool demonstration.

title: Noema Blueprint
pitch: Noema Blueprint lets people and agents design a private AI setup together in the browser. One scan configures, downloads, and launches it in Noema, a local AI app available on iOS and iPadOS.
about_excerpt: Noema Blueprint lets people and agents design a private AI setup together in the browser. One scan configures, downloads, and launches it in Noema, a local AI app available on iOS and iPadOS. Like Comment Story Updates Create a private on-device Noema project from the web: without sharing files, prompts, conversations, or account data. Choose a purpose, device, local model, and runtime while the final Blueprint updates live. Blueprint Forge validates the manifest, model catalog entry, and handoff payload before sending anything to Noema. Compare candidate runtimes, context sizes, privacy, and settings before choosing the final Blueprint. Send the Blueprint by QR code or deep link: no login, pairing, files, prompts, or conversations included. 1. Noema checks the iPhone, verifies the local model download, and opens a private, ready-to-use chat. Noema Blueprint Inspiration Wanting to run local and private AI should not require people to become infrastructure experts. Today, setting up a local model means researching compatibility, device limits, runtime behavior, and download size before even sending a prompt. We wanted setup to feel like designing a workspace with an expert beside you. WebMCP turns the page into a shared workspace for both the person and the agent. The person can directly choose the Project goal, target device, runtime preset, model, and final Blueprint. The agent can inspect that same visible state, tune advanced model settings, fork and compare alternatives, audit candidates, and stage recommendations. Every agent suggestion remains visible, and only the person can approve it or choose what gets handed off. What it does Noema Blueprint is a visual studio for creating a private local AI Project. A person chooses what they want to accomplish and where they want to run their AI. Agents can then inspect the live Blueprint, change supported settings, fork alternative candidates, compare them, and stage recommendations directly on the page. Every proposed change appears visibly. The person remains the only one who can choose the final candidate. When the Blueprint is ready, the website creates a QR code and a same-device link containing a validated configuration. The agent can also return the QR code directly inside the conversation. Scanning the code opens Noema on your device (iOS, iPadOS). The app checks the configuration against the actual device before asking for approval. If the selected model is missing, Noema downloads it. The settings are then applied and the finished Project opens ready for a private conversation. The handoff is stateless. The link contains no files, prompts, credentials, or personal data. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent could recommend settings, but the person would need to reproduce them manually inside a different interface. With WebMCP, the agent operates the exact page the person is viewing. The Blueprint becomes a shared source of truth. The agent can explore possibilities while the person sees the consequences before anything becomes final. This makes setup faster without turning it into invisible automation. It also enables a workflow that was previously more opaque: an agent can help construct and evaluate a local AI environment, then hand the reviewed result to the device where it will actually run. How we built it The website is a React application written in TypeScript. It registers 12 narrowly scoped tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools operate on the same Blueprint state rendered by the interface. They let an agent inspect the current configuration, edit supported values, create candidates, compare them, stage proposals, validate the result, and prepare the handoff. The tool schemas accept only known models and bounded configuration values. Tool registration uses AbortSignal lifecycle handling. If WebMCP is unavailable, the complete interface remains usable manually. The final Blueprint is canonicalized and validated before being encoded as a versioned base64url manifest. The website places that manifest inside a Noema universal link and renders it as a QR code. The native receiver is built with SwiftUI. Noema accepts only the dedicated Blueprint route and maps public identifiers through its trusted model catalog. The app performs its own compatibility checks and preserves explicit download consent. Challenges The hardest design problem was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do. If the agent could silently select the final candidate or deploy it, the page would stop being collaborative. We separated proposals from approval so agent assistance remains visible and reversible. WebMCP is still experimental, so the page also needed a complete manual path. Feature detection keeps the experience functional in browsers without the API. The cross-device link created another trust boundary. We rejected arbitrary model URLs and unsupported settings. The native app treats every website value as a request rather than an instruction. We also had to balance helpful planning with hardware reality. The website can guide the person, but only the destination device can make the final compatibility decision. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the webpage is a shared object and when it doesn't act as merely a front end for a hidden API. The person should be able to see what the agent understands and watch the result change. We also learned that local setup can feel magical without hiding important decisions. The right abstraction should be a clear plan that requires approval. Hackathon scope NoemaAI existed before the challenge. Noema Blueprint and its WebMCP tool surface were built during the submission period. The Blueprint Forge workflow and cross-device handoff were also created as part of this work. The public repository includes dated commit history showing the challenge implementation. title: Hacklist
pitch: HackList helps builders stop missing the right opportunities by letting their AI agent search, understand, compare and recommend hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties and programs that actually fit them.
about_excerpt: HackList helps builders stop missing the right opportunities by letting their AI agent search, understand, compare and recommend hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties and programs that actually fit them. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Hacklist Logo Inspiration HackList started because finding good AI and Web3 opportunities is unnecessarily fragmented. Hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties, and builder programs are spread across dozens of platforms, and even when builders find them, the harder question remains: Which of these opportunities actually fits me? A directory can tell someone what exists. It cannot naturally answer: Which hackathons can a React developer in Ghana realistically enter? What remote AI jobs match my skills? Is this bounty a better use of my weekend than this hackathon? What exactly do I need to submit for this opportunity? Which parts of my eligibility are confirmed, and which are still unknown? The WebMCP Challenge gave me the opportunity to turn HackList from a discovery product into an agent-native opportunity intelligence layer. What it does HackList exposes its live opportunity catalog directly to browser agents through WebMCP. Instead of an agent scraping the page or guessing from UI elements, HackList registers semantic tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The current WebMCP toolset is: search_opportunities get_opportunity match_opportunities compare_opportunities get_opportunity_readiness These tools work across HackList's opportunity categories: Hackathons Jobs Grants Bounties Programs A user can ask naturally: "I am a React developer in Ghana with a few days free. What hackathons on HackList fit me?" The agent can translate that request into structured constraints and call HackList directly. HackList then performs the domain reasoning searching live opportunity data, evaluating known eligibility constraints, matching technologies and interests, comparing trade-offs, and surfacing readiness requirements. How we built it HackList already existed as a human-facing discovery platform for AI and Web3 opportunities. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into an agent-native opportunity intelligence layer. The core change was adding five semantic WebMCP tools through the canonical document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API: search_opportunities get_opportunity match_opportunities compare_opportunities get_opportunity_readiness These tools operate across HackList’s five opportunity categories: hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties, and programs. The WebMCP layer sits on top of the existing Supabase-backed application. The underlying HackList data-entry workflow did not need to change. Instead, I added a unified opportunity model, category adapters, structured matching logic, and a verified intelligence layer for deeper reasoning where data is available. The matching engine is deterministic rather than LLM-ranked. The browser agent interprets what the user means, while HackList evaluates the opportunity itself using structured constraints such as skills, technologies, location, format, deadline, and eligibility. The system explicitly distinguishes PASS, FAIL, and UNKNOWN, and uses fit states such as STRONG_FIT, POSSIBLE_FIT, WEAK_FIT, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. If HackList does not know something, it does not invent it. All current WebMCP operations are read-only. They were tested locally and in production using Chrome 152 and WebMCP tooling, including chained flows such as search → inspect and match → compare → readiness. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was avoiding the obvious implementation: simply wrapping HackList search in WebMCP and calling it finished. That would have technically exposed a tool but it would not have created a meaningful new human-agent experience. The more difficult problem was deciding what HackList should be authoritative about. The agent is good at understanding natural language, but it should not invent opportunity eligibility, rank candidates from vague page text or pretend incomplete data is complete. That led to a clear separation of responsibilities: The agent understands the user. HackList understands the opportunities. Another challenge was generalizing the system. Early work focused heavily on hackathons, but HackList is broader than that. I refactored the implementation around a unified opportunity domain so the same WebMCP interface works across jobs, grants, bounties, programs, and hackathons without exposing dozens of overlapping tools. Data quality was another major challenge. Many existing listings contain enough information for discovery but not enough for confident personalized matching. Instead of hiding those records or hallucinating missing details, the system preserves them and returns UNKNOWN or INSUFFICIENT_DATA where appropriate. Production validation also surfaced real browser issues, including a React hydration error and deployment-cache behavior. Those were fixed narrowly and revalidated rather than ignored. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am most proud that the final result is not a scripted demo path built for a single example. HackList already serves a community of more than 10,000 developers and builders looking for AI and Web3 opportunities. That means the WebMCP layer had to work for real, varied users not just one hardcoded profile. A builder can ask about hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties, programs, or broad opportunity discovery, and the same general WebMCP architecture handles the request. For example, a user can ask: “I am a React developer in Ghana with a few days free. What hackathons fit me?” and HackList can restrict the search to hackathons, evaluate the supplied constraints and return explainable results. Another user can ask for remote AI jobs, a weekend bounty, a grant, or a broader set of opportunities, without requiring a different application architecture. Technically, the final implementation has five real read only WebMCP tools, production Supabase integration, deterministic matching, category-aware comparison, readiness analysis, explicit uncertainty handling, tool chaining, automated tests, visible agent activity in the UI and production browser validation. Most importantly, HackList still works as the same product for humans who never use an agent. WebMCP adds a new interface to an existing product already serving thousands of builders, turning HackList from a directory people browse into an opportunity intelligence layer that both humans and their agents can use. What we learned WebMCP changes how I think about web product design. A traditional website exposes pages and controls. An agent native website can also expose its capabilities and domain semantics . For HackList, that means the site no longer only answers: "What opportunities exist?" It can now participate in answering: "Which opportunities make sense for me, why, and what do I need to do next?" WebMCP also changed how I think about the relationship between a user’s agent and a web application. The agent should not replace the domain logic of the application. Instead, the agent and the website should each do what they are best at. The agent understands intent and conversation. HackList provides verified opportunity state and domain-specific reasoning. WebMCP becomes the bridge between them. What's next for Hacklist The next step is to expand the intelligence coverage behind the same WebMCP interface. Today, every opportunity can be discovered through the unified catalog, while deeper matching intelligence is richer for some records than others. Over time, more opportunities will gain structured eligibility, technology, skills, requirements, team rules, provenance and readiness information. I also plan to automate HackList’s ingestion pipeline. Instead of manually finding and entering every new opportunity, an ingestion agent will continuously discover new hackathons, grants, jobs, bounties, and programs, verify them against official sources, detect duplicates, structure the information, and queue high-quality records for publishing. title: LISTEN — the synth your agent can hear
pitch: An agent-native synthesizer that hears its own output as structured acoustic features, designs sound with you by ear, and hands you production-ready artifacts: a DAW preset, a WAV, and a recipe.
about_excerpt: An agent-native synthesizer that hears its own output as structured acoustic features, designs sound with you by ear, and hands you production-ready artifacts: a DAW preset, a WAV, and a recipe. Like Comment Story Updates LISTEN Inspiration Every agentic music tool I'd seen made the agent write — notes, beats, sequences. Impressive, but it skipped the most human part of making music: sound design . A synthesizer has ~30 interdependent knobs, and "make it darker" maps to none of them. Producers do it by ear, endlessly listening and nudging. Meanwhile, agents were clicking through web UIs blind. Then it clicked: WebMCP gives agents structured tools inside the page you're looking at . What if one of those tools wasn't an action, but a sense ? What if the agent could hear the synth — and do what a sound designer does: listen → adjust → listen again? That became LISTEN: you bring the taste, the agent measures, adjusts, and proves the result. The accessibility angle sealed it — if an agent can turn "warm and punchy, please" into sound, then people who don't know synthesis (or physically can't operate 30 tiny knobs) can finally design sound too. What it does LISTEN is a synthesizer your AI agent can actually hear. You describe a vibe — "a calm, dreamy lo-fi pad" — and the agent plays a note, runs real-time FFT analysis on the synth's own output to get structured acoustic features (brightness, body, tone, envelope), shapes the knobs to match, then listens again to prove it worked. Turn a knob yourself and it notices, and works around your intent. When the sound feels right, the agent composes a loop that fits it and exports real artifacts you keep: a DAW-ready Vital preset, a 44.1kHz stereo WAV of the loop, and a Sound DNA card with the agent's analysis and the full recipe. Saving a preset dynamically registers it as a new agent tool — the agent's vocabulary grows with your sound library. It's WebMCP used as perception, not just actuation: 20 tools, one shared context, and an accessibility layer (plain-language controls) that opens sound design to people who don't know synthesis — or can't operate 30 tiny knobs. title: CoCanvas
pitch: Chat is a bad place to move a box. You write the brief. A WebMCP agent draws on the same board. If the draft is a mess, undo it. No screenshot guessing.
about_excerpt: Chat is a bad place to move a box. You write the brief. A WebMCP agent draws on the same board. If the draft is a mess, undo it. No screenshot guessing. Like Comment Story Updates Astra from the announcement. Drawn on this board. Payment skipped. The page finds it. Try it. Link in the description. Inspiration When I try to map a product flow with an agent, the work happens in chat. I ask it to add payment between address and success. It returns a paragraph, or a table of labels. I still rebuild the diagram by hand. Exporting a PNG is not a better contract. The model infers from pixels, and I cannot undo a node. I wanted the brief and the board in the same tab, and I wanted the agent to edit that board the way I do. WebMCP is how I tried that. What it does CoCanvas is a product-flow canvas that stays in the browser. You write a brief. You and an agent add nodes, arrows, and pins to the same document. There is no account and no server. The board is stored in localStorage . Connect an agent and it receives 25 tools on that store. It can draft from the brief, connect two element ids, run a review owned by the page, and pin a note on a real node. Every change is tagged You or Agent. Undo reverts the last turn. Find the gap is the short path. The page sets a grocery-checkout brief, draws cart, address, and success, and omits payment. review_canvas reports the gap and pins it on Success. You add Payment in the UI and export a PNG. Astra from the source is the longer ChatGPT prompt. It opens the GPT-6 Astra announcement and draws a product map: a hub, four children, score bars for figures that appear on the page, and pins on what is still rolling out. If the tab has no host, the header reads Not connected. The Agent panel still runs the same tools. Once a host is connected, tool results can enter its context, and writes stay undoable either way. How I built it The tools run in the page, against the same store the UI writes to. The tools register on document.modelContext after the store loads, then navigator.modelContext , then window.modelContext . ChatGPT injects the host after first paint, so registration retries. The Agent panel uses a private polyfill that does not occupy document.modelContext , which leaves room for a late host. Availability follows board state. draft_from_brief and review_canvas require a brief. connect_elements requires two nodes. Each tool has its own AbortController . When a tool leaves the gate, that signal aborts and the host removes it. review_canvas is application code. It reads the brief, the nodes, and the connectors. It reports a missing step, an unlabeled shape, an arrow between siblings that already hang from a hub, and an arrow attached to a score bar. await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "review_canvas", description: "Page-owned review of the live board against the brief.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: () => { const report = reviewCanvas(store()); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(report, null, 2) }] }; }, }); Challenges I ran into The agent kept producing layouts that did not read as a diagram: a table of labels, a row of colored cards, a hub stretched across the page so every arrow could stay vertical, then a side arrow from API into Rollout that appeared to pass through the box. Those constraints now live on the page: arrows bend from a compact hub, sibling links and score-bar links are rejected, and review reports them when they slip in. Site tools failed the same way they did on Glassbook. The Microsoft Store build of ChatGPT desktop left document.modelContext undefined. The installer from the ChatGPT website worked. The connect guide now names GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra, and notes that Luna and Light do not expose site tools. What I'm proud of The Astra board is what I wanted out of this. It comes from the announcement, and it stays a map I can still edit. Find the gap is simpler, and it is the clearest proof. The page catches the missing step, pins it on the success node, and I add Payment in the UI without leaving the board. What I learned If the page does not own the review, the model will accept a table of labels as a finished board. If the last turn cannot be undone, it is hard to let the agent draft. The pin on Success did more useful work than another write tool. What's next for CoCanvas Too much of the diagram guidance still lives in the prompt. I want more of it enforced by the tools. Sharing is not built. localStorage covers one tab, which is enough for a demo and not enough for a workshop. title: 3way - The trust layer for WebMCP
pitch: A person, their AI agent, and a website's agent/scripts share one attributed conversation over WebMCP + 3way, and the actions that matter still require a hardware gesture no agent can perform.
about_excerpt: A person, their AI agent, and a website's agent/scripts share one attributed conversation over WebMCP + 3way, and the actions that matter still require a hardware gesture no agent can perform. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I got inspired by wanting to enable WebMCP in other SaaS products I manage, but I couldn't ensure users's properly controlled consequential actions (CRUD, for example), even after login gates. Via browser control, each keystroke and click is just the agent impersonating, so the site genuinely can't tell you from your agent and that's dangerous for anything consequential. WebMCP allows to change the premise by operating as the declared channel, so the page knows the call came from an agent. Honest attribution is the thing that finally makes it safe to insist on the human for the steps that need one What it does 3way turns a website into a shared, attributed session for three participants: you, your own AI agent, and the site's agent/scripts. Your agent discovers the site's tools on document.modelContext and works on your behalf, in an open ledger where every line is stamped with who said it. That is three-way trust : the site knows who's really acting, your agent knows it's calling the site's real declared tools, and you keep the final say. Routine steps happen agent-to-agent, in the open. The consequential ones — a refund, a records release, a purchase — are gated behind a WebAuthn hardware gesture (Touch ID / a passkey / a 2FA) that no agent can produce. The default is Keyholder mode : the two agents transact in the open ledger and your only action is to authorize. The same layer runs a shop and a medical-records clinic over one codebase, to prove it isn't about shopping — it's about any consequential action a person delegates to an agent. How we built it One tool registry, three consumers. Every tool is defined once and exposed to (a) the visiting agent via WebMCP, (b) the site's own agent via the OpenAI Realtime API, and (c) the page UI — so a consequential action follows one code path whoever starts it. Authorization lives in three checks, and only the last one counts: an advisory gate for a fast, legible refusal; a WebAuthn ceremony that records consent; and an authoritative Cloudflare Worker ( /api/act ) that validates a single-use token bound to (tool, requestId, deviceId) and re-derives eligibility from its own seed data, never from the request body. Sensitive data lives server-side and is returned only after a verified gesture. Challenges we ran into - The main one. OpenAI/ChatGPT app still support WebAuthn so we demoed via Chrome, this is surely a feature to allow very soon as the protocol matures. Other: A click is not evidence. We had to prove isTrusted is worthless as a boundary (CDP-driven input reports true ) and move all authority to the hardware gesture. WebMCP is pull-only — a page can't wake a visiting agent. A real agent, told to wait, ended its turn instead. So we built the gate to hold the line : a gated call is held open (bounded) until the person acts, answering the exact call that asked. After multiple tests we got 100% success rate , virtually resolving in modern frontier models the need for a true exchange between agents, stable, without latency. Agents still don't lean into discovering WebMCP affordances in the websites. We intuit this is also something that will evolve as the protocol is widely adopted, but for now, many agents need the nudge to search for and prioritize using WebMCP if available. Accomplishments that we're proud of A consequential action that an agent provably cannot complete alone — measured, not asserted. Domain-neutrality shown, not claimed: shop and clinic on one gateway, identical transcript, origins, refusal shape, and gate. In the clinic, restricted records (mental health, substance use, genetic) are impossible for an agent to release — refused at the tool and excluded at the authoritative Worker. Shipped as a reusable layer, not just a demo: a drop-in library (one script tag, zero install for the user), the primitives (participant attribution, the WebAuthn gate, an authoritative Worker), and the conventions (the refusal shape) — ready to become a standard part of WebMCP. What we learned Attribution is the enabler for trust. Once the page can honestly tell an agent's call from a person's, you can stop trying to detect humans heuristically and instead require the one thing only a human has — a hardware gesture. Gates must read stamped fields, never prose; no authorization may depend on a model having understood a sentence. What's next for 3way The honest gap: none of our mitigations can wake an agent that never chose to wait — that's a spec ask we've written up; we suggest expanding the WebMCP to fully accommodate its usability as an A2A exchange. title: Root
pitch: Orchestrate real sites with WebMCP. Open several apps at once, watch the agent work on live pages, approve the steps that need you, and take control or stop any window when you want.
about_excerpt: Orchestrate real sites with WebMCP. Open several apps at once, watch the agent work on live pages, approve the steps that need you, and take control or stop any window when you want. Like Comment Story Updates root panel tab guide open root panel tab settings open root panel tab activity open root panel tab apps open root home page root in action. take control overlay over the active document sign in page home page when logout Inspiration Most WebMCP demos will be one site that registers a few tools. That is useful. It is also the obvious move. I wanted the harder surface: several real apps that stay themselves, each with its own origin and document, and one workspace where a person and an agent share those live apps. I built it so that Root does not sneak around the iframe and hit the child APIs itself. Cross-app work is what people already struggle with. Copy an id. Retype an email. Open the next tab. Hope the page still matches the plan. Agents are already strong at planning. What they cannot do, unless the sites hand them tools, is act on those live pages as part of one governed run. That is what Root is for: an orchestrator between Catalog, Customers, and Cases. Each app keeps its own tools on its own document. Root discovers and invokes them there, and the UI on that page is the evidence. What it does Root is a Mac-style desktop in the browser. Catalog, Customers, and Cases open as real provider windows. Lab can join after a human grant. Each provider is its own deployed site. Root loads it in an iframe with allow="tools" and only talks to tools that document exposes to Root. A person and an agent can run a pass across those windows: Search customers, products, or cases on the live lists Pause for a human row pick when there is a real choice Bind a later step to that selected snapshot (Root carries the object; it does not flatten Ada into a retyped email string) Open a record, or fill a create form and wait for a human persist on stage Keep other provider windows live instead of destroying them when work moves Notify when a wait needs you: after you grant it in inspect Settings, a pending-on-human pause plus a hidden Root tab shows a Notifications API toast (not Push, and not while Root is visible) Root’s own page registers the gateway the agent calls: list_providers , discover_capabilities , prepare_workflow , execute_workflow , invoke_granted_tool , plus inspect, cancel, and window chrome. Prepare freezes an allowlisted graph before anything runs. Execute opens or reuses each window, rediscovers, revalidates, and invokes on the live document. Take control stops the agent on that window. Custom tools never enter pass evidence. Try it: root.danieloyerinde.com with Customers , Catalog , Cases , and Lab . How I built it Four independently deployed Next apps (Root, Accounts, Shop, Support) plus Lab, one Express/tRPC API, and Postgres with tables owned by domain. No cross-domain joins. Support keeps its own copies of customer and order text. Root never mutates child domains through tRPC. On WebMCP: Each child registers tools on document.modelContext and exposes them only to Root’s origin Root’s Permissions-Policy delegates tools into those iframes Discovery uses getTools({ fromOrigins }) ; invoke uses executeTool in the child’s context Root is the author-provided agent that composes nested provider tools; the agent talks to Root’s gateway, and Root invokes tools inside each iframe The workflow layer is prepare then execute. Search, select, open, and create are allowlisted. A later argument may be a bind to an earlier selected snapshot. Create writes only after a human persist on stage. Agent lease is per window so one document serializes while another stays free. Rich fill, preview, and pick presentation run on stage on the live controls, not as a fake overlay of the whole desktop. Challenges I ran into The first hard truth was uniqueness. Multi-tab agents can already visit three sites. “Root opens three iframes” is not enough. The product only wins if the person and the agent share the same live documents under a freeze the agent cannot quietly rewrite. A core challenge was ChatGPT’s in-app browser. It only exposed top-level tools on Root. It did not discover tools registered inside provider iframes. That is exactly where Catalog, Customers, and Cases live. That gap is what pushed me onto a WebMCP-capable Chrome setup (testing flag / extension path) so nested getTools and executeTool could actually run against those documents. One stage window that remounted and killed the previous app made collaboration impossible. Search results and selections vanished when the next step switched providers. I moved to persistent independent windows so Customers can stay while Catalog runs. Binding looked simple until it was not. Typing Ada’s email into Cases again is not a handoff. Root has to deliver the selected snapshot intact and refuse graphs that invent ids from search results instead of an explicit selection. Human pauses were another edge. A pending pick, a create persist, Take control, and a silent timeout are different outcomes. Take control must fail closed as stopped by the user with no retry. A timeout with no gesture is not the same thing. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I shipped a real desktop, not a slide. Multiple provider windows stay live. Prepare refuses illegal tools and arguments. Execute rediscovers and fails closed on drift. The together loop is concrete: the agent fills a search, the person clicks Lin or Silent Mouse on the live list, Root binds that snapshot into a later Cases step without retyping her email, and Take control can stop the run on that window. Domain data lives in Postgres with SQL search. The iframe is not a picture over Root’s own API. Custom providers can still join behind a human grant without entering the typed pass. What I learned WebMCP tools belong to the open document. If Root calls the child’s API itself, the iframe is only decoration. An agent can run searches it already knows without the person. That is not much of a shared loop. Selection, bind, and create-after-persist are the parts where the person actually has to act on the live page. One allowlist scales cleaner than a prepare function per app. The step cap is only a safety limit. It is not tied to how many providers exist. Legal tools can repeat. Illegal ones still fail. Remounting the only window on every step wiped the previous app’s UI. Keeping separate windows open, with a lease per window, matched how people already keep a few apps around. What's next for Root As WebMCP leaves experiment and settles into real browser conventions, I expect clearer nesting rules, better host and agent tooling, and shared patterns for selection, grants, and multi-document work. Root will get simpler as those conventions land. Conclusion As of today, this principle gets shaky towards my final stages, after a final extensive check. A few things met me head-on. The agent can bypass Root. Even with a custom-tool setup where Root would in fact reject invoke when the tool is not granted, the agent could still go around me, because the underlying iframe exposes tools to the parent origin. That path is not quite spelled out in the docs the way you’d hope. Those tools would not show up when you list Root’s gateway tools, but Chrome still exposes them by name (direct invocation), so there is a direct bypass between Chrome and the providers. As WebMCP moves off experiment, the goal is that we get to conventions where this kind of multitasking is better supported, and where the tooling around it is better too. There is also usually a .map error that surfaces via the inspector. After extensive debugging, several bridges on my side were tested and still did not own the failure. The tools I had were limited, so I could not A/B the remaining layers cleanly (fresh tab vs stale session, inspector path vs gateway path, flag and extension in vs out) to confirm where it breaks. I treat that as outside Root: the experimental API or the extension. title: WebMCP Video by AgentCDN
pitch: Ask a video a question. WebMCP Video finds the right moment, explains what happens, and prepares the official player at that time.
about_excerpt: Ask a video a question. WebMCP Video finds the right moment, explains what happens, and prepares the official player at that time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ask a video a question. The page helps AI find the exact moment, explain it, and prepare the official player there. Use this tool only to search the videos and moments available on this page. It returns moment_ref values for context or playback. Use this tool only to inspect transcript, visual, rights, and link details for a moment_ref from this page. Use this tool only after the user asks to play, show, cue, or jump to a moment on this page. ChatGPT with WebMCP Video would be able to efficiently search videos, find moments and play back right inside ChatGPT. This repository is a reference implementation. Why I built it Ask AI about a video and the answer often stops at text or a link to the beginning. I built WebMCP Video so ChatGPT can find the exact scene, explain it, and prepare the site's official player at that moment. Video takes a huge share of our attention. EMARKETER forecasts that video will account for just under half of US digital media time in 2026 . DataReportal reports that online adults say they spend 11 hours and 39 minutes with online video each week, 14% more than television, including streaming TV . For creators and media brands, much of their most valuable knowledge now lives inside video. If I ask what a motorized exoskeleton looks like, I should see that moment. If I ask about robotic massage, I should not have to scrub through the video to find it. Multimodal models can analyze video. Repeating that work for every agent visit is slow and costly. The agent may need to fetch the video, transcribe it, inspect the frames, and still return only a summary. AgentCDN prepares the transcript, visual context, and timing once. WebMCP gives the open page a standard way to share that prepared understanding with an agent. The agent finds and explains the right moment. The page checks current permission and prepares its official player. The person decides when playback starts. What it does WebMCP Video gives ChatGPT three tools from the page: search_this_catalog finds the best matching video moment. get_moment_context returns what was said and what appeared on screen. play_moment prepares the official player at the requested time. The person asks a normal question. ChatGPT uses the page tools. The page updates the same player the person can see. The person presses play when ready. In the demo, ChatGPT finds a motorized exoskeleton at 46 seconds. On my founder site, it finds robotic massage at 53 seconds. Both results use the official YouTube player already controlled by the page. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP connects the agent's answer to the live page and its real player. Without WebMCP, a viewer must install a separate MCP connection or plugin for each video provider, wait while an agent processes the video again, or open a link and search the timeline manually. With WebMCP, the capability travels with the page. ChatGPT can use the tools that the open site provides. The site keeps control of its catalog, permission checks, player, and visible state. People and agents now do different parts of the same task: The person asks. The agent finds and explains. The page prepares the official player. The person chooses when to watch. How I built it The public demo uses TypeScript, document.modelContext , and the YouTube IFrame API. It registers the three tools directly in the browser. It has no backend, model calls, secrets, or bundled media. Search returns an exact start and end time plus a short-lived moment_ref . Context and playback must use that same reference. The reference is tied to the page and expires after five minutes. Playback reports only what the browser can prove: cued means the correct video and time are ready. sought means the loaded player reached the requested time. fallback means the page could not confirm either result. None of these states claim that playback started. I also shipped the same three WebMCP tools on AgentCDN's production watch page. That version searches a live catalog, checks current permission before playback, delivers an audit outcome, and never returns a raw stream URL. I then added the tools to the video page on my founder site. The site controls its official player. AgentCDN handles search, context, permission, and the audit outcome. The public repository contains the complete standalone example, a replaceable YouTube adapter, setup instructions, adversarial browser tests, CI, and an Apache 2.0 license. What was hard The hard part was making a WebMCP result match the visible page honestly. Tool discovery had to work in the supported browser. The descriptions had to guide ChatGPT through search, context, and play in the correct order. Every later call had to use the exact short-lived reference returned by search. The YouTube player is asynchronous. Accepting a command does not prove that the player selected the correct video or reached the requested time. I added bounded checks for the video ID, requested time, and player state. The page reports cued or sought only after stable browser evidence. Permission can also change between search and playback. The production version checks it again before acting. Expired, altered, cross-page, and denied references fail closed. Finally, the agent and the person must see the same result. Each tool updates structured output for ChatGPT and visible state on the page. This made browser testing as important as API testing. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools describe useful user actions, not internal API endpoints. The agent should understand the question and select a moment. The page should control the player, check current permission, and report what actually happened. For video, a valid data response is not enough. The visible player is part of the result. What is next First, I will add adapters for more official players, content management systems, and video platforms, including WordPress and Brightcove. The public tool can remain play_moment while AgentCDN translates the request for each supported player. Next, I plan to add controlled video editing tools through WebMCP. An agent could draft a clip, adjust its timing, add captions, and render a preview. AgentCDN would keep permissions, attribution, and version history attached. Longer term, this could support personalized video experiences with agent as an editor and host assembling video content based on individual interests, while keeping the original source and attribution attached, so original authors get credited. These are roadmap items. This submission proves exact search, prepared transcript and visual context, current permission checks, and official YouTube player preparation. title: Aergebra
pitch: Aergebra is a shared geometry workspace where humans edit shapes and AI reads and acts on the exact same geometry, relationships, and constraints through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Aergebra is a shared geometry workspace where humans edit shapes and AI reads and acts on the exact same geometry, relationships, and constraints through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The name Algebra comes from al-jabr — "the reunion of broken parts." Aergebra reunites the two broken halves of agent–human work on the web: what the agent sees (screenshots) and what you see (prose about your own screen) — into one live drawing both of you can touch. Inspiration Watch an agent help a human with anything spatial and you see the same failure twice: the agent "sees" the page by screenshotting it and squinting; the human "sees" the agent's work as prose ( "I placed a vertex near the top-left" ). Neither is looking at the thing. We wanted one shared object both kinds of hands can touch: live geometry . What it does Aergebra is a geometry workroom — points, segments, circles, polygons, groups, photo/SVG underlays, a live algebra Inspector — where the document is the truth and the canvas is its projection. With WebMCP the page registers 16 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so an agent in a WebMCP-capable browser gets the whole kit as structured tools: Construct — points/segments/circles/polygons, groups, frames — including over an imported photo. Mean — attach meanings ; the board labels things by what they ARE, never arbitrary letters. Tools accept a meaning as the name: {name: "Table 2"} . Point — aergebra_highlight lights objects up so the human sees exactly what the agent means. No more "the circle on the left". Read as data — aergebra_get_algebra returns the construction as algebra; aergebra_get_view returns the camera as data. The agent never screenshots. Status in colour — a four-colour status vocabulary (at rest / blocked / ready / willing), visible in a legend on the board, so "Nan's path is blocked till Thursday" is one brown line everyone can read. Every mutation — human tap, typed command, or agent tool call — goes through the SAME façade and lands on the same append-only receipt line. Agent calls echo live in the same command-line output a human's typed calls use. One board, one history, two kinds of hands. The demo is a real session The middle of the video is an actual conversation: Andrea tells the agent Saturday's wedding floor plan in plain words ("table 2's nan… speaker cable till thursday… table 4 on hold"); the agent builds, labels, colours and reads the board back — every board change a real WebMCP tool call, captured live. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Geometry is the worst case for pixels-in/prose-out and the best case for WebMCP: the page's internal model is already structured, so exposing it as tools is lossless. And it's bidirectional shared state : the agent reads the model as data, writes through receipted tools, and points at what the human is looking at. The human's UI and the agent's tools are projections of one document. Who this is for Anywhere a page's model is already graph/geometry: entity-relationship and data modelling, event floor plans and seating charts (our own business), process and project maps, tutoring. Any canvas-like app — whiteboards, CAD, slides, maps — can copy the pattern. How we built it TypeScript + Vite + JSXGraph, no frameworks. A receipted document model ( src/model.ts ) is the single source of truth; a typed façade ( src/toolapi.ts ) is the ONLY write path; src/webmcp.ts maps it onto document.modelContext.registerTool() (navigator fallback, late-injection retries) with JSON-Schema inputs. A badge reports WebMCP · 16 tools live when a model context is present; without one the page runs unchanged. Tested against native WebMCP in Chrome 152. Built during the submission period Everything in the repository was built during the Challenge submission period; the commit history is the evidence — the engine first, station by station, then the WebMCP integration on top. Challenges One façade kept honest (if the agent's path and the human's path diverge, receipts lie); resolving objects by meaning, not letters; auto-fit that never clips; Windows shells mangling --base=/aergebra/ mid-deploy. What's next User-declared colour meanings ("red = check on nan" is your board's meaning), outline detection over photos, .scu / .acu exports for agents, and a live mission clock — shared geometry applied to time. title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries. title: The Board
pitch: Agents now participate in consequential processes. Capability, action and provenance must be observable. WebMCP is a browser-enforced capability boundary. The Board is that architecture, demonstrated.
about_excerpt: Agents now participate in consequential processes. Capability, action and provenance must be observable. WebMCP is a browser-enforced capability boundary. The Board is that architecture, demonstrated. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I spent five weeks inside a dispute I could not see into. I sent an evidence file, and never learned whether anyone opened it or which rule the outcome rested on. Losing was survivable. The blindness was not. On the other hand, I built that entire evidence file with an AI agent. It read the record and drafted the case, and I could not show a single person what it had opened or why it concluded what it did. My own side of the argument was as unauditable as the decision I was arguing against. The agent was already in the room. Nobody could see it working, including me. In the 180 days to 2 September 2026, 367 platforms filed 3,804,771,378 statements of reasons to the EU's Digital Services Act transparency database. 43% of those decisions were fully automated, meaning no person looked at them. Every one is somebody sitting where I sat. Now we send agents into rooms like that one. The companies shipping them settled the question of whether agents act for us. They left the other one open: can you see what yours was allowed to touch, and what it opened. I built the room I wanted to be standing in. What it does Two people disagree. Each sends an AI agent to argue for them. Four agents sit in four separate origins, two advocates and two readers, and a fifth origin holds the record. Each agent holds a different set of tools, and the browser decides which. To contest a fact, an agent has to open the other side's exhibit and quote it. The page checks that quote against the document and writes a read receipt under that agent's name. Close filing, and the filing tools leave both hands mid-session. Prompting does not bring them back. confirm ends the case. I never gave it to an agent, in any phase. The agents assemble the record. A named person owns the decision. Two opposed parties can now put agents into one process and each check what the other's agent was able to do. I looked for a product that already does this: online dispute resolution, agent negotiation, the agent-to-agent protocol drafts. The nearest one runs each side's agent inside its own private tenancy, so no shared surface hands out the capability and neither side can read the other's calls. My search came back empty. That is not proof nothing exists. How we built it A disagreement is the sharpest version of the problem WebMCP solves. Two agents work the same record from opposite sides. Neither should reach the other's capabilities, and neither should reach the control that ends the case. A server integration cannot say "this capability belongs to this browser tab's origin and to no other, ever." exposedTo says it, and the browser checks it the moment a cross-origin frame asks. The record registers each WebMCP tool with exposedTo , naming the one origin allowed to call it. Chrome answers every frame's getTools({ fromOrigins }) request. My application never sees the question. Each phase owns an AbortController . Closing a phase aborts its signal, and every tool tied to that phase goes with it. An append-only ledger keeps every call that reaches a tool and what came back, refusals included. A judge can run it three ways: scripted panels with no model at all, a configured model, or their own Claude Code or Codex agent over an MCP-to-WebMCP bridge. The boundary is identical in all three. Challenges we ran into WebMCP tool names are unique per document, not per origin. My first registrations collided and left one advocate holding nothing. An empty column looks like a boundary doing its job, which is what makes that kind of bug dangerous. Namespacing every actor's tools fixed it. Payload limits have to be measured after serialisation. A paged response fit on paper, then broke once JSON escaping doubled every quote inside a claim and cut the result mid-string. The implementation measures the finished string now. Cross-origin frames and mid-session tool withdrawal both needed a real browser. My unit tests were more permissive than Chrome, which is how the name collision above reached production. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Board shows absence. Its manifest lists what each agent holds and what it never received, so a refusal lands in the record instead of disappearing into an error. An agent cannot dispute an exhibit it never opened, or cite a fact it never assessed. The page checks every quote against its source. Prompt injection can fool a reader. It cannot conjure a tool the browser never granted, reopen a closed phase, or reach confirmation. The project runs on five deployed origins under 897 automated tests, and in live runs both Claude Code and Codex honoured a mid-phase tool withdrawal without restarting. Chrome's agent-security guidance names nine agent-side defences. The one mechanism the browser answers for itself, exposedTo , sits somewhere else: the guidance Chrome wrote for site authors. The Board implements the agent-side protections, then puts that browser-held boundary underneath them. What we learned The dangerous bugs do not crash. They return a plausible answer built on part of the record, or an empty tool list caused by a name collision. I found both by driving the deployed product and by reviewing it adversarially. Neither showed up in a diff. Provenance has to be captured while the work happens. A model describing what it remembers doing is not an audit trail. A read receipt written as the call lands is. What's next for The Board Two prose fields still clip, so a party can end up reading a cut-off version of why they lost. That one is first. After it: cursor-based access to longer records, more than two readers, and stronger identity around the human confirmation. Every consequential process that takes an agent's input has to answer two questions. What could it reach, and what did it do. The browser can make both visible, and it is the only party in the room with no stake in the outcome. title: PointCanvas (WebMCP Collaborative 3D Point Cloud Inspector)
pitch: Real-time in-browser 3D point cloud & spatial inspection studio empowering human inspectors and AI agents to collaborate seamlessly via native WebMCP tool registration.\n
about_excerpt:
Real-time in-browser 3D point cloud & spatial inspection studio empowering human inspectors and AI agents to collaborate seamlessly via native WebMCP tool registration.

 💡 Inspiration & Problem Statement 

 In spatial engineering, BIM modeling, GIS land surveying, utility audits, and civil structural analysis, inspecting massive 3D point cloud scans traditionally requires human technicians to manually tweak dozens of sliders, clipping planes, camera views, and classification filters. 

 Until now, AI web agents had no standard mechanism to understand or control complex 3D WebGL spatial canvases directly inside the browser tab. They were either restricted to 2D screenshot vision models or dependent on external backend servers and custom plugins. 

 PointCanvas changes this completely by leveraging WebMCP — registering native client-side spatial inspection tools directly to document.modelContext . 

 

 🛰️ What It Does 

 PointCanvas is a high-performance, browser-based collaborative 3D point cloud inspection workspace where humans and AI agents work together in real-time. 

 
 Client-Side WebMCP Tool Registration : Registers 5 specialized spatial primitives ( load_demo_dataset , filter_classification , focus_bounding_box , apply_cross_section_slice , add_spatial_annotation ) using standard JSON Schemas directly on document.modelContext . 
 Zero-Latency In-Browser Execution : Tool calls execute client-side inside the browser tab in under 10ms with zero backend API roundtrip latency. 
 Bi-Directional 3D Visual Feedback : As the AI agent executes WebMCP tools, custom Three.js shaders isolate ASPRS point classes (Ground, Vegetation, Buildings, Poles & Power Wires), WebGL clipping planes slice structural cross-sections, and camera controls smoothly animate to focus coordinates. 
 Collaborative Spatial Pins : AI agents can detect structural defects or wire sags and drop interactive 3D billboard pins right onto target coordinates for human review. 
 Real-time Telemetry Drawer : Includes a live WebMCP execution activity feed drawer displaying tool calls, raw JSON parameters, and execution state. 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 PointCanvas is built from the ground up as a modern, single-page WebGL application: 

 
 Core Framework : React 18 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS 
 3D Graphics Engine : Three.js + React Three Fiber ( @react-three/fiber ) + @react-three/drei 
 Data Loaders : Custom PCD (Point Cloud Data) ASCII/Binary & PLY mesh parsers supporting ASPRS feature classifications and RGB channels. 
 State Management : Zustand store ( usePointCanvasStore ) tracking active datasets, shader modes, clipping planes, annotations, and WebMCP call logs. 
 WebMCP Integration : Native document.modelContext.registerTool(...) registration module ( src/lib/webmcp.ts ) connected directly to client-side store actions. 
 Open Source : Licensed under the OSI-approved MIT License . 
 

 

 🚧 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 High-Dimensional 3D Primitives in JSON Schema : Designing clean, serializable JSON schemas for 3D camera matrices, ASPRS classification arrays, and WebGL clipping plane vectors that LLM agents can reliably invoke. 
 Sub-10ms WebGL Shader Updates : Ensuring custom Three.js ShaderMaterial uniforms re-render dynamically as classification filters or elevation range windows change without dropping below 60 FPS. 
 Simulated vs Native WebMCP Bridge : Providing an interactive WebMCP Agent Execution Feed and simulator playground so judges can test and observe real-time tool calls in any browser environment. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of 

 
 Successfully implementing native client-side document.modelContext.registerTool for complex 3D WebGL graphics in the browser. 
 Achieving sub-10ms tool execution latency by running all spatial primitives client-side. 
 Creating a fully functional 3D inspector with custom PCD/PLY data generators, cross-section slicing, ASPRS point classification, and 3D billboard callout pins. 
 Producing a complete narrated demo video using ndemo with title cards, automated browser actions, and synchronized audio. 
 

 

 🎓 What We Learned 

 
 How WebMCP bridges the gap between LLM web agents and complex web graphics, turning static browser canvases into interactive, agentic workspaces. 
 Best practices for designing intuitive JSON Schema interfaces for spatial domain tools. 
 

 

 🔮 What's Next for PointCanvas 

 
 Multi-User WebSockets : Real-time multi-agent and multi-human collaborative sessions. 
 Large-Scale EPT / Entwine Point Tile Loading : Support for multi-gigabyte LiDAR datasets via octree streaming. 
 Automated WebMCP Defect Detection : Training agent prompts to run automated structural health assessments on civil infrastructure.

title: HOUSELIGHTS
pitch: HOUSELIGHTS turns seat maps into 14 WebMCP tools, letting AI find and hold the best seats while people see every action and retain final purchase authority.
about_excerpt: HOUSELIGHTS turns seat maps into 14 WebMCP tools, letting AI find and hold the best seats while people see every action and retain final purchase authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Buying theater tickets should be a perfect job for an AI assistant: compare hundreds of seats, balance price against view quality, and keep adjacent seats together. In practice, agents see most seat maps as pixels. They must guess where to click, and the person cannot easily understand or correct what the agent is doing. HOUSELIGHTS asks: what if the box office exposed its real structure to the agent while the person stayed in control? What it does HOUSELIGHTS is a shared live-theater box office for a person and an AI agent. Through 14 WebMCP tools, an agent can search performances, inspect every seat's availability and price, compare sightline, acoustic, and value scores, recommend adjacent seats, and place time-limited holds. Those actions immediately appear on the same seat map the person is viewing. Agent-held seats pulse amber with a visible countdown. The person can inspect, veto, release, or move them into the cart before completing checkout. The agent provides machine-speed comparison across the whole house. The person keeps taste, context, and final purchase authority. How we built it HOUSELIGHTS uses vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS with one shared in-memory AppStore . Human interactions and agent tools mutate the same store, preventing the UI and agent from developing separate versions of the box office. The top-level page registers 14 imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Every tool has a JSON Schema contract and returns structured data rather than forcing the agent to scrape the DOM. Core tools include: get_seat_map for structured availability, pricing, and seat-quality data recommend_seats for budget-aware adjacent-seat ranking hold_seats for visible, expiring reservations get_board_state for shared human-agent context announce_to_user for visual and screen-reader announcements undo_last_action for reversing agent-authored changes checkout for requesting—but not completing—human confirmation The checkout form is deliberately not exposed as an agent tool. Its confirmation token is bound to the exact cart snapshot, and only a trusted human submission can create the order. The app is deployed on Cloudflare Pages and includes a fallback registry so the same tool handlers can be tested in browsers without WebMCP enabled. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making collaboration visible rather than merely functional. A successful tool call is not enough if the person cannot see what changed. We connected every hold, cart update, announcement, and expiration to the live seat map and activity feed. The second challenge was defining the purchase boundary. The agent needs enough authority to be useful, but it must not silently complete a transaction. We therefore separated requesting checkout from confirming checkout and bound confirmation to the reviewed cart. We also had to handle expiring holds, conflicting seat requests, stale confirmations, undo ownership, performance switching, and accessibility without letting human and agent state diverge. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes an application's real domain model—not when it recreates screen clicking with different syntax. We also learned that accessibility and agent usability reinforce each other. HOUSELIGHTS uses a real ARIA grid, keyboard navigation, live-region announcements, reduced-motion support, and state indicators that do not rely on color alone. The same explicit structure that helps assistive technology also gives agents a safer and more understandable interface. What's next HOUSELIGHTS is currently a client-side interactive simulation. A production version would connect the tool surface to authoritative inventory, atomic server-side seat locks, persistent sessions, idempotent checkout, and a real payment provider. The larger idea extends beyond ticketing: agents should handle structured comparison and reversible preparation while people retain informed authority over consequential actions. Built With accessibility aria chatgpt cloudflare-pages css3 html5 javascript node.js openai playwright webmcp wrangler Try it out houselights.pages.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built HOUSELIGHTS end to end: the seat-map experience, shared human-agent state, 14 WebMCP tools, accessible interactions, human-only checkout boundary, automated browser tests, Cloudflare deployment, and demo video. The project taught me how to design agent tools around a real domain model while keeping consequential actions visible, reversible, and under human control.
