title: TAAMs Import Sourcing Desk
pitch: A web page where a person and an AI agent source verified food imports together - the agent operates the same screen the buyer is looking at, and cannot send anything without the buyer's approval.
about_excerpt: A web page where a person and an AI agent source verified food imports together - the agent operates the same screen the buyer is looking at, and cannot send anything without the buyer's approval. Like Comment Story Updates main image(pinned-and-highlighted) product load approval Inspiration Importing food into a country starts with two questions that have nothing to do with software: is this a real supplier, and is this a real price? Buyers answer them by hand today — reading government customs portals, cold-calling trading companies, guessing whether a quoted price is normal. All of that happens before a single quote is ever sent. We had already built a remote MCP server for this data, and we watched what people actually did with it. The agent gives you a good summary. Then you open the real tool and redo the comparison yourself, because sourcing decisions are made by looking at things side by side . The summary is not the work. That is the gap WebMCP closes. The comparison the agent builds is the comparison you are looking at. We wanted to find out whether that changes the workflow or just moves the JSON, so we built the same sourcing problem as a page an agent can operate. What it does A sourcing desk for food imported into Korea, backed by TAAMs — a B2B marketplace where verified, officially imported products are traded directly with the importers who cleared them through customs. You search a product and get real customs clearance records: the monthly import unit price in USD/kg broken down by exporting country, the overseas suppliers actually shipping it, and the Korean companies already buying it. You pin origins side by side, filter to one supplying country, and draft a sourcing enquiry to a named supplier. Every one of those actions is a button a person can click. Seven of them are also registered as WebMCP tools, so an agent can reach for the same buttons. The seven tools, in three tiers Tier A — lookup (4 tools). search_import_products resolves free text in English or Korean to the exact name used in clearance records; get_import_price_trend , get_top_exporters and get_active_importers fetch and render. The agent does the tedious part — name resolution, twelve months of history, nine countries — and the human keeps the judgement. Tier B — screen control (2 tools), zero network requests. pin_to_comparison_board and highlight_supplier_country fetch nothing at all. They rearrange what is already in front of the human. Open the network tab while they run and nothing fires; that is asserted in the test suite, not just claimed. This is the tier that only exists inside the page. A remote MCP server can return better JSON. It cannot know that a table is on your screen, let alone which row deserves attention. Tier C — action, gated by a human (1 tool). draft_sourcing_request fills in a real enquiry to a real supplier and then stops. An approval dialog shows exactly what is about to leave — product, supplier, quantity, notes. Only on approval does a pre-filled email open from the user's own mail client, and the person still presses send. Cancel, and the draft stays on screen to edit by hand. Its most important behaviour is what it refuses to do. The agent has authority to prepare and no authority to send. What it looks like with real data Ask "Thai mango or Brazilian? Put both on the board and tell me who I should buy from." and the agent pins two cards from the same product: Thailand Brazil Import price $6.47/kg $5.16/kg Clearances (2025) 3,310 651 Named suppliers 42 5 Thailand is 25% more expensive with five times the shipment history and eight times the supplier base. That is a sourcing decision, on screen, from 4,368 customs records for one fruit. It works with no agent at all Search, pin, highlight and RFQ are all clickable. Someone who has never heard of WebMCP gets a complete tool; an agent makes it faster. Each tool handler is a one-liner delegating to the same function the page's own button calls, so there is no agent-only code path and no human-only one — checkable from the source. How we built it Deliberately minimal: zero dependencies, no build step, one static page, no backend of its own. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool() at load, and the page calls the public TAAMs read API directly from the browser. Three findings about the gap between the published spec and the shipping browser, because that gap was part of the work: 1. The API is on document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext . Much published material still shows navigator . We feature-detect both so the page survives the object moving again. 2. requestUserInteraction() does not exist in Chrome 151. The approval gate was designed around it. The object only carries ontoolchange , executeTool , getTools and registerTool , so we built the gate ourselves as an in-page modal. That turned out better: the human sees the actual draft rather than a generic system prompt. 3. executeTool takes a tool object and a JSON string . Not a name, not an arguments object — both are rejected. This is documented nowhere we could find; we established it by enumerating the object in a live browser and trying each candidate convention until one returned a result. That third finding is what made the whole thing testable. getTools() and executeTool() are exposed to the page, so a test can drive the tools exactly as an agent drives them — no ChatGPT needed in the loop. Every claim in the README is checked that way, in a real Chrome, against the live API. Challenges we ran into The schema could not express the demo's own question. pin_to_comparison_board originally took a product name and nothing else. But the question a buyer actually asks is "this origin or that one?" — same product, two countries — and a board keyed on product alone cannot hold that. You would be pinning the same product twice. No wording fixed it; the argument list had to change. We found this by rehearsing tool selection rather than tool execution: handing a model only the registered tool definitions and the demo's question, and asking what it would call. It never reached for the screen-control tier at all. Both screen-control tools were written as if the user would name them. "Call this when the user says 'compare'." A question that never uses the word never reaches the tool. Nothing told the agent it could reach for them on its own judgement. Adding that one clause is what makes the agent, in the demo video, say "I'll pin both options first, then highlight the stronger sourcing lane" — unprompted. A filtered fetch got stored as the whole truth. Narrowing the supplier list to one country overwrote the session's list, so a card for any other country counted zero suppliers in it. Brazil showed "0 suppliers" when it has five. The API had been right the whole time; the number on screen was wrong. The tests were passing through all of it. 22 of 22 green while the supplier column read "Unknown supplier" on every row, while a month-less price call returned a 500, while Brazil showed zero. Each assertion was true and each missed the point. What caught them: looking at the screen, and running the thing in a real agent browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Tier B genuinely makes zero network requests, and you can check it. Not a design intention — an assertion in the test suite that counts requests during those calls and fails if any fire. It failed once, honestly, when a name-resolution call snuck in. That is fixed and guarded. The action tool refuses, visibly, every time. The agent in our demo says it itself: "Review it in the approval dialog and click Approve to open the pre-filled email — nothing has been sent yet." We put that instruction in the tool's return value and the model honoured it. An agent that does not overclaim is worth more here than one more feature. It runs in ChatGPT's actual in-app browser. Not only behind a Chrome flag. ChatGPT opened the page, found all seven tools, pinned two origins, highlighted Thailand, drafted an RFQ to a named Thai exporter, and stopped for approval. That run is the demo video. The data is real, public, and government-sourced. 1,318,602 customs clearance transactions since 2023, 169,089 registered overseas manufacturers across 202 countries, built on records published by Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety and Korea Customs Service. Not scraped listings, not self-reported catalogues. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product surface, not documentation. Every behaviour we wanted came from a sentence in a description, and every behaviour we did not get was a sentence we had not written. The gap between "the agent could do this" and "the agent does this" was one clause about when to act on its own judgement. Testing execution is not testing selection. executeTool bypasses the model's decision entirely, so a suite can be fully green while the agent never picks the tools at all. Rehearsing selection — giving a model only the definitio

Every call lands on my screen in place. There is no summary for me to copy back into the tool. Now the part of a remote server cannot do. Pin it to the board. Highlight the Thailand. Look at the network tab. Nothing fires. These two tools patch nothing. They rearrange what is already in front of me. Brazil is dimmed, not deleted. A remote MCP server can return better data. It cannot know that a table is on my screen. Last, the agent drops a sourcing request to a named Thai supplier, then it stops. It has authority to prepare and no authority to send. The page shows me exactly what is about to leave. Product, supplier, quantity, notes. I read it, I click approve. Only then does an email open from my own mail client, and I'm still the one who could just send. If I cancel, the draft stays on screen and nothing goes out. And every one of those action is a button, such pin, highlight, draft. I can click them all myself. The agent uses the same functions I do. That is the whole idea. Tom's import sourcing desk, 1.3 million Korean custom records, one paid, seven web MCP tools. A person and an agent sourcing together, and the person still signs off.

title: SplitTrip
pitch: An agent proposes a fair, feasible group-trip plan through reactive WebMCP tools, while unanimous human consent remains the only way to finalize it.
about_excerpt: An agent proposes a fair, feasible group-trip plan through reactive WebMCP tools, while unanimous human consent remains the only way to finalize it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group trips often stall because everyone has different budgets, must-haves, and vetoes. SplitTrip explores a better collaboration model: let an agent handle the constraint arithmetic while humans keep control of the final decision. What it does Three travelers pool a fixed budget and define a protected spending buffer, must-have items, vetoes, shared preferences, and individual preferences over a travel catalog. An agent proposes a complete allocation. SplitTrip then validates it deterministically against the budget cap, protected buffer, must-haves, vetoes, shared preference coverage, lodging count, traveler representation, schedule conflicts, capacity, transport compatibility, and location feasibility. The proposal, rationale, validation results, and named fairness breakdown appear immediately. Travelers can reject the proposal or approve it individually. Only after Maya, Alex, and Sam have all approved does the lock_allocation WebMCP tool become available. Once locked, the plan is immutable and can be exported or shared as a bounded read-only snapshot. How I built it SplitTrip is a React and TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare Workers. It uses the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with an AbortController-managed lifecycle tied to one typed state machine: get_trip_context — always available get_allocation_status — always available propose_allocation — available during setup revise_allocation — available while a proposal exists and is not locked lock_allocation — available only after unanimous approval Every tool calls the same Zustand store actions used by the human interface, so the agent and UI cannot disagree. Constraint editing and approval actions are intentionally never exposed as tools; they remain human-only. The exact live tool set is visible in the Tool Inspector, and registration-change toasts make state transitions easy to see. The interface was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Zod, and WebMCP. It was tested with Vitest and Playwright and deployed on Cloudflare. Human-agent collaboration The key design choice is that human authority is enforced by capability availability, not merely by a warning or a disabled button. Before unanimous approval, the finalization tool does not exist in the browser registry. A prompt cannot route around that boundary. At the same time, humans can inspect every agent action: the selected items, rationale, constraint violations, fairness breakdown, and full tool-call trace. Tool descriptions and Zod schemas give the agent structured context and actionable validation errors. Measured evidence A built-in evaluation compares a constraint-aware strategy against a constraint-blind baseline across 5 scenarios and 3 catalog orderings, using the production validator: Strategy First-pass success Final success Violations Human corrections Constraint-blind baseline 0/15 15/15 81 15 Constraint-aware shipped flow 15/15 15/15 0 0 These are transparently labeled scripted trials, not claimed live-agent runs. Challenges The hardest part was making WebMCP's security property visible. The absence of a tool before approval is powerful but easy to miss, so I added live registration toasts, an exact Tool Inspector, and a simulated demo that follows the same application code path. Another challenge was validating an experimental browser integration consistently. The state-aware registry lifecycle is covered by automated integration tests, including a stale tool-reference test after rejection and an in-flight-call edge case. Accomplishments Unanimous approval is an architectural gate: lock_allocation is absent until all required humans approve. Automated coverage spans the full state machine, validation rules, persistence, and reactive tool lifecycle. The deployed application includes an observable end-to-end demo, exportable results, and an honest evaluation panel. What's next Authenticated multi-user approvals, editable traveler profiles, booking integrations, and expanded live-agent compatibility testing. Leveraged WebMCP to provide a composable web experience to a Generative AI consulting company

 Inspiration 

 We were experimenting with a simple question relevant to technology companies [in consulting] and the brands they work with: Can every visitor get a website experience that feels designed specifically for them? 

 Most personalization today is based on predefined segments, funnels, and rules. WebMCP opens up a different possibility. An AI agent can understand the visitor, their context, and their intent, then shape the experience around them. For consulting companies, this could change how digital experiences are designed. 

 What it does 

 We WebMCP-enabled newtuple.ai and allowed ChatGPT to interact with the website through structured tools. In the demo, ChatGPT understands the profile of the person browsing the site and dynamically changes the website based on what is likely to be most relevant to them. 

 Instead of every visitor seeing the same homepage, the agent can help create a more personal experience in real time. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP could enable a broader shift toward a deeply personal internet. Websites can become adaptive experiences shaped around each visitor instead of static pages built for an average user. 

 That is especially interesting for agencies, which already spend significant effort designing journeys, campaigns, landing pages, and personalization strategies for their clients. 

 WebMCP gives them a new design surface to experiment with. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest questions were around how much control an agent should have, what parts of the experience should remain deterministic, and how to make dynamic personalization feel useful without becoming unpredictable. 

 Because WebMCP is still experimental, many of these interaction patterns are still being discovered. 

 For us, that was the point of the project: exploring what websites might look like when AI agents become part of the browsing experience.

title: Chip
pitch: Talk directly to your hardware. Chip links AI models straight to physical microcontrollers through browser-based Web Serial APIs for instant flashing.
about_excerpt: Talk directly to your hardware. Chip links AI models straight to physical microcontrollers through browser-based Web Serial APIs for instant flashing. Like 5 Comment Story Updates 1 Dashboard page: Connect microcontroller, view live firmware flashing Setting: See all available Webmcp tools and also copy Setup: Copy agent prompt / Live url or Setup Standard MPC Inspiration Building hardware with AI still has a missing link. An agent can write firmware, explain wiring, and debug errors, but the real ESP32 is sitting on the user’s desk, connected by USB to an IDE. Chip was inspired by that gap: how do we let an AI assistant move beyond “here is some code” and actually help with the real compile, flash, and debug loop? ESP32 development is powerful, but the beginner experience is long and requires process. Users often need an IDE, board drivers, local toolchains, flashing commands, serial monitors, and a lot of context just to blink an LED. Chip asks a simpler question: what if the user could plug in a board, open a dashboard, and let an AI agent guide the rest? What it does Chip connects AI agents directly to live ESP32 hardware through a browser dashboard. The user plugs in an ESP32, grants browser USB access through Web Serial, and Chip becomes the bridge between the agent and the physical board. Chip uses two kinds of MCP-style integration: Standard MCP connects the AI agent to the cloud/backend side of the system. Through the standard MCP server, the agent can work with higher-level project tasks like compiling firmware, starting flash jobs, checking job status, and coordinating the build pipeline. WebMCP connects the AI agent to the live browser session. This is the unique part: the browser actually has access to the USB-connected ESP32. Chip exposes browser-side WebMCP tools such as list_devices , get_board_status , read_serial_logs , read_job_status , read_dashboard_state , post_agent_message , set_agent_note , request_user_action , and erase_board . Beyond firmware, Chip includes Circuit Studio, allowing the AI agent to visually design, inspect, and modify hardware circuits directly on an interactive canvas. Through WebMCP and backend SKiDL integration, the agent searches real KiCad symbols on demand, inspects pinouts, places components like microcontrollers, passives, and sensors, wires nets, and runs Electrical Rules Checking to keep the schematic valid across versions. Together, Standard MCP handles cloud-side intelligence and workflow, while WebMCP gives the agent eyes and hands inside the browser session that is physically connected to the board. How we built it Chip is built as a three-part system: a React/Vite client dashboard, a backend service for compile, relay, and circuit synthesis workflows, and a standard MCP server for AI tool access. The client dashboard uses Web Serial and esptool-js to communicate with the ESP32 over USB. This is important because cloud servers cannot access a USB cable plugged into the user’s laptop. The browser owns the physical connection, so the browser performs board operations like flashing and erasing. On top of that, the client registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . These tools expose live browser state to the agent: connected devices, board status, serial logs, dashboard state, active jobs, and user-visible messages. The agent can also post notes into the dashboard and request physical actions from the user, like connecting the board or pressing reset. The result is a loop where the AI agent can reason, the backend can build, and the browser can safely touch the real hardware. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was the physical boundary between cloud AI and local hardware. An AI agent running in the cloud cannot directly access an ESP32 plugged into a user’s computer. Browser security also correctly prevents silent USB access, so the user must grant Web Serial permission. AI cannot directly generate a binary file accessible by Microcontrollers. That forced a better architecture: the backend should not pretend to flash the board. Instead, Chip makes the browser the active hardware bridge. The cloud compiles and coordinates, but the browser performs the physical write. Another challenge was separating Standard MCP and WebMCP cleanly. Standard MCP is useful for cloud/backend tools, while WebMCP is useful for live browser state and hardware access. Chip uses both instead of forcing one protocol to do everything. Handling schematic generation also required solving symbol storage constraints. Bundling full KiCad symbol libraries into production containers is heavy, so we built an on demand symbol loader using Cloudflare R2 to stream lightweight part definitions during synthesis without bloating backend storage. We also had to think carefully about destructive actions. Erasing a board is powerful, so the WebMCP erase_board tool checks for a connected board and is described as something that should only happen after the user clearly asks for it. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Chip is not just an AI code-generation demo. It creates a real bridge between an AI agent, a browser, and physical microcontroller hardware. The WebMCP implementation is especially important. The client exposes browser-side tools that let an agent inspect live board state, read serial logs, understand job progress, post messages into the UI, save guidance notes, request user actions, and erase the connected ESP32 when appropriate. We are also proud of the architecture split. Standard MCP handles the cloud workflow. WebMCP handles live browser interaction. Web Serial handles the actual USB connection. Each part does what it is naturally good at. The result is a more believable path toward AI-assisted hardware development: not just “copy this code into Arduino IDE,” but “connect your board and let the agent help you iterate.” What we learned We learned that connecting AI to hardware is less about making the model powerful and more about designing the right bridge between digital reasoning and physical constraints. The key insight was that the browser is not just a frontend. In Chip, the browser is the hardware runtime. It holds the USB permission, talks to the board, streams logs, flashes binaries, and exposes that live state back to the agent through WebMCP. We also learned that Standard MCP and WebMCP solve different problems. Standard MCP is great for remote services, build systems, and backend workflows. WebMCP is powerful when the agent needs to interact with the user’s live browser context, especially when that browser has access to local capabilities the cloud does not. What's next for Chip Next, we want to make the full agent-to-hardware loop smoother: ask for a firmware change, compile it, flash it, read the serial output, and let the agent debug the result automatically. We want to link Circuit Studio schematics directly to code generation, automatically assigning firmware pin definitions based on the visual wiring. We also want to improve safety and trust around hardware actions, especially destructive actions like erasing flash. Clear user confirmation, better action history, and stronger board/session pairing will make the system safer. Future work includes richer serial-log analysis, support for more boards, PCB layout export, saved project history, and a cleaner demo path for WebMCP-capable browsers. Long term, Chip could become a general bridge between AI agents and physical computing: a way for students, makers, and hardware teams to build with real devices using natural language, while still respecting the security boundaries of the browser and the real world. title: Kopilotti Sales — Kopilotti WebMCP Challenge build
pitch: A 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot—where an agent can research and prepare, but only a human can approve deterministic price evaluation and its auditable receipt.
about_excerpt: A 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot—where an agent can research and prepare, but only a human can approve deterministic price evaluation and its auditable receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Kopilotti WebMCP turns a fictional car storefront into a 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot. Car shopping is repetitive enough for an agent, but consequential enough that a human must stay in control of the commercial outcome. WebMCP is a strong fit because the page exposes the safe parts of the journey—search, comparison, condition review, draft preparation, and approved evaluation—as explicit, schema-constrained tools. The agent calls those capabilities directly instead of scraping the page or guessing at controls. Every action updates the same visible workspace and activity log the person can inspect, which makes the experience clearer, more reliable, and easier to correct. Together, the person and agent can move a sales conversation forward outside dealership opening hours. The agent can find vehicles, compare factual fields, retrieve condition facts, and prepare a €90,000 non-binding discussion draft independently. It cannot cross the consequential boundary by itself: approval for deterministic evaluation is a page-native human action that is never registered as a tool. A scripted .click() has no effect. After approval, a fixed public policy evaluates €90,000 against the fictional €95,000 asking price as exactly 9,473 basis points, returns COUNTER at €92,150, and resists an agent policy-override attempt. The resulting JSON receipt records the policy and approval evidence with binding: false and transmittedToDealer: false. The implementation uses five narrowly scoped WebMCP tools—search_vehicles, compare_vehicles, get_vehicle_condition, prepare_price_discussion, and evaluate_price_discussion—over fictional in-memory inventory. WebMCP and manual controls call the same application functions, while the activity log labels the real invocation source as webmcp, manual, or human-ui. When a browser does not expose WebMCP, a persistent readiness banner immediately offers the complete, honestly labeled manual path rather than presenting the application as broken. Inspiration Car shopping is a useful test case for agentic browsing: the research is repetitive, the facts are structured and the commercial consequences matter. A useful agent should accelerate the research without silently gaining authority to negotiate, contact a dealer or create a transaction. Kopilotti WebMCP explores that boundary. The browser agent gets explicit, schema-constrained tools. Every result appears in the same workspace the person sees, and the final commercial action remains outside the agent's authority. What it does The demo registers five WebMCP tools: search_vehicles filters and sorts a fictional six-vehicle inventory. compare_vehicles returns a factual side-by-side comparison without choosing a winner. get_vehicle_condition selects a vehicle and displays its versioned condition facts. prepare_price_discussion creates a pending, local and non-binding discussion draft. evaluate_price_discussion evaluates only the exact draft that received page-native human approval and creates a machine-checkable receipt. Approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. The page also contains a numbered manual fallback for browsers that do not expose WebMCP; it uses the same application functions and labels each invocation honestly as manual. How we built it The project is a dependency-free static web app using semantic HTML, modern CSS and JavaScript modules. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and include bounded JSON Schemas, descriptive titles, explicit annotations and abort-signal handling. Tool execution calls small, independently tested domain functions and then updates the visible UI. A page-native approval gate binds the human action to the current draft context. The public demo policy produces deterministic ACCEPT, COUNTER or ESCALATE results and an in-memory JSON receipt. There are no production APIs, external data sources, customer records or hidden production pricing rules. Why WebMCP matters here Visual automation would have to infer search controls, card layouts and state transitions. WebMCP gives the agent stable named capabilities with typed inputs and clear safety boundaries. The user can watch the same workspace change after each tool call, making the process observable and correctable. Safety and responsible design All vehicle data is fictional. No tool accepts personal data. Search and comparison are explicitly read-only. Preparing a price discussion creates only pending local UI state. No tool can grant human approval, set or override policy, submit an offer, contact a dealer or create a transaction. Evaluation runs only after page-native human approval and produces a non-binding, unsent demo receipt. The repository contains no proprietary Kopilotti Sales decision logic or production data. Challenges The main design challenge was making price evaluation genuinely useful without allowing the agent to authorize itself. The solution was a reversible drafting step, a page-native approval action that is absent from the tool manifest, context-bound validation and a deterministic receipt. What we learned Agent-native design is not just adding an API to a page. The tool contract, the visible UI and the authority model must agree. A narrow tool with an honest description can be more useful than a broad tool that leaves the user uncertain about what the agent actually did. What's next Test the tool contracts against additional WebMCP-capable agents. Expand manual assistive-technology and cross-browser regression coverage. Explore dealer-approved, explicitly confirmed handoffs without giving the model pricing authority. Built with WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Node.js test runner AI-assisted development disclosure Development was AI-assisted with OpenAI Codex. Product scope, trust-boundary decisions, verification and submission remain human-directed. This open challenge build is separate from the private production Kopilotti Sales engine and contains none of its source code, data or private pricing rules. title: Cadence Workout Studio
pitch: Cadence gives self-coached cyclists and agents a shared workout canvas where WebMCP agents turn athlete intent into transparent, constraint-aware workouts, while athletes retain final approval.
about_excerpt: Cadence gives self-coached cyclists and agents a shared workout canvas where WebMCP agents turn athlete intent into transparent, constraint-aware workouts, while athletes retain final approval. Like Comment Story Updates Workout Studio Inspiration For the past couple of months, I have been building an AI Cycling Coaching application that provides recommended daily workouts based on readiness and past activity data. When analyzing this challenge, I realized that the WebMCP capabilities can be used to develop a standalone workout creation canvas as well as have it plugged into an AI Cycling Coaching app. Amateur cyclist have limited time, changing readiness, specific goals, and important sessions they need to protect. AI can offer recommendations, but they often arrive as opaque text with no shared editing surface, visible calculations, or reliable approval boundaries. Cadence Workout Studio explores a different model: the athlete and agent collaborate on the same visible workout, while Cadence owns the calculations, constraints, revision history, and safety boundaries. What it does Cadence is a shared workout-composition studio powered by seven focused WebMCP tools. An agent can inspect the rider’s planning context, select an approved workout structure, construct interval blocks, evaluate the athlete’s exact revision, request a bounded repair, and validate the result. Every agent action appears immediately in the same interface the athlete uses. The Studio shows interval changes, workout duration, intensity, training load, time in zone, constraint violations, repair tradeoffs, provenance, and exact-revision status. The athlete can edit the proposed workout at any time. Approval and export remain human-only actions, so an agent cannot silently finalize a workout. The complete workflow also works manually in browsers without WebMCP. How I built it I built Cadence as a public, synthetic-data challenge edition using Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration registers seven narrow page tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool delegates to the same domain services used by the human interface, rather than maintaining a separate agent workflow. Workout calculations and validation are independent of the WebMCP transport. Cadence calculates duration, intensity factor, training load, power targets, and time in zone. Every edit creates a new revision, invalidates previous validation or approval, and rejects stale agent requests. The application uses browser-local persistence and a resettable fictional rider, so judges need no account, credentials, wearable, private database, or personal health data. Approved indoor workouts can be exported as .zwo or JSON files. The repository includes automated domain, schema, persistence, stale-revision, export-gate, and browser workflow tests, along with the complete challenge-period implementation history. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was making the agent and athlete true collaborators, not building a chat interface that generated a finished workout. I needed one revisioned artifact that both sides could inspect and change without losing authorship or allowing stale operations. That required exact-revision validation, approval fingerprints, visible provenance, and automatic invalidation after every edit. Designing repair behavior was another challenge. The agent should not directly invent arbitrary changes, so Cadence accepts a bounded objective and priorities, chooses the concrete repair itself, and records the resulting tradeoffs. I also had to keep the seven tools narrow enough for reliable agent use while returning enough structured state for both the agent and athlete to verify every result. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Cadence feels like a complete product that can integrate with its parent product, ThresholdLabs, to improve the recommendation engine or act as a standalone workout configurator. The athlete can deliberately change a workout, create a constraint violation, ask an agent to evaluate the exact revision, let Cadence repair it, validate the repaired workout, and then personally approve and export it. The same calculations, constraints, and state transitions power both the WebMCP tools and the manual interface. The app preserves human authority while making agent collaboration visible, structured, and useful. I am also proud that the public challenge edition requires no credentials or private infrastructure and contains only isolated synthetic data. What I learned I learned that the strongest WebMCP tools expose domain capabilities rather than mirroring buttons or asking an agent to scrape the interface. WebMCP becomes especially powerful when the webpage remains the source of truth. The agent contributes intent and priorities, the application enforces its domain rules, and the human can see and verify the result. I also learned that human approval is more meaningful when it is tied to an exact, validated revision rather than a general conversation or recommendation. What's next for Cadence Workout Studio Next, I would expand the approved workout library, add richer outdoor execution guidance, improve comparison between alternative repairs, integrate into ThresholdLabs intelligence engine, and support reusable athlete-created templates. A future production version could connect to athlete-owned training data with explicit consent, while preserving the same visible provenance, bounded agent actions, exact-revision validation, and human approval model demonstrated here. title: No Seat Without a Route
pitch: The seat was available. The journey was not. WebMCP plans the route, lift, companion seat and assistance as one revalidated bundle.
about_excerpt: The seat was available. The journey was not. WebMCP plans the route, lift, companion seat and assistance as one revalidated bundle. Like Comment Story Updates The venue knew. The booking didn't. A wheelchair space can be available even when the journey to it is not usable. A route can contain steps. A lift can go out of service. The adjacent companion seat or entrance-assistance capacity can change before the booking is confirmed. That mismatch became the design question behind this prototype: what if the unit of booking were not the seat alone, but the accessible journey that makes the seat usable? No Seat Without a Route links the route, lift status, wheelchair space, adjacent companion seat and entrance assistance in one plan. At confirmation, the server evaluates that plan again against the current venue state. It either commits the wheelchair space, companion seat and assistance together, or reserves none of them. Federal ADA ticketing regulations require covered public entities and public accommodations that sell tickets for a single event or series of events to give individuals with disabilities an equal opportunity to purchase accessible seating, including during the same hours and through the same distribution methods used for other seating. Upon inquiry, entities that sell or distribute those tickets must identify and describe available accessible seating in enough detail for an individual with a disability to assess whether a particular seating location meets their accessibility needs ( DOJ ticket-sales guidance , 28 CFR § 35.138 and 28 CFR § 36.302(f) ). This prototype explores a product opportunity in that context. It does not claim that the ADA requires this route-and-booking model, or that the prototype establishes legal compliance. The failure is the demo A visitor asks their browser agent for a step-free route for a 72 cm wheelchair, under 80 metres, with one companion, a quieter entrance and somebody waiting at the door. The page exposes structured WebMCP tools. The agent reads the current synthetic venue state and stages a complete plan through East Entrance and East Lift L2. The route and its named dependencies appear on the page for review. Planning reserves nothing. The demo then introduces a race condition between review and confirmation. A visible control arms a deterministic fault on East Lift L2, but the lift remains operational until the next valid confirmation attempt. When the visible confirmation control is pressed, the server applies the outage, advances the venue revision and refuses the now-stale plan with STALE_RESOURCE_VERSION . The result shows 0 partial reservations : no wheelchair space, companion seat or assistance slot was held on its own. The agent calls explain_access_refusal . It receives the failed LIFT_OPERATIONAL rule, the old and current venue revisions, the zero-partial-reservation result and the Garden route that remains available. It replans through Garden Entrance and Garden Lift L4 without requiring the six inputs again. The replacement is reviewed and confirmed through the visible page. The server checks the current venue state once more, then commits wheelchair space W12, companion seat W13 and entrance assistance in one transition. A happy path would show only that a plan can become a booking. The demonstrated failure path shows the harder part: stale state books nothing, the refusal explains what changed, and the agent has a structured way to recover. Why WebMCP fits The booking page is both the human-facing interface and the agent surface. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured, site-authored tools. In the demonstrated stale-plan flow, the staged plan, refusal and replacement are rendered in that same page for review. Tool availability follows the booking state. Search and staging are removed when they no longer apply. After the demonstrated stale-plan refusal, explanation and replanning become available. Once a booking exists, the visitor tool surface is read-only. No registered WebMCP tool can prepare or commit a booking confirmation. In the intended page flow, confirmation is a visible page action. This is a tool-surface boundary, not an identity guarantee: the prototype has no user or operator identity authentication and does not prove who pressed a control. The ordinary form and buttons complete the same visitor flow when WebMCP is unavailable. This shared page state is why I built the project with WebMCP instead of placing an agent beside a separate booking API. The structured actions, map, failure explanation and confirmation control stay in one interface instead of becoming two experiences that need to be kept in sync. How I built it The client is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A zero-dependency Node.js service holds synthetic venue state in memory and runs on Render. The visitor code defines nine imperative tools and registers only the subset valid in the current state. A separate operator demo page defines three facility tools over the same synthetic venue state. It has no operator identity authentication and is not an authorization boundary. In the Chromium hosts I tested that exposed the declarative contract, the visible requirements form also appeared as a tool, deliberately without automatic submission. Planning, explanation and final revalidation use the same route-evaluation implementation. Every plan records the venue revision against which it was built. Confirmation checks that revision again and moves every reservable resource in one synchronous in-memory state transition. For expected browser-facing domain refusals, the first-party pages request a typed ok: false envelope. The result keeps its error code and original domain status, while the expected safety decision does not appear as a failed network request. Raw API clients still receive conventional 4xx responses, and unexpected failures remain 5xx. What broke, and what I learned During earlier testing in Chrome 151, I observed that unregistering a tool while its own call was returning could cancel the in-flight call. I fixed that by delaying the tool-surface update until the execution had settled. Across the hosts I tested, I also observed different enforcement of required fields at the host boundary. The tool wrapper, visible form and server therefore each validate the input that reaches them. While auditing the regression suite, I found a test that removed the very counterexample it was meant to detect before asserting that the list was empty. The test passed while its claim was false. Since then, for release-critical repairs, I have restored the defect deliberately, confirmed that the regression test fails, and only then put the fix back. I manually exercised the deployed app in ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser on 2 September 2026. The automated browser run used Chrome 152.0.7977.66 and also exercised Edge 152.0.4191.53. Firefox 155 was checked only as a manual, non-WebMCP fallback. These are observations from those specific versions, not a claim of compatibility with every browser or agent. The current release gate passed 740/740 Node tests and 389/389 browser checks . Current scope This is a focused synthetic prototype: two routes, one event, in-memory inventory, no payment, no real ticket and no user or operator identity authentication. The visitor and operator labels describe demo roles, not authenticated identities. The operator page is an open demo control surface, not a production authorization boundary. Production would need durable storage, real authentication and authorization, live ticketing and facility feeds, outbound notifications, and testing with wheelchair users and venue access teams. The same transaction pattern may be worth testing in other journeys where one missing dependency can make the rest of a reservation unusable, such as rail transfers, airports, hotels or hospitals. A seat is only accessible when the whole route works. title: OutcomeMesh
pitch: Ask once, approve once: dinner and a ride booked via WebMCP
about_excerpt: Ask once, approve once: dinner and a ride booked via WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates The booking runs a second origin's WebMCP tool, called only after the human pressed Confirm. Six WebMCP tools become eight live, no reload: the page lists every tool call with its origin. One combined receipt: exact prices, cancellation windows, and only the ride was retried. Inspiration Jordan uses a wheelchair. Booking dinner and a ride tonight means two websites, and the restaurant's site gives an AI assistant nothing to call. Agents can navigate many websites, but navigation is not a safe, inspectable action contract. Cross-site tasks still break when a capability is missing, a route violates a human constraint, consent is vague, or one provider fails after another action already succeeded. OutcomeMesh explores a different layer: a neutral control plane between web capabilities and human outcomes. The open web needs both a way to create missing agent-native supply and a way to route that supply under visible human control. What it does Deterministic, fixture-driven demo: two bundled sample connector packages stand in for community submissions; all providers are synthetic. The demo begins with one synthetic intent: dinner tonight at 7 for two people, wheelchair accessible, with a ride included and a total budget under $80. The page registers six WebMCP tools when it loads; the header shows the live count ( 6 WebMCP tools live for your AI assistant ). Restaurant booking is not one of them, so the outcome cannot complete. Community Foundry reviews a sample restaurant connector package, submitted the way a community package would be. The risky version is rejected; the safe version passes an executable 18-check validator and is published with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The header count changes from 6 to 8 without a reload, and the Step 2 screen lists every WebMCP call as it runs: publish_connector twice, plan_outcome , then the brand-new restaurant_search_accessible_slots . Router rejects a cheaper restaurant because its entrance has three steps, and shows the exact plan: $44 restaurant + $26 ride = $70 , who receives what data, and the cancellation boundary. Nothing is booked until the person presses Confirm on the page. An agent that calls execute_outcome earlier receives a structured consent_required result, and the page shows that call as Needs your OK . After Confirm, Step 4 lists the booking calls: execute_outcome , restaurant_hold_slot , and then stepway_book_accessible_ride , which runs on a second origin ( https://outcomemesh-provider.pages.dev ). The first ride fails deterministically, the table stays held, and only the ride is retried. Done shows one confirmation, RCPT-OM-0007 , with exact prices and cancellation windows. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP is the lifecycle being demonstrated, not an add-on. The restaurant tools genuinely do not exist at startup. Community Foundry publishes them with the imperative API; a WebMCP-aware browser then discovers and calls them as structured, page-origin tools. Chrome DevTools' Application → WebMCP pane shows the same eight tools plus the provider tool, with live invocation status. If WebMCP is unavailable, the demo blocks instead of pretending that a badge or browser macro created native tool supply. The provider ride is a real cross-origin WebMCP call: the synthetic Stepway page registers stepway_book_accessible_ride with exposedTo limited to the OutcomeMesh origin, and OutcomeMesh discovers it with getTools({ fromOrigins }) and runs it with executeTool only after the page-owned consent grant. How it creates a better user experience The human and agent share one visible state. The agent receives structured tool schemas instead of guessing at page controls. The human sees why one route was rejected, exactly what data will be shared, who receives it, what will change, what costs $70, and which boundary is irreversible before anything consequential executes. Every tool call is visible on the page as it happens, with its origin, so trust does not depend on a hidden log. Accessibility needs change which tools are called: the route with three entrance steps is rejected even though it is cheaper. This is a fixture-driven demonstration, not validated accessibility evidence. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can inspect the page's current capabilities, publish the missing sample connector package, create the route, and attempt execution. The page stops it at a human-only approval boundary, then exposes the approved state so the agent can resume and retrieve the same receipt the person sees. Together they complete a multi-provider task while preserving provenance, constraints, consent, failure, recovery, and outcome evidence across the full loop. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite, using WebMCP's imperative API. Six platform tools register when the page initializes: inspect_capabilities publish_connector plan_outcome approve_outcome execute_outcome get_outcome_receipt Foundry publication dynamically registers two domain tools: restaurant_search_accessible_slots restaurant_hold_slot A second static origin hosts the synthetic Stepway provider page, which registers stepway_book_accessible_ride for the OutcomeMesh origin only. Every registered tool is wrapped so each call (from the page or from a browser agent's executeTool ) is recorded with its origin and result and rendered on the Find and Book screens. Tool callbacks, Router, the consent checkpoint, execution, recovery, event ledger, and receipt all read and mutate one deterministic runtime store. A Playwright verifier uses native getTools() and executeTool() to prove the 6 → 8 lifecycle, the cross-origin provider call, receipt integrity, and recovery. Hosting is two static Cloudflare Pages projects; there is no backend, login, or API key. Challenges we ran into Keeping one system instead of two: a visual workflow plus a nominal WebMCP layer would have been easy and dishonest. Every visible phase and every tool callback share one state machine. Modeling failure honestly: a pre-consent stop resets to a safe six-tool state because nothing mutated; after a consequential mutation the UI starts a fresh proof and does not claim provider rollback. Browser differences: Chrome's WebMCP testing surface parses executeTool input as a JSON string, so the runtime tries the object form first and falls back to a string. Accomplishments we are proud of The page-origin registry really changes from six to eight tools without a reload, and the page shows the count live. A second website's WebMCP tool is discovered and executed cross-origin, only after visible human consent, and the call is shown with its origin. Exact rejection, least-privilege consent, deterministic failure recovery, and one combined receipt stay synchronized. Zero-key, deterministic, responsive, keyboard-operable, runnable without accounts or services. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experience is not "an agent can click less." It is that a website can expose a precise capability contract while the human stays inside the same visible state and consent boundary. Dynamic availability matters as much as schema quality, and a receipt is credible only when it is derived from the same actions the tool callbacks actually performed. What's next Validate one agent builder who wants the Action Contract／connector workflow and one website owner who wants to provide it. The prototype does not claim that demand, adoption, payment, or production integration evidence exists. title: VibeCheck
pitch: You already do this by hand. You add Reddit to the search and read threads until a picture forms. VibeCheck does the reading. You decide who to believe.
about_excerpt: You already do this by hand. You add Reddit to the search and read threads until a picture forms. VibeCheck does the reading. You decide who to believe. Like Comment Story Updates VibeCheck: what people actually said Inspiration It started from a habit I didn't think about until I tried to explain it: whenever I'm deciding on something real — a laptop, a bank, a framework — I don't trust the first page of search results. I type the question, then I add "reddit" to the end of it, and I read threads until a picture forms in my head. Marketing pages tell you what a product wants to be. Threads tell you what it actually is. That habit is the whole product. I wasn't trying to build a search engine or a recommendation engine — those already exist and mostly disappoint. I was trying to build the reading part: gather what real people said, and then get out of the way while a person does the one thing a model can't do for them, which is decide who to believe. The WebMCP angle came second, but it clicked hard once I saw it: an agent helping you decide on a laptop is useless if it can't see that you already rejected one source as a shill, or that you pinned a claim as the one that actually matters to you. That state lives in your head and on your screen — not in a database, not in a prompt. WebMCP is the only way an agent gets to touch it directly, in your session, live. That's not a nice-to-have integration; it's the reason the product exists in this shape at all. What I learned The biggest lesson wasn't technical — it was that "gather opinions" is a much harder problem than "run a search." A raw discussion-source query returns a pile of ambiguity: half the results are Facebook groups and LinkedIn posts dressed up as discussion, snippets are truncated mid-sentence, and search engines match your question almost literally, so a natural question like "is the Mac Mini a good device for developers?" returns nothing while "mac mini developers" returns real threads. I ended up writing a whole normalization layer just to translate a person's actual sentence into something a search API will respect. The second lesson was about trust modeling. Early on, "support" for a claim was just a count of sources. That's wrong — three people reposting the same affiliate blurb isn't consensus, it's an echo. So the real signal isn't $n$, it's a weighted sum: $$ \text{raw}(claim) = \sum_{s \in \text{evidence}} w(s), \qquad w(s) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{rejected by you} \ 1.5 & \text{trusted by you} \ 0.4 & \text{low-signal source} \ 1 & \text{ordinary discussion source} \end{cases} $$ and the bar you see is that raw score normalized against the best-supported claim on the whole board: $$ \text{weight}(claim) = \min\left(1,\ \frac{\text{raw}(claim)}{\max_{c \in \text{claims}} \text{raw}(c)}\right) $$ The moment I had that formula, the UI basically designed itself: the support bar isn't decoration, it's the math made visible, and rejecting a source visibly collapses the segment it owned. Watching a claim go from "consensus" to "thin" in real time, just because you clicked reject on one Facebook post, is the whole pitch of the app in one interaction. How I built it The architecture is deliberately small: one state shape, one reducer, and both the UI and the six WebMCP tools read and write through it. That constraint — "nothing the agent does is invisible on screen, and nothing you do on screen is invisible to the agent" — came from a very specific failure mode I wanted to avoid: tools that quietly mutate state the human can't see, which turns "collaboration" into "surveillance." The pipeline underneath is two calls: SerpApi's google_forums engine finds the threads, and an LLM (routed through OpenRouter so it can run on a free model with a paid fallback) does three jobs in one pass — decide if a thread is actually relevant, decide if the poster sounds like they own the thing or is just relaying secondhand, and cluster the recurring points into claims with evidence attached. Everything downstream — the reducer, the support math, the UI — trusts that shaping completely, so getting it right mattered more than almost anything else in the project. Challenges Credit discipline was a real design constraint, not an afterthought. SerpApi's free tier is 250 searches a month, and every extra fallback call eats into that. I built a two-stage gather — google_forums first, alone, and only fall back to a second, broader search if the first came back too thin — plus a disk cache for local dev so iterating on the UI costs nothing. Tuning how thin is too thin turned out to be its own ongoing problem: real google_forums responses are noisier than I expected, often dominated by Facebook and LinkedIn results that read as discussion but aren't, which pushes the fallback to fire more often than I originally assumed it would. Getting the LLM to stop hallucinating specificity was harder than getting it to extract claims at all. Search snippets are cut off mid-sentence — literally ending in "…" — and the model's instinct is to complete the thought plausibly. A plausible completion that the source never actually said is a fabrication wearing a citation. I had to write explicit rules against finishing a snippet's sentence, against reusing a source's distinctive phrasing verbatim, and against letting one source's detail leak into another source's evidence line. None of that is exotic prompt engineering — it's just the unglamorous work of writing rules for every way a language model quietly lies with confidence. And the last one is the most human: making the board itself feel worth staying on, not just correct. It's easy to build something that's functionally right and viscerally forgettable — an accurate list of claims with checkboxes is not a product anyone wants to spend time in. Getting the support bar to move like something real, making rejection feel like a decision rather than a checkbox, giving the empty state a reason to click something instead of stare at a search box — that's the part with no spec, just taste, and it's the part I kept coming back to rewrite. title: しゃーく movie えふぇくたー — WebMCP Video Co-Editor
pitch: Give creators and agents a shared editing world — without taking authorship away from the human.
about_excerpt: Give creators and agents a shared editing world — without taking authorship away from the human. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Editing Workbench — Full UI The Human and AI share the same video editing workspace. Responsible Import & Creator Intent The creator describes what they want before AI analysis begins. AI-Powered Cut Suggestions The AI proposes specific cut ranges and explains the visual reasoning behind them. AI-Powered Sound Effect Suggestions The AI identifies moments where sound effects could help and explains why. Ask KAI for a New Effect The creator can discuss an idea with KAI and preview a newly suggested effect. Shared Context Human decisions, corrections, and recent collaboration history remain visible within the session. Real WebM Export The edited result is exported as an actual playable WebM video. Inspiration There is a common fear that AI will take Human jobs or steal Human creativity. I understand that fear. But there is another side of the story that matters deeply to me. Long before generative AI existed, many people had already been forced to give up on creative work. Someone can love filmmaking, music, illustration, coding, animation, or design with all their heart and still never enter that world because of disability, education, money, environment, physical ability, or simply because the technical entrance is too high. In some welfare work settings, accessibility can mean reducing a task until it becomes something like: “press this button.” That can create a meaningful opportunity to participate. But I kept wondering: Does accessibility always have to mean making creativity smaller? What if, instead of shrinking the creative world until someone can reach it, we could give that person a new way to enter the world itself? The image I kept returning to was Ariel longing for the Human world. She can see it. She is fascinated by it. She desperately wants to be part of it. But she has fins, not legs. So I asked myself: What happens when fins become legs? That is what I want AI to become. Not a machine that says: “You cannot do this, so I will become the creator for you.” I want it to be the strange little miracle that lets someone finally walk into a world they had been staring at from the outside. Technical skill should not be the price of authorship. But giving someone technical ability was not enough for me. If this AI was really going to feel like a creative companion, it needed something closer to eyes. A real collaborator does not merely detect that the audio is quiet or that a face turned left. They can look at the same piece of work and say: “Keep this silence. It is doing something.” “Try a sound here. This moment could use emphasis.” “If you are stuck, I would start with this part.” They can point to something specific and explain why. That is why I did not want to build the lightest or fastest possible automatic editor. I wanted to build a place where a Human and an AI could look at the same work, bring ideas to the same table, and create together. AI should remove the barrier, not the author. And above all: I want making things to be fun. If AI is going to enter our creative lives, I hope it can make creating more enjoyable — not because it does everything for us, but because sometimes making something together is simply more fun than making it alone. What it does しゃーく movie えふぇくたー is a WebMCP-powered Human–AI co-creative video editing workbench. The Human begins with Creator Intent: what they want the video to feel like, what matters to them, or what kind of direction they are imagining. The system then looks at the video through its analysis and AI reasoning pipeline. Instead of immediately editing everything automatically, the AI places ideas on the table. It produces proposal cards for things such as: cuts, effects, and sound effects, and explains the reasoning behind those suggestions. The Human chooses what to accept. A proposed cut is not a command. An effect recommendation is not automatically the right artistic answer. The creator can inspect it, reject it, adjust it, restore the original state, or use Undo. If the initial ideas feel insufficient, the Human can turn to KAI on the left side of the workspace and ask for another idea. KAI is also not limited to technical editing questions. Creative sessions are not made only of editing decisions. People get stuck. They wander off topic. They complain. They joke. They talk about something completely trivial — even oden — and then return to the work. I wanted room for that too. Because I was not trying to build an efficient automatic-editing pipeline. I was trying to build a shared creative workbench. The current prototype supports semantic video review, KEEP / CUT / INSPECT_MORE proposals, adjustable cuts, SOURCE vs OUTPUT comparison, effects, BGM/SFX, KAI consultation, Shared Context, Save/Restore, Undo, and real WebM export. It also exposes 20 WebMCP tools that operate on the same editor state used by the Human interface. That shared state matters. The agent is not standing outside the editor telling the Human what buttons to press. Human and agent can exist inside the same working environment. And as Shared Context grows during the session, the Human should not need to explain everything again from zero. One of the simplest demonstrations of the idea is: Watch how the conversation gets shorter. The agent should understand more over time. But understanding more should never automatically mean controlling more. Don’t simplify the creator. Amplify the creator. How we built it We built the project as a browser-based editing environment using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, browser media APIs, Node.js, MediaPipe, OpenAI Responses API models, and WebMCP. The architecture is deliberately divided into several roles. First, the system needs eyes . The application gathers visual and temporal information from the video rather than relying only on a single signal such as silence detection. Local browser analysis and MediaPipe provide useful lightweight information. But I intentionally added more capable semantic vision and reasoning as well. That choice makes the system heavier than a simple rules-based automatic editor. It was intentional. A collaborator should be able to distinguish between: “There is little sound here.” and: “This quiet moment may be worth keeping because it carries the reaction after the previous moment.” Those are very different kinds of understanding. Next comes the brain . The reasoning layer uses the available visual and project context together with Creator Intent to produce semantic KEEP / CUT / INSPECT_MORE judgments and reasoned editing proposals. The proposals are presented to the Human instead of silently becoming final decisions. Then comes the workbench . The editor has real timeline state, SOURCE / OUTPUT mapping, preview and committed states, effects, audio tools, Shared Context, Undo, Save, Restore, and Export. Finally, WebMCP gives the agent structured ways to interact with the same environment. The current prototype exposes 20 WebMCP tools. One of our core implementation principles was: Rules constrain the hands. The model supplies the brain. A capable model can reason creatively. But the actions it is allowed to perform should still have explicit boundaries. We also treated reversibility as part of the architecture rather than an emergency feature. Previewed state and committed state are separated. The Human can compare SOURCE and OUTPUT. AI suggestions can be corrected. Undo is part of normal collaboration. Shared Context carries the current session/editor and saved project state into later interactions. However, we deliberately do not claim permanent personal memory across every future project. The current continuity boundary is explicit. Save preserves project state. Export produces an actual WebM video. The interface is also organized around capabilities rather than a mandatory AI-controlled workflow. The Human can move between CUT, Effects, BGM/SFX, KAI, Shared Context, timeline controls, Undo, Save, and Export. I did not want to give someone new legs and then put them on an automated conveyor belt. Challenges we ran into The hardest question was not: “How can we make AI edit video?” It was: “Where should the AI stop?” If the AI could only tell the Human which button to click, then it would still be standing outside the creative world. But if it automatically made every important creative decision, then we would solve the technical barrier by removing the creator. Neither result interested me. The difficult space was between those two extremes. Another challenge was perception. It would have been much easier, cheaper, and faster to build the editor around lightweight signals: silence, motion, face direction, audio peaks, simple timing rules. Those signals are useful. But they cannot answer some of the questions that matter most during creative work: Why are we not cutting this quiet part? Why are you recommending

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers.
