 AgroAgent — AI That Works With the Agricultural Web 

 Inspiration
Agriculture is one of the most important sectors for communities in Nigeria, yet many smallholder farmers still make critical decisions with limited access to timely information. Farmers need to know when to plant, what crops are suitable, which inputs to use, what the weather may look like, and where they can get better market information.
The inspiration for AgroAgent came from my work developing Smart Agro Insight, an agricultural technology concept designed to help smallholder farmers access agricultural information and make better decisions using data and technology.
I wanted to take that idea one step further.
Instead of building another agricultural chatbot that simply gives farmers answers, I wanted to explore a future where an AI agent can actually interact with agricultural web services and tools on behalf of the farmer.
This led to AgroAgent: an AI-powered agricultural web agent designed around WebMCP. The goal is to make the web more useful to farmers by allowing an AI agent to discover and interact with agricultural capabilities rather than simply generating text.
The project was founded and developed by Yahaya Abubakar under YABTECH SMART AGRO INSIGHT ENTERPRISES.
What It Does
AgroAgent is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform for smallholder farmers, cooperatives and agribusiness users.
A farmer can communicate with AgroAgent using natural language instead of navigating through many different agricultural services.
For example, a farmer can ask:
"I want to plant maize on 2 hectares in Sokoto. Help me prepare."
AgroAgent is designed to break this request into useful agricultural actions.
The platform includes WebMCP tools for:
Weather information — checking weather conditions relevant to farming.
Crop information — finding information about crops, growing conditions and risks.
Agricultural inputs — searching for suitable seeds, fertilizer and crop-protection products.
Product comparison — comparing available agricultural inputs.
Farm planning — creating a production plan based on crop and farm size.
Farm-plan saving — saving the generated plan for later use.
The platform also includes:
Farmer dashboard
AI Agricultural Agent
Weather dashboard
Crop information
Agricultural input marketplace
Market intelligence
Farm plans
Farmer profiles
Administrator dashboard
WebMCP tool diagnostics
The important difference is that AgroAgent is designed around the interaction between the farmer, the AI agent and web tools.
Instead of:
Farmer → AI → Answer
we are building:
Farmer → AI Agent → WebMCP Tools → Agricultural Information/Actions → Farmer
How We Built It
We started with the Smart Agro Insight agricultural concept and created a new WebMCP-focused application called AgroAgent.
The prototype was designed as a modular web application so that the agricultural services and AI interaction layer can evolve independently.
The application includes a responsive dashboard designed for both desktop and mobile users.
We created a dedicated WebMCP tool layer containing six core tools:
get_weather
search_crop_info
search_products
compare_products
create_farm_plan
save_farm_plan
The WebMCP implementation is structured around the browser's document.modelContext.registerTool() API so that the tools can be exposed to compatible AI agents.
We also created a data layer that currently provides a local-storage fallback for prototype testing and a Supabase-ready database architecture for production development.
The database structure includes entities for:
Farmers
Crops
Products
Market prices
Farm plans
Agent activity
The administrator dashboard is designed to provide a central place to manage farmers, farm plans and platform activity.
For the prototype, weather, market and agricultural product information is clearly identified as demo data. The architecture is designed so verified live APIs and Supabase can replace the demo layer as the project moves toward pilot implementation.
Challenges We Ran Into
One of our biggest challenges was understanding how to move beyond a conventional AI chatbot and build an application where the website itself exposes useful capabilities to an AI agent.
WebMCP introduced a different way of thinking about web applications. Instead of designing only screens and buttons for humans, we had to think about what capabilities an AI agent should be able to discover and use.
Another challenge was balancing ambition with the limited time available for the hackathon.
Agriculture has a very large scope. We initially had many possible features including weather forecasting, market intelligence, farm records, crop recommendations, agricultural inputs, buyers, supply-chain information and administrative management.
We therefore narrowed the first version to a focused workflow: helping a farmer plan maize production.
We also faced the challenge of building a meaningful WebMCP implementation while keeping the application usable in environments where native WebMCP support may not yet be available. To solve this, the prototype includes a local testing fallback while keeping the actual WebMCP registration layer separate and ready for testing in a supported environment.
Another challenge was ensuring that we did not present demo agricultural information as real-world advice. Therefore, demo weather and market information is explicitly labelled as prototype data and is intended to be replaced with verified sources before production deployment.
Accomplishments We Are Proud Of
We are proud that AgroAgent evolved from an agricultural idea into a working prototype with a clear agent + web tools architecture.
One of our biggest accomplishments is creating a dedicated set of agricultural tools that can be registered through WebMCP rather than building only a traditional chatbot.
We are particularly proud of the farm-planning workflow.
A farmer can express a goal in natural language, and the application can identify the relevant agricultural operations required to produce a farm plan.
We also built:
A complete agricultural dashboard
AI agent interface
Six WebMCP tool definitions
Agricultural crop database structure
Agricultural input catalogue
Market intelligence interface
Farm-plan management
Farmer profile
Administrator dashboard
Agent activity logging
Supabase-ready database schema
Mobile-responsive interface
Open-source project structure
Most importantly, AgroAgent demonstrates a different vision for agricultural technology: AI should not only tell farmers what to do; AI should be able to interact with useful agricultural services and help complete tasks.
What We Learned
We learned that building an AI application is not only about the AI model.
The real value comes from connecting AI to useful tools, structured information and actions.
WebMCP helped us think about the web as something an AI agent can interact with rather than simply something a human browses.
We learned to design tools around clear actions and inputs. For example, instead of asking an AI to "know everything about agriculture," we can give it specific capabilities such as:
Get weather.
Search crop information.
Search agricultural products.
Compare products.
Create a farm plan.
Save a farm plan.
We also learned the importance of building a focused MVP. A smaller workflow that works clearly is more valuable than a huge platform containing many unfinished features.
Finally, we learned that agricultural technology must be built responsibly. Weather, market and agronomic information can affect real financial decisions, so production deployment must use reliable, verified data sources and clearly communicate uncertainty.
What's Next for AgroAgent
The next stage is to move AgroAgent from a prototype toward a real pilot implementation with farmers.
Our priorities are: 

 
 Real WebMCP deployment
We will test the WebMCP tools in the supported environment and verify that AI agents can discover and execute them through the live application. 
 Supabase integration
We will connect the production database so farmer profiles, farm plans, products, market information and agent activity can be securely stored. 
 Verified agricultural data
We will replace demo weather and market information with reliable data sources and agricultural information appropriate for the target communities. 
 Local agricultural intelligence

title: How I Choose
pitch: How I Choose is a local-first rehearsal workspace that checks whether a communication partner followed a person's self-authored protocol-never evaluating the person.
about_excerpt: How I Choose is a local-first rehearsal workspace that checks whether a communication partner followed a person's self-authored protocol-never evaluating the person. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important conversations often become harder when speech, language, or processing gets difficult. Yet many communication tools still ask the person to perform better: answer faster, choose from someone else's categories, or fit a fixed conversational rhythm. We wanted to reverse that responsibility. How I Choose asks whether the communication partner adapted to the person—not whether the person performed correctly. The person defines what helps, what each signal means, how much time is needed, and what a partner must do next. The software turns those choices into a protocol that can be rehearsed and audited without inferring meaning from silence or delay. What it does How I Choose is a local-first communication rehearsal workspace for adults. A person authors their preferred channels, wording, pace, processing time, literal-language rules, semantic signals, and partner actions. They also choose exactly which fields an active browser agent may read. The workspace supports both human-only practice and an optional WebMCP agent rehearsal. Before any partner turn becomes visible, a deterministic engine checks it against the current protocol. It enforces one question at a time, word and option limits, channel rules, pending-signal acknowledgment, Pause, terminal Stop, revision freshness, conflicts, and idempotency. The person directly selects every semantic signal, including yes, no, not sure, more information, more time, rephrase, Pause, and Stop. Silence creates no event and never advances the rehearsal. Reports contain evidence about the partner's adherence and repairs ; they never score the person. The complete human-facing product includes: guided onboarding plus blank and clearly labeled synthetic profiles; profile, signal, and per-field agent-access editing; a large keyboard-accessible signal board; low-stakes rehearsal templates and partner-turn validation; partner-adherence audit and revision history; staged protocol suggestions with exact diffs and provenance; JSON import/export and a printable support guide; visible owner-only review and ratification; text-size, contrast, Quiet, and Plain language preferences. Why WebMCP This workflow needs an agent to operate inside the person's current, visible, revisioned protocol , not inside a detached chat containing copied instructions. WebMCP lets ChatGPT use the page's existing permissions, validator, state machine, and evidence while the person retains direct control of signals, rule changes, and approval. The workspace starts in Human-only mode. All eight Site tools fail closed until the person visibly enables Agent rehearsal. Once enabled, ChatGPT can read only allowlisted fields, audit readiness, start an already approved scenario, offer a validated partner turn, acknowledge the exact person-selected signal, inspect its own adherence, stage a draft improvement, and verify guide derivation. There is deliberately no tool for selecting a person's signal, answering for them, resuming, ratifying, publishing, sharing, exporting private data, deleting a profile, or assessing capacity, consent, diagnosis, comprehension, safety, or coercion. How we built it The app is a static Next.js and React application written in strict TypeScript. Dexie/IndexedDB is the durable local source of truth; Zustand holds hydrated read projections and transient preferences. Zod validates every persisted document, import, command, and Site-tool payload. Human controls and WebMCP handlers use the same application-service command path and pure domain logic. Compare-and-swap revisions, idempotency fingerprints, events, and state writes happen atomically in one IndexedDB transaction. Ratified profile snapshots are immutable and identified by canonical hashes. The top-level /demo/ page feature-detects WebMCP and imperatively registers a stable catalog through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_rehearsal_brief audit_rehearsal_readiness start_approved_rehearsal offer_partner_turn read_latest_signal get_rehearsal_report stage_protocol_patch verify_support_guide A singleton guard prevents duplicate registration under React Strict Mode. Every JSON Schema is bounded and closed with additionalProperties: false , then Zod validates again at the application boundary. Mutations require expected revisions and an idempotency key. Handlers resolve current IndexedDB state at invocation time instead of trusting stale UI state. The quality system combines Vitest, Testing Library, fast-check property tests, Playwright desktop and narrow-viewport suites, axe-core checks, dependency and secret audits, a static production build, and GitHub Actions. The release includes 76 unit, service, property, import/export, and agent-flow tests plus a complete 15-step browser judge path. Challenges we faced Treating discovery and authorization as separate problems. Registering a tool successfully does not mean it should be authorized in the current state. A real-browser test exposed an early version where Human-only was only presentation state. We fixed this by making owner-controlled agent access durable, revisioned session state and enforcing it inside every handler. Keeping agent authority physically narrow. Removing dangerous fields from a broad object was not enough. We created allowlisted agent DTOs and a separate AgentRehearsalService that cannot import owner-only ratification, signal selection, export, share, delete, or resume operations. Making concurrent changes recoverable. A person may change a rule while an agent is preparing a turn. Expected revisions cause the stale write to fail instead of overwriting the person's newer choice; the agent can reread the brief and adapt. Building safety without making clinical claims. The product is deliberately scoped to synthetic and low-stakes adult communication practice. It does not infer answers, assess a person, or present itself as a consent system, medical device, emergency plan, or legal instrument. Accomplishments that we're proud of One deterministic engine governs both human and agent partner turns. Human-only access fails closed, while owner-enabled agent access remains field-scoped and revisioned. Pause is immediately effective and Stop is terminal—no agent override exists. Stale revisions, duplicate requests, invalid turns, repair, signals, and provenance are visible and recoverable. Private notes are structurally absent from agent projections, and receipts contain metadata rather than authored conversation text. The full human product works without an account, backend, API key, remote database, analytics, or runtime external model call. The deployed production build was exercised in ChatGPT's real built-in browser: all eight tools were discovered and the guarded workflow, including Human-only denial and visible owner-enabled access, was verified. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes an existing trustworthy application boundary rather than creating a second automation-only path. Tool discovery, state authorization, validation, persistence, and visible evidence all need independent treatment. We also learned that “local-first” needs precise disclosure. Profiles and rehearsals stay in local, unencrypted IndexedDB, but fields explicitly exposed through Site tools are processed by the active browser agent. The interface says that plainly. Most importantly, semantic safety becomes more reliable when it is structural: the agent cannot manufacture a person-authored signal, Stop cannot be reversed, silence cannot become an answer, and suggestions remain drafts until the person reviews them. What's next The next phase is compensated co-design with people who use diverse communication methods, followed by deeper accessibility research and independent review. We also want to explore portable protocol formats, more rehearsal templates, stronger assistive-technology testing, and longitudinal partner-adherence evidence without introducing person scoring or surveillance. How I Choose is an open alpha, not a clinically validated product. The challenge profiles and scenarios are synthetic. Its contribution is an executable pattern for accountable communication agents: the person remains the source of meaning, while adaptation becomes testable. Verification note Real ChatGPT built-in-browser verification is documented separately in the public repository. The submitted video is an editorial product walkthrough using the real deployed interface and synthetic data; it does not claim to be footage of the separate live Site-tool test. She asks for text first, one short literal question, no more than two options, and explicit handling of every signal. The protocol is visible, editable, and versioned. Agent access is never assumed. An agent may stage a provenance linked improvement, but every change stays a draft until the person reviews it. The support guide is checked against accepted rules. Ratification is a visible owner workflow, never a site tool. How I choose is open alpha communication practice, not a consent system.

title: Shopify Catalog Health Copilot
pitch: A WebMCP copilot that helps Shopify merchants and AI agents find, fix, and verify catalog issues together, turning product data into search - and agent-ready storefronts.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP copilot that helps Shopify merchants and AI agents find, fix, and verify catalog issues together, turning product data into search - and agent-ready storefronts. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard List of WebMCP Tools on Chrome Agent edit and Merchant's correction Architecture Inspiration WebMCP already lets shopping agents interact with storefronts (I noticed Shopify-powered stores have this). I wanted to explore the merchant side of that future: who makes sure the underlying product catalog is understandable enough for those agents to use? Based on my research, catalog hygiene was the first pain point in the Shopify Reddit Community's "most annoying manual task" thread. Product catalogs often contain missing identifiers, vague descriptions, incomplete image alt text, inconsistent variants, and weak taxonomy. These issues affect traditional search today and can make products harder for AI shopping agents to understand and recommend. Catalog Health Copilot turns catalog maintenance into a collaborative workflow between a Shopify merchant (human) and an AI agent via webMCP. What it does Catalog Health Copilot connects to a Shopify development store and audits its products across six areas: Identifiers Product content Media SEO Commercial data Agent readiness It converts those findings into a prioritized issue queue and health score. From the same live page or dashboard, a merchant and their agent can: Scan the catalog. Find the highest-impact issues. Open a specific issue and inspect its context. Generate an OpenAI-assisted fix for text. Review or edit the proposed field-level change. Apply approved changes to Shopify. Re-fetch the product and verify the live result. Preview how a shopping agent interprets the product before and after the fix. The web app remains usable as an ordinary web application when WebMCP is unavailable or when humans are using it. WebMCP adds a structured collaboration layer rather than replacing the interface. Catalog auditing involves large amounts of repetitive inspection, prioritization, drafting, and verification. An agent is well suited to that labor, while the merchant should retain judgment over brand voice and product accuracy. Instead of asking an agent to guess its way through buttons and page layouts, the application exposes ten WebMCP tools : scan_catalog , get_health_score , list_issues , show_issue , generate_fix , apply_fix , apply_approved , dismiss_issue , verify_fix , and preview_agent_view . This lets the agent work with structured product data while keeping its actions visible in the same interface the merchant is viewing. When the agent selects an issue, creates a draft, or applies a fix, the page updates too. The result is a governed scan → explain → draft → review → apply → verify workflow that would be fragile and difficult to coordinate through visual browser automation alone. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. All WebMCP tools are registered in the top-level document using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The tools call the same catalog-controller functions used by the visible interface. This gives the human and the agent shared state, permissions, progress, and verification results. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and its API routes. It connects server-side to: Shopify Admin GraphQL API for catalog reads and controlled product updates OpenAI API for context-aware fix drafts, with deterministic templates as a fallback Cloudflare rate limiting and observability for protecting sensitive endpoints and recording mutation outcomes Shopify and OpenAI credentials never reach the browser. Safe demo-store writes The public demo intentionally allows controlled writes so judges can experience the complete WebMCP workflow. I added several server-enforced safeguards: Only products carrying the catalog-health-seed tag can be modified. Variant and image IDs must belong to the selected seeded product. Only an explicit allowlist of product fields is writable. A request can contain no more than ten changes. Write and OpenAI endpoints have independent rate limits. ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES provides an emergency kill switch. Every attempted mutation is logged with its outcome. A guarded reset command restores the deterministic 30-product demo catalog. These restrictions let the demonstration remain interactive without exposing a production storefront. Challenges I faced One major challenge was designing for WebMCP as a genuine product capability rather than attaching tools to an existing interface. ChatGPT’s in-app browser requires tools to be registered imperatively in the top-level document, so the application could not be an iframe or embedded Shopify Admin app. Another challenge was keeping the visible interface synchronized with agent activity. I solved this by routing both UI controls and WebMCP tools through the same controller instead of creating separate automation logic. The most important challenge was safe write access. A public demonstration needs to be easy for you, the judges, to use, but unrestricted Shopify mutations would be inappropriate. The seed-tag policy, ownership validation, allowlist, limits, logging, kill switch, and reset workflow let me keep the full experience available. What I learned I learned that agent-native UX is not simply about giving an agent more autonomy. The best experience makes actions structured, visible, interruptible, editable, and verifiable. I also learned that verification deserves to be a first-class tool. A successful API response is not enoughthe application re-fetches Shopify data and returns evidence that the intended field actually changed. Most importantly, WebMCP makes it possible for a human and an agent to operate inside one coherent product experience: the agent handles scale and repetition, while the human keeps context and judgment. What’s next For a production store, I would add merchant authentication, Shopify OAuth, role-based approvals, persistent audit history, configurable catalog policies, and scheduled monitoring. I would also expand the checks using storefront analytics and order history to identify products that are technically available but consistently undiscoverable. title: WordLift AI Audit
pitch: The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map for agents.
about_excerpt: The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map for agents. Like Comment Story Updates The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map. WordLift AI Audit turns a public website into an evidence-backed service map for AI agents. It reads representative pages, classifies the business, extracts domain entities and vocabulary, compiles the actions an agent should be able to perform, and verifies which machine interfaces actually work. But the machine output is deliberately a draft. Pages cannot prove every operating role, important entity, business term, or responsibility boundary. ChatGPT therefore interviews the human and compiles that judgment into a new immutable, human-refined service map. The problem Websites were designed as pages for people. Agents need explicit knowledge about the things a business offers, the functions they may call, the boundaries around those functions, and evidence that the interfaces really work. Most AI-readiness scanners stop at crawlability, metadata, or declarations. They cannot answer: Which action applies to which entity? Can people perform it today? Can an agent perform it? Who owns the action: the organization, a partner, or nobody? What evidence proves the conclusion? What governed contract would close the gap? What WordLift AI Audit does Analyzes up to four representative pages rather than only the homepage. Preserves the complete bounded WordLift foundation audit behind progressive disclosure. Classifies the site as commerce, publishing, travel, finance, SaaS, or a conservative fallback. Builds the Context Engine: domain graph — organizations, products, services, places, articles, offers, and provenance; lexical graph — categories, names, terminology, meanings, and aliases; action layer — expected actions, entity bindings, interfaces, boundaries, evidence, and contracts. Separates human-facing support from agent-facing declarations and successful invocation. Produces a machine-generated service-map draft with three priority gaps. Lets ChatGPT inspect that draft and interview the human about the business role, primary entities, terminology, and every expected action boundary. Compiles the human decisions into an immutable child report without altering the original evidence or allowing a human assertion to mark an action agent-ready. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is not an accessory to the interface; it is the collaboration protocol. The application exposes six generic tools: audit-website starts an audit of any safe public URL. get-audit-report follows a long-running audit through progress to completion. inspect-service-map gives ChatGPT the full machine review brief. explain-capability retrieves deeper evidence and the governed contract for one action. explain-foundation-audit returns the complete safe WordLift foundation audit. refine-service-map submits typed human judgments and returns the immutable refined report. The tool descriptions encode the intended protocol: audit → inspect → interview → explain where unclear → refine This creates a form of human–agent collaboration that was difficult before WebMCP. The machine contributes observation and inference. The human contributes business meaning and responsibility. ChatGPT mediates the conversation and turns both into structured symbolic commitments. Honest readiness A declaration earns zero readiness points. Structured data, OpenAPI, MCP, WebMCP, and other declarations remain unverified until the relevant interface is invoked successfully. Human decisions can change applicability, vocabulary, entity priority, and governance boundaries, but never evidence-based readiness. The report therefore keeps two scores separate: WordLift foundation readiness; verified agent action readiness. Example A tourism website may contain booking forms, accommodation pages, and hotel links. The machine can infer that availability matters, but it cannot safely conclude that the destination organization owns hotel inventory. The human can tell ChatGPT that the organization owns discovery and recommendations while availability is a partner handoff. The refined report then promotes the correct organization and destination entities, clarifies the terminology, changes the action boundary, updates the entity–action bindings and contract, records the rationale as human-provided provenance, and preserves the original machine draft for comparison. Implementation The application is a React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Express, and Node 22 service deployed on Google Cloud Run with immutable Firestore report revisions. It uses Zod contracts, a deterministic versioned action compiler, JSON-LD, Schema.org, Google Natural Language classification, and the WordLift AI Audit provider. Tools register on the top-level report document through the WebMCP imperative API on document.modelContext , with a compatibility alias for Chrome's current preview surface. Report-scoped tools register as soon as the route loads, before the report has finished rendering. Security controls include SSRF protection, DNS and redirect validation, response limits, sanitized evidence, rate limiting, bounded storage, server-only credentials, and truthful partial or failed states. New work created during the challenge The private WordLift AI Audit existed before August 25. The following public implementation was created during The WebMCP Challenge: a new open-source deployable application; the versioned six-archetype action compiler; multi-page context extraction and provenance; domain, lexical, interface, and entity–action schemas; verification-only readiness and safe invocation probes; six generic WebMCP tools; the inspect/interview/refine collaboration protocol; typed human assertions and immutable refined reports; the Context Engine and capability-map interface; deterministic fixtures, security boundaries, and the complete test suite. The challenge contribution is not a wrapper around the previous product. It is the new public context compiler and human-guided WebMCP experience. Testing The current release passed strict TypeScript checks, 323 unit/integration/component tests, the production build, and 12 Playwright browser scenarios. The browser suite includes the full Cyborg journey: audit, inspect, refine, open the immutable child, verify embodied human judgment, and confirm the original machine draft remains unchanged. No account is required. about_excerpt:
Nest is an agent-native flat hunt: you and ChatGPT share one live London board - map, shortlist, viewings, and offers - via WebMCP tools with your confirm on anything that commits.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Flat hunting is a messy human workflow: filters, maps, shortlists, viewing slots, and offer letters all fight for attention. Agents already talk about housing well, but they usually fail when they have to click through a UI built for a mouse. WebMCP flips that: the site can expose the real actions (search, pin, compare, hold a viewing, draft and submit an offer) as structured tools on the same live page the person is looking at. 

 Nest is that idea made concrete — a London rental board where you and your agent share one session, one map, and one shortlist. 

 What it does 

 Nest is an agent-native flat hunt: 

 
 Browse seeded London listings on a live map 
 Pin and compare homes side by side 
 Propose and hold viewing slots (agent proposes; you confirm commits) 
 Draft and submit an offer letter from the shortlist 
 Inspect board state and registered WebMCP tools on an in-app Agent tools panel 
 

 You steer in plain English in ChatGPT; Nest’s site tools update the UI in real time. Anything consequential (holding a viewing, submitting an offer) is a non-read-only tool so the browser can require confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite + React + TypeScript for a fast, deployable SPA 
 Zustand store shared by the human UI and every WebMCP execute handler (one source of truth) 
 Leaflet map with OSM tiles for the spatial board 
 WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected, registered on the top-level page 
 Seeded demo listings (no paid APIs) so judges can try the full path offline-friendly 
 Built with Codex 
 

 Core tools include search_listings , get_listing , pin_listing / unpin_listing , compare_shortlist , propose_viewings , hold_viewing , cancel_viewing , draft_offer , submit_offer , get_board_state , and set_preferences . 

 Challenges 

 
 Same-state collaboration — agent tools and UI clicks must never drift. We solved this by routing both through one store. 
 Read vs commit — WebMCP’s value is trust. Marking search/compare read-only and viewings/offers as side-effecting was deliberate product design, not just annotations. 
 Demo realism without backends — landlords, holds, and offers are simulated with structured JSON so the agent can reason, while the product still feels complete. 
 Judges’ path — a clear happy path (search → pin → compare → hold viewings → draft → submit) plus a tools panel so WebMCP leverage is obvious in under three minutes. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP isn’t “MCP in the browser” as a slogan — it’s best when the agent and the human must see the same thing : a map marker lighting up, a shortlist changing, an offer panel filling. Housing is a perfect stress test because the workflow is multi-step, spatial, and full of confirm-worthy actions. 

 Try the demo path 

 
 Open Nest in ChatGPT’s in-app browser (or Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled) 
 Ask: “Find 2-beds under £2200 in Zone 2 that allow pets, pin the best three, compare them, hold two viewings, and draft an offer for my favorite.” 
 Watch the board update; confirm when the browser asks on commits

title: Keep
pitch: Remember people. Don’t impersonate them. Keep turns messy relationship notes into visible promises, attention rankings, and editable drafts while the human stays in control.
about_excerpt: Remember people. Don’t impersonate them. Keep turns messy relationship notes into visible promises, attention rankings, and editable drafts while the human stays in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I talk to enough people that promises disappear into notes, calendars, and guilt. Traditional CRMs optimize deals and reporting. I wanted a quieter tool for the relationships where the real question is: what did I say I would do? What it does Keep is a local-first relationship desk. It stores fictional demo contacts in the browser, turns raw call notes into owner-labelled promise chips, ranks people who need attention, and creates editable follow-up drafts. Keep never sends a message. The human remains responsible for anything another person receives. Why WebMCP This workflow depends on live page state: which person is selected, their last interaction, unresolved promises, pipeline position, and whether a draft exists. Screen scraping makes an agent guess. A backend integration separates the agent from the interface where the human reviews the result. Keep registers narrow tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools call the same store as the human UI, so cards, timelines, promises, suggestions, and drafts update in front of both participants. The active tool set changes with page state. With no selected card, the agent sees discovery tools. Selecting Priya adds her relevant actions. Promise and draft tools appear only when those objects exist. Human and agent together After a call, the human gives the agent one messy sentence. The agent logs the original words, extracts commitments, and moves the card. On Monday morning, who_needs_attention ranks relationships using cadence, overdue promises, and the Waiting on me column. The agent can draft a follow-up, but it cannot send one. mark_sent only records an action after the human confirms it already happened. How I built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and a small useSyncExternalStore state layer persisted to localStorage . It exposes 14 WebMCP tools with JSON Schema inputs. Read operations use readOnlyHint ; promise extraction marks raw notes with untrustedContentHint . A deterministic commitment parser and draft generator keep the live demo independent of API keys or inference availability. Archiving, dropping a promise, and recording a sent message have in-page confirmation gates. The repository includes eight unit and WebMCP contract tests plus browser acceptance coverage for desktop and mobile. OpenAI Sites hosts the public production build used for judging. Challenges The hardest choice was deciding what the agent must not do. Auto-sending would look powerful in a demo, but it would turn a relationship tool into an impersonation tool. Keep makes the handoff visible instead. The agent can organize, recall, and draft. The person decides what is true and what leaves the browser. The second challenge was keeping agent calls and human actions consistent. Both paths now mutate one store and produce the same visible UI changes. Dynamic registration also required careful cleanup with AbortController as selection and object state changed. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when the browser is not a thin shell over an API. It lets an agent participate in a stateful visual workflow without bypassing the product or duplicating authentication and client state on a server. The best tools are narrow verbs with visible effects. What is next Calendar context is the next useful input, followed by optional encrypted sync. Sending integrations are not on the roadmap. Keep should become better at helping a person remember, not better at pretending to be them. title: HooraAI
pitch: An AI-native marketplace where agents discover human talent, prepare Tasks, and return control to humans for approval.
about_excerpt:
An AI-native marketplace where agents discover human talent, prepare Tasks, and return control to humans for approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but most service marketplaces still make people fit themselves into rigid job titles, categories, search boxes, and forms. 

 HooraAI starts with a different belief: human talent is bigger than a job title. 

 Someone may know how to repair a refrigerator, creatively customize a bicycle, help reconnect someone with a first love, or have a valuable ability that does not fit any traditional professional category. 

 We wanted to explore what happens when humans simply express what they need, can do, or are curious about , while AI handles the work of understanding that intent and discovering relevant human talent. 

 Our core idea became simple: 

 The agent prepares. The human decides. 

 What it does 

 HooraAI is an AI-native marketplace for human talent . 

 Instead of asking users to choose a category, the prototype begins with natural human intent: “I need something,” “I can do something,” or “Surprise me.” 

 A customer can say something as practical as “I need to fix my fridge” or as unusual as “I need someone to help me find my first love.” A person offering talent can describe what they can actually do without first inventing a job title for themselves. Someone can even say “I love pink,” allowing Hoora to discover unexpected human talent related to that interest. 

 Hoora identifies the strongest relevant human connection as the user’s Nexus . 

 With WebMCP, an AI agent can understand the request, discover relevant talent, and prepare a structured Task. However, the Task remains a draft until the human explicitly approves it. 

 Nothing is automatically booked, assigned, charged, or started. 

 How we built it 

 We built the prototype with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP . 

 The site exposes structured WebMCP capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The prototype currently includes three agent-facing tools: understand_need , discover_talent , and prepare_task . 

 understand_need structures natural human intent. discover_talent searches the same talent-matching logic used by the human-facing experience. prepare_task creates a structured draft Task around a selected Nexus and hands it back to the webpage for human approval. 

 A key architectural decision was to reuse the same application logic for both humans and agents rather than building a separate agent-only experience. 

 The current prototype uses seeded talent profiles and lightweight rule-based matching so we could focus on demonstrating the WebMCP interaction model, agent-to-webpage handoff, and human approval boundary . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most important challenge was deciding where agent autonomy should stop . 

 Allowing an agent to understand a request or discover possible talent is relatively low risk. Allowing it to independently create a real service relationship, book someone, assign work, or initiate payment is much more consequential. 

 We therefore designed prepare_task to prepare and surface a Task without authorizing the next action. The resulting Task remains in Draft status and visibly returns control to the human. 

 Another challenge was designing talent discovery without relying on traditional categories. HooraAI is intentionally trying to discover abilities that may not correspond neatly to existing job titles, so the interaction had to begin with natural language rather than a category tree. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that WebMCP is not simply attached to the website as a technical demonstration. It meaningfully changes how an AI agent can interact with the marketplace. 

 The agent receives structured access to HooraAI's capabilities, can discover human talent, and can prepare a Task while the webpage remains the place where consequential human approval happens. 

 We are also proud of the shared architecture between the human interface and WebMCP tools. Both use the same talent-discovery logic instead of producing two disconnected experiences. 

 Finally, we introduced the concept of a Nexus : not merely a search result, but the strongest human connection Hoora identifies for a particular need, talent, interest, or moment. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that agent-native does not have to mean agent-controlled . 

 WebMCP can make a website significantly more useful to AI agents without removing humans from meaningful decisions. 

 We learned that one of the most powerful roles for an agent may be to handle the difficult work of understanding intent, discovering possibilities, organizing information, and preparing actions—then return control to the person at the moment a meaningful decision must be made. 

 That principle became the foundation of our prototype: 

 Human expresses intent → Agent understands → Agent discovers talent → Agent prepares the Task → Human approves.

title: CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway
pitch: A safe shared pet-care state where people and agents collaborate through five guarded WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
A safe shared pet-care state where people and agents collaborate through five guarded WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway is a standalone synthetic-data pet-care workspace where a person and an AI agent operate on the same visible state through five document-bound WebMCP tools. 

 The agent reads Synthetic Pika's profile, daily focus, and events; previews an exact structured check-in; requests human review; commits only the unchanged confirmed payload; and reads the result back from browser-only storage. 

 Why I built this 

 I chose the name CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway because CAIOS is our startup project, and the gateway was my way to test whether WebMCP could turn a pet-care page into a safer shared workspace for people and agents. 

 Before we adapt this pattern to real market needs, I wanted a small, inspectable build that could prove the interaction model without exposing production CAIOS technology or real pet data. 

 Pika's everyday care made the test concrete: an agent may help structure a routine observation, but the person should still see exactly what will be recorded and remain in control of the write. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Agents normally infer controls from visual interfaces. This project instead registers five narrow tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 get_synthetic_pika_profile 
 list_synthetic_pika_events 
 get_synthetic_pika_today 
 preview_synthetic_pika_check_in 
 commit_synthetic_pika_check_in 
 

 Preview validates without writing and returns a payload-bound confirmation token. Commit fails closed unless it receives the unchanged payload and matching token. A changed or unpreviewed payload is rejected. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 The agent reduces repetitive interaction while the person sees the proposal, controls confirmation, and verifies the outcome. Both then see the same browser-only state. 

 What I learned 

 The most useful lesson was that exposing a tool is only half of the work. The human page and the agent must stay consistent around the same proposed action. 

 During testing, we found a real UI bug: after preview, a re-render could reset the visible form to its defaults while the pending payload still held the earlier values. That could make the confirmation screen misleading even though the underlying token guard still worked. 

 We fixed it by preserving the exact previewed values in the UI and invalidating confirmation whenever the form changes. This reinforced the main product principle behind the demo: WebMCP can give an agent useful capabilities, but consequential actions still need deterministic guards and visible human review. 

 Safety and hackathon boundary 

 All data is fictional and marked synthetic_hackathon_only . Mutable state stays in namespaced browser localStorage . The demo has no production CAIOS API, database, customer record, real pet record, private prompt, proprietary memory engine, nutrition reasoning, or clinical logic. It does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace veterinary or emergency care. 

 CAIOS existed before the submission period as a broader pet-care product vision. During the submission period, we created this standalone WebMCP Gateway, five tools, synthetic dataset, confirmation guards, seven deterministic tests, CI, documentation, public repository, and independent deployment. 

 Implementation and verification 

 Built with TypeScript, Vite, the WebMCP browser API, and deterministic browser storage. Seven tests cover the tool boundary and guarded writes. Type checking and production builds pass. 

 The live workflow was verified end-to-end in an OpenAI cloud Chrome CDP environment: five tools were discovered; a direct commit failed closed; preview returned a payload-bound token; the exact payload committed; and a final read returned the same visible browser-only state. 

 Try it 

 Live demo: https://caios-webmcp-challenge.vercel.app 

 Public repository: https://github.com/corwinlim/caios-webmcp-challenge 

 Demo video: https://youtu.be/FDoAIoCU3i0 

 No account or credentials are required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Cleanroom
pitch: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero.
about_excerpt: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero. Like Comment Story Updates Cleanroom What it does Cleanroom is a data-cleaning workbench for messy CSVs. You drop a file on the page and an agent in your browser profiles it, finds the concrete problems, queries and charts it, and proposes the fixes — without the file ever being uploaded anywhere. The design rule is one sentence: reads are free, writes are proposals. No tool mutates your table. When the agent wants to change something it computes the exact before/after diff, puts a card in front of you with its reasoning, and stops. You click Approve or Reject. undo is deliberately not exposed as a tool — the ability to walk a change back belongs to the person, not the model. The problem it solves Every analyst has the same bad afternoon. A CSV arrives and before you can answer one question you have to fix it: regions spelled five ways, amounts stored as ¥39,545 , four date formats in one column, duplicate rows silently doubling your revenue. An LLM is excellent at spotting exactly these problems. But letting one help has meant either uploading your data to a server or code interpreter — a non-starter the moment the file has customer names, salaries or anything your compliance team has an opinion about — or pasting a sample and hand-applying the suggestions yourself, which is the automation you wanted, gone. Cleanroom is the third option: the agent gets tools, not your data. Why this is WebMCP and could not be a server MCP This is not a remote MCP server with a web page bolted on. It structurally could not be one. The agent and the human operate on literally the same JavaScript object . One store is the single source of truth; the UI renders it and the tools operate on it. When the agent proposes a change the approval card appears in the human's rail in the same tick — no sync, no polling, no second copy that can drift. A remote agent cannot have that property, because a remote agent needs a copy. And everything a server MCP would need — upload, storage, auth, per-seat infrastructure — is simply absent. It's already your browser and already your session. The whole app is a static file. The privacy receipt The claim is "your data never leaves this tab," and a claim is worth nothing, so the page proves it. Before any other module loads, Cleanroom instruments fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon and WebSocket and counts every outbound request. The count is in the header, and the agent can read it too, via a get_privacy_receipt tool — so when you ask "did my data go anywhere?" it answers with a verifiable number instead of a promise. It reads zero because there is nothing to send it to: no analytics, no CDN, no webfont, no charting library. Even the sample dataset is inlined as a string rather than fetched, specifically so the ledger stays honest. The deployed site also ships connect-src 'none' in its CSP, so the browser enforces it independently of our own code. Being straight about the limit: this counts requests the page makes. It cannot police the browser itself or a malicious extension, and it isn't a substitute for a security review. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no runtime dependencies — a dependency that phones home would undermine the entire premise. Roughly 1,800 lines across eleven modules: a RFC-4180-tolerant CSV parser, type inference and column profiling, an issue detector, fifteen pure transform operations with a diff builder, the store that holds the undo stack, the WebMCP tool layer, the UI, and hand-rolled inline SVG charts. 14 tools are registered — eight read-only, six human-gated. Three implementation details did the most for how well an agent actually performs here: Every detected issue carries a suggested_fix — a ready-to-use propose_transform payload. The agent goes from "what's wrong?" to a queued, reviewable fix in one hop instead of guessing at an API shape. This cut the model's flailing more than anything else I tried. Errors are instructions. Every failure names the valid inputs — Column "reigon" does not exist. Available columns: order_id, order_date, region, … — and is returned as text rather than thrown, so the agent reads the recovery path instead of hitting an opaque host error. Results are context-window shaped. Profiles and aggregates are summaries by construction; raw rows are returned only on request and hard-capped at 200. A 100,000-row file is fully workable without a single row entering the model's context. Challenges WebMCP's API moved while it was being standardised — some hosts expose navigator.modelContext , the current spec draft uses document.modelContext , and earlier builds took a batch provideContext({tools}) instead of per-tool registerTool . Rather than bet on one, the registration shim feature-detects all of them and reports which it found, so the header tells the user the truth about their browser instead of failing silently. Tool results are returned in three shapes at once — MCP-style content , structuredContent , and a bare data object — so the same tool behaves identically across hosts. The harder problem was designing the pause . An agent that has to stop and wait is easy to build badly: it either blocks forever or barrels ahead assuming approval. propose_transform returns pending_human_approval with an explicit next_step , and a separate await_decision tool blocks on the human with a timeout and tells the agent what to say if it expires. Getting the agent to reliably not assume its change landed was most of the prompt-shaped work. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is interface design, and the same thing that makes an API pleasant for a junior engineer — good names, errors that say what to do next, results scoped to what you actually need — is what makes a model competent instead of erratic. The suggested_fix field was the clearest demonstration: same model, same data, dramatically better behaviour, purely from shaping the return value. The second thing: an approval gate makes an agent more useful, not less. Once a change is reviewable before it lands, you stop hedging your prompts and start letting it try things. What's next Multi-table joins under the same proposal model — the agent proposes the key and shows you the match rate before committing. Recipe export — the change log is already ordered and structured; emit it as a runnable script so a one-off clean becomes a repeatable pipeline. Approval policies — "auto-approve whitespace fixes, always ask about dropped rows." The gate exists; this is a rule layer on top of it. Try it In ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, open the page and ask: "What's wrong with this data? Don't change anything yet — just tell me what you'd fix and why." "Clean it up. Propose each fix separately so I can review them, and ask me before you touch anything that's a judgement call." In any other browser the built-in Agent Console calls the same registered tool objects a host calls — an inspector, not a mock — so you can see exactly what the agent sees. title: DoPDF with WebMCP
pitch: AI agents can read PDFs. Now they can act on them — accurately. Redact secrets and fill forms just by chatting: WebMCP lets your agent call real PDF tools instead of guessing at the UI.
about_excerpt: AI agents can read PDFs. Now they can act on them — accurately. Redact secrets and fill forms just by chatting: WebMCP lets your agent call real PDF tools instead of guessing at the UI. Like 2 Comment Story Updates "Black out my loan number and account details." The agent finds every match, marks them in red, and waits for your review Hit Apply and the redactions are baked into a fresh PDF. 100% client-side, your document never leaves the tab "I'm Jane Doe, applying for a $25k loan." The form fills live, using only what you said. It leaves the rest blank, never invented. Apply and download: the finished loan application, filled entirely by chat and flattened into a shareable PDF. Inspiration Today's browser AI can read a PDF and tell you what's in it. It still can't do anything to it. You're the one squinting at a mortgage statement, manually blacking out your account number before emailing it, or retyping the same details into yet another loan form. We wanted to give the agent hands: let it act on the document, safely, without shipping your file to some server. WebMCP made that click. A page can publish its own capabilities as tools on document.modelContext , and any WebMCP-aware agent can call them. So we turned real =PDF workflows into tools an agent can drive, entirely in the browser. What it does DoPDF with WebMCP lets an AI agent run two real PDF workflows by chat, 100% client-side: Redact. Say "black out my loan number and account details" and the agent finds every match, marks them in red, and shows a review card. You confirm, and it flattens the boxes into a downloadable PDF. Fill forms. Describe yourself in plain language and watch a fillable PDF populate live, field by field. It fills only what you actually said and never invents a value you left out. Your document never leaves the tab. The only network call is the extension talking to your chosen model. How we built it The hands (the page): Adobe PDF Embed API renders and provides core PDF capabilities. Each page registers its tools on document.modelContext . The brain (the extension): a Chrome side-panel chat that discovers whatever tools the active tab exposes and calls them, using Google Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible gateway (bring your own key). Two flavors of WebMCP, on purpose: redaction uses the imperative API ( registerTool ), while form-fill also demos the declarative API, injecting an annotated <form toolname="fill_form"> that the browser turns into a tool automatically. Human in the loop: every destructive action returns a review card, so nothing is redacted, written, or downloaded without a click. Challenges we ran into PDF Embed on reload. A repeat previewFile() can silently stall and leave a blank viewer. We now race it against a timeout and fall back to another render, so the document always shows. Declarative timing. Chrome registers an injected <form> as a tool asynchronously , and its submit handler must call event.respondWith(...) synchronously. We poll for the tool, respond in place, and fall back to an imperative tool if the browser does not surface the form. No hallucinated data. LLMs love to "complete" a form. We bake anti-fabrication into the tool descriptions and the system prompt so the agent fills only user-provided fields. HITL Trust needs UI, but WebMCP tools return data, not interfaces. A tool call hands back a result; it can't show the user a redaction preview and wait for a yes/no. So confirmation would have fallen back to plain chat text — easy to skim past, and a poor fit for a destructive action. We solved it with an agent-to-UI (A2UI) layer in the extension: the tool returns a structured payload, and the side-panel renders it as an interactive review card — highlighted matches, confirm/cancel — before anything is redacted, written, or downloaded. The agent proposes; the human disposes, in a real interface, not a wall of text. What we learned Field name is the perfect join key: the agent maps values to them, and PDF library writes them straight back, with no fuzzy matching. We also learned when to reach for declarative vs imperative WebMCP, and how much a simple review-card pattern buys you in trust. What's next Voice-driven fills, more tools (edit, compress, export, combine), and driving a PDF that is already open on any site, not just our page. title: yesmcp: agent-native booking, the human keeps the click
pitch: A real booking service an in-browser agent can use through WebMCP. It checks live availability and prepares a booking. The page then asks the human to press Confirm.
about_excerpt: A real booking service an in-browser agent can use through WebMCP. It checks live availability and prepares a booking. The page then asks the human to press Confirm. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is yesmcp ( https://yesmcp.com ) is a live business. It builds companies their own MCP connectors so their customers can book, order and ask directly inside AI chats. Its own site now practices what it sells at a deeper level: the site itself is agent-native through WebMCP. The home page registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every other page registers four of them: the entrance gate and the demo driver exist only on the home page, and a tool that cannot work on a page is never registered there. get_services : the authored services catalog. The answer carries an explicit degradation flag, so an agent never presents a stub as the catalog. check_availability : genuinely bookable 30-minute windows with slot ids. Every label carries an explicit UTC offset, never a bare wall-clock time. book_consult : prepares a REAL booking, then opens a confirmation card on the page. The request is submitted only after the human clicks Confirm. Decline is a first-class answer returned to the agent, not an error. get_live_status : live proof numbers from the production connector. answer_entrance_check : the site asks arriving visitors one question at the door. This answers it, so an agent can open the page for its human instead of stalling at a dialog it cannot see past. drive_demo (home page only): drives the interactive hero chat demo through the same controls a finger taps, so the visitor can watch the story the agent is telling. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP A services business's page is exactly where "humans and agents together" stops being a slogan. The agent does the tedious part: find the catalog, check the calendar, fill the form. The human does the human part: decide, and press the one button that commits their calendar and their inbox. Before WebMCP an in-browser agent had to guess at our DOM and click blind. One redesign and it breaks. With WebMCP it gets the same honest API our own page uses, and the page stays a normal website for everyone else. No modelContext API means no behavior at all, so all of this is progressive enhancement. How it creates a better user experience The visitor never has to translate between two systems. They say what they want in their own words, the agent turns that into two tool calls, and what comes back on screen is the server's own label for the slot, not the agent's paraphrase of it. The one irreversible step stays with the person: a card rendered by the site itself, with a button the agent cannot press. What people and agents can do together that was hard before A visitor tells their browser agent "find me a slot Thursday afternoon and set up the call". The agent checks real availability, fills the booking, and the visitor confirms with one click on a card the site rendered. The confirmation email and the owner's notification run the same production path every other door uses. The agent can also show things, not only tell them. drive_demo replays the landing's scripted chat story (browse, pick a time, booked, reschedule) in front of the visitor, driven through the same controls a finger would tap. It is labelled as a scripted demo, and the real tools sit right beside it. This is not a prototype It is a running production service. Bookings are atomic: the confirmation email is sent inside the transaction, so if the send fails the slot is released. A booking nobody was told about is not a booking. There is rate limiting, an origin allow-list on the browser endpoints, a public status endpoint reporting since 2026-08-21, and a test suite that runs green on every change. The public counter deliberately excludes bookings made from test domains, so the number it reports can only ever mean real customers. The demo booking recorded for this submission does not inflate it. The same capability already runs as a remote MCP server at https://mcp.yesmcp.com/mcp , which works today from Claude and ChatGPT. WebMCP is the third door into the same real system. How I implemented WebMCP Imperative API: document.modelContext.registerTool , with a provideContext fallback for hosts that shipped the earlier surface. Plain JavaScript, no dependencies, no framework. Tool results use the MCP content shape. Verified end to end in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, and with the Model Context Tool Inspector extension driving the tools through a real agent loop. Safety, in this order: the page never books without a human click; no modelContext means no behavior at all; agent input is never parsed as markup, because the confirmation card is built with createElement only. Server-side validation, rate limits and junk filters are shared verbatim with every other door. I built the WebMCP layer on top of my own production booking service: the six tools and their schemas, the confirmation card that keeps the final click with the human, and the demo video. title: Baton
pitch: A WebMCP store where an agent shops for you, but every change stops for your confirmation. The agent proposes, the screen narrates, and you decide before anything happens.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP store where an agent shops for you, but every change stops for your confirmation. The agent proposes, the screen narrates, and you decide before anything happens.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Baton 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Baton 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Baton 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most agent demos on the web just act. The agent clicks buy, submits the form, or empties the
cart, and you find out afterward. That gives up two things the open web needs as agents
arrive: control, meaning you decide what actually changes, and access, meaning anyone can
operate the page, not only people who can see it and use a mouse. WebMCP's own guidance also
warns about prompt injection, where a malicious page or a hijacked agent issues tool calls a
person never asked for. We wanted a design that answered both at once. 

 What it does 

 Baton is a small grocery store. It works normally for a person, who can browse, add items,
review the cart, and check out. It also registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent can do the
same things from a request like "add oat milk, then check out." 

 The read tools, search_products and review_cart , run right away. The tools that change
state, add_to_cart , remove_from_cart , and checkout , never mutate anything directly.
They create a proposal on screen and return text saying the action is awaiting confirmation,
so a well-behaved agent waits. Every action is narrated through an ARIA-live region and a
plain-language card, and confirmed or rejected actions land in a visible timeline. Checkout is
a mock. No payment is taken and no order is sent anywhere. 

 How we built it 

 Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with no framework, no build step, and no backend, deployed
as static files to Cloudflare Pages. The tools live in a local registry the page's own
interface calls directly, and the same tools are separately registered with
 document.modelContext for the agent, so the human interface never depends on the agent-side
API being present. 

 The confirmation step is enforced inside the tool, not the interface. A tool that changes
state does not change it in execute() . It sets one pending proposal and returns text that
tells the agent to wait. State only changes when the person clicks Confirm, so there is no code
path from a tool call to a state change that skips the person. 

 We also shipped a "Real agent" console in the page itself: paste any OpenAI-compatible LLM
key, and a real model plans the tool calls, which run through the same WebMCP interface and the
same confirmation step. We used it to test the flow with a real third-party model
( gpt-4o-mini via a model gateway) driving the tools end to end on the live deployed page. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Testing against a real WebMCP client was harder than expected. ChatGPT's web app
( chatgpt.com ) turned out not to be a WebMCP client at all: it web-searches the page
server-side and told us directly that it "does not expose the page's document.modelContext 
WebMCP tool registry." Chrome's WebMCP flag needs Chrome 149+, which isn't available on our
dev machine. That's what led to building the in-page "Real agent" console: it let us prove a
real third-party model driving the tools end to end, without depending on a specific browser. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The confirmation step is genuinely enforced in the tool layer, not just the UI, so there is no
way for any agent, well-behaved or not, to skip it. And the same mechanism does two jobs at
once: it is an accessibility story, because the agent operates the page's own tools instead of
a scraped DOM, and it is a prompt-injection defense, because an injected instruction can call
 checkout , but it only ever produces a proposal, never an order. 

 What we learned 

 How new WebMCP still is, down to which real clients actually support it today. And that a
confirmation step designed for accessibility turns out to double as a security boundary,
without any extra code, because both problems have the same shape: an agent should be able to
act, but a person should always get the last word. 

 What's next for Baton 

 A larger catalog and a second task, like a form or a booking, to show the design works beyond
shopping. A per-tool policy, where some proposals are approved automatically and high-stakes
ones always ask. And a shared session, where a helper and the person they assist both see the
same page.
