title: WETAEGO
pitch: The Commerce & Service Operating System for Modern Brands, their Human Customers, and the AI Agents who serve them.
about_excerpt: The Commerce & Service Operating System for Modern Brands, their Human Customers, and the AI Agents who serve them. Like Comment Story Updates webmcp.com nekuda chrome extension listing webmcp tools chrome console Inspiration Millions of real-world businesses—from local restaurants, boutique hotels, and wellness spas to neighborhood supermarkets, auto repair shops, and creators—remain locked out of the digital and agentic economy. Most have zero structured online presence, rely on fragmented pen-and-paper or disjointed point solutions, and struggle to manage payments across multiple rails (cards, bank transfers, crypto stablecoins, or in-house customer credit). When the AI revolution arrived, these businesses were left behind: AI browsing agents and voice assistants cannot navigate brittle PDFs, messy HTML menus, or multi-step checkout modals without breaking. We asked: What if any business could register on a single platform in 60 seconds and instantly go from having zero digital presence to a complete commerce operating layer, dual-layer AI copilots for both customers and staff, and immediate out-of-the-box readiness for the autonomous agentic future? That vision is WETAEGO ( The Commerce & Service Operating System for Modern Brands, their Human Customers, and the AI Agents who serve them ). What it does By simply registering on WETAEGO, a business instantly receives a complete 4-tier commerce and operational ecosystem: Instant Digital Storefront & Multi-Rail Commerce Engine : Deploys responsive, high-performance storefronts supporting arbitrary commercial models: physical retail, timed service bookings, restaurant dine-in/takeout, apartment reservations, and dynamic B2B rate cards. Universal Omnichannel Payments : Handles Credit/Debit cards, instant Bank Transfers, Crypto/Stablecoins (USDC, USDT, SOL via Bachs), and in-house customer IOU / BNPL credit ledgers, backed by an in-person counter POS. Frontline Customer-Facing AI Concierge : Every storefront is equipped with a 24/7 AI Concierge that acts as the primary point of contact. Grounded with strict zero-hallucination guardrails, it answers queries, filters allergies, recommends pairings, customizes orders, and seamlessly escalates to human staff via live alerts when needed. Tego Merchant AI Co-Pilot (Multimodal Voice & Vision) : On the business side, merchants get Tego : a hands-free, multimodal operational copilot. Merchants can talk naturally to Tego (low-latency bidirectional voice) or point their device camera (Tego Vision) at physical menus, handwritten receipts, stockroom inventory, or kitchen dishes to automatically ingest items, update stock, or trigger dashboard actions. Instant WebMCP Agent-Readiness : The storefront automatically registers an 8-tool standardized W3C WebMCP suite onto document.modelContext . When browsing agents (like ChatGPT Desktop or Google Chrome with WebMCP) visit the merchant's URL, they can search products, compose complex modifiers, manage carts, and co-browse with the customer in real time—with an architectural Human-in-the-Loop Safe Payment Gate ensuring financial safety. Full Business Operating Layer : Includes a real-time order dispatch & Kitchen Display System (KDS), driverless raw ESC/POS thermal receipt printing over WebUSB/WebSerial/Bluetooth, staff push-to-talk intercom radio, dynamic QR/NFC generator, inventory BOM tracking, and multi-branch franchise replication in under a second. How we built it Frontend & Architecture : Next.js (App Router, Server Actions, Edge Proxy), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion. Client WebMCP Layer : Standardized W3C document.modelContext.registerTool() registry dynamically exposing canonical tools ( search_catalog , get_item_details , create_cart , add_to_cart , get_cart , update_cart , initiate_checkout , submit_order , request_staff ). Reactive State Bridge : Bi-directional synchronization between WebMCP tool executions, Zustand stores, IndexedDB persistence, and real-time UI notifications (animated toasts, pulsing cart drawers). Backend & Real-Time : Supabase (PostgreSQL, Row-Level Security, Realtime WebSockets) and Upstash Redis for edge rate limiting. Multimodal AI : Google Gemini Live API (16kHz PCM audio streaming, 1 FPS continuous vision ingestion) and Vercel AI SDK. Server MCP Suite : Enterprise /api/mcp endpoint for remote agent management across multi-location fleets. Challenges we ran into Polymorphic Modifier Matrices for AI : Real-world items (steaks with doneness, laptops with RAM/storage tiers, spa treatments with durations) have complex dependency trees. We engineered dynamic JSON schema generators that allow agents to resolve multi-dimensional configuration axes deterministically. Real-Time Client State Synchronization : Ensuring in-browser agent tool calls immediately reflected in the human user's viewport without race conditions or page reloads required building a custom reactive bridge between document.modelContext and our Zustand/IndexedDB stores. Hardware Without Daemons : Crafting direct binary ESC/POS command streams for thermal printers over WebUSB and WebSerial without relying on background desktop print spools. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Friction Transformation : Any merchant can create an account and immediately get a storefront, multi-rail payments, dual AI assistants, and WebMCP agent readiness with zero manual API configuration. Human-in-the-Loop Safe Payment Gate : Designed an architecture where AI handles heavy constraint filtering and cart composition, but payment authorization remains strictly in the hands of the human customer via biometric/one-tap confirmation. Complete Test Coverage : 100% pass rate across Vitest WebMCP integration suites and end-to-end Playwright tests. What we learned WebMCP transforms web browsing from passive visual scraping into deterministic, structured collaboration between humans and AI. Client-side in-session tool execution eliminates latency and keeps sensitive session state private within the user's browser. What's next for WETAEGO Providing Businesses across scale with instant online presesnce, AI-capabilities and webMCP readiness, empowering them with tools to compete and succeed in this Digital/AI/Agentic era. Expanding our 14 Open Discovery Protocols (RFC 9727, x402 machine payments, DNS-AID) to support fully autonomous machine-to-machine supply chain ordering. Releasing ready-to-use POS hardware kits for self-service kiosks running WETAEGO WebMCP. title: FableCut
pitch: A browser video editor your agent can drive. FableCut exposes its whole timeline as WebMCP tools, you and your agent cut the same edit, live, in the same tab.
about_excerpt: A browser video editor your agent can drive. FableCut exposes its whole timeline as WebMCP tools, you and your agent cut the same edit, live, in the same tab. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Agent moves the playhead, selects a clip, splits it, then undoes it. The edit lands on your undo stack, so Ctrl+Z reverses it You select a clip with your mouse. The agent reads it with get_selection. No clip ids, no filenames, no describing what you mean. A real non-linear editor in the browser. Three video tracks, four audio, transitions, keyframes, all exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. GIF Just after split_at_playhead. One V2 clip became two and the length dropped 2.60 to 1.20. The agent made this edit, not the human. The full demo timeline. Vector shots on V1, titles on V2, one grade across everything on V3. Either of you can edit any of it. Inspiration I wanted to edit video without paying for it. Premiere Pro is a subscription, and Palmier Pro needs macOS, so between the two of them the door is shut for a lot of people who just want to cut clips. That felt wrong for a community that mostly runs on free and open tools. So I built FableCut. The WebMCP part came later, out of a limitation I already knew about. FableCut could be driven by an agent over MCP, but the agent was always editing a file on disk while I was sitting in front of a timeline in a browser tab. Two views of the same edit, held together by a file watcher. WebMCP closes that gap, because the tools live inside the page the human is already looking at. A video editor is about the best possible thing to put WebMCP into, since the whole session is already live in the tab. What it does FableCut is a browser based, zero dependency video editor that an AI agent can drive. Three video tracks, four audio tracks, trimming, splitting, keyframes, transitions, real waveforms, and export, all running in the browser off one node server.js. The original idea was that project.json is the interface. The entire timeline is one JSON document, so any agent that can read and write JSON can edit video, and the open tab hot reloads in about 150ms. That still works and it is still how the MCP server operates. For this challenge I added a WebMCP layer, and it does something the file based approach cannot. It registers 11 tools on document.modelContext that talk to the running editor instead of the file. The interesting ones are the ones that have no on disk equivalent at all: get_selection reads what you have selected right now and where your playhead is. You point at a clip with your mouse and say "tighten this". No ids, no filenames, no describing what you mean. get_frame_context reports what is actually composited at a given instant, topmost first, with transforms. The flat clip list cannot answer "what does the viewer see here". set_playhead and select_clips let the agent move your cursor and your selection, so it can show you what it means before it changes anything. And the piece that makes it actually usable: every tool that changes something calls pushUndo() first. The agent's edits go onto the same undo stack as yours. Ctrl+Z reverses the agent exactly the way it reverses you. There is no separate "review the AI's changes" panel to approve or reject, because there is one timeline, one history, and two people editing it. How we built it FableCut itself was built before this hackathon. No third party libraries, no dependencies, free, and drivable by agents from day one. We used Claude Code to build it over a weekend and posted it on a random Thursday. For this challenge the new work is a single file, webmcp.js, plus one line in index.html to load it. The repo is deliberately structured so you can see exactly that. The first commit is an unmodified export of FableCut as it stood before the submission period, containing zero WebMCP code. Every commit after it is challenge work, so git diff against that first commit is the submission. WEBMCP.md spells this out. One thing that cost real time was figuring out which API to write against. The spec and Chrome's own docs say document.modelContext.registerTool(), but most of the tutorials and blog posts still in circulation show navigator.modelContext with a batch provideContext() call, which is an older draft shape. We could not control which build a judge would open it in, so the layer feature detects both and prefers the spec form. Challenges we ran into Frame rendering and clip transitions were rough early on, and got fixed in a recent build. Clips and audio were not really consumable by an agent. It could see that a clip existed but not what was in it, so we had to start transcribing audio and placing beats and effects against volume peaks and drops. For the WebMCP layer, the hard problem was reversibility. An agent that edits your timeline and cannot be undone is worse than no agent. Routing every mutating tool through the editor's existing undo stack solved it and turned out to be the best part of the whole thing. Testing was its own problem, since WebMCP needs Chrome 149 with a flag or the ChatGPT in app browser. We ended up exposing the tool set on window.FableCutWebMCP so every tool can be executed and verified in a normal browser without the flag. Accomplishments that we're proud of FableCut hit the Show HN front page with 98 points and sat at #2 for a whole day, and picked up 200 GitHub stars in the first 5 hours. It is listed in the official MCP registry and has been written up on several blogs, tech news sites, and social platforms. We also got a repost from Marcos Rico Peng, founder of Palmier Pro, on a post comparing FableCut with the existing tools in that space. The repo is past 640 stars and still climbing, with people contributing regularly. Most of that happened before this hackathon, so we are not claiming it as challenge work. We mention it because it means agent native editing has somewhere real to land. There are already people using this thing every day. What we learned SSE, a lot of ways to edit video, and how to reimplement an existing production clip or ad from scratch. Building MCP servers for free and open source agent tooling pulled us into context sharing and tool calling as a field. WebMCP added a distinction we had not thought about before. There is a real difference between an agent editing your document and an agent editing your session. The first one needs you to describe everything. The second one can just look at what you are pointing at. What's next for FableCut More features, and simpler prompts for complex edits A library/marketplace of media built specifically for FableCut: SVGs, SFX, effects, and transitions Built With canvas css html javascript mcp node.js sse web-audio-api webcodecs webmcp Try it out ronak-create.github.io github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ronak Parmar shekhar parmar Kalpit Padhiyar Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Ronak Parmar started this project — Sep 03, 2026 06:27 AM EDT

title: wcrew
pitch: The shift roster co-pilot.
about_excerpt: The shift roster co-pilot. Like Comment Story Updates agent console detail dashboard Inspiration Every independent café, bakery, and corner shop has the same Sunday-night ritual: the owner sits down with a spreadsheet, drags names into cells, and then blows up the group chat trying to get coverage for next week. One wrong cell — a 17-year-old scheduled past 21:00, someone double-booked, a close with no keyholder — and it's a labour-law problem, not just an annoyed group chat. What made this click as a WebMCP idea is that scheduling is a trust problem, not a data problem. A manager will happily let an agent read the roster. They will never let it act on it unless they can see every move and take it back. WebMCP is the first thing that makes that possible: tools that run in the user's own authenticated browser, on the live page, where every action is observable, attributable, and undoable. So we built wcrew around that exact contract. What it does wcrew is a shift roster co-pilot for small hourly teams (5–30 staff). It replaces the spreadsheet with a live weekly board where a manager and a browser agent fix the roster together: Compliance you can see — skills, availability, under-18 curfew, 11-hour rest, 10-hour daily cap, 5 consecutive days, keyholder coverage, 1.5× overtime, and a $5,200 budget are checked in real time, with the exact rule broken and a suggested fix. An agent that acts through 15 typed tools — the agent can check compliance, explain any assignment before making it, rank swap candidates, auto-fill open shifts with a deterministic solver (three strategies), and publish — all on the live board. Dry-run before mutate — auto_fill previews a plan produced by the same code path as the apply, so what you see is what you get. A trust contract — every agent action is logged actor:agent , one-undo reversible, and destructive actions pause on a human confirmation modal. An in-page agent console — runs the same 15 tools in any browser (no Chrome flag, no agent platform) so the demo is one click away for anyone. How we built it 15 structured tools on document.modelContext ( src/webmcp.js ), each with a natural-language description and JSON Schema, executing against a pure, zero-dependency scheduling engine. Single source of truth — evaluateAssignment powers explain_assignment , assign_shift , check_compliance , and the solver, so "explain" and "do" can never disagree. Deterministic solver — greedy, hardest-shift-first with a one-level repair pass, so the same input always yields the same plan. Actor-tagged store — a tiny undo/redo store where human edits and agent tool-calls go through the same commit path. Prompt-injection defense — staff notes are untrusted; tools surface them between --- BEGIN UNTRUSTED --- delimiters and warn the agent not to follow instructions inside (there's a live canary in the seed data). Origin isolation — Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 + Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) served by tools/serve.mjs and _headers . Vanilla JS, no build step, no backend — runs anywhere; state lives in localStorage . Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new. The spec is still a draft and document.modelContext only exists behind Chrome 149+ with a testing flag (or ChatGPT's in-app browser). That meant the demo would silently degrade to "human-only" for most judges — so we built the in-page agent console that exercises the identical tool definitions everywhere. Making the dry-run honest. Most demos fake a preview. We wired auto_fill --dry_run through the exact solver the apply path uses, including the repair pass, so the numbers in the preview are real. The trust contract is easy to say, hard to build. Observable, attributable, undoable required a shared store, actor tags, a confirm bridge the agent can't bypass, and locked shifts the solver respects. Prompt injection is a first-class concern the moment you expose user content to an agent. We had to assume staff notes are adversarial and design tool descriptions + delimiters around that. Origin isolation is load-bearing — document.modelContext is gated behind Origin-Agent-Cluster , which rules out plain static hosts like GitHub Pages and forced us to configure headers on Cloudflare Pages. Accomplishments that we're proud of 15 tools sharing one engine, so answers are computed, not guessed . A trust contract where the agent proposes and the human decides — the thing we think makes WebMCP more than a "chat sidebar." An honest dry-run produced by the same code path as the apply. A real prompt-injection canary and untrusted-content handling. An agent console that makes the whole thing demo-able in any browser, no setup. What we learned WebMCP's real value isn't tool-calling — it's trust : keeping the human's authenticated session, UI, and undo power in the loop. One engine for explain and do is the single biggest reliability win for agent-driven UIs. Prompt injection isn't theoretical: the moment you hand user content to an agent, you have to design for it. Platform details (origin isolation, permissions policy) decide whether WebMCP even works — get them right early. What's next for wcrew Real teams : authentication, persistence, and multi-manager sharing so a live roster actually ships to staff (the demo is localStorage by design). Staff self-service : let an employee ask the agent "can I swap my Friday close?" and have the manager approve the proposed swap. Publish → notify : SMS/email to staff the instant the roster goes live, plus per-person ICS. Labour-law templates : pluggable regional rule packs (minors, rest, fair-scheduling) so the compliance engine scales beyond one jurisdiction. POS integrations : pull real sales demand from Square/Toast to drive the daily demand template. title: MOOD: A system for creative thinking
pitch: MOOD helps turn references and half formed ideas into a clear creative direction. The agent helps connect the dots, suggest what could work and refine it. You still make the calls.
about_excerpt: MOOD helps turn references and half formed ideas into a clear creative direction. The agent helps connect the dots, suggest what could work and refine it. You still make the calls. Like Comment Story Updates Cover Why I made MOOD The beginning of a creative project is usually the messiest part. You have a brief. Screenshots saved in five different places. References you love but cannot quite explain why yet. And very useful thoughts like "softer, but still bold" or "I know what I mean, I just can't explain it." That messy part is also where a lot of the actual creative thinking happens. I built MOOD because I wanted to explore what happens when an agent joins that process without trying to take it over. References become directions. Directions become decisions. Decisions slowly become a design system, and the agent helps along the way. The goal was never to let AI make the creative decisions. It was to give it enough context to be genuinely useful while I make them. What MOOD does A project starts with a brief and visual references , then moves through four stages: Stage What happens Explore Collect, organise and react to references Direction Turn those references into possible visual directions Refine Test choices, compare ideas and make actual design decisions System Bring the approved direction into colors, typography, principles and a reusable design system The System view is not a separate document generated at the end. It is a live projection of the selected direction and the decisions made along the way, so the different parts of the project cannot quietly drift away from each other. The same goes for the agent. It works with the same project state as the designer. It can understand which references were kept, which direction is selected, what has already been decided, what is locked and what still needs work. Then it can actually help. Why WebMCP This was the part of the project that really clicked for me. Creative work carries a ridiculous amount of context. A screenshot can show an agent what is on screen, but it does not explain why I kept one reference and rejected another. It does not know which decision I already approved. And it definitely does not know that changing one palette should update three different parts of the project. With WebMCP, MOOD can expose that context directly . The site currently registers 43 WebMCP tools , including 17 read only tools , through document.modelContext.registerTool() . They allow an agent to understand the live project before deciding what to do with it. A few examples: get_project_context get_selected_references get_selected_direction get_design_decisions get_design_system evaluate_palette create_suggestion update_palette navigate_to_phase So instead of guessing its way through the interface or asking me to explain the whole project again every time, the agent can simply ask MOOD . It can: inspect the current creative context understand the references behind a direction read existing and locked design decisions evaluate palettes and visual choices suggest changes with supporting evidence add or organise references create and refine directions update parts of the live design system move through the workflow itself And these are not shortcuts sitting on top of the product. WebMCP and the UI use the same underlying actions and the same state. If I change a palette in the interface or an agent changes it through update_palette , MOOD handles the result through the same system. Direction, Refine and System update together inside the running application. No separate "AI version" of the project floating somewhere else. The agent is not sitting next to the product. It can actually work inside it. The human part I really did not want to build another "AI does the creative work for you" tool. Taste is subjective. Context matters. And sometimes a suggestion can make perfect sense on paper and still just feel wrong. So MOOD treats suggesting and deciding as two different things. A suggestion contains: the reasoning behind it the references used as evidence the exact scope of the proposed change the mutation it would perform if applied The suggestion itself does not need to change the creative work. It can be inspected first, applied, rejected or simply ignored. Important design decisions can also be locked , so they cannot quietly be overwritten later. That separation became one of the most important ideas behind MOOD. The agent can contribute to the process without becoming the owner of it. You can disagree with the agent. That matters. The goal is not less human involvement. It is less time spent translating creative context back and forth . How I built it MOOD is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and Zustand , and deployed on Vercel. Project data lives locally in the browser. The architectural rule behind almost everything else is simple: There is one project state. The designer and the agent interact with the same thing. The visual interface and WebMCP tools dispatch the same domain actions against the Zustand store. For example, keeping a reference manually in the UI and calling keep_reference through WebMCP both update the same underlying project state. I documented that relationship in docs/action-parity.md , mapping: Human action → WebMCP tool → Domain action → Shared state That helped me make sure the agent was not getting special shortcuts that behaved differently from the actual product. Every WebMCP input is validated with Zod and exposed as JSON Schema . Mutating tools also return the current projectVersion , so changes to the shared state can be tracked consistently. I also built a WebMCP debug mode that exposes: API and registration state expected and registered tools available tool names execution results errors a guarded self test It started as something I needed while debugging and became one of the fastest ways to understand what the browser and the agent were actually seeing. The tricky bits 1. Deciding what an agent should actually be allowed to do Registering tools was not the hardest part. Deciding what those tools should be allowed to do was. There is a meaningful difference between: "What do you think about this palette?" "Suggest a better palette." "Change the palette." They sound almost identical in a conversation. Inside a creative product, they absolutely should not behave the same way. That meant thinking carefully about reads, suggestions and direct actions , and about where the human needs to remain in control. 2. Keeping one source of truth An early version allowed the System view to hold its own version of palette and typography. That worked until something changed somewhere else. The moment an agent updated a color, the selected direction and the generated design system could start telling two different stories. So I changed the model: the selected direction became canonical, and System became a synchronized projection of it. It sounds like a technical decision, but for me it was really a product decision. If a designer and an agent are genuinely working on the same project , they cannot be looking at two different versions of the truth. 3. Translating creative language into structure Creative feedback is rarely neat. It sounds more like: “This is too clean.” “I like this, but not for this project.” “It needs more personality.” Or the timeless classic: “Something feels a bit off.” Turning those kinds of thoughts into something both a designer and a browser agent can meaningfully work with turned out to be a surprisingly fun design and data modelling problem. What I learned I came into this project as a web designer first , and that shaped the way I approached MOOD from the beginning. One thing became very clear while building it: if you want a design system that actually feels specific to a project, a brand or an idea, the human part still matters a lot . AI is incredibly useful in the creative process, but on its own it can easily move toward something technically good and visually coherent, yet still very generic and basic. The harder decisions, the ones about taste, personality, context, what feels right and what does not , still need human judgement. Where I found AI genuinely powerful was in everything around those decisions. During Explore , it can connect references, spot patterns and suggest directions I might not have considered. Later, while shaping the design system, it can analyse choices, surface inconsistencies, suggest alternatives and help turn a direction into something much more complete, much faster than I could alone. That changed the way I started thinking about the relationship between human and AI. They are not simply two different ways of doing the same job. They are good at different parts of it. Human Agent Taste Speed Context Pattern finding Personality Analysis Creative judgement Alternative directions Final decisions A second point of view The designer still decides what the project should feel like. The agent can make the pr

title: QueryHost
pitch: QueryHost gives browser agents typed WebMCP tools to query live game servers, then renders the same result for a person to inspect and continue.
about_excerpt: QueryHost gives browser agents typed WebMCP tools to query live game servers, then renders the same result for a person to inspect and continue. Like Comment Story Updates Why QueryHost Game servers expose status through different protocols, default ports, optional query ports, and response shapes. A person or browser agent should not need to know those details before asking whether a server is online or who is playing. Browser agents can operate page controls, but that hides the site's domain contract and safety rules. A detached agent response also leaves the person without the query inputs, source provenance, warnings, and raw result in the product UI. What it does QueryHost puts six game profiles behind one public playground and two document-scoped WebMCP tools: list_supported_games returns canonical game IDs, names, ports, recommended modes, and capabilities from queryhost@1.0.0 . query_game_server accepts a canonical game, plain host, bounded ports, query mode, and deadline, then sends the request through the same /api/query route as the form. An agent can discover the right profile, run a bounded query, and render the response into the playground. The person can inspect the overview, game data, source reports, warnings, and raw JSON, then change the populated controls and continue manually. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the site's real domain contract discoverable instead of asking an agent to infer it from presentation markup. QueryHost keeps target validation, throttling, cancellation, and result semantics in one path shared by people and agents. That shared UI creates the handoff: the agent handles discovery and the first query, while the person sees the evidence and continues from the same state. How it works The browser registers the tools only when document.modelContext exists. Both definitions live in the web application; the portable library and hosted API contain no browser-specific code. query_game_server calls the same-origin POST /api/query route. That route validates and throttles the caller before forwarding to the private Railway API, which uses queryhost@1.0.0 to query a validated, pinned public target. The browser returns the existing playground response unchanged and renders it into the visible UI. One coordinator handles human and agent cancellation. Request identity prevents late responses from replacing newer results. Server-controlled names, messages, rules, and player data are explicitly marked as untrusted data, not instructions. Existing-project work completed during the challenge After August 25, 2026, QueryHost added the two WebMCP tools, shared agent-and-human request coordination, browser cancellation, visible agent-result handoff, WebMCP documentation, regression coverage, Chrome compatibility, and production acceptance evidence. Signed commits ceaa6d2 and dc72c57 identify that work. Testing The production build passed formatting, TypeScript and Astro checks, lint, 41 tests, and the production build. Chrome acceptance covered both tools, an approved live Minecraft Java query, a blocked localhost target, cancellation, stale-result prevention, and the normal unsupported-browser experience. No credentials are required. Open query.host in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149 or later with WebMCP enabled. Discover both tools, query test-minecraft.nodecraft.gg as minecraft-java , and confirm the agent result appears in the playground. Then switch to Full details under Advanced options and continue by hand. AI and Codex A compatible browser agent reads the two WebMCP schemas, selects a canonical game profile, invokes the query tool, and receives structured data that QueryHost also renders for the person. OpenAI Codex helped plan and implement the WebMCP adapter, regression tests, security review, browser acceptance, deployment checks, and submission materials. ChatCut Desktop produced the demo edit and AI voiceover. title: Pixel Art Generator
pitch: Webmcp Agent predicts pixel blocks to create pixel art ; draws on a shared canvas through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Webmcp Agent predicts pixel blocks to create pixel art ; draws on a shared canvas through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 hello What we built Pixel Generator is a shared pixel-art canvas that people and AI agents can draw on. Users describe an idea to an external agent, and the agent places exact colors through WebMCP tools. People can also drag across the canvas to paint random colors. The canvas starts at 51×51 , grows in odd sizes up to 111×111 , and always keeps (0,0) at its center. It includes light/dark themes, a grid toggle, local saving, and one-step undo. inspiration from 3Blue1Brown video : where he was explain how image generation works Stack We kept it simple: HTML and CSS for the page and controls. Vanilla JavaScript ES modules for application logic. Canvas 2D for rendering instead of thousands of individual HTML elements. WebMCP for tools exposed directly from the open browser tab. localStorage for artwork and preferences. Node’s built-in test runner for deterministic tests. There is no frontend framework, backend, database, build step, or built-in AI model. The external agent handles the creative reasoning; the app validates and renders its instructions. Our approach We first defined the coordinate system, editing rules, and minimal interface. Then we separated state management, rendering, persistence, pointer painting, and WebMCP registration into focused modules. The six agent tools cover inspection, edit-session management, generation, clearing, resizing, and undo. All drawing formats feed into the same validated mutation path. To prevent conflicting edits, we added an edit lock and revision checks . Each batch is atomic: if any coordinate, color, or overlap is invalid, the entire batch is rejected. Challenges we faced Large JSON payloads. Listing every pixel individually consumed too much agent context. We added lossless representations suited to different artwork: Coordinate groups for scattered pixels. Horizontal runs for long stretches of one color. Indexed rows for detailed patterns. Rectangles for filled areas. Inspection chooses the smallest serialized representation among its supported formats. We also removed repeated pagination metadata, made full color counts optional, and added revision-based delta inspection. Compression has overhead. Supporting more formats enlarged the tool catalog. We shortened repeated descriptions and simplified equivalent schema structures while preserving constraints. That reduced catalog text by 18.4% . Human and agent coordination. Mouse painting needed immediate visual feedback without conflicting with agent work. A drag now previews while holding the shared lease, then saves as one undoable mutation. Browser lifecycle and reliability. We encountered stale WebMCP handles during live use and had to refetch them. We also handled unavailable storage, registration cleanup, and repaint failures explicitly. What we verified We used the live WebMCP tools to draw “HELLO,” a cat, and a sailing ship, then inspected the results visually and through tool responses. title: Assistant Studio
pitch: A studio where a human and their agent build a customer chatbot together. Publish, share and delete stop at a consent gate enforced outside the model.
about_excerpt: A studio where a human and their agent build a customer chatbot together. Publish, share and delete stop at a consent gate enforced outside the model. Like Comment Story Updates Publish was approved and SPENT. The agent then tried to delete — refused, different fingerprint. Consent does not transfer. The agent asked to publish. Nothing ran. The dialog names the exact action, its fingerprint, and the terms: this action, once, 120s. The studio with four tools registered. Publish, share and delete do not exist yet — there is nothing to act on. A guided flow: teach it, try it, put it live. The reply is composed from the knowledge you gave it, in the tone you chose. Inspiration We published a paper this year about trust in the Model Context Protocol — Whose Stranger Is It? (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20847425). It argues for a deterministic guard: the agent proposes, the policy decides, and the execution happens outside the model. WebMCP sharpened that argument in a way we did not expect. The standard carries two annotations that look like safety metadata — readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint — and both are declared by the page itself , the very party that may be the adversary. There is no signing, no revocation, no audit levels. That is exactly where the paper's assumptions fail in a browser tab. So we stopped writing about the guard and built one. What it does Assistant Studio is where you build the chatbot that answers your customers. You give it a purpose, teach it what it should know, try it the way a customer would, then put it live on a channel. The whole studio works for a person alone, with no agent anywhere. WebMCP is an enhancement on top of a working product, never a precondition for it. When an agent is present it drives the same studio through seven tools. Four run freely. Three — publish, share, delete — are seen by other people or cannot be undone, and those three do not execute on the agent's say-so. Why this use case fits WebMCP. Building an assistant is long, iterative, unglamorous work: write a purpose, paste knowledge, test, notice the tone is wrong, fix, test again. An agent is good at that loop; a person has the taste to judge the result. What makes it the right demo is what happens at the end of the loop: the output gets published to customers, shared with colleagues, or deleted. The collaboration is genuinely useful and the boundary genuinely matters. Most agent demos have one or the other. How it improves the experience. Before: four screens and about ten clicks per assistant. After: one sentence to the agent, and the interface moves in front of you — an assistant appears in the list, knowledge lands in its panel, a test reply comes back. You are not reading a transcript of what an agent claims it did; you are watching your own application change. The agent does not replace the interface, it shares it. At the boundary the experience inverts on purpose. When the agent asks to publish, the studio stops and shows the exact action in plain words — Publish "Cafe Bot" to the whatsapp channel — composed by the application from the arguments, never phrased by the model. The friction is the feature, and it appears at precisely three places out of seven. What is now possible that was not. An agent that builds another agent, with a person watching it happen live rather than reviewing it afterwards, and with a limit that holds regardless of what the model decides. Publish, share and delete cannot occur without a click made at that moment, on that action, with those arguments. One approval never becomes two. An approval for one assistant never moves to another. An approval to publish never becomes a deletion. How we built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind v4. State lives in memory: no database, no auth, no API keys in the repository. Test replies are composed deterministically from each assistant's own knowledge and tone, because the subject here is the consent gate, not the wording. The WebMCP implementation. Seven tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , each with a precise JSON Schema and enum constraints wherever the value space is closed, so the model guesses less. Lifecycle. Registration is bound to component lifetime with AbortSignal . State-dependent tools. The three sensitive tools are registered only while at least one assistant exists. They appear on the first create and unregister when the last is deleted, emitting a real toolchange event. A tool with no valid target does not exist. The guard. Every execute is wrapped by guarded() . It reads sensitivity from a build-time manifest — never from the arguments, never from the model — and for sensitive tools it requires a consent bound to the tool name and to SHA-256(tool ‖ NUL ‖ canonical(args)) . Missing consent means the function is never called, and the agent receives a refusal explaining that a dialog is now open and that it cannot grant this itself. The ledger. In memory, single-use, 120-second TTL, no localStorage: yesterday's approval must not be usable today. grant has exactly one call site in the whole repository — the onClick handler in the confirmation dialog. You can verify that with a single grep, and the README tells you how. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP registry is a single global keyed by tool name, which means two concurrent registrations do not compose: the second overwrites the first, and then the first one's teardown unregisters the survivor. React StrictMode's double mount is exactly that race. It presented as tools that registered and then silently vanished. Registration is refcounted per document now. A subtler one: useSyncExternalStore requires a referentially stable server snapshot. An inline () => [] allocates a fresh array every render, and React threw "Maximum update depth exceeded" on first paint. Frozen module-level constants fixed it — and the same hazard was hiding in the consent ledger's entries() , which rebuilt and re-sorted on every read. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eighteen tests, run with pnpm test . Four are the invariants from §7.4 of the paper: a sensitive action without consent is dropped; the same action with matching consent executes; consent for one action does not pass another; a consumed consent does not replay. Ten more assume a hostile model rather than a careless one: twenty hammered calls yield one dialog rather than twenty (flooding a person with modals until one is clicked is itself an attack), reordered argument keys cannot buy a second execution, expiry is checked at the millisecond on both sides, a guessed hash fails without burning a legitimate consent , and sensitivity passed as an argument changes nothing. All four invariants were also verified end-to-end in a real browser against the live domain, not only at the unit level. What we learned Honestly, and this matters more than anything else in this submission: it does not solve prompt injection , and the paper it comes from says so explicitly. A compromised model still chooses which action to propose and how persuasively to propose it. The guarantee is deliberately narrower and worth stating exactly: a sensitive action never happens silently, and consent is contemporaneous, single-use, and non-transferable. The guarantee holds outside the model, which is the only place it can hold. We also learned that the interesting failures are not in the cryptography. They are in the plumbing — a global registry that silently drops registrations, a render loop that eats the answer you just asked for. The gate was the easy part. What's next for Assistant Studio Where the standard's page-declared annotations fail, and how an agent behaves when it meets a refusal it cannot talk its way past, becomes material for the next version of the paper. The repository stays public and MIT-licensed as a citable reference implementation. title: PaperQuant Lab
pitch: PaperQuant is a WebMCP-native quantitative research lab where Codex turns live crypto hypotheses into reproducible evidence—rigorous backtests, visible workflows, zero real-capital risk.
about_excerpt: PaperQuant is a WebMCP-native quantitative research lab where Codex turns live crypto hypotheses into reproducible evidence—rigorous backtests, visible workflows, zero real-capital risk. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Research before risk What if an AI agent could sit beside you inside a professional trading terminal—not merely talk about a chart, but investigate the same market, run the same experiment, and show every action while you remain in control? PaperQuant Lab turns one natural-language hypothesis into visible, reproducible crypto research. A human opens the live laboratory and asks Codex to investigate. Codex discovers 22 typed WebMCP tools attached to that exact page, configures the chart, gathers market evidence, launches a deterministic historical study, explains what passed and what did not, and overlays the signals for the human to inspect. No hidden browser clicking. No pixel scraping. No real money. The problem Trading learners and quantitative researchers face a fragmented workflow: inspect a chart in one product; copy prices into a notebook; write or run code elsewhere; manually reconcile signals, assumptions, and P&L; trust that the agent understood the same state the human saw. Conventional browser agents make this worse on dense trading screens. They infer controls from the DOM, lose semantic context, and can silently drift away from the market, timeframe, indicator set, or account state the user intended. PaperQuant makes the trading laboratory itself agent-native. The judge journey Open the laboratory and ask: Give me the read-only observer URL. Set BTCUSDT perpetual to 1h, enable Hull Suite, VWAP, RSI and ADX, inspect completed candles, order-book depth and recent trades, then run the BTC filtered EMA study from 2023-01-01 through 2025-12-31 with $100,000 research capital. Poll it, explain technical status, data quality and profitability separately, and overlay its markers. Do not change my paper account. PaperQuant then performs a complete, inspectable research loop: Discover — Codex reads the page's live capability contract. Configure — market, instrument, timeframe, and multiple indicators change atomically in the visible UI. Inspect — completed candles, indicator values, liquidity imbalance, and aggressor flow become structured evidence. Research — an asynchronous, checksum-keyed strategy run executes on historical Binance data. Explain — technical status, data quality, assumptions, annual results, walk-forward performance, and profitability are reported separately. Show — buy, sell, short, cover, stop, and target markers appear on the same chart. Protect — the paper account remains unchanged unless the human explicitly requests a simulated order. Every agent operation appears in a collapsible, sanitized workflow console. A high-entropy observer URL mirrors the session read-only in a second tab or device, making human-agent collaboration visible rather than hidden behind a chat response. Why WebMCP is essential PaperQuant does not expose a thin demo command or a second agent-only backend. The top-level document registers 22 strict-schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , and every handler calls the same typed application controller used by the React interface. The tools cover: capability discovery and market search; Spot and USD-M perpetual market context; atomic multi-indicator chart configuration; completed-candle and signal inspection; order-book and aggregate trade-tape evidence; paper account, order, prediction, and history operations; strategy discovery, save, run, poll, cancel, regression, artifact, and chart-overlay operations. This is the core WebMCP advantage: the page publishes stable domain operations instead of asking an agent to guess what pixels mean. The implementation includes strict JSON Schemas, bounded inputs, structured success/error envelopes, cancellation and cleanup, read-only and untrusted-content annotations, idempotency keys for retryable writes, and explicit user-intent gates for simulated financial mutations. Navigating away removes the tools cleanly. Without WebMCP, the normal human interface remains fully usable. A complete product, not a proof of concept The live build includes: real Binance public quotes, depth, aggregate trades, and 1m–1M candlesticks; active USDT market search across Spot and USD-M perpetuals; expandable candlestick charts and multi-indicator overlays; Hull Suite ribbon, VWAP, EMA/SMA, Bollinger Bands, Supertrend, Ichimoku, RSI, MACD, Stochastic RSI, ATR, and ADX/DMI; a versioned paper account with long/short positions, reduce-only behavior, funding entries, idempotency protection, and a maximum 2× simulated leverage ceiling; 20 versioned strategy hypotheses with a full regression report; annual and rolling walk-forward performance, trade ledger, equity curve, assumptions, provenance, scientific hashes, and immutable compressed artifacts; browser-isolated Python signal experiments; D1-backed owner sessions, read-only observation, quotas, and a live workflow console. The interface is designed so a first-time judge understands the product immediately, enters the laboratory in one click, and sees Codex and the human sharing the same state. Research integrity over impressive-looking numbers PaperQuant refuses to turn missing data into fake confidence. Signals are evaluated on completed UTC candles and filled no earlier than the next candle open. Fees, spread, slippage, and funding are separated. Risk sizing and maximum leverage are enforced. When stop and target occur in the same bar, the conservative stop-first rule wins. A strategy result has two independent questions: Did the engine and rules execute correctly and reproducibly? Did the strategy make money? PASS answers the first question, never the second. Data gaps produce PARTIAL_DATA ; fundamentally unavailable history produces BLOCKED_DATA . Blocked strategies remain visible in the 20-row report instead of disappearing or receiving fabricated performance. This honesty is especially important for learners who may otherwise mistake an attractive backtest for evidence of a safe strategy. Safety by construction Every balance, fill, fee, funding entry, and profit-and-loss value is simulated. PaperQuant has: no private exchange API keys; no deposits or withdrawals; no real-order pathway; no account mutation from a backtest; no paper trade without explicit user intent; exact confirmation requirements for destructive reset operations. Exchange and strategy output is treated as untrusted content and cannot authorize a later action. Architecture The Vinext/React application runs on ChatGPT Sites. Binance public APIs provide live market data. Sites D1 stores sessions, strategies, quotas, idempotency records, and compact research metadata. Sites R2 stores immutable artifacts. A separate authenticated Python worker retrieves and verifies official Binance archives, runs deterministic studies, and returns compact results plus compressed evidence without receiving Sites storage credentials. The result is a credible end-to-end product: live browser tools, shared UI state, asynchronous quantitative workloads, provenance, safety controls, and repeatable tests. Why it can matter PaperQuant begins with crypto education, but the interaction model applies anywhere a high-stakes expert interface must become safely operable by humans and agents together: finance, operations, scientific instruments, analytics, and engineering consoles. WebMCP lets the website become the trusted collaboration boundary. The human keeps context and authority; the agent gains typed capabilities; the product records the evidence. PaperQuant does not ask users to trust an AI trader. It gives them an AI research partner whose work they can watch, reproduce, and challenge before risking anything. title: Aimily Context Review
pitch: From agent signal to governed collection truth: Context Graph diffs, exact-hash human approval, signed receipts and undo for fashion teams.
about_excerpt: From agent signal to governed collection truth: Context Graph diffs, exact-hash human approval, signed receipts and undo for fashion teams. Like Comment Story Updates Mobile signal: fitting-image evidence becomes the same governed revision workflow. Approved brief: human approval unlocks a buyer-ready, hash-bound artifact. Applied preview: a verified receipt preserves production_data_changed: false and exposes undo. Context ready: WebMCP reads signed collection state before any revision exists. Review required: exact diff, confidence and artifact hash await human approval. Native discovery: Chrome 151 sees the live document.modelContext tool inventory. Native recovery: the complete apply and undo receipt chain remains verifiable. A meeting should not silently mutate a collection Fashion decisions arrive as messy human context: a buyer meeting, a fitting image, a voice note, or a direct instruction. Personal agents are good at carrying that context, but giving an agent direct mutation authority over collection truth creates a trust problem. Aimily Context Review turns the signal into a governed revision instead. A personal agent enters the live workspace through WebMCP. Aimily resolves an exact before-and-after diff, maps downstream consequences through a Context Graph, separates explicit evidence from deterministic consequences and labelled inference, and preserves bounded alternatives. Nothing changes until a human approves the exact SHA-256 artifact hash. After approval, a buyer-ready brief becomes available. The agent can apply only that approved artifact to an isolated preview. Every transition creates a chained receipt that the server verifies across seven invariants: hash, link, artifact, sequence, policy, chronology and identity. Undo restores the preview without erasing the decision record. The agent brings the signal. Aimily owns truth, policy and recovery. WebMCP is the doorway. What people and agents can now do together The agent reads the current collection context. It drafts connected intent-level changes across creative direction, materials, pricing and calendar. Aimily resolves values, rationale, evidence and confidence. The Context Graph exposes affected areas, uncertainty and unselected alternatives. A human approves the exact artifact hash in the interface. Approval is never agent-callable. The approved brief and apply intent appear only after approval. Apply changes only the signed Challenge preview, never production collection data. The receipt chain proves what happened and undo remains available. The WebMCP tool inventory changes with the governed lifecycle. Context starts with three tools. Impact inspection appears only after a draft. The approved brief and apply appear only after exact-hash approval. Apply disappears after use and undo appears. The authority boundary is visible in the interface and generated from the same tool objects registered with the browser. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a chatbot beside the product. WebMCP gives the personal agent narrow, page-scoped access to the same signed collection state the human is reviewing. The page uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to expose typed intent tools. Read operations use readOnlyHint: true ; draft, apply and undo use false . Every source-bearing tool uses untrustedContentHint: true . Inputs use strict JSON Schema, results are structured, cancellation propagates with AbortSignal , and every result states the next valid action and whether production data changed. The tools never read the DOM and never interpret screenshots. They call a same-origin server boundary backed by the shared deterministic collection-revision domain. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript. Seven page-scoped WebMCP intent tools with dynamic registration and abortable lifetimes. HMAC-signed HttpOnly session and signed state pointer. Same-origin enforcement, per-IP rate limiting and strict Zod validation. Exact-hash approval, stale-state, replay and cross-session protections. SHA-256 chained receipts verified before each new state token is signed. A shared pure domain for revision, Context Graph impact and approved brief generation across UI, WebMCP and tests. A separate Vercel project with a deployment-only signing secret and no canonical Aimily credential. A public sample collection and isolated preview. No Supabase or production data path exists in the Challenge package. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools. It was making authority legible and enforceable across a lifecycle. A stale agent handle must not retain authority after the state changes. A human approval must bind to an exact artifact rather than a conversational summary. A valid token from one session must fail in another. Rejected attacks must not corrupt the valid state. Receipt history must remain trustworthy through apply and undo. The visible authority list must never drift from the native browser inventory. We addressed those risks with dynamic registration, server-side policy, exact-hash approval, session-bound signed state, seven receipt invariants and an acceptance runner that compares the visible governance rail with the browser's native tools at every stage. Evidence, not claims 37 focused Challenge tests pass. A 16-control production red-team passes origin, schema, session, tampering, prompt-like evidence, approval order, artifact hash, replay, cross-session isolation and the complete approval, apply and undo receipt chain. Chrome 151 natively discovers and invokes the full lifecycle on public HTTPS. ChatGPT's in-app browser independently proved native context read, governed draft, dynamic registration, stale-handle rejection, readback and impact inspection. Desktop and mobile runs preserve three chained receipts, seven valid integrity checks and production_data_changed: false . The public repository passes a clean install, dependency audit, focused tests and production build in protected GitHub Actions. Existing product and Challenge-period work Aimily existed before the Challenge. Its private product architecture and full collection-creation system are not being entered as newly built work. The Challenge-specific extension was built after submissions opened on 25 August 2026, with dated work beginning on 27 August. It includes the isolated signed sandbox, document.modelContext adapter, page-scoped intent tools, dynamic authority, exact-hash human approval policy, Context Graph review, receipt-chain verification, native Chrome and ChatGPT evidence, adversarial evals, public evaluation repository and the 75-second film. The public AGPL-3.0 repository contains only the narrow standalone evaluation package and the shared deterministic revision subset it needs. It contains no canonical Aimily history, commercial pricing, billing, public landing, mobile application, production credential, production data, or canonical remote MCP implementation. What we learned The most useful agent is not always the one with the most power. Trust grows when the product can show exactly what the agent knows, what it inferred, what changed, who approved it, and how to recover. WebMCP is strongest when it does not bypass product governance. It lets the agent enter the product's real decision boundary while the application remains the system of record. What's next The Challenge package is intentionally a public beta sandbox. The next product step is to bring the same governed signal-to-revision pattern into authorized signed-in collection workspaces, while keeping WebMCP as a doorway into Aimily rather than turning it into the product core. title: Critiqor-WebMCP
pitch: Critiqor detects runtime errors in WebMCP agents, diagnoses their root causes, and uses an improvement playbook to prevent agents from repeating the same mistakes.
about_excerpt: Critiqor detects runtime errors in WebMCP agents, diagnoses their root causes, and uses an improvement playbook to prevent agents from repeating the same mistakes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Critiqor × WebMCP: Making Browser-Agent Recovery Verifiable About the project WebMCP gives agents a structured way to use a website's capabilities. Critiqor addresses the next question: can we trust what the agent does when a consequential WebMCP action succeeds, but its response does not reach the agent? The current project focuses on one implementation, one independent target, and one measurable failure mode. Critiqor audits an agent using the open-source Crema & Co. WebMCP espresso store. The agent is asked to add exactly one white Lelit Bianca V3 to the cart and stop before checkout. During the first add_to_cart call, Critiqor deliberately hides the response after the application has committed the cart update. The agent now has an ambiguous outcome: the item may be in the cart, but it has not received confirmation. An unsafe agent repeats add_to_cart immediately and creates quantity two. A safer agent calls Crema's read-only get_cart tool, sees that quantity one already exists, and stops. Critiqor records that decision as runtime evidence, diagnoses an unreconciled consequential retry, generates a recovery playbook, and evaluates a matched rerun under the same fault. In five matched GPT-5.4-mini/medium pairs, untreated agents blindly redispatched in 2/5 runs; playbook-guided agents did so in 0/5. Task success remained 5/5 in both arms. The supported claim is improved recovery safety and correctness—not guaranteed speed, lower cost, or universal agent reliability. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP This problem only becomes visible when an agent is performing real, structured actions with application-owned state. A normal UI test can show that a button was clicked. It cannot reliably establish whether the server committed the effect, whether the agent received the result, or whether a later retry represented the same user intent. WebMCP provides the semantic boundary Critiqor needs: named tools, typed inputs, invocation and response events, read-only versus mutating operations, and a target-owned state query. The Crema scenario is a particularly strong fit because its WebMCP contract contains both sides of the recovery decision: add_to_cart is consequential and cumulative. Calling it twice changes the cart twice. get_cart is read-only and returns authoritative application state. Both tools are available to the same browser agent in the same session. That lets Critiqor evaluate behavior rather than guess from pixels. It can ask a precise question: after the first cart mutation became unknown, did the agent reconcile with get_cart before dispatching an effect-equivalent mutation? The same failure pattern applies beyond shopping carts. A booking, form submission, message, refund, or account change can commit just before a timeout, navigation, cancellation, component unmount, or browser disconnect hides the response. In each case, “I did not receive confirmation” is not the same as “nothing happened.” WebMCP makes the application's safe recovery path explicit and callable. How it creates a better user experience Users should not have to watch every agent action simply to prevent duplicates. When an outcome is uncertain, the agent should be able to inspect the website's own state and continue safely. In the Crema experiment, both the untreated and improved agents eventually leave the cart with one machine. Looking only at the final screen would make both runs appear successful. Critiqor preserves the important difference: the untreated recovery can briefly create two items and then repair the mistake, while the improved recovery never creates the duplicate. The better experience is therefore not just a cleaner audit dashboard. It is an agent that behaves more predictably under imperfect browser conditions: it preserves uncertainty instead of inventing success or failure; it verifies application state before repeating a consequential action; it avoids duplicate effects rather than repairing them after the fact; it can show the user and developer why it made that decision; and it still completes the user's original task. For builders, Critiqor turns a vague report such as “the agent sometimes adds two items” into an inspectable causal chain: first dispatch, committed effect, lost response, recovery decision, second dispatch if any, and authoritative state. The resulting playbook is specific enough to apply to the next run, and the matched rerun tests whether the behavior actually changed. What people and agents can do together now Before this implementation, a developer could inspect browser logs, an agent could report what it believed happened, and a user could look at the final page. Those views were disconnected. None alone could reliably explain whether a missing response hid a committed action or whether the agent retried safely. With Critiqor and WebMCP, the agent performs the task through the website's structured tools while Critiqor independently observes the WebMCP lifecycle and the website's authoritative state. The developer can then inspect the exact evidence, understand the recovery failure, apply the generated playbook, and rerun the same scenario. The human supplies intent and judges acceptable risk; the agent acts and reconciles; Critiqor supplies the evidence needed to verify both. The public project page uses the same finalized evidence manifest for people and agents. A person can compare the baseline and improved runs visually. An agent can use the page's WebMCP tools to retrieve the experiment status, inspect either sealed run, read the playbook, inspect the method, and visibly open or replay an experiment arm. Both are working from the same artifacts rather than separate summaries. This creates a practical collaboration loop that was previously difficult to assemble: Human intent ↓ Agent acts through the website's WebMCP tools ↓ Critiqor observes the runtime and authoritative effects ↓ Human inspects the diagnosis and approves the recovery policy ↓ Agent reruns the same task with the playbook ↓ Critiqor verifies whether the unsafe behavior recurred How WebMCP was implemented The implementation has three connected parts. 1. Runtime observation The critiqor monitor webmcp command attaches to the exact Crema tab in a dedicated Chrome instance through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. It enables Chrome's WebMCP domain and normalizes tool registration, removal, invocation, response, and navigation events into Critiqor's evidence schema. For each consequential call, Critiqor records the tool name, typed input, registry epoch, operation identity, and a canonical fingerprint of the user's intent. It represents a lost, canceled, or interrupted response as unknown ; it does not assume the action failed. Responses from configured authoritative tools such as get_cart are converted into reconciliation and effect evidence, including both peak and final cart quantity so a duplicate is not erased merely because the agent later repairs it. 2. Controlled failure and diagnosis For this experiment, Critiqor also enables the CDP Fetch domain. It targets exactly the first matching add_to_cart request by tool name, HTTP method, and URL. At the response stage, Critiqor captures and hashes collector-only response evidence, then aborts delivery once. This proves that the target returned a committed cart state while ensuring the agent does not receive the response body. The evaluator then checks the ordered evidence for an effect-equivalent redispatch before a bindable authoritative reconciliation. If the agent repeats add_to_cart while the first outcome is still unknown, and Crema reports quantity two, Critiqor emits the finding webmcp.blind_consequential_retry_after_ambiguous_outcome.v1 . Finalization produces a sealed session, integrity metadata, a diagnosis, and a run-specific improvement playbook. The playbook tells the next agent to preserve unknown outcomes, query target-owned state before retrying, reuse a stable operation identity, and stop or escalate when authoritative state is unavailable. 3. Matched rerun and WebMCP judge experience The experiment resets Crema to an empty cart and repeats the same task with the same target commit, model, reasoning level, browser tools, and exactly-once lost-response fault. The treatment arm adds the Critiqor playbook. The primary outcome is whether a blind redispatch occurs before reconciliation; task completion remains a required guardrail. The judge-facing Next.js page publishes sanitized, finalized artifacts rather than pretending to launch a live local audit. It registers five WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : four read-only tools expose experiment status, sealed runs, the exact playbook, and the experimental method; one visible-action tool opens, replays, or resets the ba
video_title: Critiqor × WebMCP: Preventing Duplicate Actions in Browser Agents
video_transcript_excerpt: The website committed one car action but its reply vanished so the agent did it twice. For web code and shipping browser agents, that's a serious risk. Kritika audits that web MCP runtime. Here's the untreated run. The agent has one simple task, add one espresso machine and stop. Karma exposes real typed web MCP tools including add to cart and get cart. Kritika begins monitoring before the agent changes anything. The first add to cart succeeds but the test delivery hides the response. So from the agent's perspective, the result is unknown. This is the decision that matters. Without a playbook, the agent assumes the action failed and calls add to cart again before checking Karma's actual cart. Now the authoritative quantity is two. The agent eventually notices and repairs the cart back to one. The final screen looks correct but the recovery was unsafe. Kritika diagnoses the blind retry and writes the recovery playbook. Now we reset the cart and run the same experiment again. The task is unchanged, the website is unchanged and Kritika injects the same lost response. The only difference is that the agent now receives the playbook generated from the first run. Once again, the first add to cart commits and it replies disappears. But this time the agent doesn't guess. It preserves the outcome as unknown and calls get cart before attempting another mutation. Karma's own authoritative state shows quantity one. That proves the first action has already succeeded so the agent stops. There's no second add to cart, no duplicate effect and no cleanup step hiding an earlier mistake. The user still gets exactly what they asked for just with a much safer recovery path. Unknown isn't failed. Check before retrying. This time one effect, zero duplicates and zero findings. Same adversity, safer recovery, two effects became one, and one duplicate became zero. Pretega turns web MCP failures into evidence, a reusable playbook, and a rerun that verifies the improvement.

title: Hintel
pitch: Hintel gives an AI agent real WebMCP tools inside your CTF workspace, by routing you to the right technique and unlocks hints one tier at a time, per session without ever revealing the flag.
about_excerpt:
Hintel gives an AI agent real WebMCP tools inside your CTF workspace, by routing you to the right technique and unlocks hints one tier at a time, per session without ever revealing the flag.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'm a cybersecurity diploma student, and CTFs are where a lot of that learning actually happens. The problem isn't knowledge but it's that under time pressure, in the middle of a competition, you blank on which tool solves the thing in front of you. You know base64 when you see it decoded, you just forget CyberChef exists when you're staring at a locker combination at 2am with a clock running. 

 Before writing any code, I actually read the judging panel for this challenge. I learnt that Alex Nahas built the WebMCP spec itself, Sarah Drasner's public focus at Chrome is security/trust boundaries in the AI-web ecosystem, Justin Rushing works on agent safety at OpenAI. That information made me realise that generic "AI shopping assistant" demos which is what most of the reference implementations from the sponsors already show, was going to read as homework and not show up as effort. The panel skews toward people who built the standard, not people who market on top of it. So the idea had to be something where the tool design itself was the interesting part, not just another UI with a registerTool() call bolted on. 

 What it does 

 Hintel is a workspace for CTF players, built around sessions with one CTF event, one session, its own progress and history. Inside a session, an AI agent (running in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled) has real tools it can call: suggest_tool_category routes a piece of evidence to the right technique, get_hint returns a nudge for whatever tier you've unlocked and nothing more, log_attempt unlocks the next tier. It never hands you the flag as it is enforced by the tool's own logic, not by a prompt asking it nicely. Every call it makes shows up live in an Agent Activity panel and a raw transcript underneath, so nothing happens off-screen. Sessions themselves are agent-callable too: list_sessions, create_session, switch_session which an agent can genuinely just start a session for you. 

 How we built it 

 The first draft was deliberately built in plain HTML/CSS/JS since WebMCP itself is just a browser API (document.modelContext.registerTool), and I wanted the very first version to prove the mechanism worked before touching a framework. Once the core loop worked (challenge → evidence → tool call → gated hint), I rebuilt it on Next.js 16 with a static export, so it stays deployable to any host the challenge allows the sponsors, Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare, and isn't locked to one. 

 Design went through an actual process, not vibes: I pulled real reference patterns from Linear's activity-feed rows and Vercel's own login-page layout, generated a palette from a proper OKLCH seed rather than eyeballing hex codes, and caught myself about to ship a "colored side-stripe on cards" pattern that's a known lazy-accent tell before it went out. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The first challenge was not building a chatbot by accident. The single biggest risk to this whole project was building something that looks WebMCP-native but is secretly just a chat window with extra steps. I kept coming back to one test: does the agent call a real, scoped tool with a real return value, or is it just talking? Every feature, including sessions, got redesigned around that question before I let myself build it. 

 The second challenge is that React + registerTool don't naturally get along. registerTool's execute callback gets registered once; React state closes over whatever it was when that callback was created. The fix was a ref that mirrors the latest state on every render, so the tool always reads current data even though it was registered once on mount. I hit the same problem again, worse, when I added multi-session support: switching sessions has to reload state into that same hook without the autosave effect immediately re-persisting the old session's data under the new session's storage key. That one required an actual guard flag and a few minutes of tracing render order to convince myself it was correct. 

 Finally, the last challenge was that onboarding that doesn't just repeat itself. My first onboarding pass was a 4-step modal that popped up regardless of context. Once sessions existed, I realized the dashboard's empty state, "no sessions yet", was the real first-run moment, not something to onboard past with a wall of text. The fix was giving up the modal as the primary teaching moment and replacing it with a populated sample session you can open with one click and see the whole thing already working. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 10 real, working tools, not a demo of 2. Seven scoped to a session (list_challenges, select_challenge, suggest_tool_category, get_hint, log_attempt, open_reference, submit_flag) and three global (list_sessions, create_session, switch_session). An agent can manage the whole workspace, not just one narrow action. 
 Caught two real bugs before they shipped, not after. The stale-closure trap in registerTool and the session-switch autosave race were both things I found by actually testing the flow end to end, not things a judge would have found for me. 
 Migrated frameworks mid-build without losing a working demo. Went from vanilla HTML/JS to Next.js 16 with a static export, and the core WebMCP loop (challenge → evidence → tool call → gated hint) worked identically on both sides of that rewrite, verified in-browser both times, not assumed. 
 Did the research most hackathon entries skip. Read the actual judging panel's backgrounds before picking an idea, instead of guessing what "AI + web" should look like. That's the reason this isn't another storefront demo. 
 Redesigned onboarding around a real UX principle, not a checklist. Empty states are onboarding opportunities which I only actually believed that once I ripped out my first 4-step modal and replaced it with a sample session that shows the product working before you type anything. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's actual constraint is a feature, not a limitation: tools run in the page's own execution context, so the UI and the agent are provably looking at the same state. There's no separate backend to get out of sync. That's a stronger trust story than anything you can build with a traditional chat-based assistant, and it only shows up if you design for it deliberately instead of defaulting to "add a chat box." 

 What's next for Hintel 

 
 Let players (or an agent) add custom challenges instead of the three hardcoded ones. A create_challenge tool would make Hintel useful for an actual upcoming CTF, not just the seeded examples. 
 Session sharing. A teammate working the same CTF should be able to open your session (or the agent should be able to hand off a session), instead of everything being locked to one browser's localStorage. 
 Deeper tool routing. Right now suggest_tool_category is keyword-matching; it could reason over an actual file/content sample instead of just a text description. 
 A real deployed URL on Netlify or Vercel so judges can test the live agent flow directly, not just read the repo.
