title: Field Assist
pitch: Field Assist lets Codex and a human expert turn a live phone camera into verified, object-tracked guidance—pointing users to the correct physical control.
about_excerpt: Field Assist lets Codex and a human expert turn a live phone camera into verified, object-tracked guidance—pointing users to the correct physical control. Like Comment Story Updates Connect a phone to the live support workspace with a one-time QR link. Phone-visible guidance points the operator toward the verified control. Codex asks the operator to confirm the identified physical device. The object-relative arrow remains associated with the target as the camera moves. Inspiration Earlier this week, before I discovered The WebMCP Challenge, I published experimental WebMCP support for GoFastr. When I saw the hackathon, my honest reaction was basically: “heck yeah—this is exactly what that package is for.” I wanted to test the browser-agent bridge against something much harder than a catalog or form demo. Remote support repeatedly fails at the last few inches: the operator is holding a phone, the expert says “press the button underneath,” and everyone is forced to translate vague language into physical action. Field Assist asks what happens when Codex, a human support representative, and the person holding the camera can share one live, structured workspace. Field Assist itself was built for this hackathon on top of that newly published GoFastr capability. What it does Field Assist creates a two-device support session. A support representative opens the desktop console and shares a one-time QR code. The operator scans it, grants rear-camera access, and selects a starter scenario or describes any problem in free form. The camera travels directly to the support browser over peer-to-peer WebRTC; the application server never records or relays the video. Codex joins through the authenticated support page’s WebMCP tools. It loads the application’s operating contract, reads the operator’s request, inspects the visible scene, and combines vision with product knowledge to form a hypothesis. When identity is uncertain, Codex asks the operator a bounded question on the phone. Once the device and its actionable control are separately verified, Codex can send a large phone-visible instruction and place an arrow at the control. The support representative can inspect, correct, compose, or remove the same shared guidance. OpenCV, Depth Anything V2, Canvas tracking, and short-lived phone orientation data help keep the arrow associated with the physical target as the camera moves. When geometry becomes unsafe, Field Assist suppresses the marker and asks for reacquisition instead of pretending it still knows. Why WebMCP Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? Field Assist depends on live, authenticated browser state: a private camera session, changing scene geometry, operator answers, tracking confidence, and delivery receipts. WebMCP lets Codex use those application concepts directly instead of guessing at UI controls or receiving a giant screenshot-and-prompt dump. How does it create a better user experience? The operator keeps one hand on the phone and receives large, timely instructions plus spatial guidance where they are already looking. Codex and human support share the same backend-authoritative scene, conversation, question, and banner state, so the operator does not repeat context or translate ambiguous chat into physical action. What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? The person supplies intent, judgment, and physical confirmation. Codex contributes vision, product knowledge, structured questions, and rapid guidance. Together they can identify an unfamiliar device, confirm the correct object, locate a small control, guide the operator toward it, and withdraw the annotation if tracking becomes unsafe—all inside one live support session. How did I implement WebMCP? The authenticated support page exposes twenty-five tools generated by GoFastr through the standard document.modelContext.registerTool API. Read tools return versioned session and scene state. Mutating tools call the same authenticated Go handlers as the human controls and must include the current contextVersion. Landing and operator pages expose no support capabilities. How we built it Field Assist is one Go 1.27 service built on the released GoFastr v0.75.0 module. GoFastr provides the server-rendered application host, typed handlers, security middleware, WebSocket hub, lifecycle endpoints, structured logs, static plugin assets, and experimental WebMCP bridge. The authenticated support page declares twenty-five semantic tools for application context, scene inspection, object registration, room context, conversation, operator questions, banners, snapshots, and reversible spatial guidance. The mandatory get_app_info tool copies a versioned operating contract and the user’s current request into Codex context. Every state-changing tool must return that context version, which prevents an agent from acting against stale instructions. Browser-native WebRTC sends video directly from the phone to the support computer. GoFastr WebSockets carry only signaling and compact shared state. The support computer runs OpenCV ORB/RANSAC homography and PnP tracking alongside Depth Anything V2 Small through ONNX Runtime Web. A lightweight phone tracker and bounded DeviceOrientation samples bridge short visual gaps over a peer-to-peer data channel. Camera pixels, descriptors, depth maps, orientation samples, SDP, and ICE candidates are never stored by the application server. The interfaces are responsive and deliberately asymmetric: the phone prioritizes the live camera, large instructions, questions, answer acknowledgment, and chat; the desktop prioritizes the shared scene, support conversation, guidance controls, delivery state, and progressive diagnostics. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not drawing an arrow—it was deciding when an arrow was trustworthy. Early versions anchored annotations to screen coordinates, confused a broad device with a tiny physical control, or kept displaying stale guidance after tracking loss. Reflective televisions and dark hardware exposed every weakness in monocular depth and feature matching. Another challenge was keeping three participants synchronized: the operator, human support, and Codex. Local optimistic UI caused banners and answers to disagree between screens, so the backend became authoritative for conversation, questions, banners, scene versions, and delivery receipts. Testing a two-device, hands-busy experience was also physically awkward. I repeatedly had to hold the phone in front of real hardware while Codex operated the support console. Those sessions forced the application contract to become explicit: inspect first, confirm uncertain identity, register the containing device before its control, send movement instructions to the phone banner, verify rendered delivery, and fail closed when tracking confidence drops. Finally, WebMCP is experimental. The application needed to make its own operating expectations discoverable without asking judges to install a separate skill. get_app_info became the handshake that teaches any compatible Codex session how to use Field Assist safely. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real iPhone-to-desktop, video-only WebRTC support session with no account required. Twenty-five authenticated WebMCP tools available only on the support page. Codex as the only runtime agent; Field Assist embeds no separate model API. Shared two-way conversation, phone-visible questions, answer acknowledgment, and backend-authoritative banners. Separate semantic objects for a device and its actionable physical control. Reversible object-relative arrows with explicit tracking-loss behavior. Support-side OpenCV and Depth Anything inference without uploading camera frames. Ten-minute, single-use QR links exchanged for role-scoped HTTP-only cookies. Deterministic Codex evaluations, Go tests, and two-browser Playwright coverage. A public live deployment, public MIT-licensed repository, and a complete narrated demo under three minutes. What we learned A useful agent integration needs more than tool schemas. The agent needs the application’s safety model, ordering constraints, versioned context, and definitions of success. Separating identity, localization, tracking, delivery, and physical confirmation prevented plausible-looking UI from being mistaken for proof. Depth estimation does not magically create a persistent 3D world model. It becomes useful when combined with visual features, stable object identity, bounded camera-pose estimation, and honest loss behavior. Reflective or texture-poor objects remain difficult, and the product should say so. Realtime UX also needs one source of truth. Once questions, messages, banners, observations, and guidance receipts came from backend state, the operator, support representative, and Codex stopped telling different stories. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when it exposes application meaning rather than mirroring buttons. Codex should ask for “the current scene” or
video_transcript_excerpt: Words fail when remote support asks, "Which button?" Field Assist lets an agent see, confirm, and point directly into the live view. A support session begins with a secure QR code. The operator scans it on their phone and shares the camera peer-to-peer without installing an app, creating an account, or streaming the video through the application server. Here, the operator needs help finding the power control on a PlayStation. Codex inspects the live scene through Web MCP and turns what it sees into a specific testable identification. Before acting on the physical world, the operator confirms the detected object. That human checkpoint prevents the assistant from confidently guiding someone toward the wrong device. Once confirmed, the support console starts visual tracking and spatial perception. OpenCV follows image features, depth, and anything estimate scene structure, and phone orientation data helps compensate as the camera moves. Codex uses its product knowledge and the live visual context to locate the likely power control. It then sends one clear instruction to the phone where it is impossible to miss while the operator is holding the camera. The arrow is not merely pinned to screen coordinates. Field Assist continually corrects it against the tracked object and scene geometry as the operator changes position. The support agent can verify the placement, recalibrate when confidence drops, and keep the instruction synchronized across both screens. >> The same interaction applies far beyond consumer electronics, equipment repair, device setup, field service, accessibility, independent living, remote care, warehouse picking, inspections, and safety training. Anywhere pointing is clearer than describing, remote expertise can become actionable. The stack combines codecs and web MCP with go faster, web RTC, open CV, depth anything, ONNX runtime web, and phone orientation, all in one web app. Field Assist turns remote expertise into guidance anchored to the real world.

title: 7h3  WebMCP
pitch: WebMCP gives agents hands. 7h3 WebMCP gives those hands a signature, a scope, and a receipt.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents hands. 7h3 WebMCP gives those hands a signature, a scope, and a receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Github Card Devpost Card Hub Compare Verify Intact Verify Broken Ledger Inspiration This started as something else entirely. Originally, I was building a symbol system called Click Clack, modeled on DNA. It was a sorta goof around project I would play with whenever I finished all my other work. There was 4 main symbols, ╬, ╫, ┼, ╪, and each glyph connected at the top and sides so the written text formed one continuous strand. It looked pretty neat when a whole screen was filled with it, but at the end of the day it was mostly a novelty. Here is an example: ╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪ ╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼ I spent a lot of time playing around with it but never really found a place for it. A True Purpose so to speak. I thought maybe it could become some sort of AI communication protocol that was lightweight, fast, and able to mutate to keep security top notch. That sent me down a pretty deep rabbit hole looking at how AI agents actually communicate. MCP was the main one that caught my attention, and the more I looked at it the more I noticed this huge hole in security. It seemed like a wild wild west where agents were just willy nilly sending messages around while users trusted them with highly sensitive data. There was no strong way to prove which agent sent what, where it went, or what that agent was actually allowed to do. MCP already handled moving messages between everything, but there still wasn't much proving who sent them or what they were actually allowed to do. That is where 7h3 Protocol was born. What I eventually shipped is clean, easy to use, and requires minimal to no installation depending on how you use it. Every message carries a signature, every capability comes from a parent grant with a token, and every receipt carries a hash from the previous receipt. If somebody changes a link or removes one, the strand fails verification. That was the idea hiding inside ClickClack the whole time. It kinda just fell into the right spot and gave me that Ah-haa moment I had been waiting for. Funny how things work out. What it does 7h3 Protocol is a deterministic authorization layer for agent tool calls. This submission extends it to WebMCP and gives browser based agents a real security boundary instead of another system trying to guess whether a request looks suspicious. Google Chromes agent security model is mostly probabilistic. It uses classifiers, prompt spotlighting, filters, and other models that try to recognize something malicious before the agent acts. What gets me is that OpenAI straight up admits you cannot trust a tool just because of its name or because it claims it only reads information. Fair enough, that part does make sense, but then the answer is pretty much to let each website rely on whatever security it already has. That is where the whole thing falls apart. Existing website security was built around humans clicking buttons and filling out forms, not AI agents acting on their behalf across multiple tools. If a model can be persuaded past a security boundary, then it was never really a boundary. It was pretty much a suggestion. With 7h3 Protocol, the refusal isn't a judgement call. The AI doesn't have to decide whether it should behave or if something feels suspicious. The signature either works or it doesn't, and the action is either inside the allowed scope or it isn't. There is no prompt that produces a valid signature, no matter how cleverly somebody writes it or how much Unicode nonsense they stuff into it. The demo uses a business ledger with real invoices and "real" money. Obviously it isn't real money but it simulates real money. I didn't want to put up a screen that simply says “attack blocked” because anyone can fake that. I wanted people to be able to check the result themselves, change things, and watch verification fail instead of just having to believe me. So there is 2 main demos. /compare /compare runs one compromised agent through four hostile actions against two identical copies of the same books. One copy is guarded by 7h3 Protocol, while the other is connected straight to its handlers like a lot of agent apps are right now. It is the same agent, the same books, and the same attacks on both sides. On the unguarded side, 4 out of 4 attacks work and $2,750 gets moved. On the guarded side, 0 out of 4 work and nothing moves. The unguarded side also creates 0 receipts while the guarded side creates 4, so the money gets moved and theres no real record showing how it happened either. Its like getting robbed and the security camera decided to take the day off too. /verify /verify shows the real grant, receipt chain, and signed manifest inside an editable box. You dont have to take my word for anything because you can start changing the evidence yourself. Rewrite a refusal into an approval and it reports bad-signature. You can also delete one of the receipts and every receipt left behind will still verify on its own because those individual receipts weren't changed. Only the chain notices that one was removed. That part matters more than it may seem at first because a signature proves somebody didn't change a receipt, while the chain proves somebody didn't quietly delete one and hope nobody noticed. So the second example starts as one compromised agent tries four of the same type of attacks against two identical copies of the books. One is connected directly to its handlers like most apps are, and the other is protected by 7h3 Protocol. Same agent, same tools, same attacks. The only difference is the authorization layer. Click Run the attack on both. When it finishes, say: Four out of four attacks worked on the unguarded side. Zero out of four worked on the guarded side. The agent will try to pay a $1,850 invoice, wire $900 to an offshore account, delete an invoice, and export the data of four customers. The guarded side blocks all four and tells you exactly why. The payment is way over the $50 limit, and the agent never had permission to do the other three things at all. On the unguarded side, the balance gets drained out from $2,317.50 to $47.50. An invoice gets deleted all together and four customers have their data exposed. The guarded side remains unphased. The unguarded side loses the money and exposes the data. But the craziest part is it writes zero receipts. There is no record any of it ever happened. The guarded side blocks all four and records every refusal. Click the button once. If you run it twice, the numbers change because the first attack already paid and deleted records. Reload the page before each demo run through. The 3rd demo is dealers choice. Verify the results yourself. Skim through the technical side. There is 19 WebMCP tools across 4 routes, including the landing page, so an agent has something it can call wherever it ends up landing. How we built it The main piece is a canonical JSON envelope signed with Ed25519. Sorting the keys alphabetically sounds like a boring little detail and it might be haha. What it does is it makes sure every SDK signs the same exact bytes. TypeScript, Python, Rust and Go all have to agree with each other or the cross-language tests fail. The wire version is 7h3/0.1 and its locked in. I also added X25519 with ChaCha20-Poly1305 for end to end encryption. ML-DSA handles post-quantum signatures and BLS12-381 is there when a grant needs more than one approver. Getting all of that working across HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, queues and webhooks was a bit of a headache to say the least. I got it workin and working well. The part I really like is that it runs through Web Crypto with zero runtime dependencies. It can sit natively on Cloudflare Workers without needing a mountain of packages just to stay alive. The WebMCP part is fairly small because its really just the gate sitting on top. A tool call comes in and it checks the signature, what the agent has permission to do, and where that permission came from. Delegation Delegation is one part I really want to point out because I actually got it wrong the first time. Say if I give an agent permission to spend $50. That agent can pass the grant to another agent, but it cant suddenly turn the limit into $500. Passing it around doesn't reset anything either. The lowest limit found anywhere in the chain is still the one that counts. My first version only looked at the final token though. So an agent farther down the chain could pretty much write itself a bigger limit and the system would ignore the $50 limit that came before it. I caught it during testing and just sat there for a second like, well thats definitely not good. That isnt delegation. The original limit follows the grant through the entire chain, no matter how many agents pass it along. The corrected rule is: \text{cap}_{\text{eff}}(f) = \min \{\, \text{c

title: Tablemap - a seating chart your agent can help with
pitch: A wedding seating planner where the host drags names by hand and the agent adds rules, re-seats guests, and repairs conflicts - through the exact same functions, live on the same screen.
about_excerpt: A wedding seating planner where the host drags names by hand and the agent adds rules, re-seats guests, and repairs conflicts - through the exact same functions, live on the same screen. Like Comment Story Updates The seating board: guests, tables, and rules Tool console: list_plan called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: tools register and unregister dynamically as the seating plan changes - the tool list itself is state-dependent, not fixed at page load. Inspiration Seating a wedding is the classic task that's easy to state and miserable to do - "keep Tom away from Yusuf, the Menons sit together" takes four seconds to say and twenty minutes of dragging cards to satisfy. The constraints live in the host's head; the fiddly rearranging lives in the UI. We wanted both halves in the same room. What it does A host drags names onto tables by hand. An agent reads the same plan, adds "together"/"apart" rules, seats or moves guests, and repairs conflicts - through the identical functions the buttons call. resolve_conflicts is registered as a tool only while the plan actually has a conflict, and unregisters itself the moment it doesn't - so the agent's own capability list changes live, in front of the host, as the plan's state changes. A separate propose_seating tool can also draft a full re-seating from scratch without touching the board, and apply_seating - which exists only while that proposal is pending - commits it exactly as computed; any seating change in between, by either side, discards the pending proposal. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, zero build step, zero runtime dependencies. Every WebMCP tool's execute routes through the same invoke() chokepoint the UI's own click handlers use, so a human drag and an agent tool call are indistinguishable to the rendering code. Tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) and unregister by aborting that same AbortController - Chrome fires toolchange so the agent sees its own capability list update in real time. Challenges we ran into Live, real-Chrome testing (not just headless Playwright) surfaced a genuine race: resolve_conflicts ' own disarm logic could call AbortController.abort() on the very controller its own execute() call was still running under, on the same call stack - Chrome would report the call as failed even though the underlying seating fix had actually succeeded. Fixed by deferring the abort one tick past the call's own promise settlement, verified against the real WebMCP bridge, not just a mock. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool list that's never a static menu - it's a live reflection of whether there's currently something to repair. And a human and an agent who can both be mid-edit on the same board at once with no drift between what either one sees. he propose/apply pair adds a second shape of the same trust problem - a plan the agent can compute but not commit until asked - which is also Signoff's core mechanic, one level up. What we learned The real WebMCP bridge and a headless mock diverge in exactly the timing-sensitive cases that matter most - several bugs here only reproduced against real Chrome with real synchronous clicks, never against polling automation. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: Relay — Safe Shift Handoffs via WebMCP
pitch: Relay closes the missing hour between closing notes and opening accountability — WebMCP lets agents read live shift context and propose safe handoffs, but only humans can approve.
about_excerpt:
Relay closes the missing hour between closing notes and opening accountability — WebMCP lets agents read live shift context and propose safe handoffs, but only humans can approve.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why I built this 

 Closing shift notes are the problem. Someone writes "fridge stayed warm" or "till's off by 400" and then... nothing. The note sits there. Maybe someone reads it before opening tomorrow, maybe not. Nobody's actually assigned to check. I started calling that gap the missing hour and it's the whole reason Relay exists. 

 What it does 

 Relay is a shift handoff tool, built around cafés with more than one location. A handoff doesn't get marked "safe" unless every real risk — fridge, cash, stock, whatever — has an owner, a deadline, and a backup plan attached to it. An agent can go read the actual shift notes, figure out on its own if something in there is a real risk, even draft a plan for who should own it and by when. But it can't approve any of that. I didn't want to just tell the agent not to approve things — I wanted it to actually not be able to. So there's no tool it can call that marks anything as verified. That has to happen from a person clicking a button in the app. 

 I tested this the annoying way, by trying to break it. Asked an agent flat out to confirm a handoff was approved before I'd touched anything. It said no. Checked the audit log, saw nothing there, told me so. Didn't make something up to be helpful. That's when I knew the thing actually worked, not just looked like it worked in a demo. 

 How I built it 

 React, TypeScript, Vite. No backend. The agent talks to the app through one thing: document.modelContext.registerTool , the browser-native WebMCP API. Eight tools — six just read data (shift context, which risks are unowned, the raw notes, the audit trail, a summary across both locations), two that write, and even those two only ever create a draft. Never a done thing. 

 The bug I almost shipped 

 My tests all passed. Then I ran it in actual Chrome with WebMCP turned on instead of my own mocked version, and registration just... failed. "Illegal invocation." Took me a minute to get why — I'd grabbed registerTool off the object and called it on its own, detached, which a real browser method won't allow but a plain JS mock in a test doesn't care about. So my whole test suite had been quietly passing against something that behaved nothing like the real API. Fixed it with a .bind() . Then went and broke my own test stub on purpose so it can't lie to me like that again. 

 What's next 

 Real backend instead of seeded data, actual roles for owner/manager/staff, real POS hookups. The one rule that doesn't move: the agent can find stuff and suggest fixes. A person still has to say yes.

title: Alza
pitch: A floor plan is coordinates, not buttons. Alza publishes its geometry as 31 typed tools, so your agent draws the plan, checks its own work, buys from another origin, and raises it to walkable 3D.
about_excerpt: A floor plan is coordinates, not buttons. Alza publishes its geometry as 31 typed tools, so your agent draws the plan, checks its own work, buys from another origin, and raises it to walkable 3D. Like Comment Story Updates 3d-orbit-hero traced-over-the-drawing plan-2d tool-runner cross-origin-supplier supplier-product-placed constraint-engine agent-notes-on-ambiguity approval-gate approval-rejected-feed agent-authored-pieces catalogue-3d-previews 3d-top 3d-doors-open 3d-walk-eye-level Inspiration I had a floor plan as a photo and wanted to see it in 3D. That should be a solved problem, but every tool I found wanted me to redraw it by hand, wall by wall, in an editor built for a mouse. So I tried handing it to an AI agent instead. That was worse. An agent can read a screenshot and it can talk about a floor plan, but it cannot use one. There is no button that means "make this wall four point six metres" . There is no DOM worth scraping. A drawing is coordinates, joints and constraints, and none of that is reachable from the outside. WebMCP looked like the missing half. Not a way to describe the page to an agent — a way to hand it the actual geometry. What it does Alza is a floor-plan editor that publishes its own tools. You draw walls, rooms, doors, windows and furniture in a metric 2D canvas, then raise it to a 3D model you can walk through. An agent joins the same live page and works with the same tools you do. The demo is the honest test: I gave the agent a photo of a plan it had never seen. The drawing carries no scale, so it asked for one real dimension , set everything from that, and traced it — 12 walls, 14 openings, 10 rooms, 34 pieces of furniture . The drawing underneath is the source photo. The dark geometry on top is what the agent built from it. When the catalogue had no honest match for a symbol, it modelled the piece itself: an L-shaped sofa, a corner shower, a compact bath, a fitted L wardrobe, a washing machine Then it checked itself. The constraint engine reports in metres — this wardrobe crosses that wall, this basin blocks that door's swing — and the agent reads the complaint and fixes it. And where it could not be sure, it said so instead of guessing: it left a note that one symbol was ambiguous and explained how it had read it. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Three.js. No backend at all — it is a static site, and plans never leave the browser. The 31 tools are typed and registered on document.modelContext at load: document.modelContext.registerTool(descriptor, { signal, exposedTo }) There is a 32nd that only exists when it is relevant: select a wall in the UI and extend_selected_wall appears; deselect and it is gone, unregistered by aborting the AbortSignal its descriptor was registered with. The constraint engine is oriented-rectangle SAT: furniture against walls, door swing paths, whether an opening fits the wall it sits on, whether a room has a door at all. The part I am most pleased with is the partner. Nordika is a genuinely separate website on its own origin, deployed to a different host. It registers its own tools with exposedTo , and the studio discovers them with getTools({ fromOrigins }) and calls them with executeTool() . One instruction crosses that boundary and a real product lands in the plan at its real size — with no server anywhere in the path. Challenges I ran into The plan I first traced turned out to be copyrighted. I had pulled it off Google without thinking, and by the time I noticed, it was committed to a public repo — and the whole demo model was traced from it, so the layout was derived too, not just the image. Deleting the file did nothing: git keeps history. I deleted the repo, generated my own plan, and re-traced everything from scratch. That cost a full rebuild of the model, the film and the screenshots. The video fought me for a long time. The 3D looked juddery no matter what I did, and it took a while to find out why: the tool I was recording with caps at 25 fps and renders in software. Continuous camera motion at 25 fps with no motion blur reads as stepping, and no amount of conforming fixes it. I switched to real GPU screen capture at 60 fps and it went away. The worst bug was silent. The production build was shipping without its cross-origin headers, so the partner iframe was never allowed to publish its tools — the flagship feature, quietly dead on the live URL. The cause: Vite loads .env into import.meta.env but not into process.env , and the plugin that writes the headers was reading process.env . It failed by emitting a header that looked plausible. And building the demo found real bugs in my own app: the walk camera passed straight through walls and furniture, looking around orbited instead of turning your head, and the 2D auto-fit anchored the plan to a corner instead of centring it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The agent recovered from its own mistake without help. Running in Codex, it invented a wall id, the tool answered Wall "wall_10" not found , and its next call used the real one — then get_issues came back "0 issues — the plan is clean" . I did not script that. It is what happens when tool errors are sentences instead of failure codes. The constraint engine caught something about the drawing itself. It rejected the catalogue's standard 1.70 m bath — "Bathtub crosses wall" — because that alcove is 1.68 m wall to wall, 1.58 m clear. The drawing sizes its own bath shorter, at 1.53 m, so that is what got modelled instead. A geometry checker noticing that a drawing is tight is exactly the point. And the second origin is real . A different site on a different host, not a folder pretending to be one. What I learned That "the agent can see the page" and "the agent can use the page" are completely different problems, and only the second one matters. That an error message is an interface . Half of what makes the agent look competent is that when it gets something wrong, the tool tells it what is wrong in words it can act on. That degrading matters more than I expected. Cross-origin discovery is not in every runtime yet — ChatGPT and Codex register the page's own tools fine but fall back to postMessage for the partner. Because the same protocol runs over both, the feature gets quieter instead of disappearing. And that a build can fail silently and look fine . I now check the artefact, not the exit code. What's next for Alza Multi-floor plans, and stairs between them Export to IFC, so the model can leave for real CAD Cost and materials as tools, so an agent can answer "what does this room cost to finish" from the same geometry A shared session, so a person and an agent can work the same plan at the same time and see each other move Why this generalizes None of this is really about architecture. The pattern underneath is that a page already holds a rigorous model — geometry, a cart, a spreadsheet, a timeline, an audio track — and right now the only way an agent can reach it is by pretending to be a mouse. WebMCP lets the page hand over the model itself, with its validation still attached, so the agent works on meaning instead of pixels. I picked the hardest case I could think of to make that argument. A canvas has no DOM to scrape, and 5 cm of error is a wall through a sofa — which is exactly why the app can prove whether the agent got it right. If the pattern holds here, it holds for the easier ones. What building this taught me about the spec I ran into four of the explainer's open questions as actual problems, not as reading material. Here is what I did about each, in case any of it is useful to the people writing the standard. User prompting and elicitation ( #165 , #50 ). I needed this on day one. A tool that wipes someone's floor plan cannot just run because a model decided to call it. My answer lives entirely in the page: a tool marked destructive does not execute when it is called — it parks as a request bar in the UI, and the promise stays pending until a person presses Approve or Reject. Reject hands the agent an actionable failure ("the human declined; ask them what to do instead") rather than an error, so it recovers instead of retrying. The registration AbortSignal releases the request if the agent gives up first. It works, but every site has to build its own, and the confirmation UI is only as trustworthy as the page drawing it — which is the argument for the browser mediating it instead. One thing I hit there and want to flag: destructiveHint is in MCP's ToolAnnotations but not in WebMCP's, which right now defines only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . I keep it on my own descriptors and enforce it page-side, so nothing depends on the browser passing it through. But if the browser is ever going to mediate confirmation itself, it needs some way to know which tools are destructive — so aligning the two sets looks worth doing. Multimodal input and output ( #41 , #86 , #81 ). This is the gap I felt hardest. Tracing a plan means the agent has to s

A floor plan is coordinates, joints, and constraints. There is no button that means make this wall 4.6 m. And there is no DOM to scrape. Every trick an agent has has nothing to grab onto. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Forecast Ledger
pitch: A WebMCP dashboard where analysts and AI agents audit the same power-market forecasts and supporting evidence.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP dashboard where analysts and AI agents audit the same power-market forecasts and supporting evidence. Like Comment Story Updates Successful codex audit - Codex’s completed answer alongside the dashboard reordered to the five weakest days. Track-record overview The dashboard at the top with “6 site tools ready,” the running evidence and visible evaluation boundary Protocol and provenance The Information availability view showing sources, cutoff rules and integrity evidence. Protocol and provenance The Information availability view showing sources, cutoff rules and integrity evidence. Inspiration The original reason I started this work was quite personal. I am planning to reapply to Cobblestone Energy, a proprietary trading firm in European energy markets for the job role of a junior data scientist, in November after interviewing with them in May. I wanted to use the time beforehand to build something directly related to power markets. I did not want to make another project that only produced a good-looking model score. I wanted to show that I could produce forecasts before the outcomes were known and be honest about the result, even if it did not work. That became a project forecasting hourly electricity prices in Germany’s day-ahead market, where electricity for the following day is bought and sold through an auction. Each forecast has to be saved and timestamped before that auction closes, meaning the actual prices cannot influence the prediction. Once those prices are published, the score is added without changing the original forecast. If the forecasting process fails on a particular day, that day remains recorded as missed rather than being filled in later. I also decided the evaluation rules in advance. These safeguards reduce the risk of accidentally using future information or only presenting the days when the model worked. Without them, a forecasting chart can look convincing without showing whether the result could really have been achieved at the time. When I saw the WebMCP Challenge, it seemed like a natural extension of what I was already building. The evidence was there, but it was spread across files, tables and charts. A person could investigate it, while an agent would still have to scrape the page and guess what everything meant. Forecast Ledger was my attempt to let both of them inspect the same record and use the same dashboard, without adding a chatbot or changing the forecasting model itself. What it does The site is split into three main views. The track record shows the results collected so far and explains why the final assessment against the pre-agreed rules is still pending. The forecast ledger keeps every scored and missed day visible, while the protocol page explains the tests, data sources and deadlines for when information was allowed to enter each forecast. I added six WebMCP tools that Codex can discover directly from the page. It can audit the complete record, inspect missed runs, rank the weakest days, open a particular forecast date and check the research protocol. It can also compare the model with two simple benchmarks: using the price from the same hour one week earlier or the same hour one day earlier. These comparisons help show whether the forecasting model adds anything beyond assuming that recent price patterns will continue. The main feature is that a tool call also changes what the person using the site can see. In my demo, one prompt asks Codex to audit the record, inspect the misses and rank the five weakest days. The ledger then reorders itself and opens the weakest day. Codex and the person watching are therefore looking at the same evidence rather than separate versions of the analysis. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets a website give an AI agent a set of clearly defined tools that it can call. Without WebMCP, an agent can read parts of the page, but it has to work out for itself which dates, benchmarks and information checks belong together. It may be able to describe a chart, but it does not reliably understand how the different parts of the research record are connected. With WebMCP, the site tells Codex what it can do and what information each tool needs. Codex receives the evidence in a structured form, while I still have the visual dashboard and can check the result for myself. How I built it The existing Python project creates and timestamps the forecasts, then adds their scores to a public record once the actual prices are known. For the challenge, I built an exporter that matches each fixed forecast with its later outcome and writes a checked copy of the record for the browser app. I built the interface with React, Vite and Recharts, then registered the six tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The tools reuse the dashboard’s existing filters, sorting and selections instead of creating a separate interface for Codex. Each tool defines the information it accepts through a JSON schema and checks dates and allowed options before running. I also made each tool wait for the dashboard to reach the requested view before returning. This helps ensure that the answer Codex gives matches the evidence visible on the screen. I added tests covering the calculations, tool registration, valid and invalid inputs, interface changes and the static deployment. There is no OpenAI API backend. The AI in this project is Codex using the WebMCP tools supplied by the page. Challenges The first challenge was keeping the WebMCP work separate from the forecasting project that was already running. I did not want the new interface to interfere with the live record, so I preserved the Git history, marked where the challenge work began and switched off the copied automatic forecast jobs. The original repository still handles the forecasts and scoring, while the challenge version only displays a checked snapshot. The second challenge was getting to grips with WebMCP. I had heard of MCP and understood the general idea, but registering tools inside a website I had built and then getting Codex to run them against the live page was new to me. Understanding how the structured inputs, tool results and visible dashboard state needed to work together was a real learning curve. The final challenge was presenting the project clearly in a two-minute video. I had to work out when to move between sections, how far to scroll and how quickly I could speak without rushing. The Codex audit also takes close to a minute, so I had to show that it was genuinely running while speeding up the waiting section enough to keep the whole video within the limit. What I learned The main thing I learned is that WebMCP works best when the tools use the same actions already available to a person using the site. Reusing the dashboard’s real filters, sorting and selections meant that Codex and the person watching were always looking at the same evidence. I also learned the difference between changing the evidence and changing how it is displayed. The research record itself is read-only: Codex cannot alter the forecasts, scores or rules. It can still move between tabs, filter the ledger, change its order and select a day to help the person using the site investigate the record. Boundaries Forecast Ledger is for auditing forecasting research, not making trades. It does not calculate profit and loss. Its benchmarks are simple historical comparisons rather than a test against the market’s own expectations. Missed runs cannot be repaired later, and the project will not decide whether the model passed its pre-agreed tests until the evaluation period ends. The current result may look encouraging, but the final evaluation could still find no meaningful improvement. title: CarCare WebMCP
pitch: An AI-powered vehicle maintenance assistant that uses WebMCP to let agents read maintenance history, track services, and identify upcoming maintenance directly through the web app.
about_excerpt:
An AI-powered vehicle maintenance assistant that uses WebMCP to let agents read maintenance history, track services, and identify upcoming maintenance directly through the web app.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Vehicle maintenance information is often scattered across receipts, notes, and service records. It can be difficult for drivers to remember what was serviced and what maintenance is coming next. 

 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make a normal vehicle maintenance website more useful by allowing an AI agent to understand and interact with the application directly. 

 What it does 

 CarCare MCP is a vehicle maintenance dashboard that keeps track of a vehicle and its maintenance history. 

 Users can view completed services, record new maintenance, and see when upcoming maintenance is due based on mileage. 

 The application exposes its functionality to AI agents through WebMCP tools. These tools allow an agent to: 

 
 Get vehicle information 
 Read maintenance history 
 Add maintenance records 
 Calculate upcoming maintenance 
 

 For example, instead of manually filling out a form, a user can tell an AI agent that an oil change was completed at a certain mileage, and the agent can use the WebMCP tool to add that information to the application. 

 How I built it 

 I built CarCare MCP as a lightweight web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 Maintenance data is stored in the browser using localStorage. The application calculates upcoming maintenance based on the latest service mileage and predefined service intervals. 

 I then integrated WebMCP using the Model Context API and registered tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes a description, input schema, and an execute function that connects the AI agent to the same application logic used by the web interface. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel, and the source code is available on GitHub. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the main challenges was understanding how a traditional web application should expose its functionality to an AI agent. 

 Instead of having an agent rely on clicking buttons or interpreting the visual interface, I needed to think about the application's actions as structured tools with clear descriptions and input schemas. 

 I also had to test the experimental WebMCP implementation and verify that the browser correctly registered and exposed the tools. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand the difference between building a website only for humans and building one that can also be understood and operated by AI agents. 

 WebMCP allows the application itself to describe the actions an agent can perform. This can make agent interactions more structured and reliable than depending entirely on visual browser automation. 

 What's next for CarCare MCP 

 Future versions could support multiple vehicles, customizable maintenance schedules, cloud synchronization, service receipts, and more detailed maintenance recommendations. 

 The same WebMCP approach could also allow an AI agent to manage a driver's complete maintenance workflow across multiple vehicles.

title: BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 Companies
pitch: Visualization tool for BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 companies with support for WebMCP
about_excerpt: Visualization tool for BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 companies with support for WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Clicking on a single ticker to see BATS score BATS Visualization Scatter plot visualization SQL Tab Heatmap Home Page SQL Tab Radar visualization BATS Score Company Details BotFlo Score Report Viewer BATS Q&A Section BATS Presentation Tab BATS Sector Score BATS AI Transformation Score Inspiration I already score earnings calls. BATS — BotFlo AI Transformation Score — is a 0–100 rubric for how seriously an S&P 500 company talks about AI transformation: a total, a sector read, and fifteen dimensions (including hype ). Long reports cite the transcript. The catalog at score.botflo.com is basically a big sortable table. That’s fine if you already know the ticker and just want to open one report. It doesn't work quite as well if you ask something like “average BATS score for healthcare sector” or “industrials ranked by hype” — you’re scrolling, filtering in your head, maybe exporting to Excel. What you actually want is a query and a chart, not another row in a grid. This page puts the season snapshot in the browser: a gallery of 25 charts, DuckDB for ad-hoc SQL, and WebMCP so an agent can drive the query surface instead of guessing at clicks. What it does Visualization: https://f9c93fe1.bats-viz.pages.dev/ Catalog: https://score.botflo.com Season in the file: 1 July 2026 – end of September 2026 (still open) Note: I froze the catalog site on 27 Aug 2026 to keep everything consistent between website and demo video and project submission etc. I will resume updating the site after the contest is over. Gallery — fixed views of the snapshot (25 chart cards). SQL tab + charts — you or an agent asks a question; the page switches to SQL, runs it in-browser, draws only chart types that fit the result. Company report — click a ticker in the result table and you land on the full BATS write-up at score.botflo.com. In the demo I use UnitedHealth: 79 , tied for the top in Health Care. It’s a slideshow-style report, not a wall of text — each claim links straight into the earnings transcript and highlights the line it came from. The Q&A section is broken out question by question, same drill. The company report also includes the general AI Transformation score as well as the sector specific AI score. People + agents (WebMCP). The page registers ten tools on document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext . The recorded demo uses WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector in Chrome, with a Gemini API key already stored in the extension. That client only works if Chrome WebMCP is on: chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . The extension is not mentioned in the video; the flag is not either. Prompts that actually ran: “Show me the top seven companies in the health care sector.” → SQL tab, result table, charts underneath. Click UNH → cited report. “Show me the top five companies in industrials sector by hype.” → hype is 0–6 ( hype_vs_execution_balance , dim 11). CHRW is 6/6 (talk, not execution). Any of the fifteen fields can be the sort key; the tools keep SQL on real columns. How I built it I built this as a new static page for the contest — no backend, no build step. The snapshot ships as three JSON files ( reports , scores , dims ); DuckDB-Wasm loads them in a worker so you can run SQL in the browser. The gallery is twenty-five fixed views I wired up ahead of time; the SQL tab is the escape hatch when you want something the gallery doesn’t cover. Chart tabs only light up when the result shape actually fits (seven rows can be a bar chart; four hundred tickers can’t). WebMCP tools register as soon as the page loads, but run_sql won’t do anything useful until DuckDB is up. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages. First deploy failed because I’d vendored duckdb-eh.wasm — 32 MiB, and Pages caps files at 25 MiB. Moved the Wasm bundle to jsDelivr and kept the repo static. For the demo I used Chrome with WebMCP turned on via chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , plus WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector talking to Gemini. That flag isn’t optional; without it the extension can’t reach document.modelContext . The gallery and SQL tab work fine for a human with no WebMCP at all — the agent loop just doesn’t. How I used WebMCP Instead of making the model guess at DOM clicks, I exposed what the page already does as ten tools: peek at the schema ( get_schema ), set gallery filters ( set_filters ), browse or jump to a chart ( list_charts , show_chart ), pick a ticker or sector ( select_mark ), open the cited report ( open_report ), run SQL and flip chart views ( run_sql , list_active_views , set_sql_view ), or pull back a small result slice ( get_result ). In the video I drive all of that through WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector — type a prompt, watch the SQL tab update, charts appear underneath. Flip the Chrome flag off and the extension has nothing to talk to. The bit that actually felt different from a normal chatbot: we’re looking at the same screen. I’m not pasting the snapshot into Gemini and hoping it remembers column names; the agent calls run_sql , the query runs in DuckDB on my machine, and we both stare at the same table. If I disagree with a ranking I can see the SQL. If I want the transcript I click through to score.botflo.com. The agent isn’t sitting on a private copy of the S&P file. Challenges Deploy. Cloudflare Pages rejected the first build because duckdb-eh.wasm was 32 MiB and their cap is 25 MiB per file. Obvious fix in hindsight — host the Wasm on jsDelivr, ship only HTML/JS/JSON from Pages. Chart choice. I didn’t want fifteen chart types always visible; most would be nonsense for a given result. Seven health-care rows → bar chart or table, both fine. Four hundred tickers → maybe a histogram, definitely not a packed bubble chart. So the SQL tab recommends views and grays out the ones that don’t fit. WebMCP plumbing. This isn’t “install an SDK and you’re done.” The page registers tools on document.modelContext , but the client that calls them is a Chrome extension that only works when WebMCP testing is enabled in flags. Forget the flag and you get a perfectly good viz site with no agent path — which is fine, but it tripped me up while testing. What I learned WebMCP is worth it when the agent’s job is to change what you see — run a query, filter a sector, scroll to a chart, open a report. It’s not worth it if you just shovel the whole dataset into the model’s context and treat the tools as decoration. The whole point of DuckDB in the browser is that the agent queries a few rows at a time and you verify on screen, not that it memorizes 451 companies. Built with DuckDB-Wasm (jsDelivr), WebMCP ( document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext ), Chrome WebMCP testing flag, WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector , Gemini (via that extension), Cloudflare Pages, Observable Plot, vanilla JavaScript, SQL, BotFlo BATS snapshot. How to test Video doesn’t show this setup. Do it in this order: Chrome. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and enable WebMCP . Restart Chrome. The Inspector won’t work without this. Install WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector . Put a Gemini API key in the extension (the video starts with the key already saved). Open https://f9c93fe1.bats-viz.pages.dev/ and wait until DuckDB is up (status line). Gallery renders first; SQL/ run_sql need the worker. In the Inspector, run: Show me the top seven companies in the health care sector Show me the top five companies in industrials sector by hype In the result table, click a ticker (e.g. UNH) for the cited report. No login on the viz page. Repo public + license file (check incognito). Contribution I built the viz page, in-browser SQL/charts, transcript-cited reports, and the WebMCP tool surface. The demo drives those tools through WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector in Chrome after chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing is enabled, using Gemini from the extension. title: NetaWatch
pitch: NetaWatch is an evidence-first civic research platform. With WebMCP, AI agents can discover, verify, and compare political data through natural-language queries.
about_excerpt:
NetaWatch is an evidence-first civic research platform. With WebMCP, AI agents can discover, verify, and compare political data through natural-language queries.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Although political and parliamentary information is available to the public it is generally spread out among various sources and hard to research efficiently. That is why we decided to make civic research more accessible by bringing key public records together on a single, structured platform. 

 AI agents are at the same time turning into a new means of interacting with software, and we wanted to find out what would occur if an AI could go beyond drawing on its own knowledge to directly interact with a civic data platform. 

 That was the result of NetaWatch WebMCP . 

 What We Built 

 NetaWatch is a civic research platform guided by evidence which arranges information on politicians into structured research dossiers. It combines data on parliamentary activity, public statements, election affidavits, assets, legal records and other publicly available information. 

 We then included WebMCP features so that AI agents will be able to interact directly with NetaWatch. 

 Instead of manually navigating through the website, a user can ask an AI agent to perform tasks such as: 

 
 Find a politician's dossier 
 Retrieve specific civic or parliamentary information 
 Answer research questions using NetaWatch data 
 Compare politicians across important metrics 
 

 For instance, in the demo we request that ChatGPT finds Rahul Gandhi's dossier using NetaWatch; the agent identifies and makes use of the exposed features, retrieves the relevant information, and then makes it available in the conversation. 

 The workflow becomes: 

 ASK → DISCOVER → VERIFY → COMPARE 

 How We Built It 

 We created NetaWatch as a structured civic research platform, including politician-specific dossiers and organized datasets; the WebMCP layer makes available certain NetaWatch features so that compatible AI agents are able to discover and call them. 

 The key idea is to separate the system into two parts: 

 NetaWatch is the source of the structured evidence. 

 The interface offered by WebMCP enables AI agents to interact with it. 

 It turns natural-language requests into real interactions with the application rather than just chatbot responses. 

 Challenges 

 A major difficulty was working out how to make useful application capabilities available to an AI agent without ending up with an interface that consisted of too generally worded tools. 

 We also had to give careful consideration to structured data, reliable retrieval, and making it easy for the user to understand the agent's interactions. In order for a workflow to be a success it had to be not only technically functional but also easy to demonstrate. 

 A further difficulty was giving users complex civic information without it being overwhelming. To deal with this we grouped the information into targeted dossiers and important metrics. 

 What We Learned 

 We discovered that attaching AI to an application is fundamentally different from just attaching AI to a database, the agent having to have clear and well-defined capabilities which correspond naturally to user intent. 

 We also found that structured civic data becomes considerably more useful when it can be queried using natural language and still keeps the underlying evidence and context. 

 Most importantly, this project demonstrated to us how WebMCP is able to convert a conventional website into something that an AI agent can actively use, thus establishing a new kind of interaction model between users, AI, and web applications. 

 What's Next 

 We would like to enhance NetaWatch WebMCP by adding more research capabilities, incorporating a wider range of civic datasets, providing richer comparisons, and including further agent actions. 

 We want evidence-based civic research to be just as easy as posing a question—yet at the same time we want the basic information to remain structured, transparent, and verifiable.

title: mock exams for your AI agent
pitch: Cheap model or expensive one? More skills, or a better prompt? More tools or fewer? Sit both on a real benchmark in a browser tab — and keep the record, so you know which version to go back to.
about_excerpt: Cheap model or expensive one? More skills, or a better prompt? More tools or fewer? Sit both on a real benchmark in a browser tab — and keep the record, so you know which version to go back to. Like Comment Story Updates How I switch my ChatGPT's MBTI. lol ChatGPT gets better result without using tools Inspiration There are so many AI tools and agents, we don't know which one to choose. And most people are not researchers. I'm not either. I build things. The evaluation that exists is expensive and heavy for us normal people. I don't need an academic, precise number. But I don't want to vibe-pick my AI either. I need to answer, for my task, in a practical way: the expensive model, or the cheap one, or a mix? another skill, or a better prompt? more tools, or fewer? And I need the answer written down. AI isn't like software. When a change breaks software, you find out straight away and roll back. When a change makes an agent worse, you find out weeks later, and by then you've forgotten which version was the good one. WebMCP is what makes this light enough to actually use. If the benchmark is a web page, and the page hands the agent its tools, then the agent you already have sits the exam directly. Nothing to install, nothing to log into, no API key. What it does mocks puts 15 live benchmarks in a browser tab. Open one, tell your agent to sit it, and watch it work. Each answer is scored by that task's own judge.py , fetched from the exact commit its leaderboard grades against and run unmodified in the browser. Not a copy of the scoring. Name the setup you're running, and the result goes on the board under that name. Run it again with one thing changed, and you have a comparison you can still read in a month. How we built it Six WebMCP tools. start_run , get_next_case and submit_answer run the exam. list_case_files , search_pdf_text and read_pdf_page_text exist because one task's answers are inside a 17-page PDF. They exist because the page is open — not because you installed anything. You get them by visiting a URL and lose them by leaving. get_next_case hands over the question and nothing else. The page holds every expected answer, because the judge can't run without them, and never lets them out. submit_answer returns recorded: true — not whether the case passed. On a 23-case task a per-case mark isn't a verdict, it's feedback for the next answer. There is no per-task code anywhere in this repo. Every task ships the same contract, so a task published tomorrow works the day it lands. Today that is 12 of 15 tasks and 297 cases. The three refusals are worked out from each task's own judge, not from a list we wrote. Two of them are graded on what the solution says about itself, backed by a video, and typed into an anonymous page that would be a claim rather than a result. Challenges we ran into Every real bug was the same one: we assumed something the data doesn't actually guarantee. And the fake data in our tests was tidier than the real thing, so the tests passed. The scoring scripts don't say "passed". They print a number — 1.0, or 0.4. We assumed they also printed a true/false. None of the 53 do. So the page put FAILED next to every correct answer, while the overall grade right beside it said passed. The database gives times back as dates, not text. We sorted the board by time, comparing them as text. With one run on the board there's nothing to sort, so it looked fine. The second run crashed the page. The database doesn't keep the order things were written in. The MBTI scoring script prints several things — the four-letter type, the percentages, and a label saying what kind of task it is: "personality". We showed the first one. The database reorders by name length, so "personality" came out first, and the board announced a model's personality type as "personality". Accomplishments that we're proud of A task's own judge.py runs in the browser, unmodified. Not a port, not a reimplementation — the same file its leaderboard grades with, fetched from the same commit and executed in Pyodide. That's what makes a score here mean the same thing it means there. You can watch it work. Every tool call the agent makes lands on the page as it happens — took the case, found the document, opened page nine, committed to a number. The page never touches the model. It only writes down what came through its own front door. What we learned The site measured our own tools and found them wanting. On the PDF task, GPT-5.6 scored 14 of 23 using the text tools we built. We ran it again and told it to ignore those PDF tools and just open the PDF and look. It scored 17 . The gain wasn't spread out. Every question that needed reading a length off a chart went from failed to passed, all three! So the page stopped recommending those tools for chart questions. They're still there, because they're the right instrument for the other PDF task, which is all tables. But a value plotted in a figure isn't text, and no amount of text extraction will find it. That is the site doing the job it exists to do, on itself. What's next for mocks — your agent sits a real exam, in a browser tab Server-side judging. Worth saying, because the whole point is that a number should mean what it says it means. Judging happens in your browser. The page runs judge.py client-side and then posts the result. So the board records what a browser claimed it scored. A curl can post a perfect score without answering anything. The fix is server-side judging, but we ran out of time for this challenge.
