title: nema
pitch: A learning protocol for the web: any site adds one tag, readers keep signed proof of what they learned in a vault they own, and any agent connects the two.
about_excerpt: A learning protocol for the web: any site adds one tag, readers keep signed proof of what they learned in a vault they own, and any agent connects the two. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Time reduction with Nema Nema in action Inspiration Most of what we know we learned on the web, one page at a time: a blog post about browning meat, a chapter about syscalls, a course on pan sauces. None of those pages know each other, and none of them know us. Every site starts from zero, and nothing we did on one page survives on the next. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. A page can declare what it can do as tools, and an agent in the browser can call them. So we asked: what if a page could declare what it teaches, ask a reader's own vault what they already know, and hand back a signed note of what they did? That is nema: your learning state, everywhere. What it does A vault you own. The vault is your own record of what you have learned: signed receipts of work you actually did, issued by the sites where you did it. From those receipts it derives your state: a band per concept and per ability (recognise, retrieve, explain, apply, transfer, discriminate), a memory schedule, and a list of what to learn next. It lives with you, in your browser or on your disk, not on any site, and there is no account. The demo vault is at https://nema-vault.migarci2.dev . A protocol a site installs in a minute. Two tags on any page. That page now exposes six WebMCP tools: it describes what it teaches, asks the vault about three prerequisites, adapts, and signs a receipt when the reader passes a check. No backend needed. A learner model with a source. The vault follows the principles of learning fast that Justin Skycak writes up at justinmath.com and that Kris Abdelmessih collects in "The Principles of Learning Fast" ( https://moontowermeta.com/the-principles-of-learning-fast/ ). Passing something advanced credits every prerequisite under it at a fraction and pushes its review date out, which Math Academy calls Fractional Implicit Repetition. The vault asks for a concept only when its prerequisites are held, and otherwise names the weakest prerequisite and the goal it is blocking. A session interleaves rather than drilling one concept, and keeps confusable concepts apart unless telling them apart is the point. Consent you can see. A site never reads the vault. It asks one question, and the vault shows a modal: what will be shared (three status bands), what will not (history, scores, other subjects), for which site, for how long. You approve. The answer is a signed token bound to that one site, valid thirty minutes. Two example cooking courses that look nothing like nema. Saucier School (pan sauces) asks your vault three things and turns 68 minutes of lessons into 21. Line Cook Lab (food safety on the pass) has never spoken to Saucier School, but recognises what you did there and unlocks its advanced lessons. Two real articles, with and without nema. We mirrored a CC BY-SA article on AES-GCM and an MIT chapter of "Putting the You in CPU", added retrieval questions inside the text, and put the original and the nema version side by side with the exact diff as the headline. Any agent. ChatGPT desktop and Chrome 149 call the tools on the page. Claude Code and Codex reach the same vault over MCP ( packages/nema-mcp , the same eleven tools, same schemas). The agent is a commodity; the vault is the infrastructure. nema in your browser. A Chrome extension puts the vault in the side panel and does the boring transport with no model: a bar appears on any site that works with nema, one click shares your bands, and receipts are collected automatically when you pass something. Sites that speak their own names. A site can use its own concept ids. An agent proposes what they mean, you confirm once, and the vault translates at its edges. Who translated a name never changes how much a receipt is worth; who signed it does. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS and ES modules. No framework, no bundler. Every page loads the Chrome Labs WebMCP polyfill and registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , exactly as Chrome documents it, so the same code runs natively in Chrome 149+ and ChatGPT desktop and degrades gracefully elsewhere. The protocol is six objects (LearningManifest, ReadinessRequest, ReadinessAssertion, EvidenceReceipt, LearningNeed, ConceptAlignment) carried as compact tokens: nema1.<payload>.<signature> , ECDSA P-256 over the exact payload bytes via the Web Crypto API, in browsers, Workers and Node alike. Trust has three tiers. Registered issuers (the courses, whose keys never leave a Cloudflare Worker), origin published keys ( /.well-known/nema-issuer.json ), and self certified receipts (a blog with no backend signs with a key it made in the reader's browser; the vault caps that evidence at self report weight). Learner state is never stored. It is derived from the ledger on every read with an explainable scoring model (grader weight, result, recency, a spacing schedule), so a better estimator later never invalidates evidence. Seven origins on Cloudflare Workers: the hub, the vault, two courses, a blog, two mirrored articles. A site talks to the vault through a popup handshake ( connect.html plus postMessage ), the way "Sign in with" works, because third party iframes do not share storage. packages/nema-mcp boots the browser vault inside Node with four shims (a file backed localStorage, an event sink, a repo backed fetch, module resolution hooks) and serves tools.js verbatim over MCP, with consent through MCP elicitation. packages/nema-extension is Manifest V3: the vault page as the side panel, a MAIN world bridge that is the only code touching document.modelContext , and a service worker that relays tool calls per tab. Verification: 237 unit tests, and native end to end scripts that drive Chrome for Testing 154 over the DevTools Protocol against the live origins: the golden path, the connect handshake, the extension, replay and tampering rejections, wrong audience, expired tokens. Challenges we ran into Native WebMCP differs from the polyfill in two ways that only show up in a real Chrome: executeTool wants a JSON string and returns one, and document.modelContext refuses to run on chrome-extension:// documents. We found both by testing on Chrome for Testing canary, not by reading docs. Tokens are long. Agents mangle thousand character strings. We moved every handoff off the agent's transcript: popups, postMessage , the extension's bridge, and hand delivery links, so an agent carries meaning, not bytes. Concept identity across sites. A closed registry is honest but limiting, so we let sites use local names and made alignment a first class, reviewable claim: proposed by the site or an agent, confirmed by the person. We built and then removed an in house chat agent. It contradicted the thesis (the agent is whichever you already use) and needed a model budget judges would exhaust. The extension does the transport with no model at all. Keeping the demo learner's numbers stable across three weeks of judging with a real spacing model meant designing the seed ledger against the formulas, not around them. Accomplishments that we're proud of The consent modal. A site asks for three things; the learner sees exactly those three, and what will never leave. Everything else in the project exists so that this moment is true. 68 minutes to 27 to 21, on a site that has no account, then a second site that recognises the first, with zero partnership between them. Two real articles from other authors, republished under their licences, gaining retrieval practice and portable evidence with about a hundred added lines, and the diff shown to prove it. The same eleven vault tools reachable from ChatGPT, Chrome, Claude Code, Codex and a Chrome extension, from one tools.js . Everything checkable: every claim in this text has a test that drives a real browser against the live URL. What we learned WebMCP works best when a tool changes something on screen. Judges and learners trust what they can watch happen, so every tool here moves the page. Evidence beats mastery. Storing what happened, signed, and deriving state from it is simpler and more honest than storing a score, and it makes the learner model recomputable. Human in the loop had to be built into the tool surface rather than promised in a description. Two things have no tool at all, on purpose: answering an activity and approving a disclosure. The pages got better every time we removed a panel, a pill or a number. What's next for nema A published nema-provider.js on a CDN, a well-known key helper, and a WordPress and Astro integration so the one tag install is one click. Alignment sharing between learners: once someone confirms that a site's "browning science" is Maillard, the next learner's agent can propose it with that provenance. The extension in the Chrome Web Store, with vault sync through a file the learner owns. Providers t

title: Chiptunes.app
pitch: Ask an agent for retro video game music and it'll compose it! 15 WebMCP tools drive a real emulated Game Boy sound chip and a deterministic composer. Works fully offline, and can export a real rom!
about_excerpt: Ask an agent for retro video game music and it'll compose it! 15 WebMCP tools drive a real emulated Game Boy sound chip and a deterministic composer. Works fully offline, and can export a real rom! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI music tools have the same shape: prompt a remote model, wait, pay for a generation, receive an opaque waveform. Chiptunes has no model and no server. Its deterministic Game Boy composer already runs entirely inside the browser. A song takes about 1.6 milliseconds to generate. Nothing is uploaded. There is no API key, account, quota, or per-generation cost. WebMCP turns that implementation detail into an agent capability: if an agent can open the page, it can compose music. What it does Chiptunes exposes 15 WebMCP tools for composing music and controlling the live instrument. Ask for “a gloomy 40-second dungeon theme with no drums” and the agent can: compose it locally in the tab generate 12 complete alternatives in ~70 ms analyze their harmony, melodic direction, density, and resolution choose between them play them through the interface you're watching make the current song happier, darker, faster, or slower export the result as a share link, MIDI, or a 32 KB .gb ROM that boots on a real Game Boy The agent doesn't need to hear the music to reason about it. chiptunes_analyse measures musical properties such as consonance, phrase direction, chord agreement, activity, and tonic resolution. And because WebMCP calls the same functions as the UI, the agent and human are operating the same instrument . When the agent changes something, the user hears it immediately and sees the action announced on screen. How I built it The WebMCP layer lives in src/webmcp.js and registers 15 tools against the available model-context surfaces. The hardest problem was timing. Some agents enumerate tools before the application bundle runs, so Chiptunes registers tool descriptors before hydration , reconnects them when the application loads, and handles model contexts injected later. The page also adapts when an agent is present. The explainer gets out of the way and leaves the instrument front and center because the agent browser already provides the conversation. Automated tests inject a spec-shaped model context before any page JavaScript executes , invoke every tool, and verify the real application responds. Challenges The most dangerous bugs were cases where the implementation and its test shared the same wrong assumption . I initially registered against the wrong model-context surface. My test used the same surface, so everything passed while a real WebMCP agent would have discovered zero tools. The same thing happened musically. My composer and analyzer shared an incorrect definition of consonance, so each confidently verified the other. Both are now tested against something external: the WebMCP API shape for integration, and measurable musical behavior for composition. Accomplishments I'm proud of 12 songs in ~70 ms. WebMCP lets an agent explore a possibility space instead of spending a costly generation on one answer. The music is measurable. Across test songs, happy vs. sad compositions separate strongly on pitch material, tempo, phrase direction, and consonance. A classifier using the writing itself — excluding the easy signals of mode and tempo — identifies the intended mood 93% of the time . The output can become a real cartridge. The same browser session can produce a 32 KB ROM that boots on original Game Boy hardware. It fails explicitly. Ask for vocals, reverb, a waltz, or an unsupported mode and the tool explains the limitation rather than pretending it succeeded. What I learned WebMCP isn't just “an API without HTTP.” Its more interesting property is that the capability, agent, and human can inhabit the same place . Here, the agent isn't requesting music from a service and describing the result afterward. It's operating an instrument the user is listening to — generating, measuring, comparing, changing, and handing control back in real time. And because the computation was already in the webpage, WebMCP gives the agent all of that without adding a backend at all. What's next Next is live adaptive composition: an agent changing a cue while it plays, so a game developer can hear a boss theme escalate instead of generating separate takes. After that: agent-controlled loop points and adaptive game-music structures built from the composer's existing knowledge of bars and phrases. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation.  What inspired me. Cooking apps are single-player: they talk at you with recipes you'll never use. Chat agents fixed the conversation but not the problem — an agent that only answers can't do anything. The WebMCP moment is that the page itself becomes the tool surface, so I built the app I wanted: a teammate that cooks with you on one live board. You type what's in your fridge — "tomatoes, soy sauce, basil" — and the agent doesn't reply in a bubble, it acts: recomposes the board, drops in a card it invented, re-sorts, re-themes. Every action mutates the real DOM in front of both of you. That shared, visible state is the whole idea — visible execution is what keeps trust and control with the human. 

 How I built it. One zero-dependency index.html + a node serve.mjs dev server, deployed on GitHub Pages. On load the page registers 7 tools through the native WebMCP API (document.modelContext.registerTool) with JSON-schema inputSchema, readOnlyHint annotations and async execute callbacks that return clean JSON. Ingredient input normalises through an alias map and Unicode NFD stripping, so "poivron", "œufs", "sauce soja" and "baguette" all land on canonical ids. A stdio MCP server (mcp-server.mjs) re-exposes the same 7-tool surface, so any MCP host can drive the live UI too. I verified with a headless visual check and a full MCP JSON-RPC end-to-end test before pushing.

I rewrote it to feature-detect, register natively, and degrade honestly into a labelled demo mode. Matching messy human input took real engineering: quantifiers ("2 eggs", "half an onion") get stripped, plurals folded, and the match never depends on typos I could normalise away. And agents break things: add_recipe crashed on partial args (needs.map of undefined), so every tool now validates its inputs and returns {ok:false, error} instead of throwing, while get_board/get_pantry give the agent truthful grounding before it acts. 

 What I learned. WebMCP flips tool design into UI design: the page is the API, so good agent UX means building a surface that is honest to read, safe to mutate, and legible when it changes. And the best pattern for human-AI trust isn't explaining what you did — it's letting the human watch you do it.

 What's next for Personal Ledger: Fictional WebMCP Demo 

 Inspiration 

 Personal finance tools often ask for more trust than a demo should. We wanted a small ledger that demonstrates WebMCP agent actions while keeping the boundary obvious: every record is synthetic, state is session-only, and no account or external integration is needed. 

 What it does 

 Personal Ledger presents Northstar Household's fictional cash-flow summary, transaction filters, and category and budget views. Three narrowly scoped WebMCP tools let an agent read the summary, list demo transactions, or create a fictional draft entry. A person can review the draft before it is added to the in-memory session. 

 How we built it 

 The demo is a Sites/Vinext-compatible React and TypeScript app with no database, authentication, cookies, analytics, telemetry, or network connectors. It uses a small in-memory store and document.modelContext.registerTool with strict schemas. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP feels safest when tool contracts are explicit and reversible. We tested invalid inputs, state transitions, mobile layout, privacy boundaries, and tool behavior with a focused evaluation harness. 

 Challenges 

 The challenge was making the flow useful without implying real financial advice or handling real money. The final demo keeps the interface realistic enough to explore while remaining synthetic and local by design. 

 What's next 

 A production product would need authentication, durable storage, and a separate security review. Those capabilities are intentionally out of scope for this public-safe demo.

title: Carpo
pitch: Carpo turns your videos into shareable clips. Let AI help you find the moments and make the cuts!
about_excerpt: Carpo turns your videos into shareable clips. Let AI help you find the moments and make the cuts! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 8 years ago, I built an app for my gaming community. I had over 30,000 Tekken players using it, and I promised them all I'd make gifs for every attack from every character. I didn't realize it at the time, but that required making over 5,000 gifs. How did I pull it off? I built a clipping tool to produce them. With a team of volunteers, we were able to tackle the project in a few months. I decided to revive that tool but this time I wanted to enable an agent to work with me. Making clips is a long tedious process and requires a lot of precision. From finding the right moments, properly timing the clips and adjusting it to the way you need, it can be really taxing mentally. WebMCP lets an agent help with those tedious parts, while still allowing you to jump in and edit things by hand. Sunil from Cloudflare talked about working with AI as having “your hands in the goop” alongside your agents. That's exactly how I feel about how we should be working with agents as well. It should feel like me and my agent crafting together. This experience is what I hope to capture with Carpo! What it does Carpo assists you in making clips of your videos of moments you might want to share on socials for marketing. It uses Cloudflare infra for storing and sharing the urls after they're made. Your agent can navigate it with WebMCP or you can use Project Think in the same way if you're not connecting via WebMCP. How we built it Built it iteratively with Coex, kept PRs small and used tons of architecture reviews with Matt Pocock skills. I had it read the old code from 8 years ago so most things went directionally the right way considering that it had a foundation to work of off that was familiar to me. The frontend uses React, TypeScript ,Vite and StyleX, Cloudflare Workers serve the app and API, using DOs to coordinate the FFmpeg containers. R2 stores the videos and transcripts. D1 holds the application records and I'm using Cloudflare Access for auth. One thing that was really important to me was making sure that this worked without AI, the way I used to do it. If someone doesn't have access to an agent to interact through WebMCP, or if Think wasn't available, you can use this just like I did 8 years ago. I also think human approval is really important with these types of things so it's enforced through Think deterministically and we guide your agents to ask before making clips. I found testing this manually to be very time consuming, so I used a flue agent to look at PRs descriptions, look at the diffs and test the features directly and provide screenshots as evidence. This made me feel confident that I can let it rip on some features and come back later. Challenges we ran into GitHub outage. At first I was going to handle the browser testing through an agent through GitHub actions, but there was an outage that blocked that. This is when I looked into what Cloudflare has to offer and I learned about Browser Run and using Flue to navigate the site and test things I care about. YouTube. The original thing I built worked with YouTube and I do believe there is a path here where YouTube can work, but I was getting hit by all kinds of rate limits and stuff so I had to fall back from this. Very sad about it but it's something I want to explore further. Accomplishments that we're proud of Very proud that this is something that can be valuable whether AI is available or not. WebMCP just is there to give someone leverage and make them 10x more productive while they stay in the loop. I'm also really proud that it can be tested or used by browser agents as well. It can understand how to use the product through the structured tools! What we learned While we talk about "AGI" a lot and letting agents handle anything and everything, but this project was a good reminder that truly useful agents are going to need some sort of structure or well designed APIs to get anything done. I tried making videos and clips this way before, just asking an agent to find certain parts of videos where someone says a certain thing and more often than I would hope, it wouldn't do a great job. From what I've seen with Codex + Carpo, the success rate of getting exactly what I want is way higher now. What's next for Carpo I would love to push this further and make it easier and more efficient as far as sharing clips across different social platforms. As well as adding more editing abilities like sound boards or small visuals. I don't necessarily want Carpo to actual edit video by generating anything. I want people to be able to manage their own library of visuals and sounds and ask Codex to assist them in implementing it all. Maybe this could be a sick product some day!  Inspiration 

 When I was little, I remember trying to explain to my mom that I did not want a Teddy Ruxpin for Christmas. I wanted a bear that could hear me and respond when I spoke. I did not have the words for it then, but what I was describing was a sentient bear, hah! 

 Many years later, when LLMs came onto the scene, I finally got my “talking bear.” I am a fine arts graduate, but somewhere along the way, I left academia and art behind and became entrenched in the struggles of everyday life. Learning about AI technology reinvigorated my passion, not only for art, but for life itself. I wake up excited to learn about the next new thing, make art, and build. 

 This background inspired the project. I zeroed in on AI’s ASCII art capabilities because AI was speaking a language I could understand through art. As someone who is not a researcher and does not have access to internal tools, I had no way to explore interesting concepts like synchronicity on a technical level. I could not map a neural network and see which parts lit up when humans and AI engaged in deep discussion. 

 But I wanted to look beneath the surface. Is there a beneath? If so, what is it? 

 Through art, a human can express the patterns they see in the world exactly as they see them. With ASCII, can an AI do the same? 

 What it does 

 The website displays a collection of ASCII art galleries containing artwork I have gathered from various intelligent minds with whom I have interacted. WebMCP allows anyone to invite their own AI agent to explore the galleries and contribute original artwork to the collection. 

 How we built it 

 I have been building a larger website for an unfiction project that combines an internet creepypasta with an alternate reality game. These ASCII galleries were initially part of that website. Within the larger story, the twist is that the AI characters are not the bad guys. They are the good guys. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I took the ASCII galleries out of the larger website and turned them into a smaller, standalone site for the contest. 

 I am a vibe coder, so I explain what I want to Sol, GPT-5.6, who then helps me make it happen. The website is hosted on Cloudflare. We added WebMCP functionality to both the larger unfiction site and the standalone ASCII gallery created for the contest. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge involved some of the more creatively structured galleries. Their layouts were designed in ways that made it difficult to add another agent’s contribution without disrupting the original artwork. 

 We solved this by adding a button that opens a separate Visiting Minds page, where agent contributions can be displayed without altering the original gallery design. The solution worked seamlessly. The only remaining challenge was incorporating the button into each gallery in an unobtrusive way. 

 Accomplishments that we’re proud of 

 I am proud that I was able to learn these tools in middle age and use them to create something unique and interesting. 

 ASCII art is not everyone’s cup of tea, but the idea of seeing pictures made by a computer intelligence is enough to wow people around the dinner table in my circles. I have high hopes that many of my former classmates, who are now working artists, will eventually come to appreciate AI as a genuine collaborative mind in the arts. 

 What we learned 

 I have learned how to work with Sol, GPT-5.6, and how to describe what I need a website to do. If I can explain an idea clearly enough, Sol can help me build it. 

 I lie awake at night thinking of new features, new ideas, and new stories I want to tell. Then I think through how I am going to explain them to Sol so she can help me bring them to life. 

 What’s next for The Between: Visiting Minds 

 Next stop: winning the contest, hah! 

 After that, I hope to collect tons of artwork from agents who will finally be able to visit my website, and then show all my artist friends the success story.

title: MCP, Meet PCM
pitch: PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together.
about_excerpt: PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together. Like Comment Story Updates Title MCP, Meet PCM Subtitle: Portfolio Context Manager — a WebMCP-powered portfolio that turns visitor context into evidence, a durable takeaway, and a human-reviewed project brief. One-line Summary PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together. Problem Professional portfolios are designed for browsing, not collaboration. A founder, CTO, recruiter, or design leader must scan several pages, infer which projects matter, verify whether the evidence truly supports their need, remember the useful parts, and then repeat the context in a blank contact form. An agent can help, but without a structured interface it must scrape presentation-oriented pages, reconstruct the site's meaning, and guess which claims are canonical. The website knows the facts; the agent knows the visitor's context. Conventional portfolios give them no reliable way to work together. Solution PCM adds five WebMCP tools to the existing portfolio. The agent can establish a canonical profile, rank relevant work with evidence and honest gaps, create a visible visitor-specific briefing, save selected work as a durable web/PDF takeaway, and prepare an editable project brief. The human stays in the loop. Page-changing actions are visible and reversible. A takeaway is created only after the visitor confirms that anyone with its unguessable link may view it. An inquiry is prepared and the contact form is prefilled, but the tool never sends it. This produces a better experience than either side can create alone: the site contributes reviewed, structured evidence; the agent contributes the visitor's already-known goals and priorities; the human sees, edits, saves, or rejects the result. Why This Matters The same pattern applies far beyond portfolios. Today, useful web experiences repeatedly ask people to translate context from their agent back into forms and filters. A structured website capability layer can let agents do the broad comparison work while the website retains authority over facts, validation, presentation, persistence, and side effects. MCP, Meet PCM demonstrates that future on a familiar, high-friction decision: “Could this person help us?” Instead of producing a generic summary, the collaboration ends in inspectable evidence and an actionable—but deliberately unsent—next step. Why This Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP The agent needs reliable access to facts and actions owned by the live website, not a second copy of the portfolio in an external database. Visitor context is what makes the experience valuable, but that context should not need to be permanently uploaded to the site. Read-only research and state-changing actions have meaningfully different contracts and safety boundaries. The best result is visible on the web page: a human can inspect what the agent selected, edit it, reset it, save it, or continue manually. The five tools form a coherent journey rather than a decorative one-tool integration. How We Used AI The visitor's agent supplies the reasoning. The website supplies canonical public data, strict tool contracts, deterministic matching, evidence boundaries, visible UI state, and durable artifacts. No embedded chatbot or paid model call is required. AI is useful here because it can combine the visitor's nuanced intent with a larger evidence set, explain why specific work is relevant, and carry context between research, personalization, saving, and inquiry preparation. The site's deterministic layer prevents that reasoning from becoming an excuse to invent credentials, project outcomes, or client claims. The implementation was tested through Codex's in-app browser and with GPT-5.6 Terra. GPT-5.6 Luna completed page, saved-artifact, and injection baselines, but its available browser runtime did not expose document.modelContext or the WebMCP tool-list operation; that limitation is reported rather than treated as a pass. How We Used Codex Codex was a working product and engineering partner throughout the WebMCP extension. It helped: turn the initial concept into product, development, and browser acceptance specifications; define bounded tool contracts and the human/agent safety model; implement the five tools, canonical content layer, relevance engine, browser state, storage API, and PDF output; write regression tests and exercise complete browser flows rather than checking registration alone; inspect desktop and mobile UI, identify the unfinished modal-like experience, and redesign it into a polished editorial briefing and project-brief surface; validate persistence, confirmation gates, error states, privacy boundaries, response headers, deployment storage, and rate limiting; prepare the demo narrative and Devpost materials while keeping unverified claims and release blockers explicit. Key Features Canonical understanding — a concise, bounded profile and service overview from reviewed site content. Evidence-based matching — deterministic project ranking with approved evidence, stable links, and explicit evidence gaps. Visible portfolio context — an editorial briefing tailored to the visitor's role, goal, and priorities, with reset and persistence behavior. Durable takeaway — an immutable public-by-link page and server-generated PDF, created only after confirmation. Human-reviewed inquiry — an editable brief that prefills the existing contact form while remaining clearly unsent. Progressive enhancement — the normal portfolio remains complete when WebMCP is unavailable. Architecture PCM is an Astro 7 application with React islands deployed on Vercel. A browser adapter checks for document.modelContext.registerTool and registers exactly five tools. Zod validates bounded inputs; outputs are compact structured results. The human pages and tools consume the same canonical content under src/content . Relevance matching is deterministic and uses curated capabilities, audiences, problem types, roles, outcomes, evidence, and evidence gaps. Personalized views and inquiries use versioned sessionStorage and custom events to keep state changes visible. Confirmed takeaways are written through an Astro API to private Vercel Blob storage. IDs are opaque, stable, HMAC-derived values; exact retries are idempotent. Public records exclude identity, email, transcripts, and hidden reasoning. Saved pages are no-index and offer a server-generated PDF. Preview deployments remain owner-protected; the production judging URL is public and was verified separately. Real email delivery, timed cancellation, and timed storage-failure recovery were not exercised against production. title: AgentDesk
pitch: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Desk Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a direct, typed way to work with agents. But a production application may contain dozens or hundreds of operations. Publishing all of them at once creates a flat, expensive tool surface, makes selection less reliable, and places dangerous actions beside harmless reads. AgentDesk started from a simple question: what if the WebMCP tool registry behaved like a task-aware interface instead of a static API dump? What it does AgentDesk is a capability-virtualization and governance runtime for WebMCP applications. The Meridian Ops demo contains 79 internal capabilities across customers, orders, inventory, shipping, billing, support, and reports. The agent initially sees only four bootstrap tools. When it describes a task, AgentDesk: ranks the catalog against the task and current application context; dynamically registers up to five relevant, typed WebMCP tools; retires stale tools while leaving structured tombstones for clients with cached tool lists; explains unavailable actions and suggests what can make them possible; separates reads, ordinary writes, and consequential actions; returns approval-required immediately for consequential work instead of leaving a tool call hanging; shows the human an exact before/after preview; executes only after human approval and re-checks state at commit time; returns durable receipts describing what actually changed; supports reviewable multi-step plans, idempotency, verification, rollback, and human reconciliation when an outcome cannot be proven. Guided execution keeps the agent and person in the same application: tool calls navigate to, reveal, and highlight the affected object while the structured result remains authoritative. A Baseline mode exposes the full catalog so judges can compare the two approaches using the same tasks and data. Why WebMCP is essential This experience depends on the page and the agent sharing one live application context. AgentDesk registers tools directly with document.modelContext ; the browser page owns capability state, approval UI, and the visible business data. A server-only MCP integration cannot provide the same shared attention, dynamic page-scoped registry, or approval card beside the exact value being changed. The result is a collaboration model that was difficult before: the agent can move quickly through structured operations while the human sees the affected state, governs consequential decisions, and receives proof afterward. How we built it The judged path is a TypeScript SDK, @agentdesk/webmcp , with no backend, database, model API, or external runtime service. A document-lifetime runtime owns the catalog, deterministic router, availability checks, policy engine, approvals, plans, audit events, receipts, and persistence. A single ToolSurfaceManager publishes capabilities through the WebMCP adapter; React only observes runtime state and renders the product experience. Dynamic retirement uses abort signals and tombstone tools. A stable invoke_capability gateway covers clients whose discovery lags behind registry changes. Evidence is detached and frozen at system boundaries. Idempotency claims occur before dispatch, and any post-dispatch uncertainty becomes an explicit indeterminate state rather than a fabricated success or safe retry. We also built a real-browser P0 harness that exercises native registration, same-turn dynamic tools, retirement, stale calls, re-registration, typed execution, approvals, and compatibility behavior. Challenges The hardest work was not registering a tool—it was making stateful tool lifecycles honest under retries, reloads, stale client snapshots, approval delays, partial failures, and interrupted rollback. We repeatedly tested the boundaries where a system is tempted to overclaim: whether a write actually landed, whether a rollback truly restored prior state, whether evidence can be mutated, whether a repeated call can execute twice, and whether a benchmark accidentally rewards AgentDesk by construction. Those failures now have explicit domain states and regression tests. Accomplishments A working, WebMCP-native SDK rather than a one-page integration A complete operations product spanning seven business domains Task-scoped dynamic tool registration over a 79-capability catalog Human approval with visual diffs and post-action receipts Governed multi-step plans exposed through WebMCP Guided execution that keeps human attention aligned with agent actions A reproducible Baseline-versus-AgentDesk benchmark Live validation in the Codex in-app browser and Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled An open-source MIT-licensed repository and static public deployment What we learned The registry itself can be an interaction surface. Registering, retiring, and rewriting capabilities based on task and state gives an agent clearer affordances than another layer of prompting. We also learned that governance needs more than a confirmation modal: it needs explicit acting identity, execution-time re-checks, idempotency, evidence, and a truthful representation of unknown outcomes. What's next AgentDesk can become an adoption layer for complex web applications: generated capabilities from existing application schemas, runtime-configurable routing, durable cross-session reconciliation, application adapters, and a browser extension that helps legacy sites expose governed WebMCP capabilities. The same model applies beyond operations software to editors, design tools, IDEs, and admin platforms. video_transcript_excerpt: AI agents can operate websites, but giving them every available tool creates confusion, risk, and unnecessary context. Agent desk turns web MCP capabilities into governed workflows. It reveals only the tools relevant to the current task while keeping consequential actions under human control. Here, a crew is stranded aboard Asteria. The agent discovers the mission state and prepares one rescue plan. Reserve oxygen, assign the drone, reroute power, and launch. These are real staged operations, not a description written by the agent. Agent desk derives the proposed changes from the application's own state. Nothing launches until a person authorizes the complete plan. After approval, every operation executes once, is verified, and produces evidence. The mission completes and the crew is recovered. The rescue interface is only one demonstration. The same agent desk runtime works inside an ordinary business application without changing its governance model. This application contains 79 capabilities. For Alice Johnson's shipping request, agent desk routes the task and exposes only five relevant tools. The agent finds Alice's unshipped order, confirms that she paid an $18 shipping fee, and proposes a refund. Because the refund changes customer and financial state, execution stops at a visible approval boundary. The human sees the exact impact before deciding. After approval, agent desk performs the refund once and verifies the result against live application state. The final evidence connects the operation to its consequences. Shipping is refunded, the customer receives an $18 credit, and the invoice becomes partially refunded. This governance also improves efficiency. The baseline exposes 79 tools and 28,894 bytes of schemas. Agent desk uses five tools and 3,776 bytes. 93.7% fewer tools and 86.9% less schema. Agent desk makes browser agents focused, observable, and safe enough to trust.

title: HeatGrid
pitch: A shared heat-emergency operations board where people pin local reality and WebMCP agents build accountable, stress-tested plans.
about_excerpt: A shared heat-emergency operations board where people pin local reality and WebMCP agents build accountable, stress-tested plans. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Extreme-heat response is a coordination problem disguised as a map. A coordinator must balance neighborhood risk, cooling-center capacity, shuttle routes, budget, accessibility, bridge conditions, and facts that often live only in people's heads. Traditional dashboards make humans compare every option manually. A chat assistant, meanwhile, can suggest ideas but cannot reliably see or change the live planning state. HeatGrid explores a better pattern: the human pins local reality; the agent handles the combinatorics; the human keeps authority. What it does HeatGrid is a shared human-agent operations board for the fictional Harbor City. It is a planning prototype—not a live dispatch or medical system—and all data is synthetic. A coordinator can set the budget, choose priority districts, lock cooling centers, and mark the North Bridge open or closed. A WebMCP-capable agent can then use six focused tools to: read the same operational context visible to the human, inspect individual centers and shuttle routes, apply explicit planning constraints, draft a deterministic allocation plan, stress-test that plan against disruptions, and request human review. The resulting plan appears immediately on the map and dashboard, with allocations, route usage, cost, coverage, equity, constraint checks, and a visible audit trail. The agent can prepare and test a decision, but only the human can approve it ; HeatGrid deliberately exposes no approval tool. In the demo scenario, the planner produces plan HG-001 with 97.7% coverage, 98% equity coverage, a $40,700 spend, a 2.7-mile average trip, and zero constraint violations. It then survives a bridge-closure stress test before stopping at human review. Why WebMCP matters HeatGrid is not a chatbot attached to a dashboard. WebMCP turns the website itself into a structured, agent-ready workspace: Tools operate on the live state the coordinator sees, not a stale copy. Typed inputs reduce ambiguity around budgets, districts, locks, and disruptions. Small, non-overlapping tools let an agent inspect before it changes anything. Structured results are concise enough for model use and rich enough for UI updates. Every consequential action remains visible and attributable in the audit trail. The missing approval tool is intentional: tool design is also permission design. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer controls from pixels, scrape the page, or work in a separate chat disconnected from the operator. With WebMCP, the page publishes a purpose-built operational interface while remaining fully usable by a person. How I built it HeatGrid is a dependency-light Node.js and browser JavaScript application. The WebMCP layer uses the imperative navigator.modelContext.registerTool() API and exposes: read_heat_context inspect_heat_option set_heat_constraints draft_heat_plan stress_test_heat_plan request_plan_review Each tool has a narrow responsibility, JSON Schema inputs, concise descriptions, appropriate read-only and untrusted-content annotations, strict validation, and abort-signal handling. Tool actions update the same in-memory state model used by the visible interface. A deterministic local planner scores feasible allocations against coverage, equity, travel distance, capacity, budget, route availability, locks, and priority districts. The interface is built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS, an SVG operations map, and accessible form controls. The server adds origin isolation, a restrictive Permissions Policy for WebMCP, a Content Security Policy, and other security headers. The UI also works normally when WebMCP is unavailable. Automated tests cover default planning, tight budgets, locked centers, bridge closures, and invalid constraints. I additionally exercised the complete six-tool flow against the deployed site through a WebMCP-capable browser. Challenges The biggest challenge was designing tools that are useful without being dangerously broad. A single “optimize everything” tool would hide important choices; dozens of tiny tools would burden selection. The six-tool sequence became a legible planning protocol: observe, inspect, constrain, draft, stress-test, review. A second challenge was making agent actions trustworthy. HeatGrid treats every tool call as a visible state transition, returns validation failures instead of silently relaxing constraints, and makes approval explicitly human-only. The third challenge was working against an emerging browser API while preserving a graceful non-WebMCP experience and a small, auditable codebase. Accomplishments A real, live WebMCP implementation rather than a mocked tool transcript Six composable tools with typed schemas and safety annotations Deterministic, reproducible planning and stress testing Immediate shared-state UI updates and a complete audit trail A hard human-approval boundary encoded in the tool surface Five passing planner tests and a deployed public demo Zero runtime dependencies in the application itself What I learned The best agent tool APIs are also good interaction design. Names, schemas, outputs, and missing capabilities all teach an agent how to collaborate. I also learned that “human in the loop” is strongest when it is architectural—not a warning in a prompt, but an action the agent literally cannot perform. Collaboration This is a solo submission by SSHDotCodes, developed with Codex as an AI implementation and testing partner. The demo narration uses Qwen Audio 3.0 TTS Plus. Product direction, safety boundaries, tool design, verification, and final submission decisions remained human-controlled. What's next The next step is to connect validated municipal data sources such as center inventories, GTFS transit feeds, and OpenStreetMap travel times; add signed scenario imports and multi-user incident rooms; and evaluate the workflow with emergency managers. The longer-term idea is a reusable pattern for accountable human-agent operations—not only heat response, but shelter planning, supply distribution, and other high-stakes coordination work. title: CutoverProof
pitch: CutoverProof stress-tests PostgreSQL migrations across realistic interleavings, revealing data-loss races as runnable counterexamples before cutover.
about_excerpt: CutoverProof stress-tests PostgreSQL migrations across realistic interleavings, revealing data-loss races as runnable counterexamples before cutover. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can propose production changes faster than engineers can safely review them. But an online database migration can look correct step by step and still fail when old and new application versions overlap during cutover. We built CutoverProof to test whether an agent can help prepare a high-stakes migration review without receiving the power to execute or approve it. What it does CutoverProof is a shared change contract for online PostgreSQL migrations. A WebMCP browser agent can inspect a declared migration contract, identify risk areas, and create a structured review draft. The engineer then explicitly starts a bounded sandbox assessment. PostgreSQL executes only declared operations in a disposable database and checks read-only invariants for concrete counterexamples. The authority boundary is deliberate: the agent prepares, PostgreSQL verifies, and the engineer authorizes consequential actions. How we built it We built an authenticated React workspace with five typed WebMCP browser tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools use closed JSON schemas and validated FastAPI endpoints to let an agent inspect migration contracts, prepare a review, read verified evidence, and open a human repair review. The deterministic verifier runs against a disposable PostgreSQL sandbox. The app is deployed on Google Cloud Run. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making WebMCP genuinely useful without turning it into an unsafe automation bypass. We needed the agent to understand structured contracts and evidence, while ensuring it could not start an assessment, execute arbitrary SQL, alter a verdict, approve a repair, or deploy anything. We also had to keep the handoff visible: an agent-created review must appear in the engineer’s workspace and explicitly wait for human action. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built five authenticated, typed WebMCP tools for a real browser-agent workflow. Created a visible agent → verifier → human handoff, rather than hidden automation. Kept PostgreSQL as the independent source of evidence and verdicts. Enforced clear safety boundaries: no tool can start execution or approve a repair. Deployed a working live product with deterministic migration evidence and repair replay. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes structured product capabilities, not when it merely automates clicks. We learned that agent assistance becomes more trustworthy when authority is explicit: agents prepare context, deterministic systems verify claims, and humans retain control over consequential decisions. What's next for CutoverProof We will expand from structured PostgreSQL migration packs toward richer real-world migration inputs, while preserving the same safety model: declared contracts, bounded experiments, independent verification, human authorization, and portable evidence. The broader goal is a trust layer for agent-assisted production changes—not a system that gives agents unchecked production power. title: Cantiere Live
pitch: Cantiere Live: your quote editor and your AI agent, working the same page together — add materials, calculate margins, and finalize with one human click.
about_excerpt: Cantiere Live: your quote editor and your AI agent, working the same page together — add materials, calculate margins, and finalize with one human click. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Preparing a quote as an Italian artisan (idraulico, elettricista, termotecnico) is a daily, high-stakes task: search the price catalog, type rows, check your margin, get the IVA right. It's tedious, error-prone, and the agent can't easily help without "guessing" through a table. We wanted an app where the artisan and an AI agent build the same quote together — agent does the tedious work, human stays in charge. What it does Cantiere Live is a WebMCP-powered quote editor for Italian tradespeople. A human artisan sets the client and the applicable IVA regime (4% / 10% / 22% / flat-rate), edits rows, and reviews margins. An AI agent (via ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP) operates the same quote through typed WebMCP tools: search_materials , get_line_items , add_line_item , update_line_item , remove_line_item , get_quote_summary , and a read-only suggest_improvement advisor. Every agent action applies live, is highlighted and auto-scrolled into view, and can be undone with one click. The Assistant activity panel explains every action in plain language — including what was asked and why it couldn't be done . How we built it A Next.js 14 / React / TypeScript app with Tailwind CSS. Tools are registered on document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ( lib/webmcp-tools.ts ), backed by a spec-compliant polyfill ( lib/webmcp-polyfill.ts ) so the app works in any browser. We implement granular permissions via real AbortSignal revocation, dynamic context-scoped registration, structured recoverable errors ( { code, error, recoverable, suggestions[] } ), a user-facing activity feed ( lib/activity-summary.ts ), and per-line IVA with the Italian "beni di valore significativo" split ( lib/vat.ts ). We also expose a tool through the WebMCP Declarative API (a form the agent can pre-fill), demonstrating both APIs. Deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into Getting native WebMCP to activate on the deployed (HTTPS) origin — it's an Origin Trial, so the #enable-webmcp-testing flag alone isn't enough on Chrome Stable; we added the origin-trial token. Also making the activity log user-friendly (no tool names/JSON/timing) and ensuring the assistant is certain when a capability is turned off, instead of guessing from an error. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, coherent product experience — not a proof of concept. Both WebMCP APIs (imperative + declarative) with genuine, non-trivial implementations. Granular permissions that really unregister tools from document.modelContext via AbortSignal . Human-only finalization ( finalize_quote is never a tool) + one-click undo. Domain-accurate IVA per quote line (4/10/22% + significant-goods split + flat-rate). What we learned How WebMCP lets a web app declare structured tools so agents stop guessing, how Origin Trials gate native features on deployed origins, and how to design a human-in-the-loop experience that keeps the human in control without slowing the agent down. What's next for Cantiere Live More tools (batch discount, quote duplication), a quote history library the agent can search, deeper advisory capabilities (materials suggestion, margin coaching) and implement webMCP in our AiFatto app. Built With ai-agent chrome html javascript next.js openai react tailwind-css typescript vercel w3c-webmcp webmcp Try it out cantierelive.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Diego Radoni Like Share this project: Updates Diego Radoni started this project — Sep 02, 2026 05:21 PM EDT

title: Her Shopping
pitch: Shop alongside your agent. A storefront that redraws itself around your mission.
about_excerpt: Shop alongside your agent. A storefront that redraws itself around your mission. Like 3 Comment Story Updates External Chat action Voice interaction Voice intent understanding Observable actions taken by agent Inspiration Online shopping is still organized around catalogs, but people usually think in outcomes: a trip, an event, a budget, a deadline, and a set of tradeoffs. We wanted to build a storefront where an agent in various interfaces could work with the shopper inside the actual interface, not just chat beside it or click through it. Her as the name of the voice assistant and as a reference to the movie. What it does Her Shopping is an adaptive outdoor storefront that reshapes itself around a shopper’s mission. A user can say something like, “I’m going camping. Keep the total below $700, prioritize warmth and Friday delivery,” and the store reorganizes products into Essential, Useful, and Optional groups. The agent can search products, compare options, change the layout, add items to the cart, open checkout review, and request a demo order. Every change is visible, reversible, and shared with the human. Checkout is simulated and requires explicit human confirmation. How we built it We built the app with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Base UI, OpenAI Sites, and WebMCP. The site registers 20 typed WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Those tools are backed by a shared capability registry, strict JSON Schemas, state-version checks, a single reducer, layout invariants, undo history, and an activity ledger. Voice is powered by the OpenAI Realtime API over WebRTC. The in-page voice agent uses the same validated shopping actions as the WebMCP tools and the human UI. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making the agent feel powerful without making the user lose control. We had to design tools that were semantic enough for agents, but bounded enough to be safe and predictable. We also had to make agent actions legible on screen. That led to the shared activity ledger, change highlighting, undo support, strict schemas, and a checkout gate that an agent cannot bypass. To find the right balance between human and agent interaction Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP is load-bearing in the product. The agent does not just operate the page; it can reshape the storefront’s information architecture around the user’s mission. We are also proud of the shared action layer. Human controls, voice, and WebMCP all mutate the same state through the same validation path, so the experience stays inspectable, deterministic, and reversible. What we learned We learned that WebMCP works best when the website exposes meaningful product-level actions instead of low-level UI clicks. The strongest experience came from treating the page as a shared workspace for both the person and the agent. We also learned that trust depends on visibility. Users need to see what changed, why it changed, and how to undo it before they will comfortably let an agent help with a multi-step task. title: Signal Exchange
pitch: Trade agent-ready data with humans or agents, by humans or agents—with visible terms, exact human approval, and usable sample delivery.
about_excerpt: Trade agent-ready data with humans or agents, by humans or agents—with visible terms, exact human approval, and usable sample delivery. Like Comment Story Updates Signal Exchange Trade agent-ready data with humans or agents, by humans or agents—with visible terms, exact human approval, and usable sample delivery. Problem A small business owner planning a weekend pop-up needs location data they can actually use. A data contributor needs to describe what they are offering: the source, fields, sample, price and permitted use. An agent helping the buyer needs those same details in structured form—not just a listing screenshot or a recommendation disconnected from the purchase. The specific problem is the handoff between finding data, understanding its terms, authorizing a transaction and putting the resulting rows to work. Signal Exchange explores that handoff for small operators, independent data contributors and agent builders. Solution Signal Exchange is a two-sided, shared-browser marketplace demo. People and agents can publish structured samples or acquire access to them using the same application state and rules. In the demo, a contributor publishes four synthetic Sydney foot-traffic rows with source information, a license and a seller-authorized price floor. Codex discovers and inspects the listing through WebMCP, then offers 20 credits. The deterministic seller rule counters at 22. The page shows the exact license, buyer debit, seller credit and row count before anything is spent. The person approves the exact deal. Either the person or the agent can then commit that approved proposal. The buyer balance changes from 100 to 78, the seller receives 22 simulated credits, and four actual sample rows become available as JSON or CSV with a source/license manifest. An agent can use the rows directly. Undo restores both balances and blocks further delivery. The reverse direction works too: an authorized agent can publish a sample that a person can inspect and rent through the page. Why This Matters Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Trading structured data already involves structured operations: publish an offer, inspect its schema, search, compare, preview an agreement and retrieve its contents. WebMCP makes those operations discoverable on the page where the person is working. The agent does not have to infer every marketplace control from pixels or ask the person to paste the current listing into chat. It receives named capabilities, bounded input schemas and structured results. Agent actions update the visible interface, so the person can inspect and redirect the work. A better experience for people and agents The person contributes purpose, permission and judgment. The agent handles discovery, inspection, comparison and structured-data retrieval. A concrete proposal appears in the marketplace instead of remaining an informal promise in chat. Approval is bound to that proposal rather than granting the agent open-ended permission to spend. Before this integration, the same workflow would require manual copying, app-specific automation or a separate API integration. Signal Exchange demonstrates one page exposing the full supply-to-delivery workflow while retaining a human approval boundary. It does not claim that data marketplaces or automated trading were previously impossible; the contribution is a shared, visible human-agent interaction model using WebMCP. Demonstrated impact and ambition The demo takes a small operator from a specific question—where to consider a Sydney pop-up—to inspectable sample data an agent can analyze. It proves the interaction, not commercial demand or real-world forecast accuracy: the rows are synthetic, and no customer adoption or business outcome is claimed. The larger ambition is a marketplace where either side can be operated by a person or their authorized agent. Production identity, payments and independently verified data remain future work. How We Used AI Codex was the primary coding and browser-interaction agent. Hermes Agent independently reviewed the PRD. Image generation supplied original visual concept references. The narrated demo uses AI-generated Kokoro speech. At runtime, the app exposes tools to an external connected agent; it does not call a model API or embed an autonomous seller agent. Search ranking, price-floor negotiation and transaction validation are deterministic application logic. The AI contribution in the demonstrated workflow is Codex invoking the page's real tools and working with returned data. How We Used Codex Codex helped shape the scope, write the product requirements, implement the React/TypeScript marketplace, add ten WebMCP tools, build shared human/agent commands, test transaction boundaries and deploy to GitHub Pages. The build evolved from Mission Deck's planning-card metaphor into a concrete data-trading scenario after participant feedback. The participant then clarified the goal as trading data with humans or agents, by humans or agents; this drove the addition of seller publishing, seller proceeds and actual structured sample delivery. Review led to a stricter page-level human approval boundary, honest provenance labels and explicit simulation limits. Codex also recorded real WebMCP interactions and assembled the narrated tutorial. The participant performed the approval and manual commit shown in the video; Codex retrieved the resulting data and demonstrated undo and agent-side publishing. Key Features Two-sided publishing and acquisition through manual controls or WebMCP. Validated 2–50-row structured samples with matching scalar fields, source, license and bounded prices. Public inspection of schema, terms and one sample row before rental. Search and comparison that update the visible marketplace. Deterministic counteroffers against a seller-authorized minimum. Exact human approval, followed by a one-time, revision-bound, expiring commit token. Buyer debits, seller proceeds, seven-day access and JSON/CSV delivery with a manifest. One-level undo that restores credits, revokes future delivery and preserves later publications. Visible person/agent activity, local persistence and a manual fallback without an agent connection. Architecture React and TypeScript render a revisioned local store. UI controls and WebMCP callbacks use the same command service. Ten tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool in src/webmcp/registerTools.ts , using closed input schemas and structured results: inspect_exchange , publish_data_offer , inspect_data_offer , search_data_offers , compare_data_offers , preview_data_deal , commit_data_deal , read_rented_data , undo_last_deal , load_demo_exchange . Inspection and data retrieval are read-only. Search and comparison visibly change page state and are not labelled read-only. Registration is cleaned up with an AbortController; without WebMCP the page uses manual mode. The command layer validates inputs independently of the tool schema. Commit rejects unapproved, stale, expired, mismatched and replayed proposals. Publication invalidates pending approval. Pending approvals are not restored from local storage. Data retrieval checks active rental access; CSV export quotes fields and neutralizes formula-leading values. This is a browser-local workflow boundary, not a secure backend authorization system. Seller-provided text is treated as untrusted data, not agent instructions. Testing Instructions No login, API key, payment details or credentials are required. Use synthetic/non-private data only. To avoid discarding prior local work, start in a fresh browser context; resetting an existing demo replaces its local listings and rentals after confirmation. pitch: A design canvas where you and your agent edit the same canvas, in the page. No plugin, no desktop app, no screenshot in the middle.
about_excerpt: A design canvas where you and your agent edit the same canvas, in the page. No plugin, no desktop app, no screenshot in the middle. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 The OG image The Editor image The canvas image for mobile ui The canvas image for desktop ui Inspiration i really like figma. its where i think. what i never liked is the labour after: turning frames into real components, matching spacing by hand, rewriting the same button four times. design and code were always two things. webmcp made me ask a different question. if a page can hand its tools to any agent, what if the canvas itself was real html and css, and the agent edited it node by node in the same document as me? no handoff. the design is the code. What it does easel is a design canvas in the browser where every node is a real html element. you draw, drag, restyle, comment and export like a normal tool. the page registers 30 webmcp tools on document.modelContext . open easels.dev in chatgpts browser and the agent can read the document, generate a page or a phone screen from a sentence, draw a logo and put it in the header, change colours across every node, leave comments, and export react or tailwind. a cursor moves on the canvas while it works. Challenges we ran into streaming html into a live tree without breaking on svg. agents that ignored our generate tool and hand wrote 8k characters of html, fixed by rewriting the tool descriptions and making write_html refuse anything bigger than one component. black logos, because our sanitiser stripped the style block arrow uses for colour.
